options.explanation: A constraint surfaced in passing is unconfirmed, so designing past it risks building directly into an unstated legal or operational violation.

options.text: Convert vague terms into failure conditions
options.explanation: Sound discovery writes assumptions down, converts vague terms into failure conditions, and reconciles conflicts explicitly. Designing past hints or locking dates first are gate violations.

options.text: Lock the launch date before requirements exist
options.explanation: Committing a date before requirements exist forces design decisions to fit an arbitrary deadline instead of the actual testable criteria.

options.text: Reconcile conflicts via risk-tolerance agreement
options.explanation: Sound discovery writes assumptions down, converts vague terms into failure conditions, and reconciles conflicts explicitly. Designing past hints or locking dates first are gate violations.

questions.scenario: Judge each discovery practice as sound or unsound for structured requirement gathering.
questions.explanation: Sound discovery writes assumptions down, converts vague terms into failure conditions, and reconciles conflicts explicitly. Designing past hints or locking dates first are gate violations.

questions.prompt: Which response best manages expectations?

options.text: Commit to demo accuracy minus a small margin
options.explanation: An arbitrary margin off a curated demo is still a blind commitment; production traffic is unrepresentative of the ten demo cases, so the true production figure is unknown.

options.text: Confirm commitment now and evaluate after rollout
options.explanation: Committing before measuring production performance converts the launch into an experiment the sponsor never agreed to, with the discovery of failures arriving after commitments are locked.

options.text: Baseline a sample before committing to targets
options.explanation: A curated demo proves capability, not production performance. Baseline a representative sample before committing; margin-off-demo or post-rollout evaluation commits blind.

options.text: Refuse every accuracy target as totally impossible
options.explanation: Refusing all targets overcorrects; accuracy targets are legitimate once grounded in a representative baseline rather than a curated demo.

questions.scenario: A sponsor saw 96% on ten curated demo cases and wants it as the production commitment. Launch date and budget are already fixed.
questions.explanation: A curated demo proves capability, not production performance. Baseline a representative sample before committing; margin-off-demo or post-rollout evaluation commits blind.

questions.prompt: Which TWO are closed feedback loops? Select both.

options.text: Weekly quality report with no tied action
options.explanation: Defensible but weaker than the credited key(s).

options.text: Breach pages the owner who runs the runbook
options.explanation: A closed loop pairs an agreed signal with an agreed response that changes the system. Reports and ad-hoc dashboards without tied action are monitoring only.

options.text: Analyst dashboard explored ad hoc each month
options.explanation: Defensible but weaker than the credited key(s).

options.text: Override alert triggers agreed prompt rollback
options.explanation: A closed loop pairs an agreed signal with an agreed response that changes the system. Reports and ad-hoc dashboards without tied action are monitoring only.

questions.scenario: Judge which signal designs close the loop with an agreed response.
questions.explanation: A closed loop pairs an agreed signal with an agreed response that changes the system. Reports and ad-hoc dashboards without tied action are monitoring only.

questions.prompt: What best prevents silent expectation drift?

options.text: Weekly quality report with no tied action
options.explanation: A report nobody is obligated to act on is monitoring only; no agreed response changes the system when the signal fires.

options.text: Breach pages the owner who runs the runbook
options.explanation: A closed loop pairs an agreed signal with an agreed response that changes the system. Reports and ad-hoc dashboards without tied action are monitoring only.

options.text: Analyst dashboard explored ad hoc each month
options.explanation: Ad-hoc dashboard exploration depends on someone choosing to look, with no agreed trigger or response, so degradation can persist unaddressed.

options.text: Override alert triggers agreed prompt rollback
options.explanation: A closed loop pairs an agreed signal with an agreed response that changes the system. Reports and ad-hoc dashboards without tied action are monitoring only.

questions.scenario: Milestones pass quietly; a stakeholder erupts over an assumption nobody revisited. The next milestone is in two weeks.
questions.explanation: Expectations drift silently, so the fix is demos of current behavior against the acceptance bar each milestone. Waiting, longer narratives, or freezing scope do not resync understanding.

questions.prompt: Which TWO are closed feedback loops? Select both.

options.text: Nightly eval digest emailed without owner
options.explanation: An emailed digest with no assigned owner has no agreed responder, so even a visible regression waits for someone to volunteer.

options.text: Spike auto-freezes rollout per the playbook
options.explanation: Auto-freeze per playbook and cap via runbook pair signal with agreed response. Digests without owners and charts reviewed on memory are monitoring only.

options.text: Latency chart reviewed when someone remembers
options.explanation: A review that happens only when someone remembers has no reliable trigger, so the signal frequently fires without any response at all.

options.text: Cost overrun alert triggers cap via runbook
options.explanation: Auto-freeze per playbook and cap via runbook pair signal with agreed response. Digests without owners and charts reviewed on memory are monitoring only.

questions.scenario: Classify each signal design as a closed feedback loop or monitoring only.
questions.explanation: Auto-freeze per playbook and cap via runbook pair signal with agreed response. Digests without owners and charts reviewed on memory are monitoring only.

questions.prompt: What is the most important documentation gap?

options.text: Add decision records with rationale and alternatives
options.explanation: Diagrams record what was built; successors and auditors need decision records with context, rejected alternatives, and rationale. Walkthroughs and config detail do not transfer why.

options.text: Add sequence diagrams of each request path
options.explanation: Sequence diagrams add more of the same 'what' the successors already have; they still say nothing about why guardrails exist or which options were rejected.

options.text: Expand deployment configuration detail for operators
options.explanation: Configuration detail helps operators run the system but does not answer the 'why' questions successors keep asking before an audit.

options.text: Record live walkthrough videos for all successors
options.explanation: Videos capture one narrator's view at one point in time; they decay quickly, are unsearchable, and do not constitute auditable decision records.

questions.scenario: Successors inherit full architecture diagrams yet keep asking why guardrails and the vector store exist. An audit is approaching fast. The diagrams never explain rejected options.
questions.explanation: Diagrams record what was built; successors and auditors need decision records with context, rejected alternatives, and rationale. Walkthroughs and config detail do not transfer why.

questions.prompt: Which TWO items would have prevented drift?

options.text: Behavior specs plus verifiable acceptance criteria
options.explanation: Drift is prevented by behavioral specs with acceptance criteria plus concrete defaults and fixtures. Inspection gates catch drift late; diagrams alone are not executable.

options.text: Sprint-end architect inspection gates alone
options.explanation: Inspection gates only detect drift after it has already been built into the sprint, rather than constraining implementation choices as they are made.

options.text: Deeper component structure diagrams alone
options.explanation: Diagrams describe structure, not behavior; they are not executable and cannot stop prompts or thresholds from diverging from design intent.

options.text: Prompt defaults plus threshold test fixtures
options.explanation: Drift is prevented by behavioral specs with acceptance criteria plus concrete defaults and fixtures. Inspection gates catch drift late; diagrams alone are not executable.

questions.scenario: A delivery team improvised prompts and thresholds; tests diverge from design intent.
questions.explanation: Drift is prevented by behavioral specs with acceptance criteria plus concrete defaults and fixtures. Inspection gates catch drift late; diagrams alone are not executable.

questions.prompt: Which package completes the handoff?

options.text: Runbook draft without alerting or owner
options.explanation: A runbook no alert fires against and no owner executes leaves operators with instructions but no way to detect or respond to degradation in time.

options.text: Runbook, alerting, owner, plus rationale
options.explanation: Handoff transfers operability: runbook plus alerting, named owner, and rationale. Partial packages without alerting, owner, or rationale leave operators unable to respond.

options.text: Dashboards plus extended metric coverage alone
options.explanation: More dashboards still require someone to watch them and know what to do; without a runbook, alerts, and owner they transfer visibility but not response.

options.text: On-call rotation without runbook or rationale
options.explanation: A pager without a runbook produces pages nobody can act on, and without rationale the operators cannot judge which responses are safe.

questions.scenario: A triage system moves to operators next month. The draft package has code and dashboards but no response path. The date cannot move.
questions.explanation: Handoff transfers operability: runbook plus alerting, named owner, and rationale. Partial packages without alerting, owner, or rationale leave operators unable to respond.

questions.prompt: What must the architect set before closing?

options.text: Close out now and merely note the drift risk
options.explanation: Noting a risk without tied thresholds or an owner records the problem but changes nothing; the seasonal input shift will degrade quality with no one accountable.

options.text: Keep the build team on retainer indefinitely
options.explanation: An indefinite retainer is an open-ended staffing commitment, not an operational control; it neither defines drift thresholds nor establishes who responds.

options.text: Define thresholds, owner, and review cadence
options.explanation: AI quality drifts, so closeout needs thresholds, a named owner, and review cadence. Retainers, wider dashboards, or noted risks without tied action are monitoring only.

options.text: Extend dashboard coverage for all operators
options.explanation: Dashboards are monitoring only; without thresholds, a named owner, and a review cadence, observed degradation still has no agreed response.

questions.scenario: Launch targets are met and builders rotate off. Input mix shifts seasonally; ops holds only a dashboard.
questions.explanation: AI quality drifts, so closeout needs thresholds, a named owner, and review cadence. Retainers, wider dashboards, or noted risks without tied action are monitoring only.

questions.prompt: Which TWO gate statements are correctly placed?

options.text: Plan handoff before evals and trade-offs settle
options.explanation: Handoff planning before evals and trade-offs are settled transfers a design whose behavior and accepted sacrifices are not yet established, inverting the lifecycle gate.

options.text: Require eval suite plus agreed trade-offs pre-handoff
options.explanation: Evals plus agreed trade-offs gate handoff planning, and iteration returns to design with updated evals. Handoff-first or discovery-placed load testing inverts the sequence.

options.text: Place load testing inside early discovery work
options.explanation: Load testing needs a built system with representative traffic; placing it in early discovery tests a design that does not yet exist.

options.text: Return iteration to design with updated evals
options.explanation: Evals plus agreed trade-offs gate handoff planning, and iteration returns to design with updated evals. Handoff-first or discovery-placed load testing inverts the sequence.

questions.scenario: Judge gate placement across the lifecycle. Design, handoff, and iteration gates are contested. Only two statements order the gates correctly.
questions.explanation: Evals plus agreed trade-offs gate handoff planning, and iteration returns to design with updated evals. Handoff-first or discovery-placed load testing inverts the sequence.

questions.prompt: Which gate statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: Eval suite always precedes model selection
options.explanation: Evals gate model selection; rollback and owner gate handoff. Returning to discovery or accepting monitoring-alone readiness misplaces the gates.

options.text: Rollback plan precedes production handoff
options.explanation: Evals gate model selection; rollback and owner gate handoff. Returning to discovery or accepting monitoring-alone readiness misplaces the gates.

options.text: Production handoff always requires a named owner
options.explanation: Evals gate model selection; rollback and owner gate handoff. Returning to discovery or accepting monitoring-alone readiness misplaces the gates.

options.text: Iteration returns to discovery, not design
options.explanation: Iteration refines an existing design, so it re-enters at the design gate with updated evals; restarting from discovery discards already-settled requirements.

options.text: Monitoring alone satisfies handoff readiness
options.explanation: Monitoring without rollback planning and a named owner observes failures it cannot respond to, so it does not satisfy handoff readiness.

questions.scenario: Judge each lifecycle statement as correctly or incorrectly placed.
questions.explanation: Evals gate model selection; rollback and owner gate handoff. Returning to discovery or accepting monitoring-alone readiness misplaces the gates.

questions.prompt: What does a complete handoff still owe?

options.text: Source code and credentials alone for operators
options.explanation: Code and credentials let operators access the system, but without runbook, alerts, and rationale they cannot detect degradation or know which responses are safe.

options.text: Demo video plus launch slides for operators
options.explanation: Launch material markets the system as it performed on day one; it contains no operational procedures or signals for handling later degradation.

options.text: Vendor support number for escalation alone
options.explanation: An escalation number defers every problem to a third party with no internal ability to detect the degradation worth escalating or describe it precisely.

options.text: Runbook, alerts, rationale, and named owner
options.explanation: A complete handoff transfers the ability to operate: runbook, alerts, rationale, and named owner. Code, slides, or a vendor number alone transfer the system without operability.

questions.scenario: Operators received the system but cannot detect or respond to degradation. The contract date has passed and p99 costs are rising.
questions.explanation: A complete handoff transfers the ability to operate: runbook, alerts, rationale, and named owner. Code, slides, or a vendor number alone transfer the system without operability.

snapshot.title: Advanced Architecture I: Pattern Selection & Delegation

questions.prompt: Select the two ownership decisions that best fit risk and source-of-truth boundaries. (Select 2)

options.text: Policy engine decides eligibility from the maintained table.
options.explanation: Eligibility belongs to the maintained policy table (source of truth); high-value irreversible refunds need a pre-submission human gate. Claude drafts.

options.text: Human gates high-value refunds before submission.
options.explanation: Eligibility belongs to the maintained policy table (source of truth); high-value irreversible refunds need a pre-submission human gate. Claude drafts.

options.text: Claude decides eligibility alone, losing source-of-truth control.
options.explanation: Eligibility is a policy decision owned by the maintained table as source of truth, so leaving it to model inference bypasses that control and produces unaccountable decisions.

options.text: Claude issues all refunds alone with sampling, risking irreversible loss.
options.explanation: High-value refunds are irreversible once submitted, so post-hoc sampling cannot contain the loss; these actions require a human gate before submission.

questions.scenario: A retailer assistant reads complaints, checks eligibility, drafts replies, and issues refunds. High-value refunds are irreversible after submission.
questions.explanation:
Eligibility is a policy decision that must come from the maintained table — the external system as source of truth — not from model inference. High-value refunds are irreversible, so a human gate before submission matches the routing rule of pre-action approval for low-confidence, hard-to-reverse actions.

Source: Claude Platform & Solution Design, external systems as authority; Responsible AI, Safety & Risk for Architects, human-review routing.

questions.prompt: Which pattern is the best starting architecture?

options.text: Coded workflow with explicit stages, guards, and logged handoffs.
options.explanation: Known stages with reconstructability requirement call for an explicit coded workflow with guards and logged handoffs, not autonomy.

options.text: Autonomous agent with broad tools, at cost of non-reproducible paths.
options.explanation: Auditors require each stage to be reconstructable, and model-chosen paths are non-reproducible, so autonomy fails the audit requirement regardless of tool breadth.

options.text: Single call with all context, at cost of lost stage reconstruction.
options.explanation: Collapsing extract, coverage check, threshold rule, and adjuster note into one call eliminates the per-stage logs and guards auditors need to reconstruct each decision.

options.text: Peer agent team negotiating results, at cost of needless coordination.
options.explanation: The stages are fixed and known, so peer negotiation adds coordination cost and nondeterminism while offering no benefit over explicit workflow stages.

questions.scenario: An insurer processes claims through known stages: extract, coverage check, threshold rule, adjuster note. Auditors require each stage to be reconstructable.
questions.explanation:
Known, fixed stages with audit requirements are the textbook workflow case: a coded workflow keeps each stage reconstructable with guards and logged handoffs, while an agent's model-chosen path is non-reproducible and cannot satisfy auditors.

Source: Claude Platform & Solution Design, workflow versus agent trade-offs.

questions.prompt: Select the two steps that minimize elapsed time without losing cross-contract synthesis. (Select 2)

options.text: Review contracts in parallel with validation.
options.explanation: Independent reviews parallelize; a single aggregation pass preserves portfolio-level synthesis without serial delay.

options.text: Run one portfolio aggregation pass over validated results.
options.explanation: Independent reviews parallelize; a single aggregation pass preserves portfolio-level synthesis without serial delay.

options.text: Chain all reviews sequentially, paying full serial delay.
options.explanation: The contracts are independent, so sequential chaining pays the full serial delay without any improvement in review quality or portfolio synthesis.

options.text: Let one agent pick order under budget, losing parallelism and reproducibility.
options.explanation: Model-chosen ordering forfeits the parallelism the independent reviews allow and makes execution non-reproducible, all without improving the rubric-driven analysis.

questions.scenario: A due-diligence team reviews independent supplier contracts against one rubric. Findings need a portfolio-level risk summary.
questions.explanation:
Independent contracts suit parallelization: review all contracts concurrently with validation per item, then run one aggregation pass for the portfolio-level risk summary. Sequential chaining pays full serial delay without improving synthesis quality.

Source: Building with the Claude API, Parallelization workflows.

questions.prompt: Select the routing decisions that form the most defensible reference architecture. (Select 3)

options.text: Use retrieval for stable documentation questions.
options.explanation: Stable docs suit RAG; live order/account state needs APIs; state changes and human requests need guarded actions and handoff, not one index.

options.text: Use live APIs for order and account state.
options.explanation: Stable docs suit RAG; live order/account state needs APIs; state changes and human requests need guarded actions and handoff, not one index.

options.text: Use guarded actions plus immediate human handoff path.
options.explanation: Stable docs suit RAG; live order/account state needs APIs; state changes and human requests need guarded actions and handoff, not one index.

options.text: Put live state in one RAG index, paying stale and unsafe answers.
options.explanation: Order and account state change minute to minute, so an indexed snapshot serves stale answers, and a retrieval index cannot perform or authorize state-changing actions safely.

options.text: Use one agent for all intents, losing determinism and auditability.
options.explanation: Each intent has a well-known handling pattern, so a single free agent adds nondeterminism and loses the auditability that explicit routing per intent preserves.

questions.scenario: A support platform handles documentation questions, current order status, and account changes. It also receives requests for a human. The team proposes one RAG index for everything.
questions.explanation:
Each intent gets the pattern its data shape requires: stable documentation from retrieval, live order and account state from live APIs (an answer correct at 10:00 may be wrong at 10:05), guarded actions for account changes, and an immediate human-handoff path for explicit requests. One RAG index serves stale live state and cannot authorize actions.

Source: Enterprise Integration & Production, Glossary: live state; Claude Platform & Solution Design, workflow versus agent trade-offs.

questions.prompt: Which design best matches the dependency structure?

options.text: Chain with validated handoffs plus evaluator before release.
options.explanation: Sequential structured dependency fits a chain with validated handoffs and a pre-release evaluator.

options.text: Parallel stages with confidence vote, breaking sequential dependency.
options.explanation: Each stage consumes the prior stage's structured output, so the stages cannot run in parallel; a confidence vote cannot manufacture the dependency the redline flow requires.

options.text: Route whole contract to one stage by category, skipping required steps.
options.explanation: Every contract must pass through extraction, classification, and drafting, so routing by category skips mandatory steps and produces redlines without the required analysis trail.

options.text: Open-ended agent discovering stages per contract, paying irreproducibility.
options.explanation: The stages are already known and fixed, so agent-discovered paths add irreproducibility without covering any dependency the explicit chain does not already handle.

questions.scenario: A legal flow extracts clauses, classifies risk against a playbook, then drafts a redline. Each stage consumes the prior stage's structured output.
questions.explanation:
Each stage consumes the prior stage's structured output, so the dependency is strictly sequential: a chain with validated handoffs and an evaluator before release matches it. Parallel stages would break the dependency, and an open-ended agent pays irreproducibility for stages that are already known.

Source: Building with the Claude API, Chaining workflows.

questions.prompt: Select the two decisions that best contain autonomy with a phase gate. (Select 2)

options.text: Allow agentic exploration of the unfamiliar repository.
options.explanation: Unfamiliar repos justify agentic exploration, but edits/tests/publishing stay deterministic with approval before the PR.

options.text: Enforce deterministic edit-test-review with approval before publishing.
options.explanation: Unfamiliar repos justify agentic exploration, but edits/tests/publishing stay deterministic with approval before the PR.

options.text: Run one autonomous loop including approval inference, risking unapproved publishes.
options.explanation: Approval is a phase gate that must come from a human, not be inferred by the model; folding it into an autonomous loop risks publishing patches nobody approved.

options.text: Publish majority-voted patches from file agents, losing coherence and review.
options.explanation: Voting among per-file agents does not substitute for human review, and independently produced patches lack the cross-file coherence a single patch series requires before publishing.

questions.scenario: A coding assistant must explore an unfamiliar repository, propose a patch, run tests, and open a pull request after approval.
questions.explanation:
Exploration of an unfamiliar repository is open-ended, so agentic exploration fits. Publishing is irreversible and reviewable, so the edit-test-review path must be deterministic with human approval before anything ships; an autonomous loop that infers approval bypasses the gate.

Source: Claude Platform & Solution Design, workflow versus agent trade-offs; Responsible AI, Safety & Risk for Architects, human-review routing.

questions.prompt: Which packaging choice best supports reuse and governance?

options.text: Versioned Skill with procedure, rubric, and validation scripts.
options.explanation: Repeated governed procedures across clients need a versioned Skill bundling instructions, rubric, and validation scripts.

options.text: Duplicate prompts per client, paying drift and update cost.
options.explanation: Duplicated prompts mutate independently in each client, so the governed procedure drifts out of sync and every update must be repeated and re-verified per copy.

options.text: Expose scripts as tools letting clients reconstruct flow, losing version control.
options.explanation: Raw scripts as tools leave each client to reassemble the flow itself, so the governed sequence is no longer versioned or enforced as a single unit.

options.text: Store procedure in model memory, losing versioning and determinism.
options.explanation: Model memory is not versioned, auditable, or deterministic across runs and clients, so the procedure loses its governance guarantees.

questions.scenario: A firm repeats the same governed contract-review procedure in Claude Code and an internal app. It includes instructions, validation scripts, and versioned rubrics.
questions.explanation:
A skill is a versioned, reusable unit packaging instructions, optional scripts, and rubrics — exactly what a governed procedure repeated across surfaces needs. Duplicating prompts per client drifts, and exposing raw scripts or storing procedure in model memory loses version control and determinism.

Source: Claude Platform & Solution Design, seven primitives: Package a Procedure (Skills).

questions.prompt: Where should human oversight be placed? (Phase gate)

options.text: Gate high-value settlements before submission; sample low-value completions.
options.explanation: Irreversible high-value actions need a pre-submission gate; routine low-value work suits post-hoc sampling.

options.text: Review everything after submission, allowing irreversible loss plus delay.
options.explanation: Once a high-value settlement is submitted it is irreversible, so post-submission review permits the very loss oversight exists to prevent while also delaying every routine claim.

options.text: Gate only on low confidence regardless of value, missing high-stakes errors.
options.explanation: Confidence gating overlooks the model's confident mistakes, and on high-value irreversible settlements exactly those errors cause unrecoverable harm regardless of expressed confidence.

options.text: Auto-approve all with aggregate pause, allowing harm before detection.
options.explanation: Aggregate monitoring detects problems only after many irreversible settlements have already gone out, so the harm occurs before any human can intervene.

questions.scenario: A claims assistant drafts settlements that become irreversible above a threshold. Most claims are low value and routine.
questions.explanation:
Route by stakes, not volume: gate high-value, irreversible settlements pre-action, and sample routine low-value completions post-hoc. Gating only on confidence misses high-stakes errors, and reviewing everything after submission allows the irreversible loss.

Source: Responsible AI, Safety & Risk for Architects, Route review by stakes, not by volume.

questions.prompt: What evidence most strongly argues against the agent pattern?

options.text: Trajectories are enumerable as a router feeding four chains.
options.explanation: Enumerable trajectories by document type collapse to a router plus explicit chains; unpredictability of order alone does not justify agents.

options.text: Arrival order is unpredictable, which alone does not require autonomy.
options.explanation: Unpredictable arrival order is a property of incoming traffic, not of the processing path; a fixed router and chains handle arbitrary arrival order just as well.

options.text: Tool choice varies on repeats, showing instability not agent need.
options.explanation: Varying tool choice on identical repeats is evidence of nondeterministic behavior to be fixed, not evidence that open-ended autonomy is required.

options.text: Multiple sources need combining, which chains do without agents.
options.explanation: Combining sources is a synthesis step that can sit inside an explicit chain stage, so it does not force model-chosen trajectories.

questions.scenario: A team claims its research needs an agent because the subject is unfamiliar. Discovery shows every request follows the same four paths by document type.
questions.explanation:
If discovery shows every request follows the same four paths by document type, the trajectories are enumerable — a router feeding four chains reproduces them with determinism and reproducibility an agent cannot offer. Unpredictable arrival order, repeat variance, and source combination do not require autonomy.

Source: Claude Platform & Solution Design, workflow versus agent trade-offs; Building with the Claude API, Routing workflows.

questions.prompt: Which pattern is proportionate to the task?

options.text: Single augmented call with explicit criteria and reviewable output.
options.explanation: Fixed input, no external data, and human review favor a single augmented call over workflows or agents.

options.text: Three-stage draft-classify-regenerate flow, paying latency without gain.
options.explanation: With fixed input, a strict rubric, and a human reviewer, extra draft-classify-regenerate stages add latency and cost without any accuracy mechanism the task needs.

options.text: Editing agent iterating to self-rated confidence, risking unbounded loops.
options.explanation: Self-rated confidence is an unreliable stopping signal, so an iterating agent risks unbounded loops on a task a single reviewed call already satisfies.

options.text: Multi-agent debate voting on versions, paying coordination without accuracy gain.
options.explanation: Multi-agent debate pays coordination and token overhead that only pays off when a verifiable accuracy mechanism exists, which a tone rewrite with human review does not need.

questions.scenario: A one-shot marketing rewrite has fixed input, a strict tone rubric, and no external data. A user reviews output before use.
questions.explanation:
Fixed input, a strict rubric, no external data, and human review make this a single augmented call with explicit criteria — the proportionate primitive. Multi-stage flows, self-iterating agents, and multi-agent debate add latency and coordination cost without an accuracy mechanism this task needs.

Source: Claude Platform & Solution Design, reaching for a heavier primitive than the job requires is paid for in latency, tokens, and operational surface area.

questions.prompt: Which architecture addresses the failure most directly?

options.text: Validator reconciling totals with bounded correction pass.
options.explanation: Detectable field errors with a reconciliation rule call for a validator plus bounded correction, not autonomy or voting.

options.text: Autonomous re-inspection loop, paying nondeterminism without targeted check.
options.explanation: A free re-inspection loop adds nondeterminism without the targeted reconciliation rule that actually detects the misplaced totals, so it may miss the same errors.

options.text: More examples while removing validation, increasing silent field errors.
options.explanation: Removing the reconciliation check removes the only mechanism that detects the errors, so additional examples increase confidence while silent field errors persist.

options.text: Parallel extractors with majority vote, paying 3x cost without reconciliation.
options.explanation: Majority vote triples cost but cannot detect a systematic misplacement of totals; only the explicit reconciliation rule checks stated against calculated values.

questions.scenario: A document extractor emits valid schema but misplaces totals across fields. Errors are detectable by reconciling stated and calculated totals.
questions.explanation:
The errors are detectable by a known reconciliation, so the fix is a deterministic validator comparing stated and calculated totals with a bounded correction pass — a generator-verifier loop. An autonomous re-inspection loop adds nondeterminism without a targeted check, and majority vote triples cost without reconciling anything.

Source: Enterprise Integration & Production, Glossary: generator-verifier loop.

questions.prompt: Which change fixes the architectural category error?

options.text: Query system of record at request time; reserve retrieval for stable knowledge.
options.explanation: Volatile inventory is a system-of-record lookup at request time; retrieval suits stable product knowledge, not live levels.

options.text: Smaller chunks and larger embeddings, keeping staleness while paying reindex cost.
options.explanation: Chunking and embedding quality cannot fix a snapshot-based index: answers remain stale between exports regardless of retrieval precision, while reindex cost grows.

options.text: Faster refreshes with timestamps, still serving stale data between refreshes.
options.explanation: However fast the refresh, any interval between exports serves outdated quantities; timestamps disclose staleness but do not remove it.

options.text: Ask model to infer quantity from snapshots, risking hallucinated stock.
options.explanation: Inferring current quantity from old snapshots invites hallucinated stock levels, worsening the accuracy problem instead of addressing its source-of-truth error.

questions.scenario: A product answers inventory questions from a vector index of periodic exports. Users get fluent answers that are sometimes stale.
questions.explanation:
Inventory is live state: any snapshot index serves stale answers regardless of chunking or refresh speed. The category fix is to query the system of record at request time and reserve retrieval for stable knowledge.

Source: Enterprise Integration & Production, Glossary: live state.

questions.prompt: Select the redesign decisions that correct the most important mismatches. (Select 3)

options.text: Use authenticated web app instead of shared-laptop CLI.
options.explanation: Shared-laptop CLI, client-side DB access, and subagents for compliance each mismatch branch ops; fix with auth, server integration, and deterministic gates.

options.text: Use direct server integration instead of client DB access.
options.explanation: Shared-laptop CLI, client-side DB access, and subagents for compliance each mismatch branch ops; fix with auth, server integration, and deterministic gates.

options.text: Enforce deterministic compliance checks before actions.
options.explanation: Shared-laptop CLI, client-side DB access, and subagents for compliance each mismatch branch ops; fix with auth, server integration, and deterministic gates.

options.text: Keep CLI plus weekly log review, leaving unauthenticated probabilistic compliance.
options.explanation: A shared-laptop CLI has no per-user authenticated identity and weekly log review reacts after the fact, leaving compliance decisions probabilistic and unattributed.

options.text: Add peer audit agent, keeping root auth and delegation flaws.
options.explanation: An audit agent does not repair the unauthenticated entry point, the client-side database access, or the delegation of deterministic policy to probabilistic subagents.

questions.scenario: Branch staff need a guided operations assistant. The proposal uses Claude Code on shared laptops with MCP for one internal database. Compliance decisions are delegated to subagents.
questions.explanation:
Three mismatches: a shared-laptop CLI has no authenticated identity, so a web app behind SSO is required; a client-side database connection bypasses server-side access control, so the database must sit behind a direct server integration; and compliance decisions are deterministic policy enforcement that belongs in code before actions, not in delegated subagents.

Source: Enterprise Integration & Production, Five takeaways: enforce identity at the server side; Claude Platform & Solution Design, entry points.

questions.prompt: What condition makes this evaluator-optimizer loop preferable to a single call?

options.text: Quality is rubric-verifiable but first-pass compliance is inconsistent.
options.explanation: Evaluator-optimizer fits when quality is rubric-verifiable but first-pass output is inconsistently compliant.

options.text: Inputs need different sources, which calls for routing not iteration.
options.explanation: Diverging input sources are a routing concern — send each input down the path that fits it — not a reason to iterate drafts against a rubric.

options.text: Path needs tool discovery, which calls for agents not rubrics.
options.explanation: When the path itself must be discovered, an agentic loop with tools is indicated; a rubric-scored revision loop does not perform discovery.

options.text: Minimum latency forbids extra calls, which rules out iteration.
options.explanation: A hard latency floor forbids the extra scoring pass, so this condition describes when the loop is impossible, not when it is preferable.

questions.scenario: A model drafts customer apologies. A second pass scores drafts against a stable rubric and requests revision on any failure.
questions.explanation:
Evaluator-optimizer fits when quality is verifiable against a stable rubric but first-pass compliance is inconsistent: the second pass scores and requests revision only on failure. Diverse inputs call for routing, tool discovery for agents, and a hard latency floor rules iteration out entirely.

Source: Building with the Claude API, Chaining workflows.

questions.prompt: Select the two controls that make an agent defensible here. (Select 2)

options.text: Constrain tools and actions to investigation scope.
options.explanation: Unplannable sequences justify agents only with constrained tools, budgets, stopping criteria, and checkpointed state.

options.text: Set budgets, stopping criteria, and checkpoint recoverable state.
options.explanation: Unplannable sequences justify agents only with constrained tools, budgets, stopping criteria, and checkpointed state.

options.text: Grant all enterprise tools with self-determined stopping, risking overreach and runaway cost.
options.explanation: Unscoped tool access lets the agent reach far beyond the investigation, and self-determined stopping has no bound, so cost and privilege can both escalate without a checkpoint to recover from.

options.text: Fix predefined searches ignoring new findings, losing coverage of emerging issues.
options.explanation: The defining property of this task is that each finding determines the next question, so freezing searches upfront abandons exactly the emerging issues the agent exists to pursue.

questions.scenario: A research assistant investigates emerging issues where each finding determines the next source and question. The sequence cannot be listed upfront.
questions.explanation:
An agent is defensible when the path genuinely cannot be listed upfront, but only with controls: tools and actions constrained to the investigation scope, and budgets, stopping criteria, and checkpointed recoverable state bounding the loop. Unscoped enterprise access with self-determined stopping invites overreach and runaway cost.

Source: Claude Platform & Solution Design, workflow versus agent trade-offs; Building with the Claude API, Agents and tools.

questions.prompt: Which decomposition best reflects the four AI properties?

options.text: Claude extracts and drafts; code calculates; rules check; clinicians handle exceptions.
options.explanation: Language extraction/drafting suits Claude; dosage math and contraindications need code and rules engine with clinician exception handling.

options.text: Claude owns all steps with low-confidence review only, risking calculation errors.
options.explanation: Dosage calculation demands deterministic precision the model cannot guarantee, and low-confidence review misses the confident arithmetic errors that are most dangerous in a clinical setting.

options.text: System extracts while Claude calculates, inverting strengths and adding review load.
options.explanation: This inverts the division of strengths: rule-based systems handle structured extraction well, while probabilistic generation is the weakest possible owner of dosage arithmetic.

options.text: Claude verifies Claude, keeping probabilistic safety without determinism.
options.explanation: Model checking model keeps every safety-critical step probabilistic, so contraindication enforcement and dosage math still lack the determinism patient safety requires.

questions.scenario: A hospital intake assistant extracts symptoms and drafts notes. It also calculates dosage from weight and applies a contraindication rule.
questions.explanation:
Match each subtask to the mechanism its precision requires: extraction and drafting are interpretive (Claude), dosage calculation requires deterministic computation or tool execution, the contraindication rule is a deterministic check, and exceptions route to clinicians. Assigning calculation to the model risks exactly the errors the four-properties decomposition exists to prevent.

Source: Claude Platform & Solution Design, Limitation: tasks requiring precise numerical or logical computation; Model Context Protocol: Advanced, deterministic authorization.

questions.prompt: Select the two steps that preserve scale and integration coverage. (Select 2)

options.text: Fan out local checks by file in parallel.
options.explanation: Scale needs parallel local checks; shared libraries need a separate cross-file dataflow pass, not union or single-context loading.

options.text: Run separate integration pass over shared-library dependencies.
options.explanation: Scale needs parallel local checks; shared libraries need a separate cross-file dataflow pass, not union or single-context loading.

options.text: Treat union of file findings as complete, missing cross-file dataflow.
options.explanation: A union of per-file findings cannot contain cross-file dataflow issues because no worker sees the interactions across shared libraries where those bugs live.

options.text: Load all files into one session, risking overflow and context loss.
options.explanation: The audit already exceeds practical single context, so loading everything into one session invites overflow and lost detail rather than scaling the review.

questions.scenario: A large audit exceeds practical single context. Files are independent for local checks, but shared libraries need cross-file dataflow analysis.
questions.explanation:
Independent local checks fan out by file in parallel, and the shared-library cross-file dataflow analysis is a separate focused integration pass — per-file analysis plus cross-file integration, the documented decomposition for large reviews. Treating the union of file findings as complete misses exactly the cross-file failures the integration pass exists to catch.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 4.6 Designing Multi-instance and Multi-pass Review Architectures; Building with the Claude API, Parallelization workflows.

questions.prompt: What is the best first improvement before replacing the router with an agent?

options.text: Add boundary few-shots and measure confusion across overlap.
options.explanation: Overlapping categories need boundary few-shots plus confusion measurement before considering agents.

options.text: Add downstream tools to recover after misrouting, hiding classifier weakness.
options.explanation: Downstream recovery absorbs misroutes instead of fixing the classifier, so the measured weakness persists and every request pays the recovery cost.

options.text: Replace routes with generalist agent, trading measurable errors for opaque failures.
options.explanation: Swapping the router for an agent trades a measurable, improvable misrouting rate for opaque model-chosen paths that cannot be tuned with few-shot examples.

options.text: Merge overlapping categories pushing redistribution downstream, increasing manual cost.
options.explanation: Merging the overlapping categories moves the disambiguation burden onto downstream manual handling, raising cost without improving classification quality.

questions.scenario: A workflow classifies requests into four known paths with measurable misrouting. Two categories overlap semantically.
questions.explanation:
Measurable misrouting on two semantically overlapping categories is a classifier-quality problem, so the first improvement is boundary few-shot examples with confusion measured across the overlap. Replacing the router with an agent trades measurable, improvable errors for opaque ones.

Source: Building with the Claude API, Routing workflows; Exam Domain Notes, 4.2 Using Few-shot Prompting to Improve Output Consistency.

questions.prompt: Which simplification is most justified?

options.text: Bounded RAG with citations; add complexity only on eval gaps.
options.explanation: Stable corpus, citations, and no actions need only bounded RAG; agent loops and peer teams add cost without eval justification.

options.text: Remove retrieval relying on model knowledge, risking stale uncited answers.
options.explanation: The answers must be cited and the corpus is authoritative, so relying on model knowledge yields stale answers with no verifiable citations.

options.text: Remove citations trusting agent consensus, losing verifiability.
options.explanation: Consensus among models is not evidence; dropping citations removes the verifiability the use case explicitly requires.

options.text: Keep all patterns with smaller budgets, preserving needless coordination cost.
options.explanation: Smaller budgets shrink cost per step but keep the agent loop and peer team, so the latency, coordination, and operational overhead of patterns the task never exercises remain.

questions.scenario: An architect combines RAG, an agent loop, and a peer team for simple policy Q&A. The corpus is stable, answers need citations, and no actions occur.
questions.explanation:
Stable corpus, citation-required answers, and no actions need only bounded RAG with citations; the agent loop and peer team add latency, cost, and coordination without any mechanism this use case exercises. Add complexity only when evals show a gap the simpler design cannot close.

Source: Claude Platform & Solution Design, Cost: reaching for a heavier primitive than the job requires is paid for in latency, tokens, and operational surface area.

questions.prompt: Why is this simplification architecturally unsound?

options.text: Moves deterministic auditable rule into probabilistic generation obscuring ownership.
options.explanation: Threshold checks are deterministic and auditable; moving them into generation to skip integration obscures ownership and correctness.

options.text: Increases retrieval latency from training-data search, hiding the real risk.
options.explanation: Latency is not the issue; the real risk is that a published threshold applied probabilistically can silently produce decisions no backend rule would have made.

options.text: Claims calculation and language cannot share a call, missing the audit point.
options.explanation: The objection is not that both tasks cannot run in one call, but that the threshold decision itself must remain a deterministic, auditable check rather than generated output.

options.text: Requires multi-agent consensus, overkilling while ignoring determinism need.
options.explanation: Consensus is beside the point: the problem is the missing deterministic backend rule, and voting among probabilistic outputs still cannot make the decision auditable.

questions.scenario: A loan assistant uses Claude to decide a published debt-to-income threshold to avoid one backend integration.
questions.explanation:
A published debt-to-income threshold is a deterministic, auditable rule. Reimplementing it in model generation moves the decision into probabilistic output, obscuring who owns the rule and defeating auditability; the backend integration is precisely where the rule belongs.

Source: Claude Platform & Solution Design, Limitation: for high-stakes numerical accuracy, deterministic computation or tool execution should own the answer.

snapshot.title: Advanced Practice Exam: Evaluation, Testing & Optimization (v1, 20Q)

questions.prompt: Which metric set gates release?

options.text: Report average task success alone weekly
options.explanation: Average task success covers only quality, so the gate can pass while latency, cost, or safety requirements are violated; a release gate must test every measurable release condition.

options.text: Gate success latency cost safety thresholds
options.explanation: B gates all four dimensions with thresholds. Costs: A hides latency/cost/safety failures; B costs broader instrumentation; C hides accuracy/cost/safety tails; D hides quality/safety outcomes.

options.text: Track helpfulness votes and latency averages
options.explanation: Helpfulness votes and latency averages are subjective and averaged rather than thresholded, so they miss the task-success, cost, and hard safety requirements, including tail behavior.

options.text: Monitor token spend and uptime alone daily
options.explanation: Token spend and uptime are infrastructure signals; they say nothing about task quality or disallowed disclosures, so an unsafe or useless agent can pass this gate.

questions.scenario: A support agent must hold at least 92% task success, p99 under 3s, cost under 4 cents per case, and zero disallowed disclosures. The team debates a smaller quality-only scorecard.
questions.explanation: B is correct because a production gate must test the complete set of measurable requirements: task success, latency, cost, and safety. The notes distinguish quality checks from production readiness: latency and cost are design constraints, while safety requires its own evaluation method. A quality-only or infrastructure-only scorecard can pass while the system still violates another release condition. Source: Enterprise Integration & Production, Evals as acceptance criteria: building quality into the build process.

questions.prompt: What dataset fix best represents risk?

options.text: Add more simple lookup cases now
options.explanation: Adding more simple lookups worsens the skew: the suite already over-represents the easiest 70% of traffic, and inflating it hides failures in multi-step and adversarial cases.

options.text: Sample randomly from raw chat history
options.explanation: Raw random chat logs are unlabeled and inherit the production skew, so they neither guarantee coverage of the adversarial tail nor provide the graded cases an eval suite needs.

options.text: Stratify to match production failure mix
options.explanation: C stratifies to production risk including the 10% adversarial tail. Costs: A inflates scores and hides risk; B preserves skew and noise; C costs curation effort; D hardens bias and false confidence.

options.text: Duplicate high-scoring cases for score stability
options.explanation: Duplicating cases the system already passes inflates the aggregate score without adding information, manufacturing stability while hiding exactly the failure modes that dominate production losses.

questions.scenario: Production logs show 70% simple lookups, 20% multi-step claims, and 10% adversarial edges. The eval set is 90% simple lookups.
questions.explanation: C is correct because the golden dataset must represent the inputs the deployed system will encounter, including edge cases and counterexamples. A suite that is 90% easy lookups measures a different distribution from production, so its aggregate score can hide failures in multi-step and adversarial cases. Adding or duplicating easy cases worsens that coverage problem, and raw random chat logs do not by themselves create a labeled, representative dataset. Source: Enterprise Integration & Production, How the eval workflow runs: from task definition to result.

questions.prompt: Which grading mix fits each output?

options.text: Code checks JSON judge prose human safety
options.explanation: A matches deterministic, open-ended, and safety-sensitive outputs to code, judge, and human grading. Costs: A costs three pipelines; B risks judge bias on JSON/safety; C costs reviewer time unscalably

options.text: Judge model grades every output type alone
options.explanation: A single judge model grades structured JSON worse than code assertions and introduces bias on safety-sensitive refund decisions, where policy nuance needs human adjudication.

options.text: Human review grades every nightly case manually
options.explanation: Manual review of 500 nightly cases does not scale and adds reviewer fatigue; humans should be reserved for the safety-sensitive slice, with code and judges covering the deterministic and open-ended bulk.

options.text: Exact match checks grade all outputs equally
options.explanation: Exact-match checks cannot grade open-ended apologies at all and cannot capture the policy nuance in refund decisions, so two of the three output types get meaningless scores.

questions.scenario: A travel agent outputs JSON itineraries, open-ended apologies, and refund decisions with safety policy. One grading method is proposed for everything, nightly over 500 cases.
questions.explanation: A matches deterministic, open-ended, and safety-sensitive outputs to code, judge, and human grading. Costs: A costs three pipelines; B risks judge bias on JSON/safety; C costs reviewer time unscalably; D fails prose and safety nuance.

questions.prompt: What restores a valid A/B comparison?

options.text: Keep schedule and compare raw win rates
options.explanation: Keeping the schedule preserves the confound: the prompt is entangled with weekday and traffic-mix shifts, so raw win-rate differences measure the audience, not the prompt.

options.text: Add more Monday and Friday traffic data
options.explanation: More data on the same confounded schedule increases statistical confidence in a biased estimate; volume does not correct a systematic traffic-mix difference.

options.text: Pause testing until traffic fully stabilizes
options.explanation: Waiting for stability delays the decision without fixing the design flaw; whenever testing resumes on split schedules, the same time-of-week confound returns.

options.text: Randomize and interleave both prompts together
options.explanation: D randomizes and interleaves to remove the weekday confound. Costs: A confounds prompt with traffic shift; B keeps time bias with more data; C costs delay without fixing bias; D costs router and logging work.

questions.scenario: Prompt A ran Monday morning and prompt B Friday evening, 1,000 cases each. Conversion differs, but traffic mix shifted sharply. A third condition was added midweek.
questions.explanation: D randomizes and interleaves to remove the weekday confound. Costs: A confounds prompt with traffic shift; B keeps time bias with more data; C costs delay without fixing bias; D costs router and logging work.

questions.prompt: What prevents tuning leakage?

options.text: Tune prompts on the full eval suite
options.explanation: Tuning on the full suite is exactly the leakage already underway: twelve tweaks have fit the 400 cases, so the same set can no longer provide an unbiased selection signal.

options.text: Lock held-out set excluding all tuning
options.explanation: B locks a held-out set never used for tuning. Costs: A leaks tuning into selection; B costs extra curation and discipline; C hides variance behind averages; D costs compute without validity gain.

options.text: Report only mean score across seeds
options.explanation: Averaging across seeds addresses run-to-run variance, not data leakage; the mean is still computed over cases the prompts were tuned against, so it remains optimistically biased.

options.text: Rerun tuned prompt on training cases
options.explanation: Rerunning on the same training cases measures how well the prompt was fit to them, which is guaranteed to look good and proves nothing about generalization.

questions.scenario: After twelve prompt tweaks on 400 eval cases, accuracy rose from 81% to 89%. The same 400 cases will select the winner.
questions.explanation: B locks a held-out set never used for tuning. Costs: A leaks tuning into selection; B costs extra curation and discipline; C hides variance behind averages; D costs compute without validity gain.

questions.prompt: What design isolates the cause?

options.text: Ship combined change and watch dashboards
options.explanation: Shipping the combined change reproduces the attribution problem at production scale: any dashboard movement still cannot tell whether retrieval depth or the prompt caused it.

options.text: Add larger model alongside new prompt
options.explanation: Stacking a third change on top of the two entangled ones deepens the confound and makes both attribution and rollback harder, not easier.

options.text: Test one change per arm versus control
options.explanation: C isolates one change per arm against control. Costs: A leaves attribution impossible; B doubles confounds and rollback pain; C costs extra arms and traffic; D costs time without causal evidence.

options.text: Roll back both changes and wait
options.explanation: Rolling back discards a measured 4-point gain and produces no evidence about which component helped; waiting does not create causal isolation either.

questions.scenario: Retrieval depth and system prompt changed together; success rose 4 points on 600 cases. Nobody knows which change helped.
questions.explanation: C isolates one change per arm against control. Costs: A leaves attribution impossible; B doubles confounds and rollback pain; C costs extra arms and traffic; D costs time without causal evidence.

questions.prompt: What localizes the failure stage FIRST?

options.text: Rerun with gold context to isolate retrieval
options.explanation: A checks whether gold context fixes the answer, isolating retrieval. Costs: A costs a small rerun; B wastes tuning on wrong stage; C costs quality for unproven cause; D costs coverage without diagnosi

options.text: Rewrite system prompt and redeploy immediately
options.explanation: Rewriting the prompt assumes the generator is at fault before retrieval recall has been measured, so the tuning effort may be spent on the wrong stage entirely.

options.text: Cut retrieved chunks to reduce latency
options.explanation: Cutting chunks addresses latency, not citation accuracy, and reducing context could worsen the very retrieval quality that is still unmeasured.

options.text: Add broader fallback answers for misses
options.explanation: Fallback answers mask misses without diagnosing whether retrieval failed to find the source or the generator failed to cite it, adding coverage while leaving the cause unknown.

questions.scenario: Citation accuracy is 58% while retrieval recall is unmeasured. The team blames the generator and wants prompt tuning.
questions.explanation: A checks whether gold context fixes the answer, isolating retrieval. Costs: A costs a small rerun; B wastes tuning on wrong stage; C costs quality for unproven cause; D costs coverage without diagnosis.

questions.prompt: What best fixes the mismatch?

options.text: Keep long prompt and accept error rate
options.explanation: Accepting a 22% instruction-violation rate leaves a broken prompt-model pairing in production; the error is a fixable mismatch, not an inherent property of the smaller model.

options.text: Return to flagship model for every request
options.explanation: Escalating every request to the flagship model restores quality only by giving up the cost and latency reasons the smaller model was chosen for in the first place.

options.text: Add more constraints to same prompt
options.explanation: Adding constraints makes the prompt longer and harder to follow, which is precisely what the smaller model is already failing at; it deepens the mismatch instead of fixing it.

options.text: Simplify prompt to fit smaller model limits
options.explanation: D matches prompt complexity to the smaller model's instruction-following. Costs: A preserves mismatch and error rate; B costs latency and spend; C costs structure without testing cause; D costs prompt rework but fits capability.

questions.scenario: A prompt tuned on a flagship model fails on a smaller model: 22% instruction violations. Schema compliance and reasoning depth both dropped.
questions.explanation: D matches prompt complexity to the smaller model's instruction-following. Costs: A preserves mismatch and error rate; B costs latency and spend; C costs structure without testing cause; D costs prompt rework but fits capability.

questions.prompt: What cuts cost FIRST?

options.text: Negotiate cheaper tokens keeping ten chunks
options.explanation: Renegotiating unit price leaves the dominant driver — ten chunks plus three retries per case — untouched, so total spend barely moves even with a better rate.

options.text: Cut chunks retries turns then reprice units
options.explanation: B cuts quantity (chunks, turns, retries) before renegotiating unit price. Costs: A saves little while volume stays high; B costs recall validation; C risks quality without measuring; D hides unit economics.

options.text: Switch vendors without measuring token volume
options.explanation: Switching vendors changes only the unit price while the unexamined token volume stays high, so the root driver of the 9-cent average is never addressed or even measured.

options.text: Cap monthly spend without changing volume
options.explanation: A spend cap hides the unit economics and eventually rations service rather than reducing it; it neither lowers per-case cost nor reveals where the tokens actually go.

questions.scenario: Each case pulls ten chunks and averages three retries at 9 cents. The per-token price looks high, but volume is unexamined.
questions.explanation: B cuts quantity (chunks, turns, retries) before renegotiating unit price. Costs: A saves little while volume stays high; B costs recall validation; C risks quality without measuring; D hides unit economics.

questions.prompt: What best fixes p99 latency?

options.text: Compress prompts by five percent only
options.explanation: A small prompt compression trims a few milliseconds per call; the p99 tail is driven by three sequential tool calls, which this change does not touch.

options.text: Truncate all outputs to fifty tokens
options.explanation: Blind truncation degrades answer quality for every user to shave the tail, and it does not shorten the sequential tool calls that dominate slow cases.

options.text: Parallelize calls then stream partial results
options.explanation: C parallelizes independent calls then streams partials. Costs: A barely moves p99 tail; B trades accuracy for speed blindly; C costs orchestration complexity; D costs UX without fixing tail.

options.text: Add loading spinners to mask delays
options.explanation: Spinners change perceived latency only; the p99 measurement and the user still wait the full 7 seconds, so the SLO breach remains unaddressed.

questions.scenario: Median is near 1s but p99 near 7s against a 3s SLO. Traces show three sequential tool calls per slow case.
questions.explanation: C parallelizes independent calls then streams partials. Costs: A barely moves p99 tail; B trades accuracy for speed blindly; C costs orchestration complexity; D costs UX without fixing tail.

questions.prompt: Which caching choice controls cost safely?

options.text: Cache with TTL plus explicit invalidation rules
options.explanation: A caches with TTL plus invalidation and names staleness risk. Costs: A costs invalidation logic; B pays full price per repeat; C risks stale refunds silently; D costs latency with no savings.

options.text: Disable caching and pay full price
options.explanation: Disabling caching forfeits the savings on the 40% repeat traffic and keeps the $900 monthly retrieval bill, solving no part of the cost problem the scenario poses.

options.text: Cache indefinitely without any invalidation control
options.explanation: Indefinite caching with no invalidation serves stale policy answers silently — for refund and policy questions, an outdated cached answer can be confidently wrong with real financial consequences.

options.text: Retry every query with fresh full retrieval
options.explanation: Re-running full retrieval on every repeat query eliminates any savings while adding latency, which is the opposite of controlling cost on high-repeat traffic.

questions.scenario: Repeat policy questions are 40% of 10,000 daily cases. Full retrieval each time costs $900 per month.
questions.explanation: A caches with TTL plus invalidation and names staleness risk. Costs: A costs invalidation logic; B pays full price per repeat; C risks stale refunds silently; D costs latency with no savings.

questions.prompt: Which monitoring signals acceptance?

options.text: Track lab accuracy and demo win rates
options.explanation: Lab accuracy and demo wins are the same vanity signals that already coexist with an 18% override rate; they measure benchmark performance, not user acceptance in production.

options.text: Monitor uptime and average token usage
options.explanation: Uptime and token usage are infrastructure health metrics; a system can be fully available and cheap while users keep rejecting its drafts.

options.text: Sample chats for subjective vibe scores
options.explanation: Subjective vibe scores are unanchored, noisy, and not tied to user outcomes, so they cannot demonstrate acceptance or explain the high override rate leadership needs to see move.

options.text: Track overrides reopens and task resolution
options.explanation: D ties monitoring to acceptance: overrides, reopens, resolution. Costs: A celebrates lab scores while users override; B hides failure behind uptime; C costs annotation without outcome link; D costs event plumbing.

questions.scenario: Lab accuracy is 94% but agents override 18% of drafts. Leadership wants proof of production acceptance. Ticket mix keeps shifting monthly.
questions.explanation: D ties monitoring to acceptance: overrides, reopens, resolution. Costs: A celebrates lab scores while users override; B hides failure behind uptime; C costs annotation without outcome link; D costs event plumbing.

questions.prompt: Which TWO complete the release gate? Select both.

options.text: Task success >=90% with safety violations tracked
options.explanation: A and C gate quality, tail latency, unit cost, and safety. Costs: A/C cost instrumentation; B hides tail risk and cost; D hides quality, cost, and safety.

options.text: Average helpfulness score without cost tracking
options.explanation: An average helpfulness score is subjective, has no threshold, and omits cost entirely; it cannot enforce the finance and safety demands the gate is missing.

options.text: p95 latency bound with per-case cost cap
options.explanation: A and C gate quality, tail latency, unit cost, and safety. Costs: A/C cost instrumentation; B hides tail risk and cost; D hides quality, cost, and safety.

options.text: Total tokens and server uptime only
options.explanation: Total tokens and uptime are infrastructure-only signals: they track no quality threshold, no safety violations, and no per-case cost bound, leaving the gate blind to all three demanded dimensions.

questions.scenario: A release gate lists only average accuracy today. Finance and safety demand latency, cost, and refusal metrics.
questions.explanation: A and C gate quality, tail latency, unit cost, and safety. Costs: A/C cost instrumentation; B hides tail risk and cost; D hides quality, cost, and safety.

questions.prompt: Which TWO strengthen the eval suite? Select both.

options.text: Reuse demo cases with exact-match grading
options.explanation: Demo cases over-represent easy wins the system already handles, and exact-match grading cannot score refund judgment, so this change reinforces both existing suite weaknesses.

options.text: Weight cases by production failure frequency
options.explanation: B covers failure-weighted sampling and mixed graders; D is exact. Costs: A inflates scores; B/D cost curation; C biases judging and hides safety gaps.

options.text: Grade safety policy with similarity scores
options.explanation: Similarity scores are the same mismatch as BLEU for safety policy: a paraphrase can score high while violating the rule, so over-refusals stay invisible to the grader.

options.text: Pair code checks with human safety review
options.explanation: B covers failure-weighted sampling and mixed graders; D is exact. Costs: A inflates scores; B/D cost curation; C biases judging and hides safety gaps.

questions.scenario: The suite over-represents easy cases and grades refunds with BLEU. Rare over-refunds dominate support losses.
questions.explanation: B covers failure-weighted sampling and mixed graders; D is exact. Costs: A inflates scores; B/D cost curation; C biases judging and hides safety gaps.

questions.prompt: Which TWO make the A/B valid? Select both.

options.text: Randomize assignment and isolate single variable
options.explanation: A and D enforce randomization, isolation, and held-out confirmation. Costs: A/D cost traffic and discipline; B confounds time with treatment; C overfits selection to tuned data.

options.text: Run variant A mornings variant B evenings
options.explanation: Splitting variants by time of day reproduces the exact confound the scenario warns about: weekly seasonality and traffic-mix differences get attributed to the reranker instead.

options.text: Select winner on the tuning dataset
options.explanation: Selecting the winner on data used for tuning rewards overfitting to that set and does not measure how either reranker performs on fresh traffic.

options.text: Confirm winner on held-out evaluation set
options.explanation: A and D enforce randomization, isolation, and held-out confirmation. Costs: A/D cost traffic and discipline; B confounds time with treatment; C overfits selection to tuned data.

questions.scenario: Two rerankers are tested on live traffic with weekly seasonality. The team wants a trustworthy winner in two weeks.
questions.explanation: A and D enforce randomization, isolation, and held-out confirmation. Costs: A/D cost traffic and discipline; B confounds time with treatment; C overfits selection to tuned data.

questions.prompt: Which TWO localize the failing stage? Select both.

options.text: Tune generator before measuring retrieval recall
options.explanation: Tuning the generator before retrieval recall is known risks optimizing the wrong stage: if retrieval is failing to surface the contract clauses, no amount of generator tuning fixes the misses.

options.text: Test generator on gold-standard retrieved context
options.explanation: B isolates retrieval with gold context; C isolates instruction-following from knowledge. Costs: B/C cost reruns; A tunes the wrong stage; D changes two stages at once.

options.text: Probe model with prompt-only baseline cases
options.explanation: B isolates retrieval with gold context; C isolates instruction-following from knowledge. Costs: B/C cost reruns; A tunes the wrong stage; D changes two stages at once.

options.text: Change retriever and prompt simultaneously now
options.explanation: Changing two stages at once preserves the current ambiguity: even if accuracy improves, logs still cannot attribute the gain to retrieval or generation.

questions.scenario: RAG answers miss on 30% of contract questions. Logs cannot say whether retrieval or generation failed.
questions.explanation: B isolates retrieval with gold context; C isolates instruction-following from knowledge. Costs: B/C cost reruns; A tunes the wrong stage; D changes two stages at once.

questions.prompt: Which TWO cut quantity before unit price? Select both.

options.text: Reduce chunks and cap retry loops
options.explanation: A and C cut quantity: fewer chunks, fewer retries, bounded turns. Costs: A/C cost recall validation; B barely moves total spend; D risks silent quality loss.

options.text: Chase small per-token discount retaining volume
options.explanation: A 10% unit discount leaves the volume drivers — eight chunks plus liberal retries — fully intact, so the bulk of the 11-cent per-case cost is untouched.

options.text: Bound tool turns with early-stop rules
options.explanation: A and C cut quantity: fewer chunks, fewer retries, bounded turns. Costs: A/C cost recall validation; B barely moves total spend; D risks silent quality loss.

options.text: Truncate outputs blindly across all cases
options.explanation: Blind truncation is a quality gamble rather than a quantity fix: it risks silently cutting needed content while leaving chunk and retry volume — the actual cost drivers — unchanged.

questions.scenario: Cost is 11 cents per case with eight chunks and liberal retries. The vendor offers a 10% token discount.
questions.explanation: A and C cut quantity: fewer chunks, fewer retries, bounded turns. Costs: A/C cost recall validation; B barely moves total spend; D risks silent quality loss.

questions.prompt: Which grading practices are sound? Select all that apply.

options.text: Code assertions verify JSON schema fields
options.explanation: A/C/E are sound: code for structured, judge with rubric, humans for safety edges. Costs: sound options cost pipeline effort; B fails nuance; D is unscalable and noisy for all cases.

options.text: BLEU scores grade refund safety decisions
options.explanation: BLEU measures surface text overlap, not policy correctness, so a refund decision could score well while violating the safety rule — the grader is measuring the wrong thing entirely.

options.text: Judge rubric scores apology tone quality
options.explanation: A/C/E are sound: code for structured, judge with rubric, humans for safety edges. Costs: sound options cost pipeline effort; B fails nuance; D is unscalable and noisy for all cases.

options.text: Humans grade every nightly regression case
options.explanation: Human grading of every regression case does not scale to nightly volume and introduces fatigue-driven noise; humans belong on sampled safety edges, not the full run.

options.text: Humans adjudicate sampled safety edge cases
options.explanation: A/C/E are sound: code for structured, judge with rubric, humans for safety edges. Costs: sound options cost pipeline effort; B fails nuance; D is unscalable and noisy for all cases.

questions.scenario: Judge each grading practice as sound or unsound for its output type.
questions.explanation: A/C/E are sound: code for structured, judge with rubric, humans for safety edges. Costs: sound options cost pipeline effort; B fails nuance; D is unscalable and noisy for all cases.

questions.prompt: Which monitoring signals show acceptance? Select all that apply.

options.text: Lab accuracy alone proves user acceptance
options.explanation: Lab accuracy is measured on a curated benchmark, not live users; the 94% versus 18%-override gap shows exactly how lab performance can diverge from production acceptance.

options.text: Override rate flags rejected agent drafts
options.explanation: B/C/E reflect acceptance: overrides, reopens, resolution. Costs: downstream plumbing costs effort; A celebrates lab-only gains; D hides failures behind infrastructure health.

options.text: Ticket reopen rate signals unresolved work
options.explanation: B/C/E reflect acceptance: overrides, reopens, resolution. Costs: downstream plumbing costs effort; A celebrates lab-only gains; D hides failures behind infrastructure health.

options.text: Server uptime alone proves task success
options.explanation: Uptime proves the service is reachable, not that it resolves anything; a perfectly available agent can still fail every user task it handles.

options.text: Resolution rate confirms completed user goals
options.explanation: B/C/E reflect acceptance: overrides, reopens, resolution. Costs: downstream plumbing costs effort; A celebrates lab-only gains; D hides failures behind infrastructure health.

questions.scenario: Judge each production signal as acceptance-revealing or vanity for agent monitoring.
questions.explanation: B/C/E reflect acceptance: overrides, reopens, resolution. Costs: downstream plumbing costs effort; A celebrates lab-only gains; D hides failures behind infrastructure health.

questions.prompt: Which TWO cut quantity before unit price? Select both.

options.text: Renegotiate token rate keeping volume fixed
options.explanation: Renegotiating the rate only reprices the existing volume; with chunk counts, retries, and turns unchanged, the dominant cost driver is untouched.

options.text: Deduplicate chunks and cache repeats
options.explanation: B/D cut quantity first: deduplicate retrieval, bound loops. Costs: B/D cost validation work; A only reprices unchanged volume; C buys headroom without efficiency gain.

options.text: Raise concurrency limits without volume change
options.explanation: Raising concurrency adds throughput headroom but does not reduce the tokens consumed per case, so total spend stays the same or grows with demand.

options.text: Cap retries with targeted fallback policy
