options.explanation: B/D cut quantity first: deduplicate retrieval, bound loops. Costs: B/D cost validation work; A only reprices unchanged volume; C buys headroom without efficiency gain.

questions.scenario: Classify each cost action as quantity-first or unit-price-only optimization.
questions.explanation: B/D cut quantity first: deduplicate retrieval, bound loops. Costs: B/D cost validation work; A only reprices unchanged volume; C buys headroom without efficiency gain.

snapshot.title: Advanced Exam: Prompt Engineering & Structured Output (Rebalanced)

questions.prompt: Which change most directly reduces semantic reconciliation errors?

options.text: Extract stated and computed totals separately; compare in code and retry with exact mismatch.
options.explanation: Only programmatic comparison of stated vs computed totals catches semantic mismatch; schema validation alone cannot. Exact mismatch feedback makes retries actionable.

options.text: Add a self-assessed total_matches flag without any programmatic comparison.
options.explanation: A self-assessed flag is the model grading its own arithmetic, which is exactly the unreliable judgment that let the disagreement pass. Without a programmatic comparison, the semantic mismatch remains undetected.

options.text: Strictly reject off-schema fields while keeping the generic retry message.
options.explanation: Tightening schema rejection addresses structure, but the failing output already validates: the problem is semantic, not structural. Keeping a generic missing-field retry gives the model nothing specific to correct.

options.text: Add valid-invoice examples but keep the vague missing-field retry.
options.explanation: Examples of valid invoices do not teach the reconciliation rule between stated and computed totals, and the vague retry message still fails to tell the model what was wrong. The disagreement loop continues.

questions.scenario: An invoice extractor passes schema validation but totals disagree with line-item sums. Retries only flag missing fields.
questions.explanation:
Schema validation establishes structure, not whether two semantically related totals reconcile. Extracting the stated and calculated totals separately lets application code perform the deterministic comparison, then a retry can receive the exact discrepancy instead of a generic missing-field message.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 4.4 Implementing Validation, Retries, and Feedback Loops for Extraction Quality.

questions.prompt: Select each step that restores trust without sacrificing bug detection.

options.text: Pause the noisy security category until its criteria improve.
options.explanation: Pausing the noisy category stops trust erosion, refined criteria fix precision, and an independent two-pass reviewer removes self-review bias while keeping bug detection.

options.text: Refine security criteria with precise evidence thresholds.
options.explanation: Pausing the noisy category stops trust erosion, refined criteria fix precision, and an independent two-pass reviewer removes self-review bias while keeping bug detection.

options.text: Review with an independent session using local plus integration passes.
options.explanation: Pausing the noisy category stops trust erosion, refined criteria fix precision, and an independent two-pass reviewer removes self-review bias while keeping bug detection.

options.text: Keep both categories and filter only by self-rated confidence scores.
options.explanation: Self-rated confidence is uncalibrated and does not distinguish true findings from noise, so the false positives that erode trust keep flowing through. Filtering by the model's own scores preserves the same self-review bias.

options.text: Add security examples but keep the same reviewer and single pass.
options.explanation: Examples alone do not fix the imprecise criteria driving the false positives, and keeping generation and review in the same single pass retains the self-review bias that lets real bugs slip through.

questions.scenario: One model generates code and reviews it in a single pass. Noisy security findings erode trust in accurate bug findings.
questions.explanation:
The noisy category should be paused while its rules are repaired, because persistent false positives undermine trust in valid findings. The repair is explicit, evidence-based criteria; the code should then be reviewed by an independent instance, with separate local and integration passes, because a generation session is less likely to challenge its own reasoning.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 4.1 Designing Prompts with Explicit Criteria to Improve Accuracy and 4.6 Designing Multi-instance and Multi-pass Review Architectures.

questions.prompt: How should criteria and examples be combined?

options.text: Use one language-neutral example set adapted per file by the reviewer.
options.explanation: Asking the reviewer to adapt neutral examples per language re-creates the inconsistency, since each adaptation is an unguided judgment call. The cross-language leakage the scenario describes comes from exactly this kind of shared, un-calibrated set.

options.text: Write exhaustive rules for every language and omit all examples.
options.explanation: Rules without examples leave severity levels uncalibrated: the model cannot anchor what 'conservative' looks like at each level. Exhaustive rule text also grows brittle as languages evolve.

options.text: Define severity criteria per language with a small language-specific example set.
options.explanation: Shared severity plus language-specific examples prevents cross-language contamination. Neutral or exhaustive-only approaches leave severity uncalibrated.

options.text: Provide examples only for the top language and keep generic instructions elsewhere.
options.explanation: Examples for one language leave every other language without calibration, so severity rating stays inconsistent there. Generic instructions are what produced the inconsistency in the first place.

questions.scenario: A 'be conservative' prompt rates severity inconsistently across languages. Shared examples leak language-specific patterns.
questions.explanation:
Vague guidance should be replaced with concrete severity criteria, and those criteria need examples at each level. When language-specific patterns affect interpretation, the examples and criteria must make the applicable distinction explicit rather than relying on the reviewer to adapt a generic rule.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 4.1 Designing Prompts with Explicit Criteria to Improve Accuracy.

questions.prompt: Which schema and instruction design handles novel types without encouraging fabrication?

options.text: Replace the enum with unrestricted text and request precise type names.
options.explanation: Unrestricted text removes the schema constraint entirely, so output conformance and downstream handling of types are lost. Free-form naming also keeps the pressure to produce a confident-sounding category rather than honestly reporting novelty.

options.text: Add every novel label to the enum and still require a known type.
options.explanation: Enumerating labels reactively cannot keep up with novel documents, and between updates the extractor still must force every contract into a known type, perpetuating the nearest-match fabrication.

options.text: Add an unclear value used for every difficult document.
options.explanation: A single catch-all 'unclear' value invites dumping any genuinely categorizable-but-novel document into it, hiding real information. It signals difficulty, not an honest report of a category outside the predefined set.

options.text: Add other plus a conditional detail field; require other unless a definition matches.
options.explanation: An other bucket plus conditional detail gives novel types a conformant home and forces honest abstention from the enum. Expanding the enum or free text keeps fabrication pressure.

questions.scenario: A contract extractor restricts type to four enum values. Unmatched documents get the nearest value plus an invented rationale.
questions.explanation:
A strict enum alone cannot represent an in-scope but novel category. An `other` value with a conditional detail field preserves a constrained schema while allowing the extractor to report a category outside the predefined labels instead of forcing a nearest-match fabrication.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 4.3 Enforcing Structured Output with tool_use and JSON Schemas.

questions.prompt: Which few-shot strategy most directly addresses field misattribution?

options.text: Show source-to-field mappings across layouts, including why subgroup counts are excluded.
options.explanation: Source-to-field mappings across layouts plus negative examples teach the subgroup-vs-overall boundary. Output-only or single-layout examples cannot fix misattribution.

options.text: Show output JSON for several papers without the source passages behind each field.
options.explanation: Output-only examples let the model copy plausible values without learning where each field comes from in the document, so a subgroup count can still be recorded as the overall size. The provenance rule is what the examples must teach.

options.text: Use examples only for the dominant layout and rely on field names elsewhere.
options.explanation: Field names alone give no guidance when sample sizes appear in tables or footnotes instead of the dominant layout's abstract. Unusual structures remain exactly where the misattribution happens.

options.text: Place generic examples in the tool description for both selection and extraction.
options.explanation: A tool description is the wrong place for extraction-calibration examples, and generic ones do not cover the ambiguous subgroup-versus-overall case. Neither the placement nor the content addresses the misattribution.

questions.scenario: Sample sizes appear in abstracts, tables, or footnotes. The extractor sometimes records a subgroup count as the overall sample size.
questions.explanation:
Few-shot examples should cover ambiguous cases and documents with different structures. Showing the source-to-field decision, including why a subgroup count is excluded, teaches the extraction rule rather than merely displaying output that could be copied without understanding its provenance.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 4.2 Using Few-shot Prompting to Improve Output Consistency.

questions.prompt: Select each strategy needed to fix both failure patterns.

options.text: Allow null for absent evidence instead of forcing a value.
options.explanation: Nullable fields stop fabrication on absent evidence, diverse examples cover unusual layouts, and exact-mismatch feedback breaks the repeat-wrong-value loop.

options.text: Add layout-diverse examples covering unusual document structures.
options.explanation: Nullable fields stop fabrication on absent evidence, diverse examples cover unusual layouts, and exact-mismatch feedback breaks the repeat-wrong-value loop.

options.text: Return the exact extraction mismatch on every retry.
options.explanation: Nullable fields stop fabrication on absent evidence, diverse examples cover unusual layouts, and exact-mismatch feedback breaks the repeat-wrong-value loop.

options.text: Increase retries for absent fields with the existing generic loop.
options.explanation: More retries through the same generic missing-field loop cannot create source evidence that does not exist, so the model fabricates an address to satisfy the prompt. Repetition amplifies the fabrication instead of fixing it.

options.text: Keep all fields required and accept values above a confidence threshold.
options.explanation: Keeping fields required is precisely what pressures the model to invent an address when the scan lacks one, and self-rated confidence does not verify that an accepted value came from the document.

questions.scenario: Retries fabricate an absent vendor address. On unusual layouts retries repeat wrong values because feedback only says field missing.
questions.explanation:
When evidence is absent, nullable fields avoid forcing fabricated values. For layout-driven errors, targeted examples spanning different document structures improve generalization, and semantic retries need concrete validation errors; simply repeating a generic missing-field prompt cannot supply missing source evidence or identify the wrong extraction.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 4.4 Implementing Validation, Retries, and Feedback Loops for Extraction Quality.

questions.prompt: Which architecture preserves batch efficiency and recoverable validation?

options.text: Run self-contained extraction per item, validate after, then synchronously retry only failed custom_ids.
options.explanation: Self-contained batch items preserve throughput; post-batch validation plus sync retry of only failed custom_ids with exact errors restores recoverability without multi-turn inside batch.

options.text: Move all reviews to synchronous processing to keep the correction loop.
options.explanation: Moving the entire workload synchronous abandons the batch cost and throughput benefits for all items to serve a loop that only failures need. The efficient design validates after the batch and retries selectively.

options.text: Ask the model to self-correct inside one batch response and accept conformant results.
options.explanation: A single batch request cannot host a multi-turn correction loop, and self-correction inside one response is just generation, not feedback-driven repair. Schema conformance still says nothing about semantic correctness.

options.text: Submit every review twice in separate batches and keep the fuller output.
options.explanation: Double submission doubles cost and latency for every item to catch a subset of failures, and agreement between two independent runs is not the targeted validation-and-retry recovery the failed items need.

questions.scenario: A large overnight review workload uses the Message Batches API. The synchronous multi-turn correction loop cannot run inside one batch request.
questions.explanation:
A batch request must remain self-contained because the Batch API does not support a multi-turn correction loop within one request. Validate outputs after the batch, use `custom_id` to correlate results, and synchronously retry only the failed items when that correction is required.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 4.5 Designing Efficient Batch Processing Strategies.

questions.prompt: Select each change needed to robustly resolve the date swap.

options.text: Define each date by its documentary signals, not just its format.
options.explanation: Documentary-signal definitions plus contrastive examples teach the distinction, and exact field-value mismatch feedback tells the retry what to swap. Format or nullability alone cannot.

options.text: Show contrastive examples distinguishing execution from effective dates.
options.explanation: Documentary-signal definitions plus contrastive examples teach the distinction, and exact field-value mismatch feedback tells the retry what to swap. Format or nullability alone cannot.

options.text: Identify the current field-value mismatch explicitly in retry feedback.
options.explanation: Documentary-signal definitions plus contrastive examples teach the distinction, and exact field-value mismatch feedback tells the retry what to swap. Format or nullability alone cannot.

options.text: Enforce a distinct calendar format per field with regex branches.
options.explanation: In this scenario both dates are valid and can share a format, so format-based branching never distinguishes them. The swap is semantic — which date plays which role — not a formatting problem.

options.text: Make both dates nullable and return null whenever distinction is hard.
options.explanation: Nulling hard cases discards correct, extractable data whenever the distinction takes effort, trading accuracy for an escape hatch. It hides the swap rather than teaching the model to resolve it.

questions.scenario: A legal extractor swaps two valid dates. Vague 'dates may be swapped' feedback produces inconsistent retries.
questions.explanation:
Two valid dates require semantic distinctions, not merely different formats. Define each field by its documentary signals, reinforce the distinction with targeted contrastive examples, and provide the exact current mismatch in retry feedback so the correction is grounded in the validation failure.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 4.4 Implementing Validation, Retries, and Feedback Loops for Extraction Quality.

questions.prompt: How should ambiguity be represented within batch constraints?

options.text: Count every convertible den as a bedroom unless validation rejects it.
options.explanation: Counting convertible dens as bedrooms fabricates certainty the listing does not state, and schema validation cannot catch it because a higher count is perfectly conformant. This directly corrupts the bedroom data.

options.text: Pre-resolve every listing synchronously, then batch only certain documents.
options.explanation: Pre-resolving everything synchronously defeats the purpose of batching and its cost benefits, and 'certain' documents still require an interactive resolution step that a single batch request cannot host.

options.text: Run duplicate batch requests and accept values when both outputs agree.
options.explanation: Two independent runs can agree on the same arbitrary resolution of an ambiguous den, so agreement measures consistency, not correctness. It doubles cost while leaving the ambiguity unrepresented.

options.text: Separate confirmed bedroom count from ambiguity notes and flag uncertain custom_ids.
options.explanation: Separating confirmed count from ambiguity notes keeps batch conformant while preserving uncertainty for follow-up. Forcing a bedroom value fabricates certainty.

questions.scenario: Property listings batch-processed cannot ask follow-up questions. Some dens could arguably become bedrooms.
questions.explanation:
Batch processing cannot depend on interactive follow-up within a request, so ambiguity must be represented in the structured result. Keeping the confirmed count separate from an ambiguity note preserves the supported fact, while `custom_id` identifies the uncertain records for later handling.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 4.5 Designing Efficient Batch Processing Strategies.

questions.prompt: What is the likely cause and best fix?

options.text: Include relevant signatures, returns, call sites, and findings in the integration input.
options.explanation: The integration pass never received implementations, only findings, so it cannot trace the unsafe value flow. Supplying signatures, returns, and call sites restores dataflow visibility.

options.text: Shrink each per-file pass region while keeping integration input unchanged.
options.explanation: Shrinking per-file regions reduces what the local passes see but does nothing for the integration pass, which is missing the cross-module information needed to trace the unsafe value flow. The blind spot remains.

options.text: Add a cross_file flag to the finding schema without changing integration context.
options.explanation: A schema flag labels findings but supplies no signatures, returns, or call sites, so the integration pass still lacks the evidence to detect the value flow. Metadata without context cannot fix the blind spot.

options.text: Reuse the generation session so earlier context supplies implementation details.
options.explanation: Reusing the generation session forfeits reviewer independence: the same session is less likely to challenge its own code. It also conflates generation context with review context rather than constructing a purposeful integration input.

questions.scenario: Per-file reviews find local issues. The cross-file pass receives only those findings and misses an unsafe value flow between two modules.
questions.explanation:
Per-file findings alone omit the relationships required to inspect cross-file data flow. An integration pass should receive the relevant signatures, returns, and call sites with the local findings, while remaining independent of the generation context; this preserves local focus and gives the integration pass the evidence it needs.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 4.6 Designing Multi-instance and Multi-pass Review Architectures.

questions.prompt: Select each step of the most efficient and correct retry policy.

options.text: Batch-retry transient failures without changing the prompt.
options.explanation: Each failure class needs its own path: cheap batch retry for transient, exact-feedback sync correction for semantic, and honest unextractable marking when evidence is absent.

options.text: Correct semantic failures synchronously with exact feedback.
options.explanation: Each failure class needs its own path: cheap batch retry for transient, exact-feedback sync correction for semantic, and honest unextractable marking when evidence is absent.

options.text: Mark records with absent source evidence as unextractable.
options.explanation: Each failure class needs its own path: cheap batch retry for transient, exact-feedback sync correction for semantic, and honest unextractable marking when evidence is absent.

options.text: Resubmit all failures unchanged in one batch for simplicity.
options.explanation: Resubmitting semantic failures unchanged is futile: the model receives no information about what was wrong, and absent source evidence will produce the same failure again. It conflates a transient recovery with a semantic correction.

options.text: Discard failures and enlarge the next batch to hold volume constant.
options.explanation: Discarding failures silently loses both recoverable records and the signal about why extraction failed, and enlarging batches does nothing for either failure class. This trades correctness for throughput optics.

questions.scenario: After a large batch, some failures are transient API errors and others are semantic validation failures with absent source information.
questions.explanation:
Transient failures can be retried without changing the request, whereas semantic validation failures need a targeted correction path with concrete feedback. If the needed fact is absent from the source, retrying is ineffective, so the record must be marked unextractable rather than resubmitted unchanged.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 4.4 Implementing Validation, Retries, and Feedback Loops for Extraction Quality.

questions.prompt: What additional mechanism best catches this systematic error?

options.text: Expand the detected-pattern taxonomy for more precise mismatch labels.
options.explanation: A richer taxonomy still compares two plausible strings against each other with no ground truth, so both can be wrong in a newly labeled way. The missing element is an authoritative reference, not finer labels.

options.text: Add another independent reviewer and accept agreement between reviewers.
options.explanation: Two reviewers looking at the same plausible strings can agree on the same wrong name, since neither checks an authoritative source. Inter-rater agreement is not field correctness here.

options.text: Raise reviewer creativity to consider wider field interpretations.
options.explanation: More creative interpretation makes the reviewer more likely to rationalize a plausible-looking vendor name, not to verify it. The failure is absence of ground truth, not narrow thinking.

options.text: Cross-check vendor_name against an authoritative source with labeled mismatch examples.
options.explanation: Only grounding against an authoritative vendor source plus labeled mismatch examples breaks the plausible-string trap. More reviewers or labels repeat the same blind comparison.

questions.scenario: An independent reviewer approves product names in vendor_name because both are plausible strings and no ground truth is checked.
questions.explanation:
Two plausible strings can agree while both are wrong, so another reviewer does not establish field correctness. The extractor should be checked against an authoritative source, because factual lookups against authoritative data are an unambiguous behavior suitable for deterministic validation; labeled mismatch examples make the expected failure pattern explicit.

Source: Enterprise Integration & Production, Evals as acceptance criteria: building quality into the build process.

questions.prompt: Select each element of an architecture that meets all requirements without a retry-fabrication cascade.

options.text: Use nullable stated and calculated totals.
options.explanation: Nullable dual totals plus code-side comparison, exact-mismatch retries, and a stop rule on absent evidence jointly deliver conformance, reconciliation, correction, and anti-fabrication.

options.text: Compare the two totals in code, not in the model.
options.explanation: Nullable dual totals plus code-side comparison, exact-mismatch retries, and a stop rule on absent evidence jointly deliver conformance, reconciliation, correction, and anti-fabrication.

options.text: Retry only exact mismatches with specific feedback.
options.explanation: Nullable dual totals plus code-side comparison, exact-mismatch retries, and a stop rule on absent evidence jointly deliver conformance, reconciliation, correction, and anti-fabrication.

options.text: Stop retrying when source evidence is absent.
options.explanation: Nullable dual totals plus code-side comparison, exact-mismatch retries, and a stop rule on absent evidence jointly deliver conformance, reconciliation, correction, and anti-fabrication.

options.text: Require both totals non-null and retry until they match.
options.explanation: Requiring non-null totals on incomplete scans forces the model to invent numbers until two fabricated values happen to agree, which is precisely the retry-fabrication cascade the requirements forbid.

options.text: Extract totals as free text and validate only after regex parsing.
options.explanation: Free-text totals forfeit structured-output conformance and make the reconciliation comparison dependent on brittle regex parsing instead of typed fields. It undermines both the schema and validation requirements.

questions.scenario: A financial-statement pipeline needs conformant output, reconciliation checks, corrective retries, and protection against invented values from incomplete scans.
questions.explanation:
The design needs structured values that can be absent when the scan lacks evidence, a deterministic comparison of stated and calculated totals, and retries that contain the exact validation error. Retrying cannot recover a fact absent from the source, so the retry path must stop at that boundary instead of requiring non-null totals until the system fabricates them.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 4.4 Implementing Validation, Retries, and Feedback Loops for Extraction Quality.

questions.prompt: Which fix most directly uses this evidence?

options.text: Increase retries and instruct broader whole-document search each time.
options.explanation: Generic 'search harder' retries do not teach the model where signature dates actually appear, so the footer blind spot persists. Telemetry already pinpointed the specific layout, which a focused example set addresses directly.

options.text: Add contrastive footer examples and keep tracking the pattern rate.
options.explanation: Telemetry pinpoints the footer blind spot, so contrastive footer examples directly attack the dominant pattern and continued tracking verifies the fix. Generic retries or disabling the check waste the evidence.

options.text: Disable signature-date checks due to the high false-positive rate.
options.explanation: Disabling the check discards the true missing-signature findings it also produces, eliminating bug detection to escape noise. The false positives stem from a fixable example gap, not a broken check.

options.text: Require a signature_location field and treat any value as proof.
options.explanation: Treating any stated location as proof invites the model to satisfy the schema with a convenient value, converting false negatives into unfounded confirmations. It does not teach the footer distinction the examples must supply.

questions.scenario: Telemetry shows most false missing-signature findings occur when the date sits in a footer. Examples show headers only.
questions.explanation:
The evidence identifies a specific layout blind spot, so the prompt should gain targeted contrastive examples for footer placement rather than a generic retry loop. Keeping the observed pattern rate provides the feedback signal for judging whether that focused change reduces the false-positive category.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 4.2 Using Few-shot Prompting to Improve Output Consistency and 4.4 Implementing Validation, Retries, and Feedback Loops for Extraction Quality.

questions.prompt: What sequencing is architecturally sound?

options.text: Submit all documents immediately and improve the prompt for later clients.
options.explanation: Submitting everything immediately bakes unvalidated prompt errors into output that must still meet the four-hour SLA, so early clients receive defective results and there is no chance to correct course in time.

options.text: Process everything synchronously as the only deadline-compatible mode.
options.explanation: Treating synchronous as the only mode discards batch economics for the window-tolerant portion of the workload, and it still submits results from a prompt that has never been validated on a sample.

options.text: Validate on a representative sample, then route SLA work off batch.
options.explanation: Validating on a sample first avoids baking prompt errors into bulk output, then SLA-capable paths serve urgent clients while batch handles only window-tolerant work. Either-path splitting still violates the deadline for half the clients.

options.text: Split each client evenly between synchronous and batch processing.
options.explanation: Splitting evenly guarantees that half of every client's documents ride a path with no latency guarantee, arbitrarily violating the four-hour SLA regardless of urgency. Routing should follow deadline tolerance, not a fixed ratio.

questions.scenario: A large workload faces a four-hour client SLA while batch offers no latency guarantee. The prompt is not yet validated.
questions.explanation:
Message Batches offers no latency guarantee and is intended for non-blocking workloads, so it cannot be the path for a four-hour client SLA. The prompt should first be iterated on a representative sample; after validation, route SLA-bound work through a non-batch path.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 4.5 Designing Efficient Batch Processing Strategies.

questions.prompt: What is the best replacement?

options.text: Submit every survey twice and accept only matching fields.
options.explanation: Double submission doubles cost across the batch, and agreement between two runs shows consistency, not semantic correctness — both can share the same misreading. It is a poor substitute for a real verification pass.

options.text: Request extraction plus free-text verification together, parsed in code.
options.explanation: Self-verification inside the same single-turn request is just generation with extra text; the model cannot meaningfully challenge its own fresh extraction. Parsing free-text verification in code adds fragility without independent review.

options.text: Move the workload to synchronous calls to keep the two-turn interaction.
options.explanation: Moving everything synchronous abandons batch cost savings for the whole workload to preserve one interaction pattern. The verification turn can be replaced by post-hoc validation plus sampled independent review instead.

options.text: Use one structured extraction per item with validation plus sampled independent review.
options.explanation: Single structured extraction with programmatic validation fits the single-turn constraint; a risk-based independent review sample replaces the lost verification turn. Double-submission doubles cost without guaranteeing correctness.

questions.scenario: A survey extractor relied on two-turn self-verification. Batch requests are single-turn, so that interaction cannot run per request.
questions.explanation:
A single batch request cannot preserve a two-turn self-verification interaction. Use one structured extraction per item, validate deterministically after processing, and apply sampled independent review for quality evidence; JSON schema conformance alone is not a semantic review.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 4.3 Enforcing Structured Output with tool_use and JSON Schemas and 4.5 Designing Efficient Batch Processing Strategies.

questions.prompt: How should the multi-pass workflow be implemented?

options.text: Run extraction as one batch, then an independent review batch with source plus extraction.
options.explanation: Chained batches keep each pass single-turn while the review batch sees both source and extraction for genuine independence. Schema success or self-critique in one request is not independent review.

options.text: Validate extraction JSON locally and treat schema success as review.
options.explanation: Schema validation proves structure only; a well-formed extraction can still misclassify risk or omit fields. Treating conformance as review removes the independent quality check the workflow requires.

options.text: Extract, classify, and self-critique inside a single batch request.
options.explanation: A single batch request cannot host a multi-turn self-critique loop, and self-critique is not independent review — the same context that produced the extraction judges it. The requirement of independence is unmet.

options.text: Run extraction synchronously and only the review in batch.
options.explanation: The scenario requires all processing in single-turn batch requests, so running extraction synchronously violates the constraint outright rather than adapting the workflow to it.

questions.scenario: Loan applications need extraction, risk classification, and independent extraction review. All processing must use single-turn batch requests.
questions.explanation:
Batch requests are self-contained and do not support a multi-turn review loop within one request. Run extraction first, then send the source material and extraction result to a separate independent review batch; schema validation alone proves structure, not extraction correctness.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 4.5 Designing Efficient Batch Processing Strategies and 4.6 Designing Multi-instance and Multi-pass Review Architectures.

questions.prompt: Select each change that preserves cross-file coverage while reducing noise.

options.text: Define cross-file evidence thresholds with supporting examples.
options.explanation: Explicit evidence thresholds plus examples calibrate the cross-file pass, the shared severity rubric aligns it with local passes, and pausing only persistently noisy subcategories preserves coverage.

options.text: Reuse the proven severity rubric from per-file passes.
options.explanation: Explicit evidence thresholds plus examples calibrate the cross-file pass, the shared severity rubric aligns it with local passes, and pausing only persistently noisy subcategories preserves coverage.

options.text: Pause only persistently noisy subcategories, keeping the rest.
options.explanation: Explicit evidence thresholds plus examples calibrate the cross-file pass, the shared severity rubric aligns it with local passes, and pausing only persistently noisy subcategories preserves coverage.

options.text: Remove cross-file review and rely on local passes alone.
options.explanation: Removing cross-file review eliminates the only pass that can see unsafe value flows and cross-module bugs — exactly the coverage the architecture exists to provide. Local passes are structurally blind to those issues.

options.text: Merge local and integration review into one large pass.
options.explanation: Merging re-creates the vague, overloaded context that produced the false positives and forfeits the focused criteria that make the per-file passes perform well. It also enlarges each context toward lost-in-the-middle failure.

questions.scenario: A cross-file review pass has high false positives from a vague instruction. Per-file passes with explicit severity criteria perform well.
questions.explanation:
Keep the integration pass because it supplies cross-file coverage, but repair its vague instruction with explicit evidence thresholds, supporting examples, and the proven severity rubric. If a category remains noisy, pause that category rather than discarding all cross-file review.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 4.1 Designing Prompts with Explicit Criteria to Improve Accuracy and 4.6 Designing Multi-instance and Multi-pass Review Architectures.

questions.prompt: Select each fix needed for the blind spot and confidence miscalibration.

options.text: Add error-path criteria with contrastive examples.
options.explanation: Error-path criteria plus contrastive examples fix the blind spot, and calibrating routing scores on labeled failures fixes overconfidence. A new reviewer or human routing without those changes preserves the problem.

options.text: Calibrate routing scores against labeled code with known failures.
options.explanation: Error-path criteria plus contrastive examples fix the blind spot, and calibrating routing scores on labeled failures fixes overconfidence. A new reviewer or human routing without those changes preserves the problem.

options.text: Create a dedicated error-path reviewer using its own self-confidence.
options.explanation: A dedicated reviewer addresses the missing category but reuses self-rated confidence, which the scenario shows is miscalibrated on exactly these reviews. Routing would trust an unvalidated confidence signal.

options.text: Route high-confidence error-handling reviews to humans with prompts unchanged.
options.explanation: Because the reviewer reports high confidence on both correct and incorrect reviews, confidence-based routing sends a mix of sound and defective reviews to humans and leaves the blind spot in the automated path untouched.

options.text: Let the generation instance review error paths from its own context.
options.explanation: Self-review by the generation instance is less likely to challenge its own reasoning, and it does nothing about the miscalibrated confidence that must drive routing. It reproduces both defects in a weaker form.

questions.scenario: An independent reviewer misses error-handling bugs and reports high confidence on both correct and incorrect reviews there.
questions.explanation:
The reviewer needs explicit error-path criteria and contrastive examples to address the missing category. Its confidence must also be calibrated against labeled examples with known failures before it drives routing; self-rated confidence alone does not establish that the score reflects review accuracy.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 4.1 Designing Prompts with Explicit Criteria to Improve Accuracy and 4.6 Designing Multi-instance and Multi-pass Review Architectures.

questions.prompt: Which design best mitigates lost-in-the-middle effects?

options.text: Add more three-file examples and keep one integration prompt with all findings.
options.explanation: More small-file examples do not change the oversized integration prompt, so the mid-context findings remain buried where attention weakens. The lost-in-the-middle exposure is untouched.

options.text: Move the highest-severity findings to the middle of the context.
options.explanation: The middle of a long context is precisely where attention is weakest, so placing the highest-severity findings there maximizes the chance they are missed. Key evidence belongs at the foreground, not the middle.

options.text: Add identical summaries at both ends while keeping every raw finding.
options.explanation: Duplicating summaries at the ends does not shrink the oversized context, and the raw mid-context evidence still competes for attention across hundreds of findings. The structural problem remains.

options.text: Cluster findings by dependency into bounded passes with foregrounded evidence.
options.explanation: Dependency clustering with bounded passes keeps each context small and places key evidence prominently, directly countering lost-in-the-middle. More small examples or duplicated summaries keep the oversized prompt.

questions.scenario: An integration pass over findings from very many files misses mid-context evidence. Examples cover only tiny cases.
questions.explanation:
A single, oversized integration prompt is exposed to lost-in-the-middle effects. Grouping related findings into bounded passes limits context pressure, and foregrounding the decisive evidence follows the guidance to place key findings at the beginning under explicit headings.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 5.1 Managing Conversation Context to Preserve Critical Information.

snapshot.title: Advanced Exam: Context Management & Reliability (Rebalanced)

questions.prompt: Select the 2 changes that together prevent value merging and provenance loss.

options.text: Preserve separate claim records with value, source, and quote.
options.explanation: Separate records stop value merging; carrying attribution through aggregation preserves provenance.

options.text: Carry source-date attribution through aggregation to synthesis.
options.explanation: Separate records stop value merging; carrying attribution through aggregation preserves provenance.

options.text: Use a source-free facts block to simplify synthesis, losing traceability.
options.explanation: A source-free facts block discards the source links, so provenance is lost exactly as in the scenario and disputed figures can no longer be traced or annotated.

options.text: Reconstruct sources after drafting by re-searching, delaying verification.
options.explanation: Re-searching sources after drafting leaves claims unattributed while they are written and delays verification until the merged values are already in the report.

questions.scenario: A coordinator merges subagent findings, blending disputed figures and dropping source links.
questions.explanation:
Attribution is lost during summarization unless "claim → source" mappings are preserved, and conflicting figures must be annotated rather than blended. Each claim record keeps value, source, and quote, and source-date attribution carries through aggregation into synthesis so temporal differences are not misread as contradictions.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 5.6 Preserving Provenance and Handling Uncertainty in Multi-source Synthesis.

questions.prompt: Which redesign most directly breaks the failure cascade?

options.text: Retry locally and note a gap only on failure, risking silent loss.
options.explanation: Retrying locally and noting the gap only after another failure leaves the coordinator unaware during the failure window, so the drift toward generic claims continues unchecked.

options.text: Propagate typed error with partials, mark gap, persist cited findings.
options.explanation: Typed errors with partials make the gap visible and stop drift toward generic claims.

options.text: Reduce worker count for visibility, cutting parallel coverage.
options.explanation: Reducing worker count does not surface the failed domain; it merely shrinks coverage while the gap stays hidden.

options.text: Abort the workflow on any failure, sacrificing partial progress.
options.explanation: Aborting the whole workflow throws away the cited findings that did succeed and still never marks the gap for the coordinator.

questions.scenario: A worker times out on a critical domain; the coordinator hides the gap and drifts to generic claims.
questions.explanation:
Silent suppression and whole-workflow abort are both anti-patterns. The worker should propagate a typed error with its partial results so the coordinator can mark the gap, persist the cited findings that did succeed, and re-route or annotate coverage; hiding the gap is what allowed the drift into generic claims.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 5.3 Implementing Error Propagation Strategies in Multi-agent Systems.

questions.prompt: Which intervention addresses both masked performance and poor error propagation?

options.text: Lower the global threshold, increasing false passes.
options.explanation: Lowering the global threshold loosens passing everywhere and increases false passes without revealing why the one field underperforms.

options.text: Retrain only the weak field, leaving miscalibration in place.
options.explanation: Retraining only the weak field leaves confidence miscalibrated and error statuses detail-free, so both root causes persist.

options.text: Calibrate by field and type; return typed field-level errors.
options.explanation: Field-level calibration plus typed errors exposes the weak field and routes correctly.

options.text: Collapse failures into one status, hiding field-level causes.
options.explanation: Collapsing failures into a single status erases the field-level cause the coordinator needs to route and recover.

questions.scenario: A pipeline shows strong overall accuracy, but one field performs poorly and errors lack detail.
questions.explanation:
Aggregate metrics mask poor performance on specific fields, so accuracy must be analyzed and calibrated by field and document type using labeled validation sets. Errors should carry typed field-level context, because a collapsed status hides the cause the coordinator needs for recovery.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 5.5 Designing Workflows with Human Oversight and Confidence Calibration and 5.3 Implementing Error Propagation Strategies in Multi-agent Systems.

questions.prompt: Which design preserves verification data and supports the right escalation?

options.text: Resend full transcript each turn, inflating context cost.
options.explanation: Resending the full transcript each turn preserves detail only by inflating context cost, and exact values can still be lost in the noise.

options.text: Ask the customer to restate details, shifting burden to them.
options.explanation: Shifting the burden of restating details onto the customer is poor escalation practice and does nothing to surface the buried fraud alert.

options.text: Estimate missing values as uncertain, risking hallucinated facts.
options.explanation: Estimating missing values risks fabricating facts; unverifiable details should be escalated rather than guessed.

options.text: Persist exact facts, project alert fields, escalate if unverifiable.
options.explanation: Persisted facts plus projected alerts preserve verification and trigger correct escalation.

questions.scenario: A long support session summarizes a transfer vaguely while a fraud alert stays buried in tool output.
questions.explanation:
Progressive summarization condenses exact values into vague prose, so transactional facts belong in a persistent facts block outside the summarized history. Alert fields should be projected forward, and if a fact cannot be verified it should be escalated rather than estimated, since estimating risks hallucinated facts.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 5.1 Managing Conversation Context to Preserve Critical Information and 5.2 Designing Effective Escalation Patterns and Resolving Ambiguity.

questions.prompt: Select the 2 practices that together prevent evidence loss and hypothesis drift.

options.text: Record cited findings with quotes as discovered.
options.explanation: Logging evidence as found and consulting it before hypothesizing prevents drift.

options.text: Consult the log before hypotheses; summarize before phase changes.
options.explanation: Logging evidence as found and consulting it before hypothesizing prevents drift.

options.text: Compact often and treat summaries as evidence, losing early detail.
options.explanation: Treating compaction summaries as evidence loses the early quoted detail, which is exactly the mechanism that erased the file evidence.

options.text: Narrow to the familiar pattern, biasing the diagnosis.
options.explanation: Narrowing to the familiar pattern substitutes bias for the recorded evidence, producing the generic-hypothesis drift.

questions.scenario: During a long investigation the agent forgets early file evidence and substitutes a generic hypothesis.
questions.explanation:
Scratchpad files preserve key findings across context boundaries, so record cited findings with quotes as discovered and consult the log before forming hypotheses; summarize before phase changes so the next phase starts from evidence rather than a degraded summary. Treating compaction summaries as evidence or narrowing to a familiar pattern causes exactly the drift described.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 5.4 Managing Context Efficiently When Investigating Large Codebases.

questions.prompt: Phase-gate decision: how should the synthesis handle the figures?

options.text: Average close values as confirmation, overstating confidence.
options.explanation: Averaging figures from different years and methods treats them as independent confirmations and overstates confidence in a false consensus.

options.text: Preserve dates and methods; phase-gate the divergent estimate.
options.explanation: Preserving dates/methods blocks false averaging; phase-gate review handles the divergent estimate.

options.text: Publish the modal value on aggregate accuracy, hiding method gaps.
options.explanation: Publishing the modal value hides the date and method divergence and presents unverified agreement as a settled result.

options.text: Drop the lowest figure and report consensus, biasing the result.
options.explanation: Dropping the lowest figure manufactures consensus and biases the reported estimate away from the recorded evidence.

questions.scenario: Workers report similar revenue figures from different years and methods; the coordinator averages them with high confidence.
questions.explanation:
Similar figures from different years and methods are not independent confirmations; averaging them overstates confidence. Preserve dates and methods with each value, annotate the divergence, and pass it to a phase gate for reconciliation rather than publishing a consensus that hides the method gap.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 5.6 Preserving Provenance and Handling Uncertainty in Multi-source Synthesis.

questions.prompt: Which interface design prevents the false definitive claim?

options.text: Treat every empty as missing and forbid absence claims, losing valid empties.
options.explanation: Treating every empty result as missing forbids legitimate valid-empty answers and still cannot distinguish an outage from genuine absence.

options.text: Repeat every empty query via another worker, doubling outage load.
options.explanation: Duplicating every empty query doubles load during an outage and provides no systematic distinction between failure and absence.

options.text: Return access-failure vs valid-empty with source, date, coverage.
options.explanation: Distinct statuses with metadata stop the coordinator from reading outage as absence.

options.text: Suppress empty results, blinding the coordinator to coverage.
options.explanation: Suppressing empty results blinds the coordinator to coverage and prevents any distinction between outage and valid emptiness.

questions.scenario: A registry outage returns as empty success, so the coordinator claims a supplier has no certifications.
questions.explanation:
An outage must be distinguished from a valid empty result, or absence gets claimed as fact. The tool interface should return access-failure versus valid-empty explicitly, with source, date, and coverage so the coordinator knows what was actually searched and never asserts a definitive no-certifications claim from a failed lookup.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 5.3 Implementing Error Propagation Strategies in Multi-agent Systems.

questions.prompt: Select the 2 changes that fix placement, confidence, and error transparency.

options.text: Sort by self-reported confidence, rewarding overconfidence.
options.explanation: Sorting by self-reported confidence rewards the overconfidence already shown by this finding type and does nothing about mid-report burial.

options.text: Front-load critical findings; surface type-level miss rates.
options.explanation: Placement plus type-calibrated confidence and typed errors fixes burial and overconfidence.

options.text: Calibrate by finding type; attach typed error metadata.
options.explanation: Placement plus type-calibrated confidence and typed errors fixes burial and overconfidence.

options.text: Add reviewer time without reordering, keeping burial risk.
options.explanation: Adding reviewer time leaves the finding buried mid-report, so lost-in-the-middle loss and hidden miss rates persist.

questions.scenario: A critical finding sits mid-report; self-confidence is high but the type has a poor miss rate.
questions.explanation:
Key findings should be front-loaded at the beginning of aggregated data under explicit headings, since mid-report placement invites lost-in-the-middle loss. Self-rated confidence is an unreliable proxy, so calibrate by finding type using labeled data and attach typed error metadata so miss rates are visible rather than hidden behind high self-confidence.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 5.1 Managing Conversation Context to Preserve Critical Information and 5.5 Designing Workflows with Human Oversight and Confidence Calibration.

questions.prompt: Which design enables clean recovery?

options.text: Persist outputs, coverage, errors, and next steps as structured state.
options.explanation: Structured persistence of outputs, coverage, errors, and next steps enables clean resume.

options.text: Rely on session resume alone, risking lost intermediates.
options.explanation: Session resume alone restores conversation but not structured intermediates, so outputs, coverage, and the partial result can still be lost.

options.text: Restart all workers after crash, discarding partial progress.
options.explanation: Restarting all workers discards the completed outputs and the partial result that crash recovery is meant to preserve.

options.text: Avoid delegation to keep one context, losing parallel scale.
options.explanation: Avoiding delegation forfeits parallel scale and does not address crash recovery at all.

questions.scenario: A main agent crashes after workers finish, including one partial result from a transient timeout.
questions.explanation:
Structured state persistence enables crash recovery: outputs, coverage, typed errors, and next steps are stored so a restarted coordinator resumes from the partial result instead of discarding it. Session resume alone or a full worker restart loses intermediates and partial progress.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 5.4 Managing Context Efficiently When Investigating Large Codebases and 5.3 Implementing Error Propagation Strategies in Multi-agent Systems.

questions.prompt: Phase-gate decision: what should the coordinator do with the conflict?

options.text: Prefer the government source by authority, ignoring recency risk.
options.explanation: Preferring the government source by authority ignores the recency problem the coordinator could not resolve and risks reporting a stale owner.

options.text: Preserve both dated claims, mark conflict, phase-gate reconciliation.
options.explanation: Preserving both dated claims with conflict marked avoids false resolution and enables reconciliation.

options.text: Replace both with a source-free contested note, losing provenance.
options.explanation: A source-free contested note discards the provenance of both dated claims, making later reconciliation impossible.

options.text: Discard the press release as unofficial, risking staleness.
options.explanation: Discarding the press release as unofficial risks keeping the stale claim if it is in fact the more recent one.

questions.scenario: Two credible sources disagree on current patent ownership and the coordinator cannot resolve recency.
questions.explanation:
Conflicting values are preserved with annotations and passed to the coordinator for reconciliation rather than arbitrarily choosing one. Both dated claims stay in the report, the conflict is marked, and reconciliation is phase-gated; authority preference or discarding a source risks staleness and loses provenance.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 5.6 Preserving Provenance and Handling Uncertainty in Multi-source Synthesis.

questions.prompt: Which feedback-loop redesign is most appropriate?

options.text: Grow the uniform audit sample, diluting the rare-type signal.
options.explanation: Growing the uniform audit sample dilutes the rare-type failures that already vanish in aggregate accuracy.

options.text: Lower the global review threshold, flooding reviewers with noise.
options.explanation: Lowering the global review threshold floods reviewers with noise from well-performing types while still missing overconfident rare-type failures.

options.text: Oversample new types, calibrate per field, emit typed errors.
options.explanation: Targeted oversampling with per-type calibration and typed errors exposes the rare-type pattern.

options.text: Trust aggregate accuracy and review only low confidence, missing overconfidence.
options.explanation: Trusting aggregate accuracy and low confidence alone misses overconfident failures on the rare type entirely.

questions.scenario: A rare document type shows high self-confidence but poor field accuracy; uniform audits miss it.
questions.explanation:
Aggregate accuracy masks rare-type failure, so feedback must be stratified: oversample the new document type, calibrate confidence per field using labeled validation sets, and emit typed errors. Uniform audits and global thresholds dilute or flood the signal; trusting aggregate accuracy misses overconfident failures entirely.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 5.5 Designing Workflows with Human Oversight and Confidence Calibration.

questions.prompt: Select the 2 changes that best address the failure.

options.text: Delete old turns at the limit, risking cited-evidence loss.
options.explanation: Deleting old turns at the limit risks discarding cited stack-trace evidence instead of cutting the irrelevant tool noise.

options.text: Project required tool fields; drop irrelevant payload.
options.explanation: Field projection cuts noise; persisted cited findings with front-loading keeps traces in attention.

options.text: Persist cited findings; front-load key evidence in aggregates.
options.explanation: Field projection cuts noise; persisted cited findings with front-loading keeps traces in attention.

options.text: Compress every result to one sentence, stripping traceability.
options.explanation: Compressing every result to one sentence destroys traceability and quotes, which is the loss the design must prevent.

questions.scenario: A debugging tool floods context with irrelevant fields, pushing stack-trace evidence out of attention.
questions.explanation:
Tool outputs accumulate disproportionately to relevance, so project only the required fields and drop the irrelevant payload instead of deleting old turns, which risks losing cited evidence. Persist cited findings and front-load key evidence in aggregates so the stack-trace evidence stays in attention.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 5.1 Managing Conversation Context to Preserve Critical Information.

questions.prompt: Select the 2 changes that fix diagnosis, calibration, and escalation.

options.text: Define explicit policy-gap escalation triggers.
options.explanation: Explicit gap triggers plus calibrated confidence and external identifier persistence prevents miscalibrated denial.

options.text: Calibrate relevant confidence; persist identifiers outside summaries.
options.explanation: Explicit gap triggers plus calibrated confidence and external identifier persistence prevents miscalibrated denial.

options.text: Accept denial on high self-confidence, risking miscalibrated refusal.
options.explanation: Accepting the denial on high self-confidence perpetuates the miscalibration, since self-rating is an unreliable proxy for this case type.

options.text: Restore identifiers only, leaving escalation and calibration vague.
options.explanation: Restoring identifiers alone leaves escalation triggers vague and confidence miscalibrated, so the denial pattern repeats.

questions.scenario: An agent denies an ambiguous claim on high self-confidence; escalation is vague and identifiers were summarized away.
questions.explanation:
Self-confidence is an unreliable proxy for case complexity, so calibrate confidence on the relevant segment and escalate on explicit policy-gap triggers rather than trusting a high self-rating. Persist identifiers outside summaries, because summarization dropping them is what made escalation vague and unverifiable.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 5.2 Designing Effective Escalation Patterns and Resolving Ambiguity and 5.1 Managing Conversation Context to Preserve Critical Information.

questions.prompt: Which redesign preserves coverage and failure distinctions?

options.text: Weight successes higher, burying timeout and denial signals.
options.explanation: Weighting successes higher buries the timeout and denial signals, which carry different recovery decisions than success.

options.text: Retain per-supplier typed errors, partials, and coverage status.
options.explanation: Per-supplier typed errors with coverage status preserves distinctions the collapsed note destroys.

options.text: Abort on multiple non-evidence results, discarding usable signal.
options.explanation: Aborting on multiple non-evidence results discards usable partials and coverage information the synthesis needs.

options.text: Retry all failures to success, masking permission and empty cases.
options.explanation: Retrying all failures until success masks permission denials and valid empties, which are terminal states, not retryable ones.

questions.scenario: Supplier workers return mixed success, timeout, denial, and valid-empty; the coordinator collapses them into one note.
questions.explanation:
Success, timeout, denial, and valid-empty carry different recovery decisions, so collapsing them into one note destroys the distinctions the coordinator needs. Retain per-supplier typed errors, partial results, and coverage status so synthesis can annotate what is well-supported and where gaps remain.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 5.3 Implementing Error Propagation Strategies in Multi-agent Systems.

questions.prompt: Phase-gate decision: what should happen next, and what was missing?

options.text: Keep compacting until answers stabilize, deepening evidence loss.
options.explanation: Continuing to compact deepens the summarization loss, since the exact mutex evidence is already gone from the summaries.

options.text: Fork the degraded session and pick the nicer branch, hiding conflict.
options.explanation: Forking the degraded session and picking the nicer branch hides the contradiction instead of resolving it and restores no evidence.

options.text: Escalate; enforce cited scratchpad before future phase changes.
options.explanation: Once summaries destroy mutex evidence, continued compaction compounds drift; escalate and enforce scratchpad discipline.

options.text: Keep only the current conclusion, discarding contradicting findings.
options.explanation: Keeping only the current conclusion discards the contradicting findings, entrenching the drift instead of escalating it.

questions.scenario: Progressive summaries lose exact mutex evidence, producing contradictory answers and generic claims.
questions.explanation:
Progressive summarization has already condensed exact mutex evidence into vague claims, so continuing to compact deepens the loss. Escalate the contradiction and enforce a cited scratchpad (findings with quotes recorded as discovered) before future phase changes, so evidence survives context boundaries.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 5.4 Managing Context Efficiently When Investigating Large Codebases and 5.2 Designing Effective Escalation Patterns and Resolving Ambiguity.

questions.prompt: Which architecture prevents both failures?

options.text: Rebuild provenance only on auditor request, delaying detection.
options.explanation: Rebuilding provenance only on auditor request delays detection and cannot recover source links that were never captured.

options.text: Include only successes, hiding error records from the report.
options.explanation: Including only successes is precisely what hides the transient error, leaving the report's coverage overstated.

options.text: Merge prose without source fields, trading readability for loss.
options.explanation: Merging prose without source fields is the root cause of provenance loss and trades auditability for readability.

options.text: Preserve claim-source records; type failed work as coverage gaps.
options.explanation: Claim-source records plus typed attributed gaps prevent silent omission and enable audit.

questions.scenario: A coordinator merges clause-worker prose; provenance vanishes and a transient error is silently omitted.
questions.explanation:
Merging prose without source fields is what destroys provenance, and including only successes is what hides the transient failure. Preserve claim-source records through aggregation and type failed work as coverage gaps, so the report shows both what is supported and what is missing.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 5.6 Preserving Provenance and Handling Uncertainty in Multi-source Synthesis and 5.3 Implementing Error Propagation Strategies in Multi-agent Systems.

questions.prompt: Which redesign fixes routing, transparency, and attention placement?

options.text: Attach per-field source and confidence; route on risk; surface first.
options.explanation: Per-field source and calibration with risky-field routing and surfacing fixes aggregate masking.

options.text: Keep aggregate routing on high overall confidence, masking the weak field.
options.explanation: Routing on high aggregate confidence masks the one unreliable notional field, so the risky field never reaches review.

options.text: Repass middle pages of every doc, adding cost without attribution.
options.explanation: Repassing the middle pages of every document adds cost without attaching attribution to the weak field.

options.text: Lower the aggregate threshold uniformly, inflating false passes.
options.explanation: Lowering the aggregate threshold uniformly inflates false passes everywhere while leaving the field unattributed and buried.

questions.scenario: A contract shows high aggregate confidence, but one ambiguous notional field is unreliable and unattributed.
questions.explanation:
Aggregate confidence masks the weak notional field, so attach per-field source and confidence, route on risk (low-confidence or ambiguous-source fields go to review), and surface the unreliable field first rather than burying it mid-report. Uniform threshold changes mask rather than fix field-level weakness.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 5.5 Designing Workflows with Human Oversight and Confidence Calibration and 5.1 Managing Conversation Context to Preserve Critical Information.

questions.prompt: Select the 2 behaviors for the tool, agent, and context layer.

options.text: Return the first match directly, risking wrong-transaction action.
options.explanation: Returning the first match invites acting on the wrong transaction, which is exactly the guessing the scenario must stop.

options.text: Return candidate details with typed status; request identifier.
options.explanation: Detailed candidates with typed status plus persisted exact facts enable safe disambiguation.

options.text: Persist exact amount-timestamp facts outside compressed prose.
options.explanation: Detailed candidates with typed status plus persisted exact facts enable safe disambiguation.

options.text: Escalate every multi-match, overloading reviewers with safe cases.
options.explanation: Escalating every multi-match overwhelms reviewers with cases that typed candidate details could resolve safely without human effort.

questions.scenario: A transaction query returns bare matches; compressed prose lost amount facts, so the agent guesses the newest.
questions.explanation:
Multiple matches require asking for additional identifiers, not heuristic guessing, so the tool should return candidate details with typed status and request the identifier. At the context layer, exact amount-timestamp facts belong in a persistent facts block outside compressed prose, because progressive summarization is what lost them.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 5.2 Designing Effective Escalation Patterns and Resolving Ambiguity and 5.1 Managing Conversation Context to Preserve Critical Information.

questions.prompt: Select the 2 practices that make the diagram verifiable and expose the timeout.

options.text: Require file-line mappings for every architectural claim.
options.explanation: File-line mappings plus typed timeout records with gaps make the diagram auditable.

options.text: Record typed timeouts with coverage gaps in a cited scratchpad.
options.explanation: File-line mappings plus typed timeout records with gaps make the diagram auditable.

options.text: Permit typical-structure inference, hiding the timeout.
options.explanation: Permitting typical-structure inference hides the timed-out module, presenting an unverified guess as part of the architecture.

options.text: Retry timed-out workers indefinitely, blocking all output.
options.explanation: Retrying timed-out workers indefinitely blocks all output instead of recording the typed timeout with its coverage gap.

questions.scenario: Module workers produce a diagram from prose; one timed-out module is inferred and no claim has file evidence.
questions.explanation:
Claims become verifiable when every architectural claim carries a file-line mapping to its evidence. Typed timeouts with coverage gaps belong in a cited scratchpad so the inferred module is exposed as unverified; permitting typical-structure inference hides the timeout, and indefinite retry blocks all output.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 5.4 Managing Context Efficiently When Investigating Large Codebases and 5.3 Implementing Error Propagation Strategies in Multi-agent Systems.

questions.prompt: Which redesign addresses masked accuracy, calibration, and opaque errors?

options.text: Lower the global review threshold, flooding reviewers with noise.
options.explanation: Lowering the global review threshold floods reviewers with well-performing approvals while still missing overconfident rare rejections.

options.text: Send all decisions to permanent manual review, unsustainable cost.
options.explanation: Sending all decisions to permanent manual review is unsustainable and does not fix the miscalibration or opaque errors.

options.text: Retrain only on rejections keeping routing, leaving calibration broken.
options.explanation: Retraining only on rejections leaves routing, confidence calibration, and opaque error statuses untouched.

options.text: Oversample rejections, calibrate segment, route by risk, emit field errors.
options.explanation: Oversampling the rare segment with calibration, risk routing, and field errors fixes masking and opacity.

questions.scenario: A loan system reports excellent overall accuracy, but rare rejections are inaccurate and overconfident with opaque errors.
questions.explanation:
Aggregate accuracy masks rare-segment failure, so oversample the rejection segment and calibrate confidence for it using labeled data. Route by risk so overconfident rejections reach review, and emit typed field-level errors instead of opaque statuses; retraining alone leaves the calibration and error transparency broken.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 5.5 Designing Workflows with Human Oversight and Confidence Calibration and 5.3 Implementing Error Propagation Strategies in Multi-agent Systems.

snapshot.title: CCAR-P Advanced: Solution Design & Architecture v1

questions.prompt: Which architecture best meets cost, accuracy, and date together?

options.text: Rules workflow triaging cases, LLM drafting customer rationales
options.explanation: Drafting rationales addresses communication, not the manual triage effort itself, so it leaves the cost-cut goal largely unmet even though refunds stay safe.

options.text: Autonomous agent negotiating refunds directly with customers
options.explanation: Giving an agent direct negotiating authority over refunds expands the model's decision surface with no deterministic guard, putting the no-rise-in-wrong-refunds constraint at risk.

options.text: Deterministic workflow routing refunds, LLM extracting reasons only
options.explanation: Deterministic routing holds the wrong-refund rate while LLM extraction cuts handling time; full agent autonomy trades accuracy for speed under a fixed date.

options.text: Fine-tuned model replacing policy engine for refund decisions
options.explanation: Letting a fine-tuned model decide refunds removes the deterministic policy engine and its step-level guards, making the wrong-refund rate a learned property rather than an enforced rule.

questions.scenario: A retailer bleeds margin on manual returns triage. Leadership demands 30% cost cut in eight weeks without raising wrong refunds.
questions.explanation: The decisive constraint is that refund routing and policy enforcement must remain repeatable while manual effort falls. A fixed workflow can route each case through deterministic policy checks and use the LLM only for reason extraction, where it does not decide the refund. An autonomous negotiator or a model replacing the policy engine expands the model's decision surface and removes step-level deterministic guards; drafting rationales does not control the refund decision itself. Source: Claude Platform & Solution Design, Key takeaways.

questions.prompt: Which processing design fits the latency and accuracy conflict?

options.text: Augmented LLM filling templates with verified numeric fields
options.explanation: Templated generation with numeric verification meets the 2s budget and protects figures; open-ended agency improves prose at the cost of latency and errors.

options.text: Agentic researcher browsing history before writing summaries
options.explanation: Open-ended browsing before each summary blows the two-second budget, and it improves narrative color rather than the numeric accuracy that actually matters.

options.text: Multi-agent critics debating summary wording before delivery
options.explanation: Debate rounds multiply model calls and latency past the limit, and they polish wording while leaving precise numerical claims unverified.

options.text: Long-context model summarizing raw feeds without validation rules
options.explanation: Summarizing raw feeds with no validation leaves the numbers to non-deterministic generation, so a confident but wrong figure can reach a trading desk undetected.

questions.scenario: A trading ops desk needs incident summaries under two seconds. Numeric accuracy matters more than narrative fluency.
questions.explanation: Numeric correctness is the binding constraint, so verified fields must come from deterministic computation or tool execution rather than the model's fluent generation. An augmented LLM can place those verified values into a short template, preserving the two-second budget. Open-ended research, multi-agent debate, and unvalidated long-context summarization add latency and still leave precise numerical claims to a non-deterministic model. Source: Claude Platform & Solution Design, The four properties and their design consequences.

questions.prompt: Which pattern best fits regulated deterministic underwriting?

options.text: Autonomous planner choosing verification order per loan application
options.explanation: A planner-chosen verification order makes each loan's trajectory model-dependent, undermining the repeatable sequence and audit trail the regulation requires.

options.text: Supervisor agents negotiating credit decisions through open debate
options.explanation: Open debate produces trajectories that vary per decision and are hard to audit step by step, which is unacceptable for legally sensitive, rare exceptions.

options.text: Single agent calling tools until it feels confident enough
options.explanation: A confidence-based stopping rule is opaque and unbounded, so neither the number of steps nor their order can be reproduced for an auditor.

options.text: Fixed workflow sequencing checks, LLM extracting fields only
options.explanation: Fixed underwriting steps with audit needs favor deterministic workflow plus LLM extraction; an autonomous planner adds variance where compliance demands repeatability.

questions.scenario: Loan underwriting follows fixed verification steps with audit trails. Exceptions are rare but legally sensitive.
questions.explanation: The fixed verification sequence and legally sensitive exceptions make predictable, observable execution more important than runtime autonomy. A workflow keeps deterministic guards between steps for the checks and audit trail, while the LLM is limited to extracting fields. Planners, debating supervisors, and confidence-driven single agents make the trajectory model-chosen, which raises the error and observability burden without serving the repeatable process. Source: Claude Platform & Solution Design, Key takeaways.

questions.prompt: Which TWO translate the complaint into testable requirements?

options.text: Prefer flagship model for support answer quality
options.explanation: A model preference is a design choice, not a requirement; it states no business outcome or service level the support leaders actually asked for.

options.text: Cut handling time 25% without lowering resolution rate
options.explanation: Measurable requirements pair a business outcome with a constraint; vendor and model preferences are design choices, not requirements.

options.text: Use vector search for knowledge base article retrieval
options.explanation: Choosing retrieval technology is an architecture decision made after requirements exist; it does not express the speed or consistency outcome being requested.

options.text: Answer 95% chats under 5s at current staffing
options.explanation: Measurable requirements pair a business outcome with a constraint; vendor and model preferences are design choices, not requirements.

questions.scenario: Support leaders complain answers are slow and uneven. The architect must convert this into requirements before designing.
questions.explanation: Requirements should express the stakeholder outcome as measurable operating constraints: reduce handling time while preserving resolution rate, and meet a specified response-time coverage at current staffing. Model choice and vector retrieval are architecture decisions made after requirements; they do not state what business result or service level the design must meet. Source: Stakeholder Engagement, Lifecycle & GTM, What must the system cost.

questions.prompt: Which end-to-end design controls drift after launch?

options.text: Bigger model parsing invoices plus richer accuracy dashboards
options.explanation: A larger model and more dashboards observe or re-generate drifted formats but create no exception path, so bad extractions still reach payments before anyone intervenes.

options.text: Input validation plus sampled review feeding extraction improvements
