options.explanation: Upstream validation plus sampled human review closes the loop on extraction drift; downstream dashboards alone detect errors without correcting the pipeline.

options.text: Parallel agents debating each invoice field before posting
options.explanation: Agent debate at tripled volume multiplies cost and latency on every field without adding the confidence-based routing that would catch uncertain documents.

options.text: Faster OCR engine plus lower temperature for output stability
options.explanation: A faster OCR engine and lower temperature make processing quicker and more repetitive, but neither detects format drift nor routes low-confidence extractions to review.

questions.scenario: Invoice formats shift monthly. Extraction errors reach payments before anyone notices. Volume will triple next quarter.
questions.explanation: Format drift requires a control at the document-processing boundary and a route for uncertain cases, not merely a stronger generator. Validate inputs, score extraction confidence, and send low-confidence documents to human review so questionable values do not proceed unchecked; use reviewed cases to improve the extraction system. A larger model, lower temperature, or agent debate may change generation behavior but does not create the confidence-based exception path. Source: Enterprise Integration & Production, Document processing pipeline (Evaluator-optimizer).

questions.prompt: Which decomposition best handles complex contract review?

options.text: Split work by model size across contract sections
options.explanation: Splitting by model size optimizes cost per section but does not separate the responsibilities that fail, so a single prompt still performs extraction, judgment, and citation with hidden failures.

options.text: Assign agents per team preference for ownership balance
options.explanation: Team ownership preferences are an organizational concern, not an architecture; they do not create verifiable boundaries where hallucinated clauses can be caught.

options.text: Decompose into clause extraction, risk scoring, citation check
options.explanation: Decomposing by verifiable subtask isolates risk and enables parallel evaluation; decomposition by model size or by team preference confuses ownership with architecture.

options.text: Chunk documents randomly for equal processing latency
options.explanation: Random chunking balances latency but severs clauses from their context, making citation verification harder and hiding rather than exposing failures.

questions.scenario: Contract review mixes extraction, risk judgment, and citation. A single prompt hallucinates clauses and hides failures.
questions.explanation: Decompose by distinct responsibilities and failure modes: extract clauses, score their risk, then verify the citations that support the result. This exposes each stage for validation instead of asking one prompt to perform and conceal every task. Splitting by model size, team preference, or random chunks does not establish responsibility-level checks for the hallucinated clauses and unsupported citations. Source: Claude Platform & Solution Design, Key takeaways.

questions.prompt: Which TWO orchestration choices fit parallel claims extraction?

options.text: Run independent extractors in parallel for each field
options.explanation: Parallel extraction with a supervisor merge fits independent fields plus conflict resolution; chained debate on every field wastes latency for little accuracy gain.

options.text: Chain all agents sequentially debating every extracted field
options.explanation: Sequential debate on independent signals adds latency for no accuracy gain, since the fields have no dependency requiring serial resolution.

options.text: Add supervisor merging outputs and resolving field conflicts
options.explanation: Parallel extraction with a supervisor merge fits independent fields plus conflict resolution; chained debate on every field wastes latency for little accuracy gain.

options.text: Let agents bid for tasks in open marketplace negotiation
options.explanation: Marketplace bidding has no mechanism for the explicit conflict-resolution rule the scenario demands, and its allocation overhead adds cost without structure.

questions.scenario: Claims packets hold independent medical, billing, and fraud signals. Conflicts are rare but must be resolved explicitly.
questions.explanation: The medical, billing, and fraud signals are independent, so separate extractors can run in parallel rather than serially adding delay. Because conflicts must be handled explicitly, a supervisor should reconcile the field outputs using a stated conflict rule. Sequential debate wastes latency on independent work, while marketplace bidding does not supply the required synthesis and conflict-resolution boundary. Source: Claude Platform & Solution Design, The parts an architect assembles solutions from.

questions.prompt: Which design meets volume, cost, and quality together?

options.text: Tiered routing with cheap model first, flagship on ambiguity
options.explanation: Tiered routing reserves flagship reasoning for ambiguous tickets while cheap models clear routine ones; uniform flagship use buys accuracy at unsustainable cost.

options.text: Flagship model answering every ticket for maximum quality
options.explanation: Running the flagship model on two million mostly routine tickets destroys the fixed budget, spending premium cost where a cheaper path is sufficient.

options.text: Agentic web research enriching each routine ticket response
options.explanation: Web research per routine ticket adds tool-call cost and latency to the bulk of volume, eroding the budget while giving routine answers no quality they need.

options.text: Multi-agent voting on every ticket before sending reply
options.explanation: Voting multiplies inference cost by the number of voters on every single ticket, which is financially impossible at two million monthly volume.

questions.scenario: A helpdesk faces two million monthly tickets. Budget is fixed, but escalation quality cannot drop. Most tickets are routine.
questions.explanation: At high volume with a fixed budget, the architecture should reserve expensive capability for cases that need it. Routing routine tickets to a lower-cost model and escalating ambiguous cases to a stronger model controls average spend while protecting escalation quality. Using the flagship model, web research, or multi-agent voting for every ticket applies the costly path even when the routine path is sufficient. Source: Claude Platform & Solution Design, Key takeaways.

questions.prompt: Which design lifts productivity without breaking accountability?

options.text: Autonomous agent filing briefs without lawyer approval step
options.explanation: Filing without lawyer sign-off eliminates the accountability the firm requires, and unverifiable citations in a filed brief create direct professional liability.

options.text: General chatbot answering legal questions without source citations
options.explanation: Uncited answers cannot satisfy the cited-precedent requirement, and chat responses never reach the draft-and-approval path filings must go through.

options.text: Batch summarizer rewriting all precedents without review queue
options.explanation: Batch rewriting with no review queue produces unverified precedent text at scale, so errors in authority reach filings before any lawyer sees them.

options.text: Draft-then-verify workflow with lawyer approval and citations
options.explanation: Draft-then-verify keeps the lawyer accountable while cutting drafting time; autonomous filing optimizes speed while violating the accountability constraint.

questions.scenario: A law firm wants faster brief drafting. Every filing needs lawyer sign-off and cited precedent. Deadlines are non-negotiable.
questions.explanation: The model should draft the brief, but a lawyer remains responsible for approval and needs verifiable precedent citations. A draft-then-verify workflow separates generative assistance from the human decision and adds a check for factual support. Autonomous filing removes the required accountability, while uncited chat and unreviewed batch rewriting do not provide the required verification path. Source: Claude Platform & Solution Design, From property to design consequence.

questions.prompt: Which pattern statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: Agentic loops always beat fixed workflows on cost
options.explanation: Agentic loops usually cost more, not less: iterative tool calls, retries, and growing context accumulate tokens, so they are justified by open-endedness, not economy.

options.text: Fixed workflows suit auditable repeatable compliance steps
options.explanation: Workflows suit fixed auditable steps, agency suits open-ended search, and retrieval grounds answers; autonomy never removes evaluation and debate is not free.

options.text: Autonomy removes the need for output evaluation suites
options.explanation: More autonomy increases rather than removes evaluation need, because model-chosen trajectories must be checked for correctness and safety before production.

options.text: Retrieval grounding reduces hallucination on known content
options.explanation: Workflows suit fixed auditable steps, agency suits open-ended search, and retrieval grounds answers; autonomy never removes evaluation and debate is not free.

options.text: Open-ended research favors agentic exploration over scripts
options.explanation: Workflows suit fixed auditable steps, agency suits open-ended search, and retrieval grounds answers; autonomy never removes evaluation and debate is not free.

questions.scenario: Judge each architecture pattern claim as true or false for solution design.
questions.explanation: Fixed workflows fit auditable, repeatable steps because deterministic guards can be placed between stages. Retrieval grounds a response in an external source of truth for knowledge the model should not answer from memory, reducing unsupported generation for known content. Agentic loops are not inherently cheaper: iterative tool use, retries, and growing context increase cost and latency, and autonomy never removes the need for evaluation. Open-ended research is the case that can justify an agent because the path cannot be fully enumerated in advance. Source: Claude Platform & Solution Design, Key takeaways.

questions.prompt: Which proposal represents transformation rather than efficiency?

options.text: Faster dashboard showing existing underwriting queue status
options.explanation: A dashboard improves visibility into the current queue but leaves the days-long manual underwriting process itself untouched, so turnaround barely moves.

options.text: Straight-through pipeline auto-deciding all standard loan applications
options.explanation: Transformation changes the operating model with measured turnaround gains; a faster dashboard improves visibility without redesigning underwriting itself.

options.text: Better search across current policy document store
options.explanation: Better search speeds up document lookup as a tooling gain, but the application still moves through the same handoffs that produce multi-day turnaround.

options.text: Copilot autocompleting underwriter notes without process change
options.explanation: Autocompleting notes is incremental efficiency for the writer; the underwriting decision path and its turnaround structure remain exactly as slow as before.

questions.scenario: A bank wants transformation in underwriting, not incremental tooling. Turnaround must fall from days to minutes for standard cases.
questions.explanation: Transformation changes the operating process that produces the outcome, not only the information around the current queue. A straight-through path for standard applications can convert a days-long manual sequence into a minutes-long automated decision flow. A dashboard, document search, or note-completion copilot can improve the existing process, but leaves the underwriting handoff and turnaround structure in place. Source: Claude Platform & Solution Design, Decomposition.

questions.prompt: Which fix targets the failing pipeline stage?

options.text: Upgrade reasoning model for better field interpretation logic
options.explanation: A stronger reasoning model still ingests the same low-resolution scans, so the dominant error source upstream of processing is untouched.

options.text: Add multi-agent review debating each garbled scan result
options.explanation: Debating results downstream of a bad scan spends heavy compute trying to interpret pixels that were unreadable on arrival, rather than stopping bad inputs at the source.

options.text: Add capture validation rejecting all low-quality scans upstream
options.explanation: Garbled scans are an input-quality failure, so capture validation gates the pipeline; a stronger reasoning model improves processing but ingests the same noise.

options.text: Expand context window to include more invoice history
options.explanation: More invoice history gives the model surrounding context but cannot reconstruct fields that were never legibly captured in the scan itself.

questions.scenario: Extraction fails on garbled scans. The team proposes a larger reasoning model. Errors cluster on low-resolution uploads from one channel.
questions.explanation: The failure originates before extraction: a single upload channel supplies low-resolution scans. Add an upstream capture-quality validation gate so unsuitable inputs are stopped or corrected before they enter the extractor. A larger reasoning model, agent review, or more historical context operates after the degraded input has already reached processing and therefore does not address the failing boundary. Source: Enterprise Integration & Production, Document processing pipeline (Evaluator-optimizer).

questions.prompt: Which THREE belong in the decomposition gate? Select three.

options.text: Define subtask boundaries with measurable acceptance criteria
options.explanation: Decomposition gates on measurable subtasks, interfaces, and evals; model choice and launch date belong to later selection and planning gates.

options.text: Select flagship model before splitting the overall task
options.explanation: Choosing a model before the task is split inverts the gate order, locking in capacity decisions that the subtask boundaries should drive.

options.text: Specify interfaces and data contracts between decomposed subtasks
options.explanation: Decomposition gates on measurable subtasks, interfaces, and evals; model choice and launch date belong to later selection and planning gates.

options.text: Commit launch date before validating subtask feasibility
options.explanation: A committed launch date before subtask feasibility is known guarantees schedule pressure overrides whatever the decomposition actually supports.

options.text: Build per-subtask evals before choosing orchestration pattern
options.explanation: Decomposition gates on measurable subtasks, interfaces, and evals; model choice and launch date belong to later selection and planning gates.

questions.scenario: A fraud-review task spans document intake, signal scoring, and narrative generation. The team debates where decomposition planning should stop. Decomposition must complete before orchestration choice.
questions.explanation: Decomposition gates on measurable subtasks, interfaces, and evals; model choice and launch date belong to later selection and planning gates.

questions.prompt: What must be true before building the feedback loop?

options.text: Freeze versioned output schema and baseline quality metrics
options.explanation: Feedback loops need a versioned output baseline to attribute change; tuning prompts from raw complaints skips the measurement that makes iteration meaningful.

options.text: Tune prompts weekly from anecdotal support ticket complaints
options.explanation: Anecdotal tuning without a versioned baseline cannot tell whether quality improved, so it generates churn that may itself introduce new drift.

options.text: Add more agents to explore alternative answer styles
options.explanation: More agents exploring styles multiply output variation while 'good' remains undefined, making the drift problem larger rather than measurable.

options.text: Collect user thumbs signals without defined response owner
options.explanation: Signals with no owner produce data nobody responds to; without a responder they cannot close a loop no matter how much is collected.

questions.scenario: A support copilot drifts monthly. No one agrees what good output was. Telemetry exists but lacks owners and baselines.
questions.explanation: A feedback loop requires a stable definition of the output being assessed and a baseline against which future behavior can be compared. Versioning the output schema and setting quality baselines makes later measurements interpretable; only then can the team detect drift and decide whether a change helped. Anecdotal prompt tuning, extra agents, or ownerless thumbs signals generate activity without defining the controlled artifact or the reference level of quality. Source: Claude Platform & Solution Design, Key takeaways.

questions.prompt: Which TWO are agentic patterns? Select both.

options.text: Fixed triage rules with LLM extracting fields
options.explanation: The triage path is written in code and the LLM only performs a bounded extraction step, so no runtime decision about the sequence of work is made by the model.

options.text: Planner choosing tool order per investigation goal
options.explanation: Full mapping: A workflow (fixed triage rules with LLM extraction); B agentic (planner choosing tool order per goal); C workflow (template filling with validation); D agentic (supervisor delegating sub

options.text: Template filling with validation rules before sending
options.explanation: Template filling with validation follows a predetermined path with deterministic checks, leaving the model no authority over what happens next.

options.text: Supervisor delegating subtasks to specialists at runtime
options.explanation: Full mapping: A workflow (fixed triage rules with LLM extraction); B agentic (planner choosing tool order per goal); C workflow (template filling with validation); D agentic (supervisor delegating sub

questions.scenario: Classify each design as agentic or workflow-augmented based on runtime autonomy.
questions.explanation: A design is agentic when the model makes runtime choices about the sequence of work. A planner that chooses tool order and a supervisor that delegates tasks to specialists both determine the next action dynamically. Fixed rules plus extraction and template filling plus validation are workflows: the path is written in code, so the LLM augments a bounded step rather than controlling the trajectory. Source: Claude Platform & Solution Design, The parts an architect assembles solutions from.

questions.prompt: Which multi-agent configuration respects cost and latency?

options.text: Unbounded agent debate improving answer depth and creativity
options.explanation: Unbounded debate has no stopping criterion, so latency and inference cost grow past both the 3s p99 budget and the quarterly cap.

options.text: Endless retrieval expansion ensuring complete context coverage
options.explanation: Endless retrieval chases completeness with unbounded tool calls and context growth, directly violating both budget constraints.

options.text: Full-model ensemble reviewing every routine customer reply
options.explanation: A full ensemble on every routine reply multiplies inference cost across all traffic, exhausting the quarterly cap on cases that need no review.

options.text: Bounded parallel critics with adjudicator under latency budget
options.explanation: Parallel critics with adjudication names both the recall gain and the latency-cost control; unbounded debate names collaboration benefits without latency or cost bounds.

questions.scenario: A product team proposes multi-agent review for every reply. P99 latency budget is 3s and inference budget is capped quarterly.
questions.explanation: If multi-agent review is justified, its work must have explicit limits that honor both the latency and inference budgets. Parallel critics reduce elapsed time relative to serial review, and an adjudicator provides a defined synthesis point; turn and tool budgets can bound the runtime. Unbounded debate, endless retrieval, and full ensembles for routine replies make cost and latency grow without a stopping criterion. Source: Enterprise Integration & Production, Architecture What breaks first Mitigation.

questions.prompt: Which TWO make the performance SLA enforceable?

options.text: Promise median latency observed during vendor demo
options.explanation: Demo medians hide exactly the long-document p99 breaches the telemetry shows, so a median promise is unmeasurable in practice and guarantees disputes over compliance.

options.text: Define percentile targets per query class separately
options.explanation: Enforceable SLAs separate query classes and tie percentile targets to fallbacks; medians and demo figures hide tail risk the business will feel.

options.text: Report average accuracy across all document types
options.explanation: Averages blend the breaching long-document tail into routine traffic, masking the very failures the SLA is supposed to make enforceable.

options.text: Pair SLA with fallback path when targets breach
options.explanation: Enforceable SLAs separate query classes and tie percentile targets to fallbacks; medians and demo figures hide tail risk the business will feel.

questions.scenario: Procurement demands 99% accuracy in 2s for all queries. Telemetry shows long documents breach p99 badly.
questions.explanation: Enforceable SLAs separate query classes and tie percentile targets to fallbacks; medians and demo figures hide tail risk the business will feel.

questions.prompt: Which architecture fits the fixed-date audited rollout?

options.text: Platform-wide autonomous agents resolving cases end to end
options.explanation: End-to-end autonomy with no eval harness cannot satisfy regulators' audit-trail requirements, and the safety maturity it needs cannot be built inside six weeks.

options.text: Proven workflow plus LLM drafting with human approval
options.explanation: A six-week audited rollout favors proven workflow plus targeted LLM assistance; platform-wide autonomous agents need eval and safety maturity the date forbids.

options.text: Custom multi-agent swarm learning policies from live traffic
options.explanation: A swarm learning from live traffic produces non-deterministic, unauditable decisions on real disputes, which regulators cannot certify in a fixed window.

options.text: Experimental planner discovering new resolution paths in production
options.explanation: Discovering resolution paths in production makes real customers the experiment, with no evaluated behavior to show auditors before launch.

questions.scenario: A telecom must launch dispute handling in six weeks. Regulators require audit trails. The team has no agent eval harness yet.
questions.explanation: A six-week audited rollout favors proven workflow plus targeted LLM assistance; platform-wide autonomous agents need eval and safety maturity the date forbids.

questions.prompt: Which pipeline gate statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: Input validation gates processing on capture quality
options.explanation: Input validation, versioned outputs, and owned feedback signals gate each stage; tuning processing before input quality or collecting signals without owners are misplaced.

options.text: Processing upgrades fix upstream capture quality failures
options.explanation: Processing operates downstream of capture, so upgrades cannot repair inputs that were already garbled; capture quality needs its own upstream gate.

options.text: Versioned outputs precede any meaningful feedback measurement
options.explanation: Input validation, versioned outputs, and owned feedback signals gate each stage; tuning processing before input quality or collecting signals without owners are misplaced.

options.text: Signals without owners still form feedback loops
options.explanation: A signal nobody owns triggers no agreed response, so it remains observation; without a responder the loop never closes.

options.text: Feedback needs threshold, owner, and response action
options.explanation: Input validation, versioned outputs, and owned feedback signals gate each stage; tuning processing before input quality or collecting signals without owners are misplaced.

questions.scenario: Judge each end-to-end pipeline statement as correctly or incorrectly placed.
questions.explanation: Input validation, versioned outputs, and owned feedback signals gate each stage; tuning processing before input quality or collecting signals without owners are misplaced.

questions.prompt: Which design proves efficiency value without SLA harm?

options.text: Automate standard renewals while preserving 2s SLA compliance
options.explanation: Efficiency requires both unit-cost reduction and SLA preservation; pure automation without the guardrail converts cost savings into breach penalties.

options.text: Automate renewals ignoring latency to maximize throughput gains
options.explanation: Maximizing throughput while ignoring latency breaches the SLA the board explicitly protected, so penalty costs can erase the entire unit-cost saving.

options.text: Add agents researching each renewal history before quoting
options.explanation: Per-ticket agent research multiplies cost and latency on routine renewals, raising unit cost and risking the SLA — the opposite of the efficiency goal.

options.text: Hire reviewers checking every automated renewal manually
options.explanation: Manual review of every renewal re-adds the labor cost automation was meant to remove, so unit cost never actually falls.

questions.scenario: An insurer wants efficiency from renewal automation. The board demands lower unit cost with no SLA regression.
questions.explanation: Efficiency requires both unit-cost reduction and SLA preservation; pure automation without the guardrail converts cost savings into breach penalties.

snapshot.title: Advanced Architecture III: Agent Control & Reliability

questions.prompt: Which control guarantees the ordering?

options.text: Instruct the model to verify before transfer, accepting bypass under drift
options.explanation: Instructions give only probabilistic compliance: under drift or a subtle prompt the model can skip verification, so no ordering guarantee exists.

options.text: Enforce a pre-execution guard on transfer_funds checking verified state
options.explanation: Ordering guarantees need deterministic enforcement. A pre-execution guard checks verified state in the current transaction and blocks transfer_funds otherwise; prompts, reminders, and temperature do n

options.text: Remind the model after verify_payee, risking skipped verification silently
options.explanation: A reminder is still just a prompt-level nudge; when it is ignored the skip happens silently and the transfer runs unverified.

options.text: Lower temperature with examples, leaving edge-case transfers unverified
options.explanation: Lowering temperature makes outputs more predictable but never makes compliance certain, so edge cases can still transfer funds unverified.

questions.scenario: A payment agent must never run transfer_funds unless verify_payee succeeded in the current transaction.
questions.explanation:
Ordering between verification and fund transfer is a deterministic guarantee, so it belongs in a pre-execution guard on transfer_funds that checks verified state; prompts and reminders provide only probabilistic compliance and fail silently under drift.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 1.4 Implementing Multi-step Workflows with Enforcement and Handoff Patterns and 1.5 Agent SDK Hooks for Intercepting Tool Calls and Normalizing Data.

questions.prompt: What is the best next move?

options.text: Restart empty, losing findings and repeating completed work
options.explanation: Restarting empty discards the scratchpad's preserved findings and forces the investigation to redo work already completed.

options.text: Compact or restart from the scratchpad, dropping verbose history
options.explanation: The scratchpad preserves decisions while verbose history can be dropped. Compacting or restarting from it retains findings and frees context; restarting empty, waiting for limits, or deleting findings

options.text: Continue unchanged, risking truncation and failed requests
options.explanation: Continuing unchanged consumes the remaining context window and eventually fails on truncation instead of acting on the available compact state.

options.text: Delete earliest findings, discarding decisions still needed later
options.explanation: Deleting early findings discards decisions the investigation still depends on, trading correct conclusions for temporary context space.

questions.scenario: Verbose tool outputs exhaust context, but key findings persist in a structured scratchpad.
questions.explanation:
Scratchpad files preserve key findings across context boundaries, so the reliable move is to compact or restart while carrying the scratchpad forward and dropping the verbose tool history. Continuing unchanged risks truncation; restarting empty repeats work and loses findings.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 5.4 Managing Context Efficiently When Investigating Large Codebases.

questions.prompt: Where should normalization occur?

options.text: Ask the model to convert dates mentally, inviting sorting errors
options.explanation: Mental conversion of conflicting formats is exactly the probabilistic behavior that produced the wrong ordering; it does not fix the data.

options.text: Fix each vendor service, blocking on external owners
options.explanation: The vendors cannot be changed, so this blocks the fix on external owners who are unavailable and out of the architect's control.

options.text: Normalize in a post-tool hook before context entry
options.explanation: Models should not mentally normalize mixed formats. A post-tool hook normalizes dates to one schema before context entry, fixing ordering without depending on external vendors or post-hoc relabeling.

options.text: Relabel dates after ordering, preserving the wrong sequence
options.explanation: Relabeling after ordering applies correct formats to an already-wrong sequence, so the underlying ordering error persists.

questions.scenario: Three services return dates in conflicting formats, so the agent orders events incorrectly. The vendors cannot be changed.
questions.explanation:
Data-format normalization is a PostToolUse hook pattern: intercept tool results and normalize (ISO 8601 dates) before the model consumes them. The model converting mentally invites sorting errors, and relabeling after ordering preserves the wrong sequence.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 1.5 Agent SDK Hooks for Intercepting Tool Calls and Normalizing Data.

questions.prompt: Which TWO controls must hold at the budget gate before any continuation? Select both.

options.text: Grant extra calls on request, allowing unbounded spend
options.explanation: Granting extra calls on request makes the budget advisory rather than binding, allowing spend to grow without bound past the boundary.

options.text: Block pending side effects at the boundary
options.explanation: Budget exhaustion is a hard gate: the loop must not execute the pending financial side effect, and must persist state, report incompleteness, and require authorized continuation. Extra calls on reques

options.text: Persist state, report incompleteness, require authorized resume
options.explanation: Budget exhaustion is a hard gate: the loop must not execute the pending financial side effect, and must persist state, report incompleteness, and require authorized continuation. Extra calls on reques

options.text: Discard the session silently, hiding the unfinished operation
options.explanation: Silently discarding the session hides a half-prepared financial operation with no persisted state or report, leaving it impossible to resume safely.

questions.scenario: An agent hits its tool-call budget with a financial operation partially prepared.
questions.explanation:
A budget boundary must block pending side effects so no financial operation completes on an exhausted budget, persist state, and report incompleteness with a required authorized resume. Granting extra calls unbounds spend, and silent session loss hides an unfinished financial operation.

Source: Responsible AI, Safety & Risk for Architects, fail-closed controls and evidence artifacts.

questions.prompt: What should govern loop termination?

options.text: API stop reason: continue on tool use, stop on end turn
options.explanation: Only the API stop reason is authoritative: tool-use means continue the loop, end-turn means stop. Text matching, fixed counts, or error absence confuse fluency or success with completion.

options.text: Confidence classifier, stopping early on fluent text
options.explanation: A classifier over fluent text stops on confidence rather than completion, cutting off the pending tool result that requests more work.

options.text: Fixed five iterations, cutting off needed work
options.explanation: A fixed iteration count is arbitrary: it cuts off legitimate work still requested by tool results or wastes cycles after the task is done.

options.text: Absence of errors, confusing success with completion
options.explanation: An error-free run says nothing about completion; the pending tool result requesting another action proves the task is unfinished.

questions.scenario: An agent stops when its text says 'complete', ignoring a tool result that requests another action.
questions.explanation:
Loop termination is governed by the API stop reason: continue when stop_reason is tool_use and stop only on end_turn. Parsing the agent's own text for 'complete' is a documented anti-pattern and ignored the pending tool result requesting another action.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 1.1 Designing Agentic Loops for Autonomous Task Execution.

questions.prompt: Which continuation strategy is most reliable?

options.text: Restart fresh with valid decisions, current schema, and change summary
options.explanation: Stale identifiers invalidate resume/compact paths. Restarting fresh with still-valid decisions, current schema, and an explicit change summary preserves intent without reasoning over renamed tables.

options.text: Resume unchanged, reasoning over stale table names
options.explanation: Resuming unchanged forces the model to reason over renamed tables, so stale identifiers contaminate every downstream step.

options.text: Fork twice and pick fewer steps, keeping stale schema
options.explanation: Forking copies the contaminated context into both branches, so choosing the shorter one still carries the stale schema forward.

options.text: Compact until names vanish, hiding the schema change
options.explanation: Compacting until the renamed tables disappear hides the schema change instead of resolving it, leaving the model to rediscover it wrongly.

questions.scenario: A migration session references renamed tables, but prior business decisions remain valid.
questions.explanation:
When resumed context contains stale references, a fresh session with the still-valid business decisions, the current schema, and an explicit change summary is more reliable than resuming, forking, or compacting — all of which carry the renamed-table references forward.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 1.7 Session State, Resuming, and Forking.

questions.prompt: How should the loop react?

options.text: Append the denial, continue, and follow the allowed escalation path
options.explanation: A guard denial is loop input, not session death. Appending the block result and continuing lets the model follow the allowed escalation path instead of bypassing limits or blinding itself.

options.text: Terminate the session, abandoning legitimate escalation
options.explanation: Terminating on a guard denial abandons the legitimate escalation path the guard explicitly returned, turning a policy block into a dead end.

options.text: Execute the refund anyway, violating the limit
options.explanation: Executing anyway defeats the guard's purpose and performs the exact over-limit action the policy exists to prevent.

options.text: Hide the denial, reasoning without the policy result
options.explanation: Hiding the denial removes the policy result from the model's reasoning, so it cannot choose the allowed escalation path it was given.

questions.scenario: A refund guard blocks an over-limit call and returns an escalation instruction.
questions.explanation:
A guard denial is a tool result: append it and continue the loop so the agent can follow the allowed escalation path. Terminating abandons legitimate escalation, executing violates the limit, and hiding the denial removes the policy result from reasoning.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 1.5 Agent SDK Hooks for Intercepting Tool Calls and Normalizing Data.

questions.prompt: Which TWO describe the permission set that enforces least privilege? Select both.

options.text: Allow all tools by instruction, leaving deletion and exfiltration open
options.explanation: Instruction-only limits leave every tool technically reachable, so deletion and exfiltration remain one prompt away despite the task scope.

options.text: Allow email and delete with confirmation, keeping unneeded risk
options.explanation: Confirmation reduces but does not remove risk; least privilege requires powers the task never needs, like email and delete, to be removed entirely.

options.text: Allow only read and save-copy
options.explanation: Least privilege removes unneeded email and delete powers entirely. Read plus save-copy with a completed-scan gate before save preserves the redaction task while eliminating exfiltration and destructio

options.text: Require a completed scan before any save
options.explanation: Least privilege removes unneeded email and delete powers entirely. Read plus save-copy with a completed-scan gate before save preserves the redaction task while eliminating exfiltration and destructio

questions.scenario: A subagent tasked only with redacted copies can read, save, email, and delete source files.
questions.explanation:
Least privilege grants only what the task needs: a redacted-copies subagent gets read and save-copy only, with any save gated on a completed scan. Email and delete paths are removed entirely rather than merely confirmed, and instruction-only limits leave every tool reachable.

Source: Responsible AI, Safety & Risk for Architects, tool-call authorization.

questions.prompt: Which tool response design enables correct stopping?

options.text: Shorten text, forcing the model to guess productivity
options.explanation: Shorter responses give the model even less information to distinguish no-match from failure, deepening the guessing that caused the loop.

options.text: Raise generic exceptions, masking real errors
options.explanation: Generic exceptions collapse retryable, permission, and no-match cases into one signal, so the loop cannot choose the right recovery.

options.text: Return bare empty arrays, confusing no-match with failure
options.explanation: Bare empty arrays are the current defect: the model cannot tell a valid empty result from a transient or permission failure, so it keeps searching.

options.text: Return explicit no-match status distinct from transient and permission errors
options.explanation: Retry loops need machine-readable status. An explicit no-match status distinct from transient, permission, and validation errors lets the loop stop correctly instead of inferring from brevity or crash

questions.scenario: An agent loops on search because every empty result lacks status metadata.
questions.explanation:
Access failures (retry decision), valid empty results (no matches), and permission errors require different recovery actions, so the tool must return an explicit no-match status distinct from transient and permission errors. Bare empty arrays are exactly what caused the loop.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 2.2 Implementing Structured Error Responses for MCP Tools.

questions.prompt: Which TWO checks must pass at the deploy gate? Select both.

options.text: Trust the stale flag, risking deploy of untested code
options.explanation: The flag describes tests against an older commit; trusting it can deploy code that was never tested after the repository changed.

options.text: Bind test success to an immutable commit or artifact digest
options.explanation: Boolean flags go stale when code changes. Binding test success to an immutable commit or artifact digest and rechecking it immediately before deploy blocks deployment against stale validation.

options.text: Revalidate the digest immediately before deploy
options.explanation: Boolean flags go stale when code changes. Binding test success to an immutable commit or artifact digest and rechecking it immediately before deploy blocks deployment against stale validation.

options.text: Accept a confident model review as equivalent to tests
options.explanation: A confident review is not execution evidence; it cannot substitute for tests bound to the exact artifact being deployed.

questions.scenario: A deployment agent passed tests, then the repository changed before deploy. Session state still claims tests_passed=true.
questions.explanation: verified fix explanation

questions.prompt: Which control should trip at the dependency boundary?

options.text: Prompt agents to avoid slowness, leaving retry storms unchecked
options.explanation: A prompt does not shed load; agents keep retrying at the transport layer, so the storm exhausts the service pool regardless of instructions.

options.text: Stuff timeout logs into context, wasting attention without shedding load
options.explanation: Adding logs consumes context and attention but changes no retry behavior, so the retry storm continues to drain the pool.

options.text: Trip a circuit breaker and fail fast during cooldown
options.explanation: Repeated timeouts need load shedding, not reminders or more logs. A circuit breaker trips after the error threshold and fails fast during cooldown, protecting the service pool.

options.text: Debate root causes in a worker while overload spreads
options.explanation: Root-cause debate happens after stabilization; while overload spreads, the priority is shedding load, not analysis.

questions.scenario: A dependency times out repeatedly, and agents keep retrying until the service pool is exhausted.
questions.explanation:
Repeated timeouts exhausting the service pool are the circuit breaker's trigger: when errors exceed the threshold it blocks further requests and fails fast during cooldown, preventing the retry storm from consuming the calling system's capacity. Prompts and log stuffing do not shed load.

Source: Enterprise Integration & Production, Glossary: circuit breaker.

questions.prompt: Which reliability action belongs in orchestration?

options.text: Retry indefinitely, stalling the user task
options.explanation: Retries are already exhausted, so continuing to retry only stalls the task while the endpoint stays overloaded.

options.text: Route to an evaluated fallback and mark degraded telemetry
options.explanation: Exhausted retries with quality tolerance call for graceful degradation. Routing to an evaluated fallback model and marking the degraded path in telemetry preserves the task with explicit quality bound

options.text: Strip quality checks, risking silent bad output
options.explanation: Removing quality checks removes the safety net exactly when running on a reduced-quality fallback, risking silent bad output.

options.text: Return partial text as complete, hiding the failure
options.explanation: Presenting partial output as complete misrepresents the degraded state to the user and hides the failure instead of bounding it.

questions.scenario: The primary model endpoint keeps returning overload errors with retries exhausted, but the task tolerates reduced quality.
questions.explanation:
With retries exhausted and quality tolerance available, the orchestration-layer control is a fallback chain: route to an evaluated fallback and mark degraded telemetry so the degradation is visible. Indefinite retry stalls the task; stripping checks or returning partial text as complete hides failures.

Source: Enterprise Integration & Production, Glossary: fallback chains; POC-to-production reliability patterns.

questions.prompt: Which oversight design addresses the blind spot?

options.text: Trust the aggregate, ignoring the failing segment
options.explanation: Trusting the aggregate is the current blind spot: high overall accuracy conceals the rare document type where misses concentrate.

options.text: Calibrate by type and sample high-confidence outputs per segment
options.explanation: Aggregates hide rare-type failures and confidence misleads. Calibrating by document type and sampling high-confidence outputs within each risk segment exposes confident misses where harm concentrates.

options.text: Review only low confidence, missing confident misses
options.explanation: Confidence-based routing misses exactly the confident errors this segment produces, since its scores stay high while its miss rate climbs.

options.text: Raise the global threshold, overloading review without targeting risk
options.explanation: A higher global threshold floods review with low-risk items while still never sampling the high-confidence outputs where the rare-type errors live.

questions.scenario: Moderation shows high overall accuracy, but one rare document type has a high miss rate despite confident scores.
questions.explanation:
Aggregate accuracy masks segment failure, so calibrate confidence by document type using labeled validation sets and apply stratified sampling to measure error rates even in high-confidence extractions. Reviewing only low confidence misses confident misses — precisely the documented blind spot.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 5.5 Designing Workflows with Human Oversight and Confidence Calibration.

questions.prompt: Which TWO entries belong in the model context? Select both.

options.text: Pass only the relevant fields plus provenance
options.explanation: Attention needs minimal sufficient context with provenance. Passing only relevant fields plus source into the model while retaining the full result outside context preserves grounding without dilution

options.text: Retain the full result outside context for audit or lookup
options.explanation: Attention needs minimal sufficient context with provenance. Passing only relevant fields plus source into the model while retaining the full result outside context preserves grounding without dilution

options.text: Pass all fields, diluting attention with noise
options.explanation: Passing dozens of irrelevant fields dilutes the model's attention with noise and increases the chance the decision-relevant fields are overlooked.

options.text: Pass prose without sources, losing verifiability
options.explanation: Prose without provenance cannot be verified or traced back to the source record, so any decision built on it is ungrounded.

questions.scenario: A tool returns dozens of fields, but only status, owner, deadline, risk, and source matter for the next decision.
questions.explanation:
Tool outputs accumulate disproportionately to relevance, so trim to the relevant fields plus provenance and retain the full result outside context for audit or lookup. Passing all fields dilutes attention with noise, and prose without sources loses verifiability.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 5.1 Managing Conversation Context to Preserve Critical Information.

questions.prompt: Which TWO conditions must hold at the open-account gate? Select both.

options.text: Infer confirmation from sentiment, opening without consent
options.explanation: Inferred sentiment is not recorded consent; opening an irreversible account on an inference bypasses the explicit customer confirmation policy requires.

options.text: Open after KYC then confirm, making reversal impossible
options.explanation: Opening before confirmation reverses the gate order, so the irreversible action happens before the consent that must precede it.

options.text: Require current KYC success
options.explanation: Irreversible actions need conjunctive gates. Account creation must require both current KYC success and an explicit confirmation record; sentiment inference, deferred confirmation, or either/or logic

options.text: Require an explicit confirmation record
options.explanation: Irreversible actions need conjunctive gates. Account creation must require both current KYC success and an explicit confirmation record; sentiment inference, deferred confirmation, or either/or logic

questions.scenario: An account-opening agent may collect data and run KYC, but opening is irreversible. Policy needs KYC success plus explicit customer confirmation.
questions.explanation:
Account opening is irreversible, so the pre-action gate requires both a current KYC success record and an explicit customer confirmation record — deterministic, recorded evidence, not inferred sentiment. Opening before confirmation makes reversal impossible.

Source: Responsible AI, Safety & Risk for Architects, human-review routing and evidence artifacts.

questions.prompt: Which approval model is safer?

options.text: Treat old prose as durable approval, enabling stale authorization
options.explanation: Prose from an hour-old conversation is stale authorization: nothing binds it to the current change, so the agent can fish for permissive-sounding sentences.

options.text: Require fresh structured approval bound to the exact change and actor
options.explanation: Old conversation text is not authorization. Production changes need fresh, structured approval bound to the exact proposed change and actor, preventing stale or inferred consent.

options.text: Let the agent infer approval, inviting self-authorization
options.explanation: Agent-inferred approval is self-authorization: the same system proposing the change also decides the consent exists, with no independent evidence.

options.text: Accept two agents agreeing the tone sounds permissive
options.explanation: Two agents agreeing on tone is still inference, not authorization; neither is an accountable human actor bound to the specific change.

questions.scenario: An agent proposes a production config change citing an approval sentence from an hour-old conversation.
questions.explanation:
Prose approval from an old conversation is stale, unverifiable authorization. The safer model is a fresh, structured approval bound to the exact change and the approving actor — a provable, replayable record rather than a quoted sentence an agent can fish for.

Source: Responsible AI, Safety & Risk for Architects, tool-call authorization and evidence artifacts.

questions.prompt: Which TWO elements make the log sufficient? Select both.

options.text: Log actor, action, argument digest, and timestamps with trace ID
options.explanation: Reconstruction needs full attempt history. Sufficient logs capture actor, action, argument digest, timestamps with trace ID plus policy decision and result, explicitly including blocked attempts that

options.text: Log policy decision and result, including blocked attempts
options.explanation: Reconstruction needs full attempt history. Sufficient logs capture actor, action, argument digest, timestamps with trace ID plus policy decision and result, explicitly including blocked attempts that

options.text: Log only successes, erasing blocked and failed attempts
options.explanation: Logging only successes erases the blocked and failed attempts the audit is explicitly required to reconstruct.

options.text: Log only final messages, losing tool-level evidence
options.explanation: Final messages summarize outcomes but drop the per-call evidence — actor, arguments, decisions — needed to reconstruct every attempt.

questions.scenario: An agent can create, update, and delete customer records. Audit must reconstruct every attempt, including blocked ones.
questions.explanation:
Reconstruction requires decision logging: actor, action, argument digest, timestamps, and trace ID per call, plus the policy decision and result — including blocked and failed attempts. Logging only successes or only final messages erases exactly the evidence audit needs.

Source: Responsible AI, Safety & Risk for Architects, decision logging.

questions.prompt: Which continuation approach is proportionate?

options.text: Resume, refresh live health, and retain unchanged topology
options.explanation: Only health values are stale while topology holds. The proportionate move resumes the session, explicitly refreshes live health data, and retains unchanged topology findings instead of trusting stalen

options.text: Trust old health, acting on stale availability
options.explanation: Acting on stale health values means routing decisions based on availability that may no longer hold, the exact hazard the refresh exists to remove.

options.text: Discard topology and restart, repeating settled analysis
options.explanation: Restarting discards still-valid configuration and topology analysis, repeating settled work for no reliability gain.

options.text: Average old and new health, fabricating a value
options.explanation: Averaging old and new health readings fabricates a value that matches neither the current nor the prior state, corrupting the basis for action.

questions.scenario: A resumed incident session has stale health values, but configuration and topology are unchanged.
questions.explanation:
Resume is proportionate when most context is still valid: keep the unchanged configuration and topology, and refresh only the live health values that went stale. Restarting repeats settled analysis; averaging old and new health fabricates a value.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 1.7 Session State, Resuming, and Forking.

questions.prompt: Which TWO designs prevent duplicate side effects? Select both.

options.text: Rely on model memory, risking duplicate tickets
options.explanation: Model memory of a prior attempt is not durable state; after the timeout the model can still re-issue the call and create a duplicate ticket.

options.text: Shorten timeouts and retry faster, multiplying duplicates
options.explanation: Faster retries increase the number of attempts racing an unknown outcome, multiplying duplicates instead of preventing them.

options.text: Send an idempotency key with the request
options.explanation: Timeouts after side effects need exactly-once mechanics. An idempotency key plus querying operation status before repeating prevents duplicate tickets without disabling all retries.

options.text: Check operation status before repeating the side effect
options.explanation: Timeouts after side effects need exactly-once mechanics. An idempotency key plus querying operation status before repeating prevents duplicate tickets without disabling all retries.

questions.scenario: A ticket-creation call times out before confirmation, and retry could duplicate the side effect.
questions.explanation:
A timeout before confirmation leaves the side effect's state unknown, so prevent duplication structurally: send an idempotency key so a repeat resolves to the same ticket, and check the operation's status before repeating the side effect. Model memory and faster retries both multiply duplicates.

Source: Enterprise Integration & Production, reliability patterns (retries and transient errors).

questions.prompt: Which stopping criterion is more reliable?

options.text: Stop at a URL count, counting duplicates as coverage
options.explanation: A URL count treats syndicated duplicates as independent coverage, so the agent can stop while several evidence areas rest on a single underlying article.

options.text: Stop on model confidence, ignoring provenance diversity
options.explanation: Self-reported confidence is an unreliable stopping signal and ignores whether sources are independent, letting duplicated coverage look sufficient.

options.text: Stop on token budget, leaving evidence gaps uncovered
options.explanation: A token budget measures spending, not evidence coverage, so the agent stops with evidence gaps still unfilled.

options.text: Stop when evidence categories and independent-source criteria are met
options.explanation: URL counts and confidence confuse quantity with coverage. Stopping when required evidence categories and independent-source criteria are satisfied handles syndication duplicates and enforces provenanc

questions.scenario: A research agent can stop after five sources, but several sources repeat the same syndicated article.
questions.explanation:
A URL count counts duplicates as coverage, and self-confidence is an unreliable proxy. The reliable criterion is evidence-based: stop when the required evidence categories are covered and each rests on independent sources, so syndicated duplicates do not masquerade as breadth.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 5.6 Preserving Provenance and Handling Uncertainty in Multi-source Synthesis.

snapshot.title: Advanced Architecture II: Multi-Agent Orchestration

questions.prompt: Which invariant should synthesis enforce before publishing?

options.text: Require equal token counts from every worker, delaying merge on verbosity.
options.explanation: Token counts measure verbosity, not coverage; a verbose report can still omit its assigned sections while a terse one covers them fully.

options.text: Require every worker to use two tools, wasting calls on irrelevant sections.
options.explanation: Tool usage is effort, not coverage — forcing a fixed number of calls wastes work on sections that need none and still proves nothing about whether required sections were returned.

options.text: Reconcile returned section IDs against required IDs or declared exceptions.
options.explanation: Synthesis cannot prove completeness without reconciling returned IDs against required IDs or declared exceptions.

options.text: Require an odd number of reports, dropping valid work arbitrarily.
options.explanation: Parity of report count has no relationship to section completeness and would discard valid work simply for making the count even.

questions.scenario: A coordinator must assemble a ten-section report. Workers were spawned dynamically with no record of assignments or returns.
questions.explanation:
With dynamic spawning, the only verifiable invariant is coverage: reconcile the returned section IDs against the required IDs, accepting declared exceptions. Token counts, tool counts, or parity of report numbers have no bearing on completeness.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 1.2 Orchestrating Multi-agent Systems (Coordinator–Subagent).

questions.prompt: What should the coordinator change first?

options.text: Define disjoint coverage assignments and reconcile submitted units before synthesis.
options.explanation: Disjoint assignments plus reconciliation prevent overlap and expose the missing jurisdiction before synthesis.

options.text: Let workers negotiate coverage peer-to-peer, causing races and lost ownership.
options.explanation: Peer-to-peer negotiation has no single owner of the coverage map, so races and duplicate work persist and the missing jurisdiction can still go unclaimed.

options.text: Raise every source budget and treat overlap as validation, hiding the gap.
options.explanation: More sources per worker increases cost and deepens overlap without addressing the structural problem, and the unassigned jurisdiction remains uncovered regardless of budget.

options.text: Ask synthesis to infer the missing jurisdiction, fabricating coverage.
options.explanation: Inference is not coverage: synthesis would be inventing content for a jurisdiction no worker actually investigated, manufacturing false completeness.

questions.scenario: Four workers cover regulations, incidents, vendors, and evidence. Their reports overlap and omit one jurisdiction.
questions.explanation:
Overlap and a missing jurisdiction are coverage failures, so the coordinator should define disjoint coverage assignments and reconcile submitted units against them before synthesis. Peer-to-peer negotiation races, and inferring the missing jurisdiction fabricates coverage.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 1.2 Orchestrating Multi-agent Systems (Coordinator–Subagent).

questions.prompt: Which context strategy best fixes the loss?

options.text: Shuffle report order each run and accept the average omission rate.
options.explanation: Shuffling changes which reports land in the forgotten middle; it redistributes the loss rather than fixing it, and accepting a nonzero omission rate abandons the evidence entirely.

options.text: Repeat middle reports verbatim at start and end, doubling tokens.
options.explanation: Verbatim duplication doubles token cost and still relies on raw sequential prose, so the structural cause of middle-position loss remains.

options.text: Compress every report to one sentence, destroying nuance and conflicts.
options.explanation: One-sentence compression destroys the nuance, conflicts, and claim-source links synthesis needs, trading omission for distortion.

options.text: Aggregate into structured findings, front-load critical items, keep claim-source links.
options.explanation: Structured aggregation with front-loaded critical items and claim-source links survives middle-position loss.

questions.scenario: Synthesis receives twelve long worker reports. Evidence from the middle reports is repeatedly omitted.
questions.explanation:
Omitted middle evidence is the lost-in-the-middle effect. Aggregate the twelve reports into structured findings, front-load critical items at the beginning under explicit headings, and keep claim-source links so synthesis reads from an ordered structure rather than raw sequential prose.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 5.1 Managing Conversation Context to Preserve Critical Information and 5.6 Preserving Provenance and Handling Uncertainty in Multi-source Synthesis.

questions.prompt: Select the two tool-allocation fixes that enforce least privilege.

options.text: Restrict the worker to read-only schema tools by default.
options.explanation: Least privilege requires both a minimal default toolset and an explicit approval gate for destructive calls.

options.text: Require explicit approval before any migration or deploy call.
options.explanation: Least privilege requires both a minimal default toolset and an explicit approval gate for destructive calls.

options.text: Keep all tools with warning text, leaving destructive actions reachable.
options.explanation: Prompt warnings do not constrain execution: migration writes, deploy, email, and billing remain one bad call away, which is precisely the least-privilege violation being fixed.

options.text: Route every tool call through free-form chat, losing auditability.
options.explanation: Free-form chat is not a deterministic authorization gate — it removes the structured, auditable approval trail that tool-call authorization requires.

questions.scenario: A database worker holds search, schema read, migration write, email, billing, and deploy tools.
questions.explanation:
Least privilege means defaulting the worker to read-only schema tools, with destructive actions (migration writes, deploy) behind explicit approval — deterministic gates on side-effecting calls. Warning text leaves destructive tools reachable, which is the risk being closed.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 2.3 Allocating Tools Across Agents and Configuring tool_choice; Responsible AI, Safety & Risk for Architects, tool-call authorization.

questions.prompt: Phase 1 stabilize, Phase 2 complete: which recovery sequence?

options.text: Abort the whole run, discarding seven complete regions.
options.explanation: Aborting discards seven fully successful regions to punish one partial failure, destroying useful work the recovery could simply have completed.

options.text: Silently omit the failed region and claim global coverage.
options.explanation: Silent omission fabricates global coverage, hiding a known gap from consumers who may rely on the missing region's evidence.

options.text: Retry missing work, preserve partial evidence, annotate any remaining gap.
options.explanation: Preserving partial evidence, retrying only missing work, and annotating gaps maintains coverage honesty.

options.text: Ask a finished worker to infer the missing region, fabricating evidence.
options.explanation: A finished worker has no data for the missing region, so its inference would be fabricated evidence presented as review findings.

questions.scenario: Eight workers review independent regions. One times out after returning two of five sources. The other seven finished successfully.
questions.explanation:
Recover incrementally: retry only the missing work, preserve the two sources already returned, and annotate any remaining gap in coverage. Aborting discards seven complete regions, silent omission fabricates coverage, and inference fabricates evidence.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 5.3 Implementing Error Propagation Strategies in Multi-agent Systems.

questions.prompt: Select the two observability fixes that restore traceability.

options.text: Propagate one trace ID across coordinator, workers, and retries.
options.explanation: A shared trace ID plus linked per-worker coverage events makes the missing finding attributable.

options.text: Emit per-worker coverage events linked to that trace ID.
options.explanation: A shared trace ID plus linked per-worker coverage events makes the missing finding attributable.

options.text: Give each worker an isolated trace, making loss unlinkable.
options.explanation: Isolated per-worker traces are exactly what made the loss unlinkable: with no shared ID, worker calls cannot be tied back to the originating request or to each other.

options.text: Store only final prose, destroying diagnosis.
options.explanation: Final prose alone discards the per-worker events and linkage needed for diagnosis, so a lost finding remains impossible to attribute or reconstruct.

questions.scenario: A final report lost one worker's findings. Logs cannot link worker calls to the originating request.
questions.explanation:
Traceability requires one trace ID propagated across coordinator, workers, and retries, plus per-worker coverage events linked to that ID — so the lost findings can be located and attributed. Isolated per-worker traces and final-prose-only storage are what made the loss unlinkable.

Source: Enterprise Integration & Production, A/B testing and observability: per-request observability.

questions.prompt: How should synthesis handle the conflict?

options.text: Keep the newer figure and delete the older source, hiding the trend.
options.explanation: Deleting the older figure discards provenance and hides the trend the six-month comparison reveals; the difference is temporal, not an error to be pruned.

options.text: Average both values, inventing a number neither source reported.
options.explanation: Averaging manufactures a market-share figure neither source ever stated and erases the dated movement between the two measurement points.

options.text: Pick the figure from the more confident worker, confusing confidence with recency.
options.explanation: Worker confidence says nothing about which measurement is current; selecting on confidence conflates model self-assessment with source recency.

options.text: Preserve both values with source and date, explaining the temporal difference.
options.explanation: Dated, sourced preservation explains the difference as temporal rather than forcing a false single truth.

questions.scenario: Two credible sources report different market-share figures six months apart.
questions.explanation:
Six months apart is a temporal difference, not a contradiction: preserve both values with source and date and explain the temporal difference, rather than deleting, averaging, or substituting confidence for recency.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 5.6 Preserving Provenance and Handling Uncertainty in Multi-source Synthesis.

questions.prompt: What change enables true parallelism?

options.text: Lower each token budget, sacrificing depth without parallelism.
options.explanation: Token budgets do not affect execution order, so cutting them only sacrifices worker depth while the Task calls still run sequentially.

options.text: Split into three turns, forcing sequential waits.
options.explanation: Separate turns guarantee one call completes before the next is issued, which is the very serialization causing the missing latency gain.

options.text: Use one worker with three tools, reintroducing a bottleneck.
options.explanation: Consolidating into one worker removes the parallel workers entirely, reintroducing a single point of sequential execution.

options.text: Dispatch all Task calls together and await the full result set.
options.explanation: True parallelism requires dispatching all Task calls together in one turn before awaiting the set.

questions.scenario: A coordinator requests three workers in one turn. The runtime runs the Task calls sequentially with no latency gain.
questions.explanation:
Parallel subagents are spawned via multiple Task calls dispatched together in a single coordinator turn, and the coordinator awaits the full result set. If the runtime serialized them, the fix is dispatching all calls together, not shrinking budgets or forcing separate turns.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 1.3 Configuring Subagent Calls, Context Passing, and Spawning.

questions.prompt: Match each outcome to its handling: which three judgments are correct?

options.text: Escalate the permission error instead of blindly retrying it.
options.explanation: Permission needs escalation, no-match is valid acceptance, timeout needs backoff retry with partial data kept.

options.text: Accept the empty result as valid when no records exist.
options.explanation: Permission needs escalation, no-match is valid acceptance, timeout needs backoff retry with partial data kept.

options.text: Retry the timeout with backoff while keeping partial data.
options.explanation: Permission needs escalation, no-match is valid acceptance, timeout needs backoff retry with partial data kept.

options.text: Abort the whole orchestration on any mixed outcome, discarding useful work.
options.explanation: Mixed outcomes are normal and each has its own handling; aborting everything discards two fully useful results because a third needs escalation or retry.

questions.scenario: Three results arrive together. One shows a permission error, one shows no matching records, one shows a timeout with partial data. The coordinator must not conflate them.
questions.explanation:
The three outcomes require different handling: a permission error is escalated (retrying cannot fix authorization), a valid empty result is accepted as a legitimate answer when no records exist, and a timeout is retried with backoff while keeping the partial data. Aborting on mixed outcomes discards useful work.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 2.2 Implementing Structured Error Responses for MCP Tools and 5.3 Implementing Error Propagation Strategies in Multi-agent Systems.

questions.prompt: Which handoff is most reliable?

options.text: Send only the preferred figure, baking in confirmation bias.
options.explanation: Passing only the preferred figure starves the worker of the other claims and bakes the coordinator's conclusion into the input, guaranteeing confirmation bias.

options.text: Send all claims, sources, dates, and the exact reconciliation question structurally.
options.explanation: Reconciliation needs all claims with sources, dates, and the exact question in structured form.

options.text: Resume the first session and overwrite its task, losing provenance.
options.explanation: Overwriting an existing session's task destroys the provenance of what that session already concluded and grafts a new question onto stale context.

options.text: Send nothing and demand independent search, duplicating work.
options.explanation: Withholding the claims and sources forces the worker to rediscover facts the coordinator already holds, duplicating effort and risking it finds different figures than the ones under dispute.

questions.scenario: A new worker must reconcile three contradictory pricing figures. It receives only a one-sentence summary.
questions.explanation:
Subagent context must be explicit: send all three claims with their sources and dates, plus the exact reconciliation question, in a structured handoff. A one-sentence summary or a preferred figure biases or starves the worker; demanding independent search duplicates work.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 1.3 Configuring Subagent Calls, Context Passing, and Spawning and 5.6 Preserving Provenance and Handling Uncertainty in Multi-source Synthesis.

questions.prompt: How should the prompt be redesigned?

options.text: Add steps for every failure and enforce exact order, causing brittleness.
options.explanation: Adding prescriptive steps doubles down on the existing problem: rigid sequencing cannot anticipate every failure and makes the prompt brittle instead of guiding judgment.

options.text: State the goal, decision criteria, required evidence, and output contract.
options.explanation: Goals, decision criteria, required evidence, and output contract guide judgment without brittle scripting.

options.text: Remove all criteria and let purpose emerge, drifting without standards.
options.explanation: Removing all criteria leaves workers with no standard to judge conclusions against, so outputs drift aimlessly rather than improve.

options.text: Replace judgment with majority vote, amplifying shared blind spots.
options.explanation: Majority vote substitutes counting for reasoning and amplifies any shared blind spot among workers rather than strengthening the conclusions themselves.

questions.scenario: Workers return correct facts but conclusions stay weak. The coordinator prompt enforces 25 rigid steps.
questions.explanation:
Coordinator prompts should be written in terms of the goal, decision criteria, required evidence, and output contract rather than 25 rigid steps; workers return correct facts, so the missing piece is the standard the conclusions must meet, not more sequencing.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 1.3 Configuring Subagent Calls, Context Passing, and Spawning.

questions.prompt: Which additional stage closes the gap?

options.text: Add an integration worker over interfaces, call paths, and local findings.
options.explanation: Per-file workers cannot see cross-service paths; an integration pass over interfaces is required.

options.text: Double local reviewers, multiplying cost without cross-service view.
options.explanation: Duplicating per-file reviewers multiplies cost but each reviewer still sees only one file, so the cross-service authorization break remains invisible.

options.text: Concatenate local reports unchanged, preserving fragmentation.
options.explanation: Concatenation preserves the per-file fragmentation that caused the miss; no step ever examines the interfaces and call paths across the four services.

options.text: Assign the largest service to a stronger model, mistaking size for coverage.
options.explanation: The break spans four services, so assigning a stronger model to the largest single file mistakes size for cross-service coverage and still leaves three services unexamined at the boundary.

questions.scenario: One worker per file finds local issues. No worker detects an authorization break spanning four services.
questions.explanation:
Per-file workers cannot see cross-service relationships, so the missing stage is an integration worker over interfaces, call paths, and the local findings — per-file analysis plus a cross-file integration pass. More local reviewers or a stronger model on the largest service do not create the cross-service view.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 4.6 Designing Multi-instance and Multi-pass Review Architectures.

questions.prompt: Select the two correct strategy-to-mechanism matches.

options.text: Competing strategies -> fork shared context into isolated sessions, then compare.
options.explanation: Forking shared context isolates explorations while preserving grounding; sequential reuse leaks bias.

options.text: Bias avoidance -> avoid sequential reuse carrying prior results.
options.explanation: Forking shared context isolates explorations while preserving grounding; sequential reuse leaks bias.

options.text: Independence -> strip schema analysis, losing grounding and causing divergence.
options.explanation: Stripping the shared schema analysis achieves separation by removing grounding, so both explorations start uninformed and diverge from the actual schema rather than from each other.

options.text: Efficiency -> use one worker for both, confusing verbosity with quality.
options.explanation: One worker handling both explorations reintroduces the bias the design exists to avoid; saving tokens says nothing about the quality of the comparison.

questions.scenario: Two workers must explore competing migrations from one schema analysis. Neither exploration may bias the other.
questions.explanation:
Correct matches: competing explorations fork the shared schema analysis into isolated sessions and compare afterward; bias avoidance means not reusing sequential context that carries prior results into later analysis. Stripping the shared analysis loses grounding, and one worker for both reintroduces the bias.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 1.7 Session State, Resuming, and Forking.

questions.prompt: Select the two contract requirements that enable synthesis.

options.text: Require findings with claim-to-source links.
options.explanation: Synthesis needs claim-source links plus coverage units and structured errors; prose length is not verifiable.

options.text: Require coverage units plus structured error metadata.
options.explanation: Synthesis needs claim-source links plus coverage units and structured errors; prose length is not verifiable.

options.text: Require longer narratives, burying gaps in prose.
options.explanation: Longer prose buries gaps and ambiguities inside narrative rather than making them explicit; unverifiable volume is not synthesis-ready structure.

options.text: Require identical word counts, rewarding padding over completeness.
options.explanation: Word count measures padding, not coverage or source quality, and equal lengths across different scopes are meaningless as a completeness signal.

questions.scenario: Workers return prose with inconsistent headings. Sources checked, units completed, and errors stay unclear.
questions.explanation:
Synthesis needs structure, not volume: every finding must carry a claim-to-source link, and each worker must report its coverage units plus structured error metadata so gaps and failures are explicit. Longer narratives and identical word counts reward padding, not completeness.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 5.6 Preserving Provenance and Handling Uncertainty in Multi-source Synthesis and 5.3 Implementing Error Propagation Strategies in Multi-agent Systems.

questions.prompt: Phase-gate before parallel work: what must come first?
