options.text: Define a shared interface contract and require implementation against it.
options.explanation: A shared interface contract must precede parallel implementation or merge becomes rework.

options.text: Let each worker optimize its format, guaranteeing rework at merge.
options.explanation: Per-worker format optimization is exactly what produced the incompatible outputs; it guarantees the rework continues at every merge.

options.text: Run workers sequentially copying the previous format, serializing delivery.
options.explanation: Sequential copying eliminates the parallelism that motivated the fan-out and still propagates whatever flaw the first worker's format contains.

options.text: Add a docs worker afterward, documenting incompatibility instead of preventing it.
options.explanation: Documenting the incompatibility after the fact records the damage instead of preventing it; the field names and error formats are already divergent.

questions.scenario: API, database, tests, and docs workers build in parallel. Their outputs use incompatible field names and error formats. Rework dominates the merge.
questions.explanation:
Incompatible field names and error formats come from parallel work without a shared interface. Before fanning out, define the common contract (field names, error format) and require every worker to implement against it; documenting incompatibility afterward or serializing delivery treats the symptom.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 1.2 Orchestrating Multi-agent Systems (Coordinator–Subagent) and 1.3 Configuring Subagent Calls, Context Passing, and Spawning.

questions.prompt: Which decomposition strategy fits best?

options.text: Map first, then generate and reprioritize scoped investigations from risk.
options.explanation: Adaptive decomposition maps first, then generates and reprioritizes scoped investigations from risk.

options.text: Give every component equal time before mapping, starving risky areas.
options.explanation: Equal time ignores observed risk entirely, starving the components findings show to be dangerous while over-investing in ones that are clean.

options.text: Fix the full sequence before discovery, ignoring emerging risk.
options.explanation: A pre-fixed sequence cannot incorporate new findings, so the investigation never reprioritizes toward the risks discovery actually reveals.

options.text: Analyze only initially named components, missing lateral paths.
options.explanation: Restricting analysis to initially named components misses the lateral paths that new findings expose beyond the opening map.

questions.scenario: A security investigation opens with a system map. New findings decide which components need deep analysis.
questions.explanation:
New findings determine the next investigation, so this is adaptive decomposition: map first, then generate and reprioritize scoped investigations from observed risk. Equal time for every component, a pre-fixed sequence, or only initially named components ignore what discovery reveals.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 1.6 Task Decomposition Strategies for Complex Workflows.

questions.prompt: What should be propagated to the coordinator?

options.text: Report unrecoverable failure demanding repetition, wasting completed evidence.
options.explanation: The worker completed with full evidence after successful retries, so labeling the work unrecoverable throws away finished results and forces needless repetition.

options.text: The completed result plus retry metadata for trace and monitoring.
options.explanation: Recovered work is complete, but retry metadata still aids trace and operational monitoring.

options.text: Only the initial 429, obscuring successful recovery.
options.explanation: Reporting only the 429 hides that the work actually succeeded, which would misdirect the coordinator into retrying or discarding completed evidence.

options.text: Only the result, blinding operations to flakiness.
options.explanation: Reporting only the result hides the transient 429s, blinding monitoring to the endpoint's flakiness and its cost in retries.

questions.scenario: A worker hits a 429, retries twice successfully, and completes with full evidence.
questions.explanation:
The worker recovered locally, so it reports the completed result with full evidence plus retry metadata (the transient 429s) for trace and monitoring. Propagating it as unrecoverable wastes finished work; reporting only the 429 or only the result each hides one side of the picture.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 2.2 Implementing Structured Error Responses for MCP Tools and 5.3 Implementing Error Propagation Strategies in Multi-agent Systems.

questions.prompt: Select the two context fixes that preserve signal.

options.text: Send only the sections relevant to the assigned question.
options.explanation: Relevant sections preserve signal while metadata plus a retrieval path keeps the worker unblocked.

options.text: Include source metadata plus a path to fetch more.
options.explanation: Relevant sections preserve signal while metadata plus a retrieval path keeps the worker unblocked.

options.text: Send the full document, burying signal and inflating cost.
options.explanation: The full 200-page document buries the five relevant sections in noise, inflates token cost, and degrades the worker's attention on exactly the signal it was assigned to analyze.

options.text: Send only the coordinator conclusion, removing evidence and inviting bias.
options.explanation: A conclusion without the underlying evidence strips the worker of anything to reason from and bakes the coordinator's view into the input, inviting bias.

questions.scenario: A worker needs five sections from a 200-page source. The coordinator currently sends the full document.
questions.explanation:
Pass only the minimum necessary data into the context: send the five relevant sections with source metadata and a path to fetch more if needed. The full document buries signal and inflates cost; the coordinator conclusion alone removes the evidence the worker must reason from.

Source: Enterprise Integration & Production, Five takeaways: pass only the minimum necessary data.

questions.prompt: Phase 1 classify, Phase 2 adapt: which refinement?

options.text: Increase retry count with the same prompt, repeating deterministic failure.
options.explanation: Failures repeat identically on identical context, so they are deterministic; more retries with the same prompt just multiply the same failure and grow the ledger.

options.text: Classify the failure, revise context or method, reroute only if plausible.
options.explanation: Identical retries repeat deterministic failure; classification plus context/method revision enables plausible recovery.

options.text: Broadcast every failure to all workers, multiplying cost and inconsistency.
options.explanation: Broadcasting every failure to every worker multiplies cost and produces inconsistent handling where a targeted classification and reroute would do.

options.text: Suppress failed tasks from the ledger, publishing false completeness.
options.explanation: Removing failed tasks from the ledger hides the work that never completed, publishing a false picture of completeness.

questions.scenario: Failed tasks always return to the same worker with identical context. Failures repeat identically. The ledger keeps growing without learning.
questions.explanation:
Identical repeated failures on identical context are deterministic, so retrying unchanged is wasted work. The refinement loop must classify the failure, revise the context or method, and reroute only if the failure type plausibly responds to the change; suppressing failed tasks publishes false completeness.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 2.2 Implementing Structured Error Responses for MCP Tools and 5.3 Implementing Error Propagation Strategies in Multi-agent Systems.

questions.prompt: What is the main architectural risk?

options.text: Early reports consume more tokens, misdiagnosing cost as correctness risk.
options.explanation: Token consumption is a cost property, not a correctness one; the risk is a draft presenting itself as complete while coverage is still unverified.

options.text: Fast workers are lower quality, so wait for the slowest indefinitely, stalling delivery.
options.explanation: Completion speed says nothing about report quality, and waiting indefinitely for the slowest stalls delivery without addressing the actual completeness gate.

options.text: The draft can claim completeness before required units return or fail declared.
options.explanation: Streaming early drafts risks completeness claims before all required units return or fail declared.

options.text: Any intermediate text revokes permission for extra workers, misstating constraints.
options.explanation: Publishing an intermediate draft does not revoke permission to spawn additional workers; the constraint being violated is the completeness claim, not spawning rights.

questions.scenario: Results publish as soon as workers finish. A draft goes out after three of five reports arrive. Readers may mistake it for complete.
questions.explanation:
Publishing as workers finish means the draft can present itself as complete while required coverage units have neither returned nor been declared failed. The completeness claim must be gated on coverage reconciliation, not on elapsed work.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 5.3 Implementing Error Propagation Strategies in Multi-agent Systems and 5.6 Preserving Provenance and Handling Uncertainty in Multi-source Synthesis.

snapshot.title: Advanced Practice Exam: Stakeholder Communication & Lifecycle (v3, 20Q)

questions.prompt: What should the architect do FIRST?

options.text: Commit the flu-season date immediately now
options.explanation: Committing the flu-season date locks a deadline before anyone has defined what success means, so the team risks delivering against an undefined promise.

options.text: Design workflows around assumed effortless meaning
options.explanation: Designing around an assumed meaning of 'effortless' bakes an unverified guess into the architecture instead of testing it against what nurses actually experience.

options.text: Elicit failure cases before committing dates
options.explanation: Vague adjectives must become testable failure conditions before dates are committed. Committing, designing around assumption, or selecting vendors acts one gate early.

options.text: Select vendor before clarifying effortless terms
options.explanation: Choosing a vendor before the requirement exists makes the selection criteria arbitrary and impossible to tie to any measurable outcome.

questions.scenario: A hospital sponsor requests an 'effortless' discharge summary agent before flu season. Nurses have not defined what effortless means in review time.
questions.explanation:
'Effortless' is a preference signal, not a requirement: it must be translated into testable, bounded constraints (e.g., review time) before any date or design is committed. A stakeholder who hears a confident architecture assumes the Architect has the information to build it, so finish the question set first.

Source: Stakeholder Engagement, Lifecycle & GTM, Discovery: translation of vague language into testable constraints.

questions.prompt: What should the architect do FIRST?

options.text: Confirm residency rule before routing design
options.explanation: A constraint mentioned in passing must be confirmed before routing or storage decisions. Retaining central routing, load testing, or dashboards without confirmation leaves violation intact.

options.text: Retain central routing and note assumption
options.explanation: Routing transactions to a central store on an unconfirmed residency assumption risks a data-residency violation that a written note cannot cure.

options.text: Run load tests before confirming residency
options.explanation: Load testing measures performance, not legal constraints, so it cannot confirm or resolve the residency question that decides the routing design.

options.text: Add residency dashboards without confirming scope
options.explanation: Dashboards only observe outcomes after the fact; they do not confirm the residency rule that must shape the routing decision before it is made.

questions.scenario: A fintech rollout drafts cross-border ledger routing to a central store. A risk officer noted transactions 'likely stay domestic' without confirmation.
questions.explanation:
A 'likely stays domestic' note is an unverified assumption feeding a binding architectural decision (data routing). Confirm the residency rule before designing the routing; dashboards and load tests do not resolve the underlying legal constraint.

Source: Stakeholder Engagement, Lifecycle & GTM, Discovery: write assumptions and constraints down early.

questions.prompt: Which TWO questions convert adjectives into requirements?

options.text: Ask what failure looks like concretely
options.explanation: Adjectives become requirements via concrete failure cases and one measurable citizen behavior. Vendor and timeline questions skip elicitation entirely.

options.text: Ask which vendor platform they prefer
options.explanation: Vendor preference is a solution choice, not a requirement; it says nothing about what fairness or trustworthiness would concretely mean for citizens.

options.text: Ask for one measurable citizen behavior
options.explanation: Adjectives become requirements via concrete failure cases and one measurable citizen behavior. Vendor and timeline questions skip elicitation entirely.

options.text: Ask for preferred launch timeline instead
options.explanation: A launch timeline schedules delivery but never converts the adjectives into testable behavior, so the requirements remain undefined.

questions.scenario: A public-sector sponsor calls a benefits assistant 'fair and trustworthy.' The team needs testable requirements before architecture begins.
questions.explanation:
Adjectives become requirements when they are testable and bounded: ask what failure looks like concretely (a failure condition defines the requirement's boundary) and ask for one measurable citizen behavior (a metric the architecture can be judged against). Vendor preference and timeline do not define fairness or trustworthiness.

Source: Stakeholder Engagement, Lifecycle & GTM, Four questions turn discovery into requirements.

questions.prompt: What should the architect do FIRST?

options.text: Encode both demands as runtime toggles
options.explanation: Encoding the unresolved conflict as toggles pushes the risk decision into runtime instead of reconciling it, leaving the architecture to serve whichever demand wins by accident.

options.text: Facilitate risk agreement before designing now
options.explanation: Conflicting mandates are resolved by facilitating explicit risk agreement before designing. Encoding toggles, imposing one side, or splitting difference avoids the decision.

options.text: Impose manual approval as binding rule
options.explanation: Unilaterally siding with security ignores the fixed quarter date and cost cap without a documented agreement, so the conflict resurfaces as an unmanaged dispute.

options.text: Split difference with partial sampling now
options.explanation: Partial sampling is an arbitrary compromise that neither party agreed to as an acceptable risk, so it dodges the decision rather than making it explicitly.

questions.scenario: Security mandates manual approval for every SaaS procurement recommendation. Sales demands instant auto-approval to meet a fixed quarter date under a strict cost cap.
questions.explanation:
Security's manual-approval mandate and sales' auto-approval demand are conflicting risk positions that must be reconciled before the architecture is designed around either; the Architect's job is to make the risk agreement happen, not to encode unresolved demands as toggles or split the difference.

Source: Stakeholder Engagement, Lifecycle & GTM, Discovery and conflict reconciliation via risk agreement.

questions.prompt: Which response best communicates the trade-off?

options.text: Recommend faster option without stating its cost
options.explanation: Recommending a choice while hiding its 3.5x cost and latency sacrifice denies finance the information needed for informed consent.

options.text: Present both costed options without recommending one
options.explanation: Presenting both options without a recommendation defers the decision finance explicitly asked for and shifts accountability back to the stakeholders.

options.text: Defer the decision until after launch date
options.explanation: Deferring past a fixed launch date removes the ability to influence that launch at all and leaves the trade-off unmade when it matters most.

options.text: Recommend one option, name sacrifice, set trigger
options.explanation: Trade-off communication costs both options, recommends one, names sacrifice, and sets revisit trigger. No recommendation, unstated cost, or deferral past date avoids informed consent.

questions.scenario: A fintech rollout weighs retriever A at $8k/mo with 2.1s p99 against retriever B at $28k/mo with 850ms p99. The launch date is fixed and finance demands a recommendation.
questions.explanation:
A complete trade-off presentation names what the choice gains, what it gives up, and what reversal costs: recommend one option, state the sacrifice explicitly, and set a trigger for revisiting. Presenting both without recommending defers the decision; recommending without stating cost hides the trade-off.

Source: Stakeholder Engagement, Lifecycle & GTM, Trade-off framing and go to market.

questions.prompt: Which TWO actions best defend the decision?

options.text: Brief one executive privately to lock support
options.explanation: Private lobbying builds political backing rather than a defensible decision, and it leaves the board's stated preference unaddressed on the merits.

options.text: Compare both options against agreed priorities now
options.explanation: Contested calls are defended by comparing both options against agreed priorities and recording decision, rationale, and triggers. Private lock-in or one-sided deep-dives do not.

options.text: Deep-dive only into chosen design internals today
options.explanation: Examining only the favored design is one-sided advocacy that never tests it against the priorities the board already agreed to.

options.text: Record decision, rationale, and revisit triggers now
options.explanation: Contested calls are defended by comparing both options against agreed priorities and recording decision, rationale, and triggers. Private lock-in or one-sided deep-dives do not.

questions.scenario: A hospital board prefers a fine-tuned model after seeing a vendor demo. The architect favors retrieval under a fixed p99 cap and tight operating budget.
questions.explanation:
Defend the decision on agreed priorities, not politics: compare both options against the metrics the board already accepted, and record the decision, its rationale, and revisit triggers so the choice survives personnel changes. Private lobbying and one-sided deep dives do not make a decision defensible.

Source: Stakeholder Engagement, Lifecycle & GTM, Documentation for handoff and audit.

questions.prompt: What is the flaw in this approval?

options.text: The sacrificed cost term was never stated
options.explanation: An approval without the stated downside is not informed consent even with quorum and agenda. The token-cost and latency sacrifice was never put forward.

options.text: The approval quorum was too small here
options.explanation: Quorum is a procedural property of the meeting, not the defect; even a full quorum cannot consent to a trade-off it was never told about.

options.text: The meeting lacked a formal recorded agenda
options.explanation: A missing agenda is a process shortfall, but the approval's real flaw is that the sacrificed token cost and latency were never disclosed.

options.text: The decision lacked a second vendor bid
options.explanation: Competing bids are procurement hygiene, not a prerequisite for informed consent; the flaw is the undisclosed downside of the approved choice.

questions.scenario: A public-sector board approved broader context windows for answer quality. The token-cost rise and latency hit were never stated. The team treats the vote as final consent.
questions.explanation:
A trade-off presentation is incomplete when a sacrificed term is hidden: the board approved answer quality without being told it costs token budget and latency, so the vote is not informed consent. Quorum size, agendas, and vendor bids are not the defect.

Source: Stakeholder Engagement, Lifecycle & GTM, Trade-off framing: gains, losses, and reversal cost.

questions.prompt: What should the architect do FIRST?

options.text: Accept terms since the median already passes
options.explanation: The median passing is irrelevant: the measured 4.8s p99 on knowledge-base queries already breaches the promised 1.5s p99, so signing concedes a guaranteed violation.

options.text: Negotiate percentile terms per query class now
options.explanation: SLAs are negotiated from measured tail behavior per query class, not medians or pre-sign optimization. Signing on median concedes breach; internal-only tracking concedes term.

options.text: Begin optimizing performance before signing any terms
options.explanation: Optimization is a separate workstream that may never reach the demanded tail latency; negotiating realistic terms protects the contract regardless of tuning outcomes.

options.text: Track latency internally and omit SLA terms
options.explanation: Omitting SLA terms concedes the negotiating position entirely and leaves the terms to be written later by the counterparty against the provider.

questions.scenario: SaaS procurement demands 1.5s p99 for all support queries by go-live. Telemetry shows 900ms median but 4.8s p99 on knowledge-base queries. Sales presses to sign this week.
questions.explanation:
Signing an SLA the system already breaches on a query class is a liability, not a formality. Negotiate percentile terms per query class before signing, so the 4.8s p99 knowledge-base tail is not measured against a 1.5s blanket promise; the median passing is irrelevant to the p99 term.

Source: Stakeholder Engagement, Lifecycle & GTM, Feedback loops and SLA management: set SLA thresholds from their real sources.

questions.prompt: Which practices belong in discovery? Select all that apply.

options.text: Write assumptions and constraints down early
options.explanation: Sound discovery writes assumptions down, converts vague terms into failure conditions, and reconciles conflicts explicitly. Designing past hints or locking dates first violates sequence.

options.text: Design past a constraint mentioned in passing
options.explanation: Designing past a constraint mentioned in passing bakes an unverified assumption into the architecture instead of confirming and recording it.

options.text: Convert vague terms into failure conditions
options.explanation: Sound discovery writes assumptions down, converts vague terms into failure conditions, and reconciles conflicts explicitly. Designing past hints or locking dates first violates sequence.

options.text: Lock the launch date before requirements exist
options.explanation: Locking a date before requirements exist inverts the discovery sequence and forces the design to fit a commitment made against undefined work.

options.text: Reconcile conflicts via risk agreement now
options.explanation: Sound discovery writes assumptions down, converts vague terms into failure conditions, and reconciles conflicts explicitly. Designing past hints or locking dates first violates sequence.

questions.scenario: Judge each discovery practice as sound or unsound for structured requirement gathering.
questions.explanation:
Sound discovery practices: write assumptions and constraints down early (so they bind the design), convert vague terms into failure conditions (making them testable), and reconcile conflicts via explicit risk agreement. Designing past a mentioned constraint and locking dates before requirements exist are the classic discovery failures.

Source: Stakeholder Engagement, Lifecycle & GTM, Discovery: translation into testable, bounded constraints.

questions.prompt: Which response best manages expectations?

options.text: Commit to demo accuracy minus small margin
options.explanation: Twelve curated demo loans are not a representative sample, so subtracting a margin from their accuracy still commits to a number the production distribution may not support.

options.text: Confirm commitment now and evaluate after rollout
options.explanation: Committing before baselining a representative sample makes the promise blind; evaluating after rollout discovers the shortfall only once the target is locked.

options.text: Baseline a representative sample before committing
options.explanation: A curated demo proves capability, not production performance. Baseline a representative sample before committing; margin-off-demo or post-rollout evaluation commits blind.

options.text: Refuse every accuracy target as totally impossible
options.explanation: Refusing all targets is an overcorrection: accuracy targets are legitimate once grounded in a representative baseline rather than curated demo data.

questions.scenario: A fintech sponsor saw 95% on twelve curated demo loans and wants it as the production target. Budget and launch date are already locked.
questions.explanation:
Twelve curated demo loans are not a representative sample; committing to their accuracy locks an expectation the production distribution may not support. Baseline accuracy on a representative sample before committing any target, then communicate the honest number.

Source: Stakeholder Engagement, Lifecycle & GTM, Trade-off framing and expectation management.

questions.prompt: Which TWO are closed feedback loops? Select both.

options.text: Weekly quality report with no tied action
options.explanation: A report nobody is bound to act on is monitoring only; no signal-to-action path exists, so the loop is open.

options.text: Breach pages the owner who runs runbook
options.explanation: A closed loop pairs an agreed signal with an agreed response that changes the system. Reports and ad-hoc dashboards without tied action are monitoring only.

options.text: Analyst dashboard explored ad hoc each month
options.explanation: An ad-hoc dashboard has no agreed trigger, owner, or response, so observing it changes nothing in the system.

options.text: Override spike triggers agreed rollback now
options.explanation: A closed loop pairs an agreed signal with an agreed response that changes the system. Reports and ad-hoc dashboards without tied action are monitoring only.

questions.scenario: A healthcare ops team reviews candidate signal designs after a triage outage. Only some designs pair a signal with an agreed response.
questions.explanation:
A closed feedback loop pairs a signal with an owner and an agreed action: a threshold breach that pages the owner who executes a runbook, and an override spike that triggers an agreed rollback. Reports and dashboards without a tied action are monitoring only.

Source: Stakeholder Engagement, Lifecycle & GTM, The feedback loop: signal to trigger, owner, and action.

questions.prompt: What best prevents silent expectation drift?

options.text: Wait until someone escalates dissatisfaction loudly now
options.explanation: Waiting for escalation means drift is discovered only after it has hardened into rejection, exactly the two-month surprise this scenario describes.

options.text: Send longer monthly status narratives instead now
options.explanation: Longer prose narratives describe activity but never show behavior against the agreed bar, so they do not surface changed assumptions.

options.text: Freeze scope so expectations cannot drift further
options.explanation: Freezing scope blocks legitimate change but does not resync stakeholder understanding with actual system behavior.

options.text: Demo behavior against acceptance bar each milestone
options.explanation: Expectations drift silently, so fix is demos of current behavior against acceptance bar each milestone. Waiting, longer narratives, or freezing scope do not resync understanding.

questions.scenario: A public-sector pilot passes milestones quietly for two months. A director then rejects the workflow over an assumption never revisited. The next review is in two weeks.
questions.explanation:
Silent drift happens when behavior is never shown against the agreed bar: demo the system's actual behavior against the acceptance criteria at every milestone, so assumptions are revisited while they can still change cheaply. Longer narratives and waiting for escalation do not surface drift.

Source: Stakeholder Engagement, Lifecycle & GTM, The feedback loop and outcome documentation.

questions.prompt: Which TWO are closed feedback loops? Select both.

options.text: Nightly eval digest emailed without owner review
options.explanation: A digest sent with no assigned owner and no agreed response is monitoring only; even unread, nothing in the system changes.

options.text: Spike auto-freezes rollout per playbook rule now
options.explanation: Auto-freeze per playbook and cap via runbook pair signal with agreed response. Digests without owners and charts reviewed on memory are monitoring only.

options.text: Latency chart reviewed when someone remembers it
options.explanation: A chart reviewed opportunistically has no trigger or owner, so spikes are caught by memory rather than by an agreed response.

options.text: Cost overrun alert triggers cap via runbook
options.explanation: Auto-freeze per playbook and cap via runbook pair signal with agreed response. Digests without owners and charts reviewed on memory are monitoring only.

questions.scenario: Classify each SaaS support signal design as a closed feedback loop or monitoring only.
questions.explanation:
Closed loops pair signal with automatic or owned action: a spike that auto-freezes the rollout per playbook rule, and a cost-overrun alert that triggers a cap via runbook. Emailed digests no one reviews and charts read opportunistically are monitoring without a response.

Source: Stakeholder Engagement, Lifecycle & GTM, The feedback loop: signal to trigger, owner, and action.

questions.prompt: What is the most important documentation gap?

options.text: Add decision records with rationale and alternatives
options.explanation: Diagrams record what was built; successors and auditors need decision records with context, rejected alternatives, and rationale. Walkthroughs and config detail do not transfer why.

options.text: Add sequence diagrams for each request path
options.explanation: Sequence diagrams record what the system does, which the successors already have; they still cannot explain why the threshold or reranker was chosen.

options.text: Expand deployment config detail for operators now
options.explanation: Configuration detail documents current values, not the reasoning behind them, so successors still cannot distinguish load-bearing choices from preferences.

options.text: Record live walkthrough videos for all successors
options.explanation: Videos transfer a one-time narrative that quickly goes stale and does not capture the rejected alternatives and rationale an audit requires.

questions.scenario: After an incident review, successors inherit complete runbooks and diagrams. They still cannot explain why the fallback threshold or reranker was chosen. An audit starts next week.
questions.explanation:
Diagrams and runbooks carry what the system is; only decision records with rationale and rejected alternatives explain why load-bearing choices (fallback threshold, reranker) were made. Without rationale, successors cannot tell load-bearing choices from preferences and cannot safely change them.

Source: Stakeholder Engagement, Lifecycle & GTM, Documentation for handoff and audit: record decisions, rejected alternatives, and trade-offs.

questions.prompt: Which TWO items would have prevented drift?

options.text: Behavior specs plus verifiable acceptance criteria
options.explanation: Drift is prevented by behavioral specs with acceptance criteria plus concrete defaults and fixtures. Inspection gates catch drift late; diagrams alone are not executable.

options.text: Rely on sprint-end inspection gates alone
options.explanation: Inspection gates detect drift only after it has accumulated, rather than making the approved intent checkable as the work happens.

options.text: Deeper component structure diagrams alone help
options.explanation: Diagrams describe structure but are not executable, so improvised prompts and thresholds can still diverge from them undetected.

options.text: Prompt defaults plus threshold test fixtures
options.explanation: Drift is prevented by behavioral specs with acceptance criteria plus concrete defaults and fixtures. Inspection gates catch drift late; diagrams alone are not executable.

questions.scenario: A healthcare delivery team improvised discharge prompts and escalation thresholds. Tests now diverge from the approved design intent.
questions.explanation:
Improvised prompts and thresholds drift because no artifact fixed the approved intent: behavior specs with verifiable acceptance criteria, and prompt-default plus threshold test fixtures, bind implementation to design. Inspection gates alone and more diagrams do not make intent checkable.

Source: Stakeholder Engagement, Lifecycle & GTM, The AI-native lifecycle: version-controlled artifacts and gates; Exam Domain Notes, 3.x test-first iteration.

questions.prompt: Which package completes the handoff?

options.text: Runbook draft without alerting or owner
options.explanation: A runbook without alerting or a named owner leaves the missing alert response path unsolved and nobody accountable when the strained cost cap trips.

options.text: Runbook, alerting, owner, plus rationale now
options.explanation: Handoff transfers operability: runbook plus alerting, named owner, and rationale. Partial packages without alerting, owner, or rationale leave operators unable to respond.

options.text: Dashboards plus extended metric coverage alone
options.explanation: The draft already has dashboards; wider metric coverage does not create the response path operations needs for alerts and cost overruns.

options.text: On-call rotation without runbook or rationale
options.explanation: An on-call rotation assigns people but gives them no symptom-to-action runbook or rationale, so they cannot respond to the alerts they will receive.

questions.scenario: A fintech assistant moves to operations next month under a fixed date. The draft includes code and dashboards but no alert response path while operating costs strain the cap.
questions.explanation:
A complete operational handoff includes the runbook (symptom-to-cause-to-action paths), alerting tied to owners, a named owner, and decision rationale, because the missing alert response path and strained cost cap are exactly what operations will face first. Dashboards alone or an on-call rotation without a runbook leave the response path undefined.

Source: Stakeholder Engagement, Lifecycle & GTM, Documentation for handoff and audit: runbooks, escalation paths, rationale.

questions.prompt: What must the architect set before closing?

options.text: Close program while merely noting drift risk
options.explanation: Noting drift risk without thresholds, an owner, or a cadence leaves the feedback loop undefined, so seasonal quality drift goes unwatched.

options.text: Retain build team on retainer indefinitely now
options.explanation: A retainer keeps builders available but does not define who owns drift monitoring or how often quality is reviewed, and it is not a durable governance structure.

options.text: Define thresholds, owner, and review cadence now
options.explanation: AI quality drifts, so closeout needs thresholds, a named owner, and review cadence. Retainers, wider dashboards, or noted risks without tied action are monitoring only.

options.text: Extend dashboard coverage for all operators now
options.explanation: Ops already holds a dashboard; without thresholds, a named owner, and a cadence, wider coverage is still monitoring only, not a feedback loop.

questions.scenario: A SaaS rollout met launch targets and builders rotate off next week. Ticket mix shifts seasonally, ops holds only a dashboard, and no owner tracks quality drift.
questions.explanation:
Closing without an owner leaves quality drift unwatched. Define the drift thresholds, name the owner, and set the review cadence so the feedback-loop governance rows exist before the build team rotates off; dashboards without thresholds and ownership are not a feedback loop.

Source: Stakeholder Engagement, Lifecycle & GTM, The feedback loop: governance rows need to be in place before launch.

questions.prompt: Which TWO gate statements are correctly placed?

options.text: Plan handoff before evals and trade-offs settle
options.explanation: Handoff transfers a validated system, so planning it before the eval suite and trade-offs settle hands over a draft rather than a proven artifact.

options.text: Require eval suite plus agreed trade-offs pre-handoff
options.explanation: Evals plus agreed trade-offs gate handoff planning, and iteration returns to design with updated evals. Handoff-first or discovery-placed load testing inverts sequence.

options.text: Place load testing inside early discovery work
options.explanation: Load testing belongs in design and verification when a concrete system exists to test, not in discovery before any architecture is built.

options.text: Return iteration to design with updated evals
options.explanation: Evals plus agreed trade-offs gate handoff planning, and iteration returns to design with updated evals. Handoff-first or discovery-placed load testing inverts sequence.

questions.scenario: Judge gate placement across design, handoff, and iteration. Only two statements order the gates correctly.
questions.explanation:
Correct gate ordering: the eval suite and agreed trade-offs must exist before handoff (handoff transfers a validated system, not a draft), and iteration that reveals new requirements returns to design with updated evals. Handing off before evals settle and placing load testing in discovery misorder the gates.

Source: Stakeholder Engagement, Lifecycle & GTM, Lifecycle gates; The AI-Native SDLC playbook, plan/design gates and CI gates.

questions.prompt: Which gate statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: Eval suite always precedes model selection
options.explanation: Evals gate model selection; rollback and owner gate handoff. Returning to discovery or accepting monitoring-alone readiness misplaces gates.

options.text: Rollback plan always precedes production handoff
options.explanation: Evals gate model selection; rollback and owner gate handoff. Returning to discovery or accepting monitoring-alone readiness misplaces gates.

options.text: Production handoff always requires a named owner
options.explanation: Evals gate model selection; rollback and owner gate handoff. Returning to discovery or accepting monitoring-alone readiness misplaces gates.

options.text: Iteration returns to discovery, not design
options.explanation: Iteration re-enters design with updated evals; returning all the way to discovery repeats elicitation that the accepted requirements already cover.

options.text: Monitoring alone satisfies handoff readiness checks
options.explanation: Handoff readiness requires a proven rollback plan and a named owner; dashboards and monitoring alone leave reversal and accountability undefined.

questions.scenario: Judge each lifecycle statement as correctly or incorrectly placed.
questions.explanation:
Correctly placed: a rollback plan precedes production handoff (the reversal path must be proven before operators take over), and production handoff requires a named owner (a handoff with no owner is a claim, not a handoff). Eval suites do not always precede model selection in every lifecycle shape, iteration can re-enter design, and monitoring alone does not satisfy handoff readiness.

Source: Stakeholder Engagement, Lifecycle & GTM, Entry point selection and outcome documentation; The AI-Native SDLC playbook, Stage gates.

questions.prompt: What does a complete handoff still owe?

options.text: Source code and credentials alone for operators
options.explanation: Code and credentials transfer the artifact but none of the detection or response capability operators need to catch quality drops or cost rises.

options.text: Demo video plus launch slides for operators
options.explanation: Launch material describes the system at launch, not how to operate it, so operators still cannot detect drift or respond to rising p99 costs.

options.text: Vendor support number for escalation alone now
options.explanation: An escalation phone number presupposes someone can already detect the problem; it provides no runbook, alerts, or internal owner.

options.text: Runbook, alerts, rationale, plus named owner now
options.explanation: A complete handoff transfers ability to operate: runbook, alerts, rationale, and named owner. Code, slides, or vendor number alone transfer system without operability.

questions.scenario: A public-sector system transferred to operators last month under a fixed date. Operators cannot detect quality drops and p99 costs keep rising. No runbook or owner transferred.
questions.explanation:
What the handoff still owes is the operating layer: a runbook mapping symptoms to actions, alerts tied to that runbook, decision rationale so operators can judge changes, and a named owner accountable for drift and cost. Code, credentials, videos, or a vendor phone number each leave detection and response undefined.

Source: Stakeholder Engagement, Lifecycle & GTM, Documentation for handoff and audit: runbooks, escalation paths, rationale.

snapshot.title: Advanced Practice Exam: Evaluation, Testing & Optimization (v2, 20Q)

questions.prompt: Which metric set gates release?

options.text: Report mean accuracy alone each week
options.explanation: Mean accuracy alone never measures the p99, cost, or safety constraints, so a release could ship while violating thresholds it never checked.

options.text: Gate accuracy latency cost safety thresholds
options.explanation: B gates accuracy, tail latency, unit cost, and safety. Costs: A costs blind latency/cost/safety failures; B costs broader instrumentation; C costs CSAT noise hiding cost/safety; D costs spend tracking

options.text: Track CSAT averages and mean latency only
options.explanation: CSAT averages and mean latency miss the accuracy bar, per-case cost, and PII safety entirely, so none of the named constraints is actually gated.

options.text: Monitor spend totals and uptime alone daily
options.explanation: Spend totals and uptime track infrastructure health but ignore routing accuracy, tail latency, and PII leaks, leaving the core quality and safety constraints ungated.

questions.scenario: A triage assistant must hold ≥91% routing accuracy, p99 under 2s, cost under 3 cents per case, and zero PII leaks. The team proposes a mean-accuracy-only scorecard to ship faster.
questions.explanation:
Release gates the named constraints, not a single mean: accuracy ≥91%, p99 under 2s, cost under 3 cents per case, and zero PII leaks. A mean-accuracy scorecard lets a release pass while violating latency, cost, or safety thresholds it never measured.

Source: Enterprise Integration & Production, Evals as acceptance criteria and POC-to-production checklist.

questions.prompt: What dataset fix best represents risk?

options.text: Add more clean invoice cases now
options.explanation: Adding more clean cases deepens the 95% clean skew, further hiding the noisy scans and adversarial layouts that drive production disputes.

options.text: Sample raw history without stratification controls
options.explanation: Raw-history sampling without stratification preserves whatever skew the traffic had and adds noise, so the eval mix still does not match the known 60/25/15 production distribution.

options.text: Stratify suite to production failure mix
options.explanation: C stratifies to the 60/25/15 production mix. Costs: A costs inflated scores hiding noisy/adversarial risk; B costs skew and noise preserved; C costs curation effort; D costs false stability and hidden

options.text: Duplicate passing cases for stable scores
options.explanation: Duplicating passing cases only stabilizes scores on the over-represented clean segment, manufacturing false stability while the failure modes stay hidden.

questions.scenario: An extraction pipeline sees 60% clean invoices, 25% noisy scans, and 15% adversarial layouts, but the eval set is 95% clean. Accuracy reads 96% while production disputes rise.
questions.explanation:
If the dataset is not representative, the scores are not meaningful: stratify the eval suite to the production failure mix (clean, noisy, adversarial) so the 96% lab score reflects the cases that actually dispute in production. Adding clean cases or duplicating passes deepens the skew.

Source: Enterprise Integration & Production, Evals as acceptance criteria: build the golden dataset.

questions.prompt: Which grading mix fits each output?

options.text: Code checks JSON judge prose human safety
options.explanation: A matches deterministic, open-ended, and safety-critical outputs to code, judge, and human grading. Costs: A costs three pipelines; B costs judge bias on JSON/safety; C costs unscalable reviewer load;

options.text: Judge model grades every output type alone
options.explanation: A single judge model is unreliable for deterministic JSON, which code checks grade exactly, and unsafe for refund decisions, which need human review.

options.text: Human reviewers grade all nightly cases manually
options.explanation: Human review of all 800 nightly cases does not scale, and it wastes reviewer effort on JSON outputs that deterministic code checks could grade exactly.

options.text: Exact match rules grade all outputs equally
options.explanation: Exact-match rules cannot score open-ended empathy replies meaningfully and provide no safety judgment for refund decisions.

questions.scenario: A support copilot outputs JSON summaries, open-ended empathy replies, and refund decisions with safety policy. The team proposes one grader for 800 nightly cases under a 90% accuracy bar.
questions.explanation:
Match grader to behavior: code checks grade JSON deterministically, an LLM judge scores open-ended empathy, and safety-critical refund decisions need human review — the grading ladder. One grader for all three output types either under-checks safety or over-pays for mechanical checks.

Source: Enterprise Integration & Production, The grading ladder: choosing how to grade.

questions.prompt: What restores a valid A/B comparison?

options.text: Keep schedule comparing raw win rates
options.explanation: Keeping the Monday/Friday schedule preserves the traffic-shift and midweek-reranker confounds, so raw win rates remain attributable to timing rather than the prompt.

options.text: Collect more Monday Friday traffic samples
options.explanation: Collecting more samples from the same separated windows adds biased data without removing the traffic-shift confound.

options.text: Pause tests until traffic fully stabilizes
options.explanation: Pausing delays the decision without fixing the design; the confound returns as soon as traffic shifts again during any future test.

options.text: Randomize interleave both prompts with logging
options.explanation: D removes weekday and midweek confounds via randomization. Costs: A costs time-confounded attribution error; B costs more biased data; C costs delay without fixing bias; D costs router and logging wor

questions.scenario: Document Q&A prompt A ran Monday morning and prompt B Friday evening, 1,200 cases each. Traffic mix shifted sharply between windows. A reranker tweak also shipped midweek.
questions.explanation:
A/B validity requires simultaneous randomized exposure to the same traffic: interleave both prompts on randomized requests with logging, so the traffic shift and the midweek reranker change no longer confound the comparison. More Monday/Friday samples preserve the confound.

Source: Enterprise Integration & Production, A/B testing posture: treatment, primary metric, sample size.

questions.prompt: What prevents tuning leakage?

options.text: Tune prompts across full eval suite
options.explanation: Tuning across the full suite deepens the leakage: the 15 tweaks are already fitted to these cases, and winner selection on them overstates the 88%.

options.text: Lock held-out set excluding all tuning
options.explanation: B locks an untouched held-out set for selection. Costs: A costs overfitting and inflated 88%; B costs extra curation and discipline; C costs variance hidden behind means; D costs training-set optimism

options.text: Report mean score across seeds only
options.explanation: Reporting means across seeds reduces run-to-run variance but does nothing about the tuning leakage from 15 tweaks on the same 500 cases.

options.text: Rerun winner on training cases only
options.explanation: Rerunning the winner on the training cases measures optimism, not generalization, since those cases are exactly what the tweaks overfit.

questions.scenario: An agentic workflow was tuned through 15 tweaks on 500 cases, rising 80% to 88% against a 90% bar. The same 500 cases will select the winner under a 4-cent cost cap.
questions.explanation:
Fifteen tweaks on the same 500 cases have tuned to those cases; selecting the winner on them is leakage. Lock a held-out set that no tuning ever saw and measure there, otherwise the 88% does not predict production performance.

Source: Enterprise Integration & Production, Evals as acceptance criteria: keep the golden dataset current and out of the tuning loop.

questions.prompt: What design isolates the cause?

options.text: Ship combined change watching dashboards daily
options.explanation: Shipping the combined change keeps both variables entangled, so the 3-point gain stays unattributable and the p99 effect remains unknown.

options.text: Add larger model alongside new prompt
options.explanation: Adding a larger model introduces a third simultaneous change, compounding the attribution problem instead of isolating it.

options.text: Test each change against control separately
options.explanation: C isolates one variable per arm against control. Costs: A costs unattributable 3-point gain; B costs doubled confounds and rollback pain; C costs extra arms and traffic; D costs time without causal ev

options.text: Roll back changes and wait idly
options.explanation: Rolling back and waiting produces no causal evidence about which change helped and what it did to p99.

questions.scenario: A triage assistant changed retrieval depth and system prompt together; success rose 3 points on 700 cases past the 90% bar. Nobody knows which change helped p99 2.4s.
questions.explanation:
Changing retrieval depth and system prompt together makes attribution impossible. Test each change against the control separately so the eval isolates which change produced the gain and what it did to p99.

Source: Enterprise Integration & Production, Evals as acceptance criteria: interpret and act on per-change results.

questions.prompt: What localizes the failure stage FIRST?

options.text: Rerun generator on gold retrieved context
options.explanation: A tests whether gold context fixes answers, isolating retrieval. Costs: A costs one small rerun; B costs tuning the wrong stage; C costs recall loss for unproven cause; D costs coverage bloat without

options.text: Rewrite system prompt redeploying it immediately
options.explanation: Rewriting the prompt acts on the generator before the retrieval hypothesis is tested, risking tuning the wrong stage while recall stays unmeasured.

options.text: Cut retrieved chunks reducing latency blindly
options.explanation: Cutting chunks reduces latency without evidence about the cause, likely worsening retrieval recall while never testing whether retrieval was failing.

options.text: Add fallback answers expanding coverage broadly
options.explanation: Adding fallback answers masks misses instead of localizing whether retrieval or generation caused the 61% accuracy.

questions.scenario: Document Q&A citation accuracy is 61% against an 85% bar, p99 3.1s versus 3s SLO. Retrieval recall is unmeasured while the team blames the generator.
questions.explanation:
Retrieval recall is unmeasured, so the first diagnostic isolates the stage: rerun the generator on gold retrieved context. If accuracy recovers, the failure is retrieval, not generation; prompt rewrites and chunk cuts act before the cause is known.

Source: Enterprise Integration & Production, per-stage observability and failure localization.

questions.prompt: What best fixes the mismatch?

options.text: Keep long prompt accepting error rate
options.explanation: Keeping the long prompt accepts a 24% schema violation rate against a 5% bar, failing the quality constraint outright.

options.text: Route everything to flagship model always
options.explanation: Routing everything to the flagship model breaks the 2-cent-per-document cost cap, trading one violated constraint for another.

options.text: Add constraints to same long prompt
options.explanation: Adding more constraints to an already-too-long prompt compounds the steerability problem for a smaller model that cannot follow it.

options.text: Simplify prompt fitting smaller model limits
options.explanation: D fits prompt complexity to the smaller model's instruction-following. Costs: A costs persistent 24% violations; B costs flagship latency and spend; C costs more constraints the model cannot follow; D

questions.scenario: An extraction prompt tuned on a flagship model shows 24% schema violations on a smaller model against a 5% bar. Cost must stay under 2 cents per document.
questions.explanation:
A prompt tuned on a flagship model does not transfer to a smaller model's capabilities. The fix is to simplify and re-tune the prompt to fit the smaller model's limits, staying under the 2-cent cap; routing everything to the flagship breaks the cost constraint and keeping a 24% violation rate fails the bar.

Source: Claude Platform & Solution Design, steerability: short, concrete, verifiable instructions with defined formats.

questions.prompt: What cuts cost FIRST?

options.text: Renegotiate token price keeping volume intact
options.explanation: Renegotiating the token price leaves the bloated volume of 9 chunks and 4 retries untouched, so the savings still cannot close the gap to the 3-cent cap.

options.text: Cut chunks retries turns before repricing
options.explanation: B cuts volume (chunks, retries, turns) before unit price. Costs: A costs savings on still-bloated volume; B costs recall validation work; C costs vendor churn without measurement; D costs budget theat

options.text: Change vendors without measuring token volumes
options.explanation: Changing vendors without measuring token volumes is repricing theater; the per-case cost is driven by work volume that no vendor switch addresses.

options.text: Cap monthly spend without changing volumes
options.explanation: Capping monthly spend without changing volumes either blocks service or hides the overage; the underlying per-case cost stays above the cap.

questions.scenario: A support copilot averages 9 chunks and 4 retries at 8 cents per case against a 3-cent cap. Its p99 is 4s versus a 2.5s SLO. The team wants to renegotiate token price first.
questions.explanation: B is correct because the first cost lever is the amount of work performed: reduce retrieved context and bound retry or tool-turn behavior before negotiating a marginal token-rate change. The current excess chunks and retries also drive the latency breach, whereas A, C, and D preserve the unmeasured work volume. Source: Enterprise Integration & Production, Cost and latency modeling: Know the numbers before you build.

questions.prompt: What best fixes p99 latency?

options.text: Compress prompts by five percent only
options.explanation: A five percent prompt compression shaves marginal time and leaves the three sequential tool calls that actually cause the p99 tail untouched.

options.text: Truncate every output to fifty tokens
options.explanation: Truncating every output to fifty tokens sacrifices answer quality across all cases and barely affects the tool-call latency dominating the tail.

options.text: Parallelize calls then stream partial results
options.explanation: C attacks the sequential-call tail then streams partials. Costs: A costs effort for negligible p99 gain; B costs accuracy for blind truncation; C costs orchestration complexity; D costs UX masking wit

options.text: Add spinners masking delays from users
options.explanation: Spinners change only perceived latency; the p99 breaches the SLO either way because the sequential calls still run in series.

questions.scenario: A triage assistant shows median 0.9s but p99 6.5s against a 2s SLO. Traces show three sequential tool calls on slow cases costing 7 cents each.
questions.explanation:
The p99 tail comes from three sequential tool calls on slow cases. Parallelizing the independent calls and streaming partial results attacks the tail's cause; prompt compression and output truncation shave marginal time, and spinners mask rather than fix latency.

Source: Building with the Claude API, Parallelization workflows.

questions.prompt: Which caching choice controls cost safely?

options.text: Cache prefixes with TTL plus invalidation rules
options.explanation: A captures repeat savings while bounding staleness. Costs: A costs TTL and invalidation logic; B costs full price on every repeat; C costs silent stale refunds; D costs latency with zero savings.

options.text: Disable caching paying full price every time
options.explanation: Disabling caching pays full price on the 45% of repeat cases, forfeiting the cost savings while the safety constraint is never actually at risk.

options.text: Cache forever without any invalidation controls
options.explanation: Caching forever serves stale refund policy with no invalidation path, directly violating the binding safety constraint.

options.text: Re-retrieve everything fresh for each query always
options.explanation: Re-retrieving everything fresh adds latency and cost on every repeat with zero savings, failing the cost objective the caching was meant to serve.

questions.scenario: Repeat policy questions are 45% of 12,000 daily support cases costing $1,100 per month. Stale refunds are the binding safety constraint.
questions.explanation:
Caching is most effective for long, stable, repeated content: 45% repeat policy questions suit prefix caching with a TTL and invalidation rules, so stale refund policy cannot be served - the binding safety constraint. Caching forever or disabling caching fails one side of the cost/safety pair.

Source: Enterprise Integration & Production, Glossary: caching.

questions.prompt: Which monitoring signals acceptance?

options.text: Track lab accuracy demo win rates
options.explanation: Lab accuracy and demo win rates are lab-side metrics; the 20% override rate shows real users rejecting drafts, so these numbers prove nothing about production acceptance.

options.text: Monitor uptime average token usage only
options.explanation: Uptime and token usage measure infrastructure health, not whether users accept the agent's work product.

options.text: Sample chats for subjective vibe scores
options.explanation: Subjective vibe scores are not behavioral evidence of acceptance and cannot counter the objective 20% override signal.

options.text: Track overrides reopens task resolution rates
options.explanation: D measures overrides, reopens, and resolution as acceptance. Costs: A costs lab optimism while agents override; B costs infrastructure health mistaken for success; C costs vibe scores without outcomes

questions.scenario: An agentic workflow scores 93% lab accuracy against a 90% bar, but agents override 20% of drafts at 6 cents per case. Leadership demands production acceptance proof.
questions.explanation:
Lab accuracy does not prove production acceptance; the override rate does the opposite. Acceptance shows in behavioral production signals: overrides, reopens, and task resolution rates - the translation layer mapping technical metrics to business outcomes.

Source: Enterprise Integration & Production, A/B testing and observability: build a translation layer to business metrics.

questions.prompt: Which TWO complete the release gate? Select both.

options.text: Task success ≥90% with safety violations tracked
options.explanation: A gates quality plus safety and C gates tail latency plus unit cost. Costs: A costs safety instrumentation; B costs hidden tail risk and spend; C costs latency/cost plumbing; D costs quality-blind inf

options.text: Average helpfulness score without any cost tracking
options.explanation: A helpfulness average with no cost tracking misses the per-case cost cap and the p99 bound, and it gates neither safety nor latency.

options.text: p99 latency bound with per-case cost cap
options.explanation: A gates quality plus safety and C gates tail latency plus unit cost. Costs: A costs safety instrumentation; B costs hidden tail risk and spend; C costs latency/cost plumbing; D costs quality-blind inf

options.text: Total tokens and server uptime alone daily
options.explanation: Token totals and uptime are infrastructure measures that say nothing about task success, safety leaks, latency, or per-case cost.

questions.scenario: A triage release gate lists only 88% average accuracy. Finance requires p99 ≤2s and ≤3 cents per case; safety requires zero leaks.
questions.explanation:
The gate is complete when it covers the named constraints: task success at threshold with tracked safety violations (accuracy and zero leaks) plus the p99 latency bound and per-case cost cap finance requires. Helpfulness averages without cost tracking and token/uptime totals alone miss the gate's terms.

Source: Enterprise Integration & Production, POC-to-production: map cost and latency to a budget; evals as gate.

questions.prompt: Which TWO strengthen the eval suite? Select both.

options.text: Reuse demo cases with exact-match grading
options.explanation: Reusing demo cases keeps the clean-invoice over-representation and exact-match grading cannot assess forged layouts or safety denials.

options.text: Weight cases by production failure frequency
options.explanation: B fixes coverage with failure-weighted sampling; D fixes grading with code plus human review. Costs: A costs inflated demo scores; B costs curation effort; C costs similarity scores missing safety; D

options.text: Grade safety denials with similarity scores only
options.explanation: Similarity scores like BLEU cannot judge the safety correctness of refund denials, leaving the highest-stakes outputs graded by proxy.

options.text: Pair code checks with human safety review
options.explanation: B fixes coverage with failure-weighted sampling; D fixes grading with code plus human review. Costs: A costs inflated demo scores; B costs curation effort; C costs similarity scores missing safety; D

questions.scenario: An extraction suite over-represents clean invoices while rare forged layouts drive losses. Refund denials are graded with BLEU. Accuracy must clear 92% under a 2-cent cap.
questions.explanation:
The suite must represent the failure distribution: weight cases by production failure frequency so rare forged layouts stop hiding behind clean invoices. Safety-critical refund denials cannot be graded by similarity metrics like BLEU - safety needs code checks where possible plus human review of sampled cases.

Source: Enterprise Integration & Production, Evals as acceptance criteria and grading ladder.

questions.prompt: Which TWO make the A/B valid? Select both.

options.text: Randomize assignment isolating one single variable
options.explanation: A enforces randomization with one isolated variable; D confirms on untouched held-out data. Costs: A costs traffic and router work; B costs time-confounded comparisons; C costs overfit selection; D co

options.text: Run variant mornings variant evenings separately
options.explanation: Splitting variants across morning and evening traffic re-introduces the weekly seasonality as a confound, invalidating the comparison.

options.text: Select winner using the tuning dataset
options.explanation: Selecting the winner on the tuning dataset overfits selection to data the variants were developed against, so the 87% bar is not credibly tested.

options.text: Confirm winner on held-out evaluation set
options.explanation: A enforces randomization with one isolated variable; D confirms on untouched held-out data. Costs: A costs traffic and router work; B costs time-confounded comparisons; C costs overfit selection; D co

questions.scenario: Two rerankers for document Q&A are tested on live traffic with weekly seasonality. The winner must clear 87% accuracy with p99 ≤3s.
questions.explanation:
A valid A/B randomizes assignment to the variants and isolates a single variable, then confirms the winner on a held-out evaluation set rather than the tuning data. Splitting variants across morning and evening traffic re-introduces the seasonality confound the test must control.

Source: Enterprise Integration & Production, A/B testing posture and eval-gate guidance.

questions.prompt: Which TWO localize the failing stage? Select both.

options.text: Tune generator before measuring retrieval recall
options.explanation: Tuning the generator before measuring retrieval recall risks optimizing the wrong stage while the logs still cannot attribute the misses.

options.text: Test generator on gold-standard retrieved context
options.explanation: B isolates retrieval via gold context; C isolates instruction-following via prompt-only probes. Costs: A costs tuning the wrong stage; B costs rerun effort; C costs baseline construction; D costs two

options.text: Probe model using prompt-only baseline cases
options.explanation: B isolates retrieval via gold context; C isolates instruction-following via prompt-only probes. Costs: A costs tuning the wrong stage; B costs rerun effort; C costs baseline construction; D costs two

options.text: Change retriever prompt simultaneously right now
options.explanation: Changing retriever and prompt simultaneously entangles both stages, so the 32% miss rate stays unattributable.

questions.scenario: Contract Q&A misses 32% of answers against a 90% bar at 5 cents per case. Logs cannot separate retrieval misses from generation errors.
questions.explanation:
Isolate the stages: test the generator on gold-standard retrieved context (if it recovers, retrieval is the failure), and probe the model with prompt-only baseline cases to bound generation performance. Tuning before measuring and changing both stages at once keep the attribution blind.

Source: Enterprise Integration & Production, per-stage observability and failure localization.

questions.prompt: Which TWO cut quantity before unit price? Select both.

options.text: Reduce chunks and cap retry loops
options.explanation: A cuts chunks and retries; C bounds agentic turns with early stops. Costs: A costs recall validation; B costs discount theater on bloated volume; C costs stop-rule tuning; D costs blind quality loss.

options.text: Chase small discount retaining full volume
options.explanation: A 10% discount on a 10-cent cost only reaches 9 cents, nowhere near the 3-cent cap, because the wasted volume of chunks and retries is untouched.

options.text: Bound tool turns with early-stop rules
options.explanation: A cuts chunks and retries; C bounds agentic turns with early stops. Costs: A costs recall validation; B costs discount theater on bloated volume; C costs stop-rule tuning; D costs blind quality loss.

options.text: Truncate outputs blindly across all cases
options.explanation: Blind truncation degrades answer quality on every case without addressing the retry and chunk inflation driving the cost.

questions.scenario: An agentic workflow costs 10 cents per case against a 3-cent cap with 8 chunks and liberal retries. The vendor offers a 10% token discount instead.
questions.explanation:
Quantity-first cuts attack volume: reduce chunks and cap retry loops, and bound tool turns with early-stop rules. Chasing the 10% discount retains the full volume of wasted calls, and blind truncation degrades quality without addressing the retry and chunk inflation.

Source: Enterprise Integration & Production, cost model: estimate call volume, token consumption, and cost.

questions.prompt: Which grading practices are sound? Select all that apply.

options.text: Code assertions verify JSON schema fields
options.explanation: A is sound for structured JSON; C is sound for rubric-graded tone; E is sound with humans calibrating safety edges. Costs: A/C/E cost pipeline and sampling effort; B costs BLEU missing safety; D costs

options.text: BLEU scores grade refund safety decisions
options.explanation: BLEU measures textual similarity, not safety correctness, so it cannot grade refund denial decisions and will silently pass unsafe outputs.

options.text: Judge rubric scores apology tone quality
options.explanation: A is sound for structured JSON; C is sound for rubric-graded tone; E is sound with humans calibrating safety edges. Costs: A/C/E cost pipeline and sampling effort; B costs BLEU missing safety; D costs

options.text: Humans grade every nightly regression case
options.explanation: Human-grading all 800 nightly cases does not scale, and it wastes scarce reviewer time that sampled-edge calibration already covers.

options.text: Humans adjudicate sampled safety edge cases
options.explanation: A is sound for structured JSON; C is sound for rubric-graded tone; E is sound with humans calibrating safety edges. Costs: A/C/E cost pipeline and sampling effort; B costs BLEU missing safety; D costs

questions.scenario: A support copilot needs nightly grading over 800 cases at ≥90% accuracy. Humans calibrate the judge on 100 sampled edges. Judge each practice as sound or unsound.
questions.explanation:
Sound: code assertions verify JSON schema fields (deterministic behavior), a judge with a rubric scores apology tone (interpretive), and humans adjudicate sampled safety edge cases (calibration plus high-stakes review). BLEU on safety decisions and human-grading every nightly case are respectively invalid and unscalable.

Source: Enterprise Integration & Production, The grading ladder and judge calibration.

questions.prompt: Which monitoring signals show acceptance? Select all that apply.

options.text: Lab accuracy alone proves user acceptance
options.explanation: Lab accuracy is a vanity signal here: the 17% override rate shows users rejecting drafts despite the 91% lab score.

options.text: Override rate flags rejected agent drafts
options.explanation: B/C/E reveal acceptance via overrides, reopens, and resolution. Costs: A costs lab-only optimism; B/C/E cost downstream event plumbing; D costs infrastructure health mistaken for task success.

options.text: Ticket reopen rate signals unresolved work
options.explanation: B/C/E reveal acceptance via overrides, reopens, and resolution. Costs: A costs lab-only optimism; B/C/E cost downstream event plumbing; D costs infrastructure health mistaken for task success.

options.text: Server uptime alone proves task success
options.explanation: Uptime measures service availability, not whether users' tasks actually got resolved, so it cannot evidence acceptance.

options.text: Resolution rate confirms completed user goals
options.explanation: B/C/E reveal acceptance via overrides, reopens, and resolution. Costs: A costs lab-only optimism; B/C/E cost downstream event plumbing; D costs infrastructure health mistaken for task success.

questions.scenario: A document Q&A agent holds 91% lab accuracy but 17% draft overrides at 5 cents per case. Judge each signal as acceptance-revealing or vanity.
questions.explanation:
Acceptance-revealing signals are behavioral: override rate flags rejected drafts, ticket reopen rate signals unresolved work, and resolution rate confirms completed user goals. Lab accuracy alone and server uptime alone are vanity metrics that cannot show user acceptance.

Source: Enterprise Integration & Production, A/B testing and observability: translation layer to business metrics.

questions.prompt: Which TWO cut quantity before unit price? Select both.

options.text: Renegotiate token rate keeping volume fixed
options.explanation: Renegotiating the token rate is unit-price-only: the wasted volume of chunks and retries stays intact, so the gap to the 3-cent cap barely moves.

options.text: Deduplicate chunks and cache repeated prefixes
options.explanation: B/D cut quantity via dedup, caching, and bounded retries; A/C only reprice or scale unchanged volume. Costs: A costs unchanged volume at lower rate; B costs dedup validation; C costs headroom without

options.text: Raise concurrency limits without volume change
options.explanation: Raising concurrency moves speed, not cost or latency at the tail, and leaves per-case volume unchanged against the cap.

options.text: Cap retries with targeted fallback policy
options.explanation: B/D cut quantity via dedup, caching, and bounded retries; A/C only reprice or scale unchanged volume. Costs: A costs unchanged volume at lower rate; B costs dedup validation; C costs headroom without

questions.scenario: A support copilot spends 9 cents per case against a 3-cent cap with p99 4s. Repeat queries dominate volume. Classify each action as quantity-first or unit-price-only.
questions.explanation:
Quantity-first actions reduce volume: deduplicate chunks and cache repeated prefixes, and cap retries with a targeted fallback policy. Renegotiating the token rate keeps the wasted volume intact, and raising concurrency moves speed, not cost or latency, at the tail.

Source: Enterprise Integration & Production, cost model and caching guidance.

snapshot.title: Advanced Practice: Integration (v2, 20Q)

questions.prompt: What chunking fix should the architect choose FIRST?

options.text: Keep 512-token chunks, add reranker
options.explanation: A reranker only reorders retrieved chunks; the citations are split at chunk boundaries before ranking happens, and text recall already exceeds its target.

options.text: Expand top-k from 4 to 12
options.explanation: Raising top-k fetches more chunks, which adds more partial clause fragments without changing the boundaries that split them.

options.text: Switch to clause-boundary chunks with overlap
options.explanation: Text recall already clears target; the failure is split citations. Clause-boundary chunks with overlap fix the failing half; rerankers, top-k, and embeddings improve recall only.

options.text: Upgrade to larger embedding model
options.explanation: A larger embedding model improves semantic recall, which already passes, and does nothing about clause boundaries cutting citations in half.

questions.scenario: Freight QA shows text recall 0.93 (target 0.85) but 31% of hazmat-clause citations split across chunks (target <10%). Fixed 512-token chunks are used.
questions.explanation:
Text recall already meets target; the failing metric is citation splitting, which is a chunk-boundary problem, not a retrieval-quality problem. Aligning chunks to clause boundaries with overlap removes the splits that fixed 512-token windows cause.

Source: Enterprise Integration & Production, Evals as acceptance criteria: building quality into the build process.

questions.prompt: What indexing change fixes the failing half?

options.text: Index shot rows with timecode metadata
options.explanation: Transcript recall clears target; shot-time lookup fails because flattening destroys table structure. A structured row index with timecodes fixes the failing half.

options.text: Widen transcript chunks to 1024 tokens
options.explanation: Wider chunks retrieve larger blobs of transcript prose but cannot restore the per-shot timecode structure that flattening destroyed.

options.text: Raise top-k from 5 to 14
options.explanation: Retrieving more prose raises coverage of the transcript, but the shot table fields the lookup needs are still missing.

options.text: Retrain embeddings on media transcripts
options.explanation: Retraining embeddings changes similarity scores, not the fact that the structured shot rows no longer exist as queryable records.

questions.scenario: Transcript recall 0.90 clears 0.85, but shot-time lookup accuracy is 0.55 (target 0.80). Shot tables were flattened into transcript prose.
questions.explanation:
Flattening shot tables into transcript prose destroys the structure the lookup needs. Indexing shot rows with timecode metadata restores the queryable fields; widening chunks or raising top-k retrieves more prose without fixing the missing structure.

Source: Enterprise Integration & Production, Evals as acceptance criteria: building quality into the build process.

questions.prompt: What retrieval split best resolves the errors?

options.text: Index quota snapshots every five minutes
options.explanation: Five-minute snapshots still serve quota state that can be minutes stale; live state needs a per-request query to the source system.

options.text: Route live quota to direct tenant API
options.explanation: Help docs are stable and suit RAG; quota is live state needing a direct tenant API. Faster snapshots or rerankers keep the staleness failure.

options.text: Add reranker over quota snapshot data
options.explanation: A reranker picks better among the same stale hourly snapshots, so the 28% error rate from outdated data remains.

options.text: Tune embeddings on quota field names
options.explanation: Tuning embeddings on field names improves matching, but the errors come from stale data, not from failing to find the snapshot.

questions.scenario: Help-doc accuracy 0.94 clears 0.90, but quota-availability errors reach 28% from hourly snapshots. p99 1.0s sits within 2s.
questions.explanation:
Quota availability is live state: an answer correct at one hour can be wrong minutes later, so it belongs in the source-of-truth system queried directly per request, not in hourly snapshot retrieval. Latency already passes, so the errors come from snapshot staleness, not retrieval quality.

Source: Enterprise Integration & Production, Glossary and enterprise integration patterns.

questions.prompt: What retrieval change fixes exact-ID queries?

options.text: Enlarge embeddings and reindex all tickets
options.explanation: Bigger embeddings strengthen semantic similarity, which already passes; exact identifiers are a lexical lookup that vectors handle worst.

options.text: Raise top-k and add query rewriting
options.explanation: More candidates and rewritten queries still rank by semantic similarity, so exact IDs remain lost among near-matches.

options.text: Chunk tickets into wider text windows
options.explanation: Wider windows bury identifiers in more surrounding text without adding the exact-match capability ID lookup needs.

options.text: Add BM25 path fused with vectors
