options.explanation: Semantic recall clears target; exact ticket IDs need keyword matching. A BM25 path fused with vectors fixes IDs without harming conceptual queries.

questions.scenario: Semantic recall 0.92 clears 0.85 across knowledge articles. Exact ticket-ID queries like SUP-44710 succeed only 0.44 (target 0.95). IDs were embedded as ordinary prose.
questions.explanation:
Exact identifiers are an unambiguous lookup, which semantic embedding handles poorly. A hybrid path that fuses BM25 keyword matching with vectors restores exact-ID precision while keeping the semantic recall that already passes.

Source: Enterprise Integration & Production, Evals as acceptance criteria: building quality into the build process.

questions.prompt: Which integration shape best fits this scale?

options.text: Duplicate direct client code per team
options.explanation: Duplicating client code per team is precisely what produced the divergent auth implementations and rising incidents.

options.text: Share wiki docs without shared code
options.explanation: Documentation alone leaves every team maintaining its own auth and pagination code, so the diverging copies and incidents continue.

options.text: Publish one MCP server for warehouse
options.explanation: One warehouse API with seven consumers justifies a single MCP server: one auth, pagination, and retry surface instead of seven diverging copies.

options.text: Merge seven teams into one agent
options.explanation: Collapsing teams into one agent is an organizational change that does nothing to centralize the duplicated auth code.

questions.scenario: One warehouse API serves seven analyst teams, each reimplementing auth and pagination. p95 850ms is within 1.5s; duplicate auth incidents keep rising.
questions.explanation:
When many clients need the same API, MCP servers are the reuse mechanism: one server exposes the warehouse once, so auth and pagination are implemented and audited centrally instead of duplicated per team. Duplicate client-side auth implementations are the direct cause of the rising incidents.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 2.4 Integrating MCP Servers into Claude Code and Agent Workflows.

questions.prompt: What should the architect choose for Monday launch?

options.text: Keep the direct carrier API call
options.explanation: With one consumer the direct call already meets p99 and avoids MCP hop, host, and date risk. MCP pays off with many consumers, not one Friday launch.

options.text: Wrap carrier in new MCP server
options.explanation: The MCP wrapper breaches the p99 budget and needs a new host, so it violates both the latency constraint and the launch date.

options.text: Add MCP cache before Monday launch
options.explanation: A cache added days before launch cannot make an unmeasured prototype meet a hard p99 budget by Monday.

options.text: Proxy carrier calls through chat agent
options.explanation: Routing through a chat agent adds another hop and dependency on the critical path, worsening latency and launch risk.

questions.scenario: Direct carrier API p99 is 650ms (budget 800ms) at 99.9% success. The MCP prototype adds 200ms, breaches p99, and needs a new host.
questions.explanation:
The direct call meets latency and success targets; the MCP prototype breaches p99 and needs new infrastructure before a fixed launch date. Ship on the path that meets the constraints and defer the MCP migration; adding a cache cannot make an unmeasured prototype meet a hard deadline.

Source: Claude Platform & Solution Design, delivery routes and latency trade-offs.

questions.prompt: Which pattern fits this negotiation need?

options.text: Return bigger one-shot MCP verdicts now
options.explanation: A larger single verdict is still a one-shot response; it cannot carry the 4-6 turns of back-and-forth the negotiation requires.

options.text: Use agent-to-agent evidence dialogue now
options.explanation: Multi-turn rights negotiation needs agent-to-agent dialogue, not a one-shot tool. Single verdict calls cannot deliberate evidence across turns.

options.text: Add more rights inputs to MCP
options.explanation: More input fields enrich a single verdict but do not add the multi-turn deliberation the 0.87 score shows is missing.

options.text: Cache past verdicts to cut latency
options.explanation: Caching speeds up repeated verdicts but does not introduce the interactive negotiation turns that are absent entirely.

questions.scenario: Rights clearance needs 4-6 turns between licensing and editing agents. A one-shot MCP verdict scores 0.87 (target 0.90) with no dialogue.
questions.explanation:
A one-shot MCP verdict cannot deliberate across turns, so a negotiation requiring 4-6 exchanges needs agent-to-agent dialogue; the 0.87 score reflects the missing interaction shape, not missing inputs or caching.

Source: Enterprise Integration & Production, integration pattern selection.

questions.prompt: What context change meets the token budget?

options.text: Add few-shot examples per tool entry
options.explanation: Few-shot examples add tokens on top of the 150 injected schemas, pushing the 39k-token context further past the 12k budget.

options.text: Upgrade to a larger base model
options.explanation: A larger model may tolerate more input tokens but does not reduce the 39k tokens injected each turn, so latency and cost stay breached.

options.text: Cache the full tool catalog longer
options.explanation: Caching cuts cost of repeated tokens but the full 150-schema catalog still occupies the context window and drives the p99 breach.

options.text: Expose tool search, load schemas on demand
options.explanation: Accuracy clears target; tokens and p99 breach. Searchable on-demand schemas fix the failing cost and latency half; model or cache boosters worsen it.

questions.scenario: With 150 tools injected each turn, accuracy 0.92 clears 0.85, but inputs reach 39k tokens (budget 12k) and p99 6.4s vs 2.5s.
questions.explanation:
Injecting 150 tool schemas every turn is a monolithic-context design that inflates tokens and latency. Progressive discovery — a searchable tool catalog with schemas loaded on demand — keeps accuracy while meeting the token budget; caching the full catalog or adding examples grows context further.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 2.4 Integrating MCP Servers into Claude Code and Agent Workflows.

questions.prompt: What scoping fix cuts misrouting FIRST?

options.text: Lengthen every tool description text passage
options.explanation: Longer descriptions add more context to choose among the same 38 tools, worsening token load without fixing the overload that causes misrouting.

options.text: Add retries on wrong-tool call events
options.explanation: Retrying after a wrong-tool call treats the symptom after the fact and does not reduce the 21% misrouting rate at selection time.

options.text: Upgrade model to follow instructions better
options.explanation: Accuracy once routed correctly is already 0.93, so the model follows fine; the failure is having 38 tools to choose from at once.

options.text: Scope minimal tool subset per task
options.explanation: Correct-tool accuracy clears target; excess capability drives misrouting. Least-privilege per-task subsets cut the failing wrong-tool rate first.

questions.scenario: Tenant admin agent holds 38 tools with 21% wrong-tool calls (target <5%). Accuracy once routed correctly is 0.93, clearing 0.88.
questions.explanation:
Wrong-tool rate at 38 available tools matches the documented effect that too many tools per agent reduces selection reliability, while accuracy once routed correctly already passes. Scoping the minimal tool subset per task fixes the selection stage; longer descriptions or a model upgrade do not address the overload.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 2.3 Allocating Tools Across Agents and Configuring tool_choice.

questions.prompt: What auth fix blocks this bypass?

options.text: Verify identity and scopes server-side
options.explanation: Client-asserted tiers are forgeable. Identity and scopes must be verified and enforced server-side regardless of prompt claims.

options.text: Harden system prompt role wording text
options.explanation: Prompt wording is user-visible text, not an authorization control; a forged tier inside prompt text bypasses it exactly as the pentest showed.

options.text: Hide priority tool descriptions from prompts
options.explanation: Hiding descriptions is cosmetic; the privilege decision must come from verified server-side identity, not from what the prompt happens to reveal.

options.text: Embed longer tokens inside prompt text
options.explanation: Any token or tier value carried in prompt text is client-asserted input that an attacker can rewrite, which is the very bypass demonstrated.

questions.scenario: Functional tests pass 100% on shipment refunds. Pentest forges tenant tier from basic to priority inside prompt text. Identity arrives asserted by the client.
questions.explanation:
Identity asserted by the client is spoofable by prompt text. Identity and authorization must be enforced server-side: the caller's tenant tier comes from the verified identity layer, never from prompt content; prompt wording and tool-description hiding are not authorization controls.

Source: Enterprise Integration & Production, Five takeaways: enforce identity at the server side.

questions.prompt: What authorization change stops the bypass?

options.text: Add retries on delete failure events
options.explanation: Retries re-issue the delete after a failure; they cannot detect that the caller's role was demoted mid-session.

options.text: Cache session auth for 24 hours
options.explanation: Caching authorization longer widens the window in which a demoted role can still act, making the bypass worse.

options.text: Authorize every invocation server-side now
options.explanation: Success rate clears SLO; the failure is stale session trust. Every privileged invocation needs fresh server-side authorization checks.

options.text: Log prompt text more verbosely daily
options.explanation: Logging records the bypass after it happens; it does not prevent a demoted role from performing the next delete.

questions.scenario: Delete success 99.2% clears SLO, but a mid-session role demotion still permits drops. Token is checked once at session start; 2 bypasses occurred.
questions.explanation:
Authorization checked once at session start cannot observe a mid-session role demotion. Each privileged invocation must be authorized server-side at call time, so the demoted role is blocked immediately; caching auth longer or improving logging does not close the bypass window.

Source: Enterprise Integration & Production, Five takeaways: enforce identity at the server side.

questions.prompt: Which justified trade meets all constraints?

options.text: Keep reranker, slip the release date
options.explanation: The release date is fixed and immovable, so slipping it violates a stated constraint regardless of accuracy or latency gains.

options.text: Drop reranker, hold 0.92 within p99
options.explanation: Accuracy clears 0.90 with headroom, but p99 breaches a fixed budget with capped GPUs and date. Trading 0.95 to 0.92 buys p99 with explicit budget.

options.text: Keep reranker, double GPU spend cap
options.explanation: Doubling GPU spend breaks the explicitly capped budget, which cannot be traded away to keep the reranker.

options.text: Add cache, tolerate the p99 breach
options.explanation: Tolerating the breach leaves a hard p99 budget violated; a cache added under a fixed date cannot be validated in time to close the gap.

questions.scenario: Reranked clip accuracy 0.95 clears 0.90, but p99 is 4.1s vs 1.5s budget. Release date is fixed and GPU spend is capped.
questions.explanation:
The fixed release date and capped GPU spend are the immovable constraints, and p99 is a hard budget. Dropping the reranker holds 0.92, above the 0.90 target, within p99; the other options each violate a named constraint.

Source: Claude Platform & Solution Design, cost-complexity-risk trade-off framing.

questions.prompt: Which TWO indexing moves fix the failing halves?

options.text: Use 2048-token chunks for all sources
options.explanation: One uniform large chunk size optimizes the already-passing pod manuals while further fragmenting short driver tickets and blurring tariff table rows.

options.text: Use ticket-level chunks with thread metadata
options.explanation: Driver tickets need small thread-aware chunks; tariff tables need row-structured indexing. Uniform large chunks optimize the already-passing manuals.

options.text: Index tariff tables as structured rows
options.explanation: Driver tickets need small thread-aware chunks; tariff tables need row-structured indexing. Uniform large chunks optimize the already-passing manuals.

options.text: Merge sources into one flat index
options.explanation: Merging into one flat index erases the per-source structure that ticket threads and tariff fields need, keeping the failing metrics unchanged.

questions.scenario: Pod manifests, 35k short driver tickets, and 250 tariff tables share one chunk size. Text recall 0.89 clears 0.85; ticket and table QA miss targets.
questions.explanation:
One chunk size cannot fit three document shapes. Short driver tickets should be indexed at ticket level with thread metadata so complete threads are retrieved, and tariff tables should be indexed as structured rows so field lookups hit exact cells; a single uniform chunk size either fragments tickets or blurs tables.

Source: Enterprise Integration & Production, Evals as acceptance criteria: building quality into the build process.

questions.prompt: Which TWO moves fix work-order lookups?

options.text: RAG for guides, live API for orders
options.explanation: Conceptual guides suit semantic RAG with a live order API; exact IDs also need keyword fusion. Snapshots or one index preserve staleness.

options.text: Fuse BM25 with vectors for identifiers
options.explanation: Conceptual guides suit semantic RAG with a live order API; exact IDs also need keyword fusion. Snapshots or one index preserve staleness.

options.text: Snapshot work orders nightly into vectors
options.explanation: Nightly snapshots are exactly what produces the 24% stale answers; work-order state changes during the day and must be queried live.

options.text: Use one semantic index for everything
options.explanation: A single semantic index keeps the exact-ID failure at 0.47 and still serves stale snapshot data for live work orders.

questions.scenario: Concept recall 0.93 clears 0.90, but WID-7734 lookups succeed 0.47 with 24% stale answers from nightly snapshots.
questions.explanation:
Two separate failures need two separate fixes: exact WID identifiers are an unambiguous lookup best served by a BM25-keyword path fused with vectors, and the 24% stale answers come from nightly snapshots of data that changes during the day, so live work orders must be queried from the source system rather than indexed nightly. Guides are static content and stay in RAG.

Source: Enterprise Integration & Production, Glossary: live state, and eval guidance.

questions.prompt: Which TWO changes fix tokens and misrouting?

options.text: Add searchable tool discovery on demand
options.explanation: On-demand discovery plus per-intent scoping fix tokens and misrouting together. Bigger windows or retries preserve the bloated context.

options.text: Inject full catalog into bigger window
options.explanation: Enlarging the window to fit all 150 schemas keeps the full catalog in every prompt, so token bloat and wrong-tool selection both persist.

options.text: Inject task-scoped tool subsets only
options.explanation: On-demand discovery plus per-intent scoping fix tokens and misrouting together. Bigger windows or retries preserve the bloated context.

options.text: Retry wrong-tool calls automatically always
options.explanation: Automatic retries act after a wrong-tool call has already happened; they reduce neither the 42k-token prompts nor the 18% misrouting rate.

questions.scenario: A 150-tool render catalog yields 42k-token prompts and 18% wrong-tool calls. Correct-tool accuracy 0.94 already clears its target.
questions.explanation:
Token bloat and misrouting both come from injecting the full 150-tool catalog every turn. A searchable tool discovery layer loads schemas on demand, and injecting only the task-scoped subset keeps each turn's context small and selection reliable; enlarging the window or auto-retrying does not fix either metric.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 2.4 Integrating MCP Servers into Claude Code and Agent Workflows and 2.3 Allocating Tools Across Agents and Configuring tool_choice.

questions.prompt: Which TWO integration choices fit these shapes?

options.text: Keep bulk exports on direct CLI script
options.explanation: One-off pipeline callers stay direct and bulk exports stay on CLI scripts, while eight billing tenants share one MCP server. Wrapping the single caller or chatting exports adds latency.

options.text: Publish one MCP server for billing
options.explanation: One-off pipeline callers stay direct and bulk exports stay on CLI scripts, while eight billing tenants share one MCP server. Wrapping the single caller or chatting exports adds latency.

options.text: Wrap single transcode caller in MCP server
options.explanation: A single caller gains no reuse from an MCP wrapper, and the added hop plus new host risks the fixed Friday ship date.

options.text: Route nightly exports through chat agent
options.explanation: Unattended bulk jobs need no conversational surface; pushing 50GB nightly exports through a chat agent adds overhead with no interaction benefit.

questions.scenario: A transcoding service has one pipeline caller and must ship Friday. Billing API serves eight tenants with diverging auth copies. Nightly 50GB exports run unattended without chat.
questions.explanation:
A single-caller pipeline shipping Friday gains nothing from an MCP wrapper's reuse benefit, so it stays direct. The billing API with eight diverging tenant auth implementations is exactly the multi-client reuse case one MCP server solves. Unattended bulk exports need no conversational tool surface and do not belong in a chat agent.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 2.4 Integrating MCP Servers into Claude Code and Agent Workflows.

questions.prompt: Which TWO fixes close both gaps?

options.text: Check caller roles via prompt instructions
options.explanation: Prompt instructions are not authorization; privilege checks in prompt text are exactly what allowed the two bypasses.

options.text: Authorize each payout call server-side
options.explanation: Bypasses need per-invocation server-side checks; untraceable payouts need I/O spans with outcome labels. Prompt checks and counters do neither.

options.text: Track aggregate success counters only now
options.explanation: Aggregate counters hide both failures: they cannot attribute a payout write to an approval or expose a per-call privilege bypass.

options.text: Trace tool I/O with outcome labels
options.explanation: Bypasses need per-invocation server-side checks; untraceable payouts need I/O spans with outcome labels. Prompt checks and counters do neither.

questions.scenario: Refund agent success 0.96 clears 0.92, but 2 privilege bypasses occurred and payout writes cannot be traced to an approval.
questions.explanation:
Bypasses happen because privilege checks live in prompt instructions, which are not authorization. Authorize each payout call server-side so the decision is provable and replayable, and trace tool I/O with outcome labels so every write can be attributed to an approval; aggregate success counters hide both failures.

Source: Enterprise Integration & Production, Five takeaways and observability guidance.

questions.prompt: Which gate statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: Single dispatch caller uses direct call
options.explanation: Single dispatch callers stay direct, shared routing APIs gain one MCP server, and bulk manifest exports stay on CLI scripts. One-shot exception tools and full-catalog injection are unsound.

options.text: Shared routing API uses one MCP server
options.explanation: Single dispatch callers stay direct, shared routing APIs gain one MCP server, and bulk manifest exports stay on CLI scripts. One-shot exception tools and full-catalog injection are unsound.

options.text: Multi-turn exception handling uses one-shot tool
options.explanation: A one-shot tool cannot deliberate across the multiple turns exception handling requires, so this interaction shape mismatches the tool type.

options.text: Inject all 150 schemas every turn
options.explanation: Injecting every schema each turn is monolithic context that bloats tokens and latency instead of loading schemas on demand per intent.

options.text: Bulk manifest export uses direct CLI script
options.explanation: Single dispatch callers stay direct, shared routing APIs gain one MCP server, and bulk manifest exports stay on CLI scripts. One-shot exception tools and full-catalog injection are unsound.

questions.scenario: Judge each integration choice as sound or unsound for its consumer count and interaction shape. One-shot calls cannot deliberate across turns. Bulk jobs need no conversational tool surface.
questions.explanation:
Sound choices: a single dispatch caller uses a direct call (no reuse benefit to an MCP wrapper); a shared routing API uses one MCP server (multi-client reuse); and bulk manifest export uses a direct CLI script (no conversational surface needed). Unsound: multi-turn exception handling cannot deliberate inside a one-shot tool, and injecting all 150 schemas every turn is monolithic context, not progressive discovery.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 2.4 Integrating MCP Servers into Claude Code and Agent Workflows.

questions.prompt: Which gate statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: Live inventory uses nightly vector snapshot
options.explanation: Inventory is live state that changes during the day, so a nightly snapshot serves stale answers exactly when availability matters.

options.text: Exact shipment IDs use hybrid keyword-vector path
options.explanation: Shipment IDs need hybrid paths, privileged calls need per-invocation server checks, and incidents need I/O traces with outcomes. Snapshots and prompt trust fail.

options.text: Trust tenant tier asserted in prompt text
options.explanation: A tier asserted inside prompt text is client-supplied and spoofable; identity must come from a verified server-side layer instead.

options.text: Authorize each privileged call server-side now
options.explanation: Shipment IDs need hybrid paths, privileged calls need per-invocation server checks, and incidents need I/O traces with outcomes. Snapshots and prompt trust fail.

options.text: Trace tool I/O with outcome labels
options.explanation: Shipment IDs need hybrid paths, privileged calls need per-invocation server checks, and incidents need I/O traces with outcomes. Snapshots and prompt trust fail.

questions.scenario: Judge each retrieval, auth, and observability statement as sound or unsound practice.
questions.explanation:
Sound: exact shipment IDs use a hybrid keyword-vector path (identifiers are unambiguous lookups); each privileged call is authorized server-side (deterministic, replayable); tool I/O is traced with outcome labels (per-request observability). Unsound: live inventory is live state and cannot come from a nightly snapshot, and a tenant tier asserted in prompt text is client-asserted, spoofable input, not identity.

Source: Enterprise Integration & Production, Glossary and Five takeaways.

questions.prompt: Which TWO are progressive discovery? Select both.

options.text: Searchable catalog loading schemas on demand
options.explanation: Progressive discovery loads schemas on demand and scopes per intent; full injection and prompt-stuffed secrets are monolithic context.

options.text: Full 150 schemas injected every turn
options.explanation: Injecting all 150 schemas each turn is monolithic context: it bloats every request regardless of the current intent.

options.text: Task-scoped subset injected per intent now
options.explanation: Progressive discovery loads schemas on demand and scopes per intent; full injection and prompt-stuffed secrets are monolithic context.

options.text: All runbooks plus secrets in system prompt
options.explanation: Stuffing runbooks and secrets into the system prompt injects everything on every request — the definition of monolithic context — and leaks secrets besides.

questions.scenario: Classify each tool-context design as progressive discovery or monolithic context. Progressive means schemas load on demand per intent. Monolithic injects everything every turn.
questions.explanation:
Progressive discovery loads context on demand per intent: the searchable catalog that loads schemas when needed, and the task-scoped subset injected per intent. Injecting all 150 schemas every turn and stuffing runbooks plus secrets into the system prompt are monolithic-context designs that bloat every request.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 2.4 Integrating MCP Servers into Claude Code and Agent Workflows.

snapshot.title: Advanced: Developer Productivity & Operational Enablement (v1, 20Q)

questions.prompt: Where should shared build conventions live?

options.text: Each developer personal CLAUDE.md file
options.explanation: Personal files fragment the baseline: each developer keeps different habits, which is the very problem the team wants to eliminate.

options.text: Versioned shared project CLAUDE.md file
options.explanation: Team conventions must be versioned and shared, so they belong in project CLAUDE.md. User-level config is for personal preferences only.

options.text: Private chat transcripts shared by leads
options.explanation: Chat transcripts are unstructured, unversioned, and not read by the tool, so they cannot act as an enforced shared baseline.

options.text: Local IDE defaults kept fully unversioned
options.explanation: Unversioned local defaults drift per machine and cannot be centrally updated or shared across the ten developers.

questions.scenario: A platform team onboards ten developers who each keep different build and test habits. Leads want one shared baseline.
questions.explanation:
A team baseline is shared configuration: a versioned project CLAUDE.md gives all ten developers the same build and test conventions, travels with the repo, and is centrally updatable. Personal files, chat transcripts, and unversioned IDE defaults cannot serve as a shared baseline.

Source: Team Enablement & Operational Productivity, Deploy the environment as a shared configuration.

questions.prompt: Which configuration best scopes frontend rules?

options.text: Single root rule applied to all paths
options.explanation: A root-wide rule is what already misfires: it forces one set of conventions across both subsystems with conflicting styles.

options.text: Personal user override for every developer
options.explanation: Per-developer overrides fragment the shared baseline and reintroduce the inconsistent habits the monorepo needs to eliminate.

options.text: Directory CLAUDE.md inside frontend folder
options.explanation: Subsystem differences call for directory-scoped CLAUDE.md. A root-wide rule would force frontend conventions onto backend code.

options.text: Standalone slash command run each time
options.explanation: A slash command is a manual prompt shortcut run on demand, not persistent scoped configuration that applies to the right files automatically.

questions.scenario: A monorepo mixes React frontend and Go backend with conflicting style and test rules. A root rule keeps misfiring.
questions.explanation:
Conflicting conventions per directory belong in directory-level CLAUDE.md files: a CLAUDE.md inside the frontend folder scopes React rules to that tree while the Go backend keeps its own. One root rule misfires across the boundary; per-developer overrides fragment the baseline.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 3.1 Configuring CLAUDE.md with Hierarchy, Scope, and Modular Organization.

questions.prompt: Which rule design controls migration risk?

options.text: Glob-scoped rule for migration file paths
options.explanation: High-risk paths need glob-scoped rules that trigger only on migrations. Global rules add friction everywhere else.

options.text: Global rule applied to every source file
options.explanation: A global rule applies the backup check to every edit, exactly the slowdown the scenario says is unacceptable.

options.text: Personal memory entry on each laptop
options.explanation: Personal memories are per-machine and unenforced, so the mandatory backup check would be inconsistently applied and easily missed.

options.text: Repeated ad-hoc prompt every review
options.explanation: Relying on an ad-hoc prompt each review is manual and error-prone; it does not enforce the check automatically on migration edits.

questions.scenario: Schema migrations need mandatory backup checks, but applying that check globally slows every unrelated edit.
questions.explanation:
Path-specific rules load only when editing matching files: a glob-scoped rule for migration paths enforces the backup check exactly where it matters without taxing unrelated edits, saving context and tokens versus a global rule.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 3.3 Using Path-specific Rules for Conditional Convention Loading.

questions.prompt: Which mechanism best packages this workflow?

options.text: Simple slash command prompt shortcut
options.explanation: A slash command is only a prompt shortcut; it cannot package the scripts, checklist execution, and fixed report format the audit requires.

options.text: Global CLAUDE.md style rule entry
options.explanation: A style rule in CLAUDE.md shapes conventions passively; it does not execute a multi-step audit workflow or produce a report artifact.

options.text: Permission allowlist entry for shell
options.explanation: An allowlist entry only grants permission to run commands; it carries none of the audit procedure or report contract.

options.text: Packaged Skill with helper scripts
options.explanation: Executable multi-step workflows with scripts belong in a Skill. A slash command alone is only a prompt shortcut.

questions.scenario: The security team repeats a dependency audit using scripts, an API checklist, and a fixed report format.
questions.explanation:
A repeatable procedure with instructions plus optional scripts and a fixed report format is exactly what a packaged Skill is for: versioned, reusable, and shareable. A slash-command prompt, a style rule, or an allowlist entry cannot package executable workflow steps and a report contract.

Source: Claude Platform & Solution Design, seven primitives: Package a Procedure (Skills).

questions.prompt: Which TWO permission moves balance speed and safety?

options.text: Auto-allow scoped test and format tools
options.explanation: Allowlist safe, reversible tools and gate destructive ones. Broad auto-allow or disabling prompts trades safety for speed.

options.text: Auto-allow shell deletion and force push
options.explanation: Auto-allowing deletion and force push repeats last quarter's outage: destructive, hard-to-reverse actions must require approval, not frictionless access.

options.text: Require approval for destructive database drops
options.explanation: Allowlist safe, reversible tools and gate destructive ones. Broad auto-allow or disabling prompts trades safety for speed.

options.text: Disable all permission prompts team-wide
options.explanation: Disabling prompts removes the only guardrail on destructive commands, repeating the outage with no human checkpoint at all.

questions.scenario: Developers want frictionless formatting and tests, while security fears accidental data loss. Destructive commands caused an outage last quarter. The team must choose default permissions this sprint.
questions.explanation:
Balance by risk: auto-allow the safe, high-frequency operations (scoped test and format tools) to remove friction, and require approval for destructive actions like database drops, which caused the outage. Auto-allowing deletions or disabling prompts team-wide repeats the failure.

Source: Claude Code in Action, permissions; Team Enablement & Operational Productivity, shared permission posture.

questions.prompt: What should the architect choose FIRST?

options.text: Enter plan mode to align the approach
options.explanation: Ambiguous scope plus high blast radius demands plan mode alignment first. Direct execution locks in untested assumptions.

options.text: Execute the full refactor directly now
options.explanation: Executing directly on an unclear-boundary legacy module locks in untested assumptions and risks breaking payments with no agreed approach.

options.text: Generate broad new files immediately
options.explanation: Generating broad new files before understanding the module's boundaries multiplies the blast radius and duplicates the old behavior blindly.

options.text: Skip tests for faster initial iteration
options.explanation: Skipping tests on payment logic removes the only safety net during a high-risk change, trading short-term speed for unverified correctness.

questions.scenario: A legacy payment module has unclear boundaries and no owner. A deadline tempts the team to rewrite immediately.
questions.explanation:
Large changes with unclear boundaries and multiple viable approaches are the planning-mode case: enter plan mode so Claude can explore the legacy module read-only and align the approach before any edit; direct execution or skipping tests forfeits the safety the plan provides.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 3.4 Deciding When to Use Planning Mode vs Direct Execution.

questions.prompt: Which workflow fits this fix best?

options.text: Open formal plan mode for alignment
options.explanation: Plan mode is for large ambiguous changes; a single-file typo with known expected text needs no alignment overhead.

options.text: Draft design doc before any change
options.explanation: A design doc for a one-line typo fix is pure overhead; the change is fully understood before any work begins.

options.text: Edit directly then run focused tests
options.explanation: A small well-understood fix does not need plan overhead. Direct execution with tests is faster and sufficient.

options.text: Schedule architecture review before fixing
options.explanation: An architecture review cannot improve a single error-message typo and stalls a trivial fix behind a heavyweight process.

questions.scenario: A typo breaks one error message in a single file. Tests and expected text are already clear.
questions.explanation:
A single-file typo with clear tests and expected text is the direct-execution case: edit directly and run the focused tests. Formal plan mode and architecture review are overhead this fix does not need.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 3.4 Deciding When to Use Planning Mode vs Direct Execution.

questions.prompt: Which TWO choices make the command reusable?

options.text: Store team command in user home only
options.explanation: A user-home command is personal to one machine, so other squads never discover or share the /new-service definition.

options.text: Store command in project commands directory
options.explanation: Team commands must be project-scoped with descriptive frontmatter and parameters. User-scoped or undescribed commands do not scale.

options.text: Omit description to keep files shorter
options.explanation: Without a description the command is undiscoverable — users cannot see what it does or when to invoke it in the command list.

options.text: Add frontmatter with args and description
options.explanation: Team commands must be project-scoped with descriptive frontmatter and parameters. User-scoped or undescribed commands do not scale.

questions.scenario: Every squad scaffolds services differently. The team wants one /new-service command everyone discovers and reuses.
questions.explanation:
Reusability comes from placement plus metadata: store the command in the project commands directory (shared via VCS so every squad discovers it) and add frontmatter with the argument hint and description so users know how to invoke it. A user-home copy is personal and a description-less file is undiscoverable.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 3.2 Creating and Configuring Custom Slash Commands and Skills.

questions.prompt: Which TDD loop should Claude follow?

options.text: Generate full code then add tests later
options.explanation: Generating code first bakes in whatever rounding behavior the model produced; tests written afterward tend to assert that behavior instead of the spec.

options.text: Write failing test then minimal code
options.explanation: TDD uses a tight failing-test loop with minimal implementation. Generating all code first defeats regression protection.

options.text: Copy similar tests without running them
options.explanation: Copied tests that are never run prove nothing; they may not compile, may not match the helper's contract, and provide no regression safety.

options.text: Skip red phase to save iteration time
options.explanation: Skipping the red phase means the test is never shown to fail, so it may pass vacuously and never actually guard the rounding behavior.

questions.scenario: A billing helper needs exact rounding behavior. The team wants AI assistance without losing regression safety.
questions.explanation:
Test-driven iteration writes the failing test first, then the minimal code to pass it: the rounding test encodes the expected behavior before implementation, so regression safety is structural rather than hoped for. Generating code first and adding tests later bakes in whatever behavior the model produced.

Source: Claude Code in Action, test-driven iteration; Exam Domain Notes, 3.x build test sets with expected behavior.

questions.prompt: Which CI invocation avoids hanging runners?

options.text: Run interactive session with open prompts
options.explanation: An interactive session blocks forever when an approval prompt appears with no developer present — the exact hang already happening in CI.

options.text: Pause pipeline awaiting developer input
options.explanation: Pausing for input overnight leaves runners idle and queues builds, which is the current failure mode rather than a fix.

options.text: Reuse personal login session in CI
options.explanation: A personal login in CI is an unmanaged credential with broad rights; it does not solve prompting and violates least-privilege for runners.

options.text: Run headless with fixed permissions flags
options.explanation: CI must run headless with explicit permissions and timeouts. Interactive prompts hang runners indefinitely.

questions.scenario: Claude runs hang in CI waiting for approval prompts. Builds queue while runners idle overnight.
questions.explanation:
Unattended CI runs must never wait on an approval prompt nobody is there to give. Run headless in non-interactive mode with pre-approved permission flags, so only allowlisted tools execute and anything else is auto-denied instead of hanging the runner.

Source: Claude Code in Action, headless mode and don't-ask for unattended runs.

questions.prompt: Which CI practices are sound? Select all that apply.

options.text: Pin exact Claude agent version in CI
options.explanation: Pin versions, run non-interactive, and gate risky merges by humans. Auto-merge on bot approval and secret leakage are failures.

options.text: Run agents in non-interactive CI mode
options.explanation: Pin versions, run non-interactive, and gate risky merges by humans. Auto-merge on bot approval and secret leakage are failures.

options.text: Auto-merge whenever bot review passes
options.explanation: Bot-passed auto-merge removes the human gate on irreversible merges, which is how the silent risky merges already slipped through.

options.text: Paste production secrets into prompts
options.explanation: Secrets pasted into prompts leak into logs, transcripts, and model context; credentials must stay in secret stores injected at runtime.

options.text: Require human gate for risky migrations
options.explanation: Pin versions, run non-interactive, and gate risky merges by humans. Auto-merge on bot approval and secret leakage are failures.

questions.scenario: Judge each CI integration practice as sound or unsound for team pipelines. The team mixes generated code, secrets, and auto-merge proposals. Review history shows silent risky merges already happened.
questions.explanation:
Sound: pin the agent version (reproducible pipelines), run non-interactive mode (no hanging prompts), and require a human gate for risky migrations (deterministic safety on irreversible actions). Auto-merging whenever a bot approves repeats the silent risky merges, and secrets never belong in prompts.

Source: Claude Code in Action, CI/CD pipelines; The AI-Native SDLC playbook, hooks as approval gates.

questions.prompt: What best prevents tests baking in bugs?

options.text: Anchor tests on spec plus edge cases
options.explanation: Tests must be anchored on the specification and edge cases, not on current code. Mirroring buggy output bakes bugs in.

options.text: Mirror current code output as oracle
options.explanation: Using current output as the oracle asserts the rounding bug as expected behavior, which is exactly how the generated tests already missed it.

options.text: Maximize line coverage without assertions
options.explanation: Coverage without assertions executes code but checks nothing, so the rounding bug would pass untouched no matter how much is covered.

options.text: Accept generated tests without review
options.explanation: Accepting generated tests unreviewed leaves the spec-mirroring problem in place; a human must check tests against the spec and edge cases.

questions.scenario: AI-generated tests pass yet miss a known rounding bug because they assert the buggy output.
questions.explanation:
Tests that mirror current output assert the bug as the oracle. Anchor them on the specification and edge cases (rounding boundaries, negatives), so a known bug fails the suite instead of passing it.

Source: Claude Code in Action, test-driven iteration; Exam Domain Notes, 3.x provide concrete test cases with expected outputs for edge cases.

questions.prompt: Which change best restores review trust?

options.text: Comment on every possible style nit
options.explanation: Commenting on every nit multiplies the trivial-comment flood that made developers ignore the reviewer in the first place.

options.text: Repost identical findings on each commit
options.explanation: Reposting duplicate findings on every commit adds noise without new signal, burying real defects further.

options.text: Tier severity and suppress low confidence
options.explanation: Precision comes from scoped rules, severity tiers, and suppressing low-confidence findings. More comments without tuning increases ignore rates.

options.text: Run review without scoping any paths
options.explanation: Unscoped review ranges over everything and surfaces more marginal findings, increasing the false-positive flood that eroded trust.

questions.scenario: Developers ignore the AI reviewer after floods of trivial and duplicate comments bury real defects.
questions.explanation:
High false-positive rates in some categories undermine trust in accurate ones: tier findings by severity and suppress low-confidence output so real defects are not buried under nits and duplicates. Commenting on everything and reposting findings recreate the flood.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 4.1 Designing Prompts with Explicit Criteria to Improve Accuracy.

questions.prompt: Which TWO steps should come FIRST?

options.text: Build minimal reproduction script first
options.explanation: Reproduce first, then narrow with traces and bisect. Rewriting or broadening scope before isolation wastes effort and hides cause.

options.text: Rewrite service before isolating the cause
options.explanation: Rewriting before isolating the trigger risks re-creating the same bug in new code and discards the evidence in the working service.

options.text: Broaden refactor across unrelated modules
options.explanation: Broadening scope across unrelated modules mixes unrelated changes with the investigation, making attribution of the latency spike impossible.

options.text: Narrow scope using traces and bisect runs
options.explanation: Reproduce first, then narrow with traces and bisect. Rewriting or broadening scope before isolation wastes effort and hides cause.

questions.scenario: Production checkout latency spikes only under a specific coupon mix. Logs and traces exist but nobody isolated the trigger. Pressure pushes for an immediate full rewrite.
questions.explanation:
Before touching the service, isolate the trigger: build a minimal reproduction of the failing coupon mix, and use the existing traces plus bisect runs to narrow scope. A rewrite before isolation risks re-creating the bug in new code.

Source: Claude Code in Action, debugging discipline; Team Enablement & Operational Productivity, symptom-to-cause diagnosis.

questions.prompt: Which mechanism best standardizes response?

options.text: Freeform prompt written per incident
options.explanation: Per-incident freeform prompts are the source of the divergence; each operator's improvised steps guarantee different resolutions.

options.text: Packaged Skill embedding runbook checks
options.explanation: On-call needs a packaged Skill embedding the runbook, checks, and escalation. Freeform prompting varies by operator.

options.text: Personal user memory from last on-call
options.explanation: A personal memory is one operator's recollection on one machine; it cannot standardize the response across the whole on-call rotation.

options.text: Global style rule describing incidents
options.explanation: A style rule governs code conventions passively; it does not execute the incident runbook steps or enforce escalation paths.

questions.scenario: Night incidents resolve differently per operator because each prompts Claude from memory without shared steps.
questions.explanation:
Standardizing incident response means packaging the shared steps: a Skill embedding the runbook checks gives every operator the same procedure and report, while personal memories and per-incident freeform prompts are exactly why responses diverge.

Source: Claude Platform & Solution Design, seven primitives: Skills; Team Enablement & Operational Productivity, runbooks and shared standards.

questions.prompt: Which TWO pairings place the mechanism correctly?

options.text: Team standards stored in home directory
options.explanation: A home directory is per-user storage; team standards placed there become personal configuration that never reaches the rest of the team.

options.text: Personal aliases stored in user config
options.explanation: Personal prefs belong in user config; executable workflows belong in Skills. Team standards do not belong in home dirs, nor do one-shot prompts replace Skills.

options.text: Multi-step audit as one-shot prompt
options.explanation: A one-shot prompt cannot carry the state, scripts, and step sequencing an executable multi-step audit needs to run reliably.

options.text: Executable audit workflow as Skill
options.explanation: Personal prefs belong in user config; executable workflows belong in Skills. Team standards do not belong in home dirs, nor do one-shot prompts replace Skills.

questions.scenario: Classify each mechanism-to-layer pairing as correctly or incorrectly placed. The team confuses personal config, shared config, prompts, and Skills. Several workflows broke after a misplaced config change.
questions.explanation:
Correct pairings: personal aliases belong in user config, and an executable multi-step audit workflow belongs in a Skill. Team standards in a home directory make them personal instead of shared, and a one-shot prompt cannot carry multi-step executable workflow state.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 3.1 CLAUDE.md hierarchy and 3.2 slash commands and Skills.

questions.prompt: Which resolution satisfies both constraints?

options.text: Allow all network access permanently
options.explanation: Permanent unrestricted network access removes security's control entirely, violating the constraint the denial exists to protect.

options.text: Deny installs and break the build
options.explanation: A blanket deny keeps the builds broken and releases stalled, satisfying security but failing the operational need for the registry.

options.text: Share personal credentials across runners
options.explanation: Shared personal credentials are an unmanaged, unauditable secret with broad rights; they solve neither governance nor traceability.

options.text: Scope registry exception with audit log
options.explanation: Resolve with a narrowly scoped exception plus audit, not a global allow or a blocking deny. Both extremes fail one constraint.

questions.scenario: Security denies CI network access, but builds need one trusted package registry. Releases stall while both sides refuse exceptions.
questions.explanation:
The resolution that respects both constraints is a narrowly scoped exception: allow network access only to the trusted registry, with the access audited via logs, so security keeps its control while builds unblock. Broad access, broken builds, or shared personal credentials each violate one side.

Source: Team Enablement & Operational Productivity, spend posture and guardrails; Responsible AI, Safety & Risk for Architects, least-privilege controls.

questions.prompt: Which TWO artifacts must the plan include?

options.text: Record success criteria and rollback plan
options.explanation: Plans need explicit success criteria and rollback plus phased steps. Log dumps or immediate execution skip the alignment value.

options.text: Attach raw log dumps without success criteria
options.explanation: Raw log dumps without defined criteria give no shared definition of done, which is exactly why the migration keeps restarting.

options.text: Break work into phased verifiable steps
options.explanation: Plans need explicit success criteria and rollback plus phased steps. Log dumps or immediate execution skip the alignment value.

options.text: Skip planning and execute directly now
options.explanation: Skipping planning reproduces the churn: without agreed phases and done criteria, the migration restarts yet again.

questions.scenario: A cross-service migration keeps restarting because phases and done criteria were never agreed before coding.
questions.explanation:
Plans that prevent restarts include success criteria with a rollback plan and phased, verifiable steps: each phase has a done criterion that can be checked before proceeding. Raw log dumps without criteria and skipping planning reproduce the churn.

Source: Claude Code in Action, plan mode; The AI-Native SDLC playbook, plan gates.

questions.prompt: Which debugging statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: Reproduce the failure before changing code
options.explanation: Reproduce first, change one variable at a time, and keep observability context. Fix-first or unreviewed generated fixes hide causes.

options.text: Apply generated fix before any reproduction
options.explanation: Applying a fix before reproduction is guesswork; without a repro you cannot tell whether the fix addressed the real cause or even changed anything.

options.text: Change one variable per test iteration
options.explanation: Reproduce first, change one variable at a time, and keep observability context. Fix-first or unreviewed generated fixes hide causes.

options.text: Commit AI fixes without human review
options.explanation: Committing AI fixes unreviewed repeats the past failures: unverified changes reach the codebase with no human accountable checkpoint.

options.text: Attach logs and traces to debug context
options.explanation: Reproduce first, change one variable at a time, and keep observability context. Fix-first or unreviewed generated fixes hide causes.

questions.scenario: Judge each debugging claim as sound or unsound for operational issues. The team faces flaky failures with mixed logs and traces. Past fixes were committed without reproduction or review.
questions.explanation:
Sound debugging discipline: reproduce the failure before changing code, change one variable per iteration so attribution is clean, and attach logs and traces to the debug context. Applying fixes before reproduction and committing AI fixes without review repeat the past failures.

Source: Claude Code in Action, debugging; Team Enablement & Operational Productivity, verification checklist.

questions.prompt: Which context setup best resolves the incident?

options.text: Paste only the suspect function text
options.explanation: Code review of the function alone already showed no defect; the fault only appears under load, so code text cannot contain the answer.

options.text: Ask for broad rewrite without evidence
options.explanation: Requesting a rewrite with no evidence guesses at a cause that code review already failed to reveal, risking new defects without fixing the timeout.

options.text: Feed logs, metrics, traces with scope
options.explanation: Operational faults need logs, metrics, and traces bounding the prompt. Code-only context misses environment and timing causes.

options.text: Retry same prompt with higher temperature
options.explanation: Raising temperature only randomizes responses; without load evidence the model still lacks the data the dashboards hold.

questions.scenario: An API times out only at peak load. Code review alone shows no defect, but dashboards hold the pattern.
questions.explanation:
Peak-load-only timeouts are invisible in code review; the evidence lives in telemetry. Feed the logs, metrics, and traces with a scoped question so the diagnosis is grounded in the dashboards where the pattern is observable.

Source: Claude Code in Action, debugging; Enterprise Integration & Production, observability instrumentation.

snapshot.title: Advanced Exam: Agent Architecture & Orchestration (Rebalanced)

questions.prompt: Before the refund tool runs, should you enforce verified identity in session state?

options.text: Block the refund tool unless session state holds a verified ID, adding one state check.
options.explanation: Refunds executed because verification was prompt-only and post-use. The fix is a deterministic pre-use gate on verified customer ID in session state; text parsing is spoofable and caps do not enforce

options.text: Parse assistant text for a verified token before continuing, risking spoofed text bypass.
options.explanation: Parsing assistant text for a verified token is spoofable, because the model can generate a fake 'verified' token; this adds no deterministic guarantee that identity was actually checked in state.

options.text: Stop the loop on any tool request, adding latency and breaking valid refund flows.
options.explanation: Stopping the loop on any tool request blocks every legitimate tool call, adds latency, and breaks valid refund flows; it does nothing to enforce identity verification.

options.text: Cap iterations at three to limit skips, leaving unverified refunds still executable.
options.explanation: Capping iterations only limits loop length; it does not gate the refund on verified identity, so unverified refunds remain fully executable within the cap.

questions.scenario: A refund workflow relies on a prompt plus a post-use check for identity verification. Some refunds still execute without verified state.
questions.explanation:
Identity verification before a financial operation is a deterministic guarantee, and prompt instructions provide only probabilistic compliance. A pre-use state check that blocks the refund tool unless session state holds a verified ID enforces the rule the post-use check cannot retroactively prevent.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 1.4 Implementing Multi-step Workflows with Enforcement and Handoff Patterns and 1.5 Agent SDK Hooks for Intercepting Tool Calls and Normalizing Data.

questions.prompt: What is the best architectural response to recall degradation?

options.text: Raise the cap and continue in the same context, keeping degraded recall and higher cost.
options.explanation: Raising the cap keeps the agent in the same degraded long context, so recall loss and cost grow rather than recovering; the fix is persisting findings and delegating to fresh agents.

options.text: Replace investigation with a fixed pipeline, losing adaptivity for unexpected findings.
options.explanation: A fixed pipeline strips the investigation of its adaptive loop, so unexpected findings can no longer redirect the work; it sidesteps the recall degradation instead of fixing it.

options.text: Persist findings and delegate remainder to fresh agents, ending on model completion.
options.explanation: Degradation comes from long-context recall loss, not the cap value. Persist findings, delegate remainder to fresh agents, and stop on model completion; raising the cap keeps degraded recall and cost.

options.text: Compress every result to one line after each call, discarding decisive investigation evidence.
options.explanation: Compressing every result to one line destroys decisive investigation evidence, so later synthesis loses exactly the detail the recall problem threatened.

questions.scenario: An adaptive security investigation degrades after many iterations and loses specific findings. Raising the fixed iteration cap is proposed as the main control.
questions.explanation:
Long single-context runs degrade recall, and raising an iteration cap keeps the degraded context. The adaptive value comes from persisting findings, delegating the remaining work to fresh agents, and ending on model completion rather than an arbitrary cap; a fixed pipeline would trade away the adaptivity the investigation needs.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 1.1 Designing Agentic Loops for Autonomous Task Execution and 1.6 Task Decomposition Strategies for Complex Workflows.

questions.prompt: What context must the fresh subagent receive?

options.text: Pass no context since subagents inherit history, causing blind re-investigation.
options.explanation: Subagents do not inherit coordinator history, so passing no context leaves the subagent blindly re-investigating everything instead of targeting the known inconsistency.

options.text: Pass only the summary without file evidence, forcing unverifiable conclusions.
options.explanation: A summary without the underlying file outputs is unverifiable, forcing the subagent to draw conclusions it cannot check against evidence.

options.text: Pass relevant file outputs plus the inconsistency in a structured prompt.
options.explanation: Fresh subagents do not inherit coordinator history. They need relevant per-file outputs plus the specific inconsistency framed in a structured prompt; summaries without evidence force unverifiable con

options.text: Force a first tool call with no prior findings, adding latency without direction.
options.explanation: Forcing a first tool call with no prior findings redoes work already completed and adds latency without giving the subagent direction about the inconsistency.

questions.scenario: A coordinator detects a cross-module inconsistency and reroutes a fresh subagent to investigate it. The subagent starts without prior file outputs.
questions.explanation:
Subagents do not inherit parent context, so the coordinator must explicitly include what the subagent needs: the relevant file outputs plus the inconsistency to investigate, in a structured prompt. Passing only a summary forces unverifiable conclusions; passing nothing causes blind re-investigation.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 1.3 Configuring Subagent Calls, Context Passing, and Spawning.

questions.prompt: Which declarations must each parallel subagent return? Select all that apply.

options.text: Lists the prior research inputs it actually consumed.
options.explanation: Plausible results hide missing inputs. Require each subagent to declare consumed inputs, sources, and coverage/gaps. Double execution doubles cost and sequential execution kills parallelism without gu

options.text: Names the sources consulted for its reported findings.
options.explanation: Plausible results hide missing inputs. Require each subagent to declare consumed inputs, sources, and coverage/gaps. Double execution doubles cost and sequential execution kills parallelism without gu

options.text: States coverage and gaps versus its assignment.
options.explanation: Plausible results hide missing inputs. Require each subagent to declare consumed inputs, sources, and coverage/gaps. Double execution doubles cost and sequential execution kills parallelism without gu

options.text: Runs every task twice to guarantee completeness, doubling cost.
options.explanation: Running every task twice doubles cost and still cannot reveal which inputs were skipped; explicit declarations of consumed inputs, sources, and coverage gaps are what make incompleteness detectable.

options.text: Runs all tasks sequentially to guarantee completeness, adding latency.
options.explanation: Sequential execution sacrifices parallelism and still cannot detect an omitted prior input inside a plausible result; declared coverage and gaps, not reordering, expose the incompleteness.

questions.scenario: One parallel subagent omits a required prior output but returns a plausible result. The coordinator cannot detect the incomplete input.
questions.explanation:
A coordinator cannot detect an incomplete input inside a plausible-looking result, so each subagent must declare the prior inputs it actually consumed, the sources behind its findings, and its coverage and gaps versus its assignment. Rerunning tasks sequentially or in duplicate adds cost without making incompleteness detectable.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 1.3 Configuring Subagent Calls, Context Passing, and Spawning and 5.6 Preserving Provenance and Handling Uncertainty in Multi-source Synthesis.

questions.prompt: Before assessment and handoff, which two controls guarantee order and quality?

options.text: Gate assessment on verified identity state before using retrieval results.
options.explanation: Order and handoff quality need two deterministic controls: gate assessment on verified state and validate the 3-field escalation payload before submission. Prompt examples and chaining improve style b

options.text: Validate the escalation payload with all three fields before submission.
options.explanation: Order and handoff quality need two deterministic controls: gate assessment on verified state and validate the 3-field escalation payload before submission. Prompt examples and chaining improve style b

options.text: Add prompt instructions plus a handoff example, leaving spoofed order possible.
options.explanation: Prompt instructions and examples are probabilistic, so a spoofed or skipped verification can still reorder the flow; deterministic order needs a state gate and validated payload.

options.text: Use fixed prompt chaining and trust each prompt to enforce order and format.
options.explanation: Fixed prompt chaining trusts each prompt to enforce order and format, but prompts are bypassable, leaving spoofed ordering and malformed handoffs possible.

questions.scenario: A customer workflow needs ordered retrieval and identity verification, then a validated human handoff with three required fields.
questions.explanation:
Ordering between retrieval, verification, and assessment is a deterministic guarantee, so gate assessment on verified identity state rather than trusting prompts. The human handoff should carry a structured, validated escalation payload with all required fields, since prompt guidance alone permits spoofed order and malformed handoffs.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 1.4 Implementing Multi-step Workflows with Enforcement and Handoff Patterns.

questions.prompt: How should work continue after the schema changed?

options.text: Resume the old session and reread only the schema, keeping stale assumptions.
options.explanation: Resuming the old session carries two-week-old stale schema assumptions; rereading only the schema does not correct the invalid references already baked into the context.

options.text: Start fresh with valid decisions, the new schema, and an explicit change list.
options.explanation: Two-week-old schema references are stale; resuming, forking, or compacting preserves invalid assumptions. Start fresh with valid decisions, the new schema, and an explicit change list.

options.text: Fork the stale session to explore the new schema, carrying over invalid context.
options.explanation: Forking copies the stale session, so invalid schema references are carried into the new branch instead of being replaced by the current schema.

options.text: Compact the old session before resuming, preserving outdated schema references.
options.explanation: Compaction summarizes old context but preserves its outdated schema references, so invalid assumptions survive into the resumed work.

questions.scenario: A migration session is two weeks old and its schema references are stale after renames and dropped columns.
questions.explanation:
When resumed context is stale, a fresh session with a structured summary is more reliable than resuming. The new session needs the still-valid decisions, the current schema, and an explicit change list; resuming, forking, or compacting the old session carries invalid schema references forward.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 1.7 Session State, Resuming, and Forking.

questions.prompt: What is the consequence and correct behavior for early synthesis?

options.text: Early synthesis improves latency with no completeness risk to the final answer.
options.explanation: Synthesizing after only the first result is inherently incomplete because the other parallel results have not returned, so the latency gain produces a wrong final answer.

options.text: The loop cannot continue because parallel tool calls are architecturally unsupported.
options.explanation: Parallel tool calls are fully supported; the turn simply completes once all results are incorporated, so architecture is not the limitation here.

options.text: A later automatic synthesis always overwrites the early partial synthesis result.
options.explanation: There is no mechanism that automatically overwrites an early partial synthesis; the actual problem is that early synthesis stays incomplete until all results return.

options.text: Early synthesis is incomplete; wait until all results arrive and the turn ends.
options.explanation: Three parallel tools in one turn complete only when all results are incorporated and the model ends the turn. Early custom synthesis after the first result is incomplete; later synthesis does not auto

questions.scenario: Three parallel tasks launch in one turn. Custom code synthesizes after the first result instead of waiting for loop completion.
questions.explanation:
Synthesis that runs after the first result arrives is inherently incomplete: the remaining parallel results have not returned and the turn has not ended. The coordinator must wait until all parallel results are collected and the turn completes before synthesizing.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 1.1 Designing Agentic Loops for Autonomous Task Execution and 1.3 Configuring Subagent Calls, Context Passing, and Spawning.

questions.prompt: Before execution and on timeouts, which two designs are correct?

options.text: Block amounts above $5,000 before tool execution for deterministic safety.
options.explanation: Safety needs a pre-use block above $5,000; resilience needs local retry of transient timeouts inside the subagent. Prompt-only thresholds are bypassable, post-checks act too late, and escalating every

options.text: Retry transaction-service timeouts locally inside the subagent for resilience.
options.explanation: Safety needs a pre-use block above $5,000; resilience needs local retry of transient timeouts inside the subagent. Prompt-only thresholds are bypassable, post-checks act too late, and escalating every

options.text: Put the threshold in the prompt and retry timeouts via a post-use hook.
options.explanation: A prompt-stated threshold is probabilistic and bypassable, and a post-use hook retries only after the failure has already leaked; safety needs a pre-use block and local in-subagent retry.

options.text: Check the threshold after refund and escalate every timeout upward immediately.
options.explanation: Checking the amount after the refund executes lets over-limit refunds complete, and escalating every transient timeout discards cheap local retries that would have succeeded.

questions.scenario: A refund subagent must never execute amounts above $5,000 and should handle transaction-service timeouts. Prompt-only limits are proposed.
questions.explanation:
A hard financial threshold must be enforced deterministically before execution, since prompts offer only probabilistic compliance. Transient timeouts should be retried locally inside the subagent, with only unrecoverable errors propagated upward; post-hoc checks and immediate escalation of every timeout misplace both controls.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 1.5 Agent SDK Hooks for Intercepting Tool Calls and Normalizing Data and 2.2 Implementing Structured Error Responses for MCP Tools.

questions.prompt: What is the cause and fix for the misordering?

options.text: Move normalization before tool execution, leaving old raw values still mixed.
options.explanation: Moving normalization before execution does not touch the already-recorded raw values, so old and new formats remain mixed and misordering persists.

options.text: Restart with the hook active or reissue queries so every result is normalized.
options.explanation: The hook only normalizes new results; old raw timestamps remain, so mixed formats misorder. Restart with the hook active or reissue queries so every result is normalized; moving normalization pre-exec

options.text: Tell the model to assume old values are ISO 8601, risking silent misordering.
options.explanation: Telling the model to assume old values are ISO 8601 is a probabilistic guess; wrong assumptions produce silent misordering instead of true normalization.

options.text: Rewrite the full conversation each iteration via another hook, adding heavy cost.
options.explanation: Rewriting the entire conversation each iteration is disproportionately expensive and remains a prompt-level workaround rather than normalizing the actual data.

questions.scenario: A timestamp-normalizing hook deployed mid-session leaves old raw values alongside new normalized ones. Transactions are now misordered.
questions.explanation:
A hook deployed mid-session applies only to new tool results, so old raw values and new normalized values coexist and ordering breaks. The correct behavior is to restart with the hook active or reissue the queries so every value passes through normalization; instructing the model to assume a format leaves silent misordering possible.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 1.5 Agent SDK Hooks for Intercepting Tool Calls and Normalizing Data.

questions.prompt: Match each work type to its strategy using the shared set. Select the correct mappings.

options.text: Uniform checks across 60 files -> chained convention checks. [Set: chained / focused / single / fan-out]
options.explanation: Uniform checks scale via chained convention checks; the coupled 8-file dataflow needs separate focused integration. A single open investigation blurs concerns and 60-way fan-out explodes synthesis cos

options.text: 8-file dataflow change -> focused separate integration. [Set: chained / focused / single / fan-out]
options.explanation: Uniform checks scale via chained convention checks; the coupled 8-file dataflow needs separate focused integration. A single open investigation blurs concerns and 60-way fan-out explodes synthesis cos

options.text: All files plus dataflow -> single open-ended investigation. [Set: chained / focused / single / fan-out]
options.explanation: One open-ended investigation mixes uniform convention checks with the coupled cross-file dataflow change, blurring concerns and producing neither reliable checks nor focused integration.

options.text: All 60 files -> 60 parallel agents with one-pass synthesis. [Set: chained / focused / single / fan-out]
options.explanation: Spawning 60 parallel agents for uniform checks explodes synthesis cost; uniform convention work scales better with chained checks, keeping the dataflow pass separate.

questions.scenario: A sixty-file review has uniform API checks plus one cross-file dataflow change across eight files. Decomposition is disputed.
questions.explanation:
Uniform checks across many files suit fan-out: parallel subagents with a single synthesis pass. The cross-file dataflow change is a separate focused integration pass, matching the pattern of splitting per-file analysis from cross-file integration; one open-ended investigation or chained convention checks mismatches the work's structure.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 1.6 Task Decomposition Strategies for Complex Workflows.

questions.prompt: How should the two alternatives be investigated and compared?

options.text: Explore both sequentially in one session, forcing costly mental backtracking.
options.explanation: Exploring both strategies sequentially in one session forces costly mental backtracking and risks cross-contaminating the two branches' findings.

options.text: Start two sessions from scratch without the shared analysis, redoing prior work.
options.explanation: Two from-scratch sessions discard the shared analysis, redoing work a fork would have preserved and adding cost without improving comparison quality.

options.text: Keep one path in the parent and delegate only the other, biasing comparison.
options.explanation: Keeping one path in the parent biases the comparison: the parent-held path gets richer context and attention than the delegated one.

options.text: Fork the shared context into two branches and synthesize their outputs.
options.explanation: Both strategies need the shared analysis without cross-contamination. Fork the shared context into two branches and synthesize outputs; sequential exploration forces backtracking and scratch sessions

questions.scenario: A shared analysis supports two viable migration strategies. They should be explored independently and then compared.
questions.explanation:
`fork_session` creates independent branches from the shared analysis, so both alternatives get full exploration without redoing prior work; outputs are then synthesized for comparison. Sequential exploration forces mental backtracking, and running only one path in the parent biases the comparison.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 1.7 Session State, Resuming, and Forking.

questions.prompt: Before saving, which two controls enforce least privilege and ordering?

options.text: Restrict tools to read and write only, removing email exfiltration risk.
options.explanation: Least privilege plus state gating is required: restrict tools to read/write only and gate writes on recorded scan completion. Prompt-only email bans are bypassable and checking after reading without g

options.text: Gate writes on recorded scan-completion state before any save occurs.
options.explanation: Least privilege plus state gating is required: restrict tools to read/write only and gate writes on recorded scan completion. Prompt-only email bans are bypassable and checking after reading without g

options.text: Allow email but forbid it in the prompt, leaving exfiltration still possible.
options.explanation: A prompt prohibition leaves the email tool attached, so exfiltration remains technically possible; least privilege requires removing the capability, not asking the model to avoid it.

options.text: Check completeness after reading without gating writes, allowing early saves.
options.explanation: Checking completeness only after reading provides no enforcement, so the subagent can still save before the scan completes; writes must be gated on recorded scan-completion state.

questions.scenario: A PII-redaction subagent needs read and write tools, must never email, and may save only after scan completion.
questions.explanation:
Least privilege is enforced by restricting the toolset to read and write only, removing the email exfiltration path entirely; a prompt prohibition still leaves the tool available. Ordering is enforced by gating writes on recorded scan-completion state, since prompt guidance cannot guarantee the scan finished before any save.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 1.4 Implementing Multi-step Workflows with Enforcement and Handoff Patterns.

questions.prompt: Before deploy runs, should you require a recorded test success?

options.text: Parse assistant text for a pass phrase before deploy, risking spoofed approval.
options.explanation: Assistant text is generated and spoofable, so a pass phrase proves nothing about the actual test result; deploy must gate on the recorded tool success.

options.text: Gate deploy on a recorded success result from the test tool execution.
options.explanation: Text parsing for 'tests passed' is spoofable and ordering definitions does not enforce results. Gate deploy on a recorded success result from the test tool; caps control length, not dependencies.

options.text: Order tool definitions so deploy appears after test, without checking results.
options.explanation: The order of tool definitions has no effect on execution ordering or dependencies, so deploy can still run before a successful test.

options.text: Use an iteration cap so deploy cannot occur too early, ignoring test outcome.
options.explanation: An iteration cap limits loop length only; it cannot express a dependency on the test tool's outcome, so deploy can still precede a test pass.

questions.scenario: Deployment must run only after a successful test tool result. Parsing assistant text for confirmation is proposed.
questions.explanation:
Parsing assistant text for a confirmation phrase is a documented anti-pattern: generated text can be spoofed or mistaken. The deploy must be gated on the recorded success result of the test tool execution, a programmatic precondition that cannot pass without an actual test pass.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 1.1 Designing Agentic Loops for Autonomous Task Execution and 1.4 Implementing Multi-step Workflows with Enforcement and Handoff Patterns.

questions.prompt: What is the most reliable continuation strategy near the context limit?

options.text: Discard the session and reconstruct from memory, losing provenance and accuracy.
options.explanation: Reconstructing a three-day investigation from memory loses provenance and detail, degrading accuracy even though the facts are still current.

options.text: Fork the full long context without reducing it, keeping bloat and high cost.
options.explanation: Forking the full context copies the bloat verbatim, so the new branch stays near the limit with the same high cost and no compaction benefit.

options.text: Resume the session, compact it, and continue from preserved findings.
options.explanation: Facts are still current but verbose tool output fills context. Resume, compact, and continue from preserved findings; discarding, forking full context, or deleting arbitrary messages loses provenance

options.text: Delete arbitrary prior tool messages before resuming, risking key evidence loss.
