options.explanation: Deleting arbitrary tool messages can silently remove decisive evidence; compaction summarizes deliberately and preserves findings instead.

questions.scenario: A three-day-old investigation is still factually current but near its context limit. Verbose old tool output is no longer useful.
questions.explanation:
When context is current but near its limit, resume the session and compact it: compaction summarizes the conversation so work continues from preserved findings, and `/compact` accepts instructions to keep what matters. Deleting arbitrary tool messages or reconstructing from memory risks losing decisive evidence.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 1.7 Session State, Resuming, and Forking.

questions.prompt: How should the loop behave after a pre-use block?

options.text: Terminate immediately because any blocked tool call ends the agent loop.
options.explanation: A blocked tool call does not terminate the agent loop; the denial is appended as a normal tool result, so terminating is based on a false premise.

options.text: Convert the block reason to end_turn automatically, skipping model recovery.
options.explanation: Auto-converting the denial to end_turn skips the model's chance to recover or escalate, discarding the control flow the structured denial was designed for.

options.text: Make the hook call escalation itself and end the conversation immediately.
options.explanation: The hook should not hijack the flow by calling escalation itself and ending the conversation; its job is to deny the tool and let the model choose the recovery path.

options.text: Append the denial result and continue so the model can choose escalation.
options.explanation: A pre-use block does not end the loop; its structured denial result is appended so the model can choose escalation. Treating blocks as terminal or auto-ending the turn removes the model's recovery pat

questions.scenario: A pre-use hook blocks a prohibited refund and returns a structured escalation message. The developer fears the loop will terminate.
questions.explanation:
A pre-use block does not end the agent loop: the hook's denial is appended as a tool result and the loop continues, letting the model choose an escalation path. Terminating or auto-converting the denial to `end_turn` would discard the model's opportunity to recover, and the hook itself should not hijack escalation.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 1.1 Designing Agentic Loops for Autonomous Task Execution and 1.5 Agent SDK Hooks for Intercepting Tool Calls and Normalizing Data.

questions.prompt: Match each coordinator duty to its mechanism using the shared set.

options.text: Avoid overlap -> assign non-overlapping source sets. [Set: partition / provenance / negotiate / sequence]
options.explanation: The coordinator must partition sources and require provenance for dedup. Direct negotiation adds coordination latency and sequential execution only hides overlap without attribution.

options.text: Enable dedup -> require provenance with each finding. [Set: partition / provenance / negotiate / sequence]
options.explanation: The coordinator must partition sources and require provenance for dedup. Direct negotiation adds coordination latency and sequential execution only hides overlap without attribution.

options.text: Coordinate sources -> let subagents negotiate access directly. [Set: partition / provenance / negotiate / sequence]
options.explanation: Peer-to-peer negotiation of source access adds coordination latency and races; the coordinator should own source routing and assign non-overlapping sets.

options.text: Ensure coverage -> run sequentially so later agents infer prior coverage. [Set: partition / provenance / negotiate / sequence]
options.explanation: Running sequentially does not create coverage, because later agents cannot reliably infer what was already covered; only explicit non-overlapping partitioning guarantees it.

questions.scenario: Four research subagents get no source partition. Two query the same source and synthesis duplicates findings without attribution.
questions.explanation:
The coordinator splits research coverage by assigning non-overlapping source sets, and deduplication becomes possible when every finding carries provenance. Source access is routed through the coordinator rather than negotiated peer-to-peer, and sequential execution is not what ensures coverage—explicit partitioning is.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 1.2 Orchestrating Multi-agent Systems (Coordinator–Subagent).

questions.prompt: Which THREE placements are correct? Select three.

options.text: Normalize extraction deterministically to avoid ordering errors.
options.explanation: With limited hook budget, hook what needs determinism (normalization, PII-public block) and prompt for style preference. Hooking everything wastes budget; hooking only sensitivity leaves ordering erro

options.text: Block PII labeled public deterministically for safety enforcement.
options.explanation: With limited hook budget, hook what needs determinism (normalization, PII-public block) and prompt for style preference. Hooking everything wastes budget; hooking only sensitivity leaves ordering erro

options.text: Guide summary style via prompt to save hook budget and latency.
options.explanation: With limited hook budget, hook what needs determinism (normalization, PII-public block) and prompt for style preference. Hooking everything wastes budget; hooking only sensitivity leaves ordering erro

options.text: Hook every stage including style, wasting budget and adding latency.
options.explanation: Hooking every stage including the soft style preference spends scarce deterministic-hook budget where a prompt suffices and adds latency on every call.

options.text: Hook only sensitivity and leave normalization entirely to prose.
options.explanation: Leaving normalization entirely to prose reintroduces the ordering errors the hook exists to prevent; a prompt-based format instruction is not deterministic.

questions.scenario: A document flow needs normalized extraction, a ban on labeling PII as public, and a preferred summary style. Hook budget is limited.
questions.explanation:
Hooks are deterministic guarantees, so spend them where guarantees are required: normalize the extraction format deterministically and block PII labeled public deterministically. Summary style is a soft preference that belongs in the prompt; hooking style wastes budget and latency, and leaving normalization to prose reintroduces ordering errors.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 1.5 Agent SDK Hooks for Intercepting Tool Calls and Normalizing Data.

questions.prompt: What decomposition fix prevents incompatible data shapes?

options.text: Give each agent a longer procedure but keep their inputs fully independent.
options.explanation: Longer procedures with fully independent inputs do not create a shared interface, so each agent still invents its own data shape and the incompatibility remains.

options.text: Merge all work into one agent and avoid decomposition, losing parallelism.
options.explanation: Merging everything into one agent abandons decomposition and parallelism to solve a contract problem that a shared interface fixes directly.

options.text: Define a common contract first, delegate against it, then verify integration.
options.explanation: Incompatible shapes come from independent delegation without a shared interface. Define a common contract first, delegate against it, then verify integration; longer isolated procedures or end-stage r

options.text: Let the coordinator rewrite conflicting components at the end, adding rework.
options.explanation: Rewriting conflicting components at the end is expensive rework; a shared contract defined before delegation prevents the shape conflicts from arising.

questions.scenario: Route, model, tests, and docs are delegated independently without a shared interface. Four incompatible data shapes result.
questions.explanation:
Independent delegation without a shared interface produces incompatible outputs. The fix is to define the common contract first, delegate each component against it, and then verify integration; merging everything into one agent or rewriting conflicts afterward trades away parallelism or adds rework.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 1.2 Orchestrating Multi-agent Systems (Coordinator–Subagent) and 1.3 Configuring Subagent Calls, Context Passing, and Spawning.

questions.prompt: How should delegation be reframed after brittle procedural compliance?

options.text: Specify the goal, quality criteria, and tools, allowing adaptive tool decisions.
options.explanation: Exact procedures go brittle when intermediate data surprises; mechanical completion misses quality goals. Specify goal, quality criteria, and tools while allowing adaptive tool decisions; further rest

options.text: Restrict tools further so deviation from the procedure becomes impossible.
options.explanation: Restricting tools further reduces the subagent's ability to adapt when intermediate data surprises it, deepening the brittleness instead of fixing the prompt framing.

options.text: Assign one subagent to each procedural step, multiplying handoff overhead.
options.explanation: One subagent per procedural step multiplies handoff overhead and still encodes the brittle procedure, only spread across more agents.

options.text: Add an iteration cap equal to the listed steps, preserving procedural rigidity.
options.explanation: An iteration cap equal to the step count enforces the same rigid procedure; it does not let tool decisions adapt to unexpected intermediate data.

questions.scenario: A coordinator gives an exact fifteen-step tool procedure. Unexpected intermediate data makes it complete mechanically but miss the quality goal.
questions.explanation:
Coordinator prompts should be written in terms of goals, quality criteria, and available tools rather than step-by-step procedures, so the subagent can adapt its tool decisions to intermediate results; rigid procedural compliance completed mechanically but missed the quality goal.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 1.3 Configuring Subagent Calls, Context Passing, and Spawning.

questions.prompt: Before account opening, should you require recorded KYC success and stop on end_turn?

options.text: Keep text parsing and add a sequence example, leaving spoofed completion possible.
options.explanation: Keeping text parsing leaves completion spoofable, and adding a sequence example still relies on probabilistic prompt compliance for KYC ordering.

options.text: Use a fixed iteration count and order tools in the definition list for control.
options.explanation: A fixed iteration count and tool-definition ordering control neither when the loop stops correctly nor whether KYC actually succeeded before account opening.

options.text: Stop on tool_use so the first requested action ends the loop prematurely.
options.explanation: Stopping on tool_use ends the loop at the very first requested action, before the KYC flow or onboarding work can complete.

options.text: Stop on end_turn and gate account opening on recorded KYC success.
options.explanation: Text matching 'done' is spoofable and prompt-only KYC is unenforceable. Stop on end_turn and gate account opening on recorded KYC success; fixed counts and tool ordering do not enforce outcomes.

questions.scenario: An onboarding loop stops when generated text contains 'done' and relies on a prompt to require KYC before account opening.
questions.explanation:
Parsing generated text for a completion word is an anti-pattern; the loop should stop on `stop_reason = end_turn`. Account opening is a gated action that must be blocked until the KYC tool records a success result, since prompt-based sequencing provides only probabilistic compliance.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 1.1 Designing Agentic Loops for Autonomous Task Execution and 1.4 Implementing Multi-step Workflows with Enforcement and Handoff Patterns.

questions.prompt: What indexing change fixes the failing half?

options.text: Index table rows with cell metadata
options.explanation: Text recall clears target; table-cell lookup fails because flattening destroys structure. A row-level structured index fixes the failing half.

options.text: Widen prose chunks to 1024 tokens
options.explanation: Wider prose chunks still contain flattened tables, so cell-level lookups keep failing even though more text is retrieved per hit.

options.text: Raise top-k from 5 to 15
options.explanation: Retrieving more passages cannot restore cell structure that flattening destroyed, so extra prose still lacks the row and column boundaries the metric measures.

options.text: Retrain embeddings on manuals
options.explanation: Embedding quality is not the failure; the source text lost its table structure before indexing, so retraining embeddings cannot bring cell boundaries back.

questions.scenario: Manual QA has text recall 0.90 (target 0.85) but table-cell accuracy 0.52 (target 0.80). Tables were flattened into prose before indexing.
questions.explanation: Text recall clears target; table-cell lookup fails because flattening destroys structure. A row-level structured index fixes the failing half.

questions.prompt: Which architecture best meets cost, accuracy, and date together?

options.text: Rules workflow triaging cases, LLM drafting customer rationales
options.explanation: Pure rule-based triage cannot cover the variety of return reasons, so escalations keep manual labor high and the 30% cost cut slips.

options.text: Autonomous agent negotiating refunds directly with customers
options.explanation: An agent negotiating refunds directly with customers makes probabilistic decisions on money, raising exactly the wrong-refund rate leadership froze.

options.text: Deterministic workflow routing refunds, LLM extracting reasons only
options.explanation: Deterministic routing holds the wrong-refund rate while LLM extraction cuts handling time; full agent autonomy trades accuracy for speed under a fixed date.

options.text: Fine-tuned model replacing policy engine for refund decisions
options.explanation: A fine-tuned model replacing the policy engine is probabilistic and needs retraining on every policy change, so wrong refunds rise and auditability drops.

questions.scenario: A retailer bleeds margin on manual returns triage. Leadership demands 30% cost cut in eight weeks without raising wrong refunds.
questions.explanation: Deterministic routing holds the wrong-refund rate while LLM extraction cuts handling time; full agent autonomy trades accuracy for speed under a fixed date.

questions.prompt: What dataset fix best represents risk?

options.text: Add more simple lookup cases now
options.explanation: Adding more of the case type already overrepresented deepens the skew and inflates scores while the 10% adversarial tail stays unmeasured.

options.text: Sample randomly from raw chat history
options.explanation: Random sampling from raw history reproduces noise and still underrepresents rare adversarial edges in any finite draw, so measured risk stays distorted.

options.text: Stratify to match production failure mix
options.explanation: C stratifies to production risk including the 10% adversarial tail. Costs: A inflates scores and hides risk; B preserves skew and noise; C costs curation effort; D hardens bias and false confidence.

options.text: Duplicate high-scoring cases for score stability
options.explanation: Duplicating cases the system already passes pads stability numbers without measuring anything new, hardening false confidence in the eval.

questions.scenario: Production logs show 70% simple lookups, 20% multi-step claims, and 10% adversarial edges. The eval set is 90% simple lookups.
questions.explanation: C stratifies to production risk including the 10% adversarial tail. Costs: A inflates scores and hides risk; B preserves skew and noise; C costs curation effort; D hardens bias and false confidence.

questions.prompt: How should refund authorization be enforced?

options.text: Ask the model to self-check refunds
options.explanation: A model self-check is probabilistic and steerable by prompt content, so it can approve over-limit refunds and leaves no deterministic audit trail.

options.text: Log refunds for monthly sampling review
options.explanation: Monthly sampling reviews refunds after they have already issued, so over-limit payouts still occur and are only caught late.

options.text: Enforce refund policy in tool authorization
options.explanation: Tool calls need deterministic policy enforcement on amount, recipient, and approval state. A model self-check is bypassable and unauditable.

options.text: Add agents researching each renewal history before quoting
options.explanation: Agents researching each renewal history before quoting add latency and cost per case, jeopardizing the SLA and the unit-cost goal.

options.text: Hire reviewers checking every automated renewal manually
options.explanation: Reviewers checking every automated renewal manually reintroduce human cost per case, erasing the efficiency the automation was meant to deliver.

questions.scenario: An insurer wants efficiency from renewal automation. The board demands lower unit cost with no SLA regression.
questions.explanation: Efficiency requires both unit-cost reduction and SLA preservation; pure automation without the guardrail converts cost savings into breach penalties.

questions.prompt: Which TWO are progressive discovery? Select both.

options.text: Searchable catalog loading schemas on demand
options.explanation: Progressive discovery loads schemas on demand and scopes per intent; full injection and prompt-stuffed secrets are monolithic context. Full mapping: A progressive, B monolithic, C progressive, D monol

options.text: Full 150 schemas injected every turn
options.explanation: Injecting all 150 schemas every turn is monolithic context by definition, the opposite of loading schemas on demand per intent.

options.text: Task-scoped subset injected per intent now
options.explanation: Progressive discovery loads schemas on demand and scopes per intent; full injection and prompt-stuffed secrets are monolithic context. Full mapping: A progressive, B monolithic, C progressive, D monol

options.text: All runbooks plus secrets in system prompt
options.explanation: All runbooks plus secrets in the system prompt is monolithic injection, and it also exposes secrets regardless of intent.

questions.scenario: Classify each tool-context design as progressive discovery or monolithic context. Progressive means schemas load on demand per intent. Monolithic injects everything every turn.
questions.explanation: Progressive discovery loads schemas on demand and scopes per intent; full injection and prompt-stuffed secrets are monolithic context. Full mapping: A progressive, B monolithic, C progressive, D monolithic.

snapshot.description: Full-length 63-question mock, blueprint-weighted: Integration 12, Solution Design 11, Evaluation 10, Governance 9, Stakeholder 9, Models/Prompting/Context 8, Developer 4. New-format v1-short-multiresponse. 120 minutes.

snapshot.title: Advanced Exam: Tool Design & MCP Integration (Rebalanced)

questions.prompt: Which redesign addresses routing and failure semantics?

options.text: Keep both tools and steer compliance searches via prompt preference.
options.explanation: Prompt preferences cannot fix the underlying problem: the two overlapping tool descriptions still leave the model to guess which applies, and a silent success with empty results during an archive outage would still trigger the refund. Steering by prose leaves both failure modes untouched.

options.text: Split the tools by scope and return a structured access error on outage.
options.explanation: Overlapping tools cause misrouting, and silent success on outage causes the refund cascade. Differentiated tools plus a structured access error fix both routing and failure semantics.

options.text: Force the archive tool for every compliance-related user message.
options.explanation: Forcing a tool guarantees it is called but does nothing about the overlapping descriptions that cause misrouting, and it still lets an unreachable archive surface as success with empty results. The refund cascade would continue unchanged.

options.text: Merge all sources and keep successful empty results during outages.
options.explanation: Merging makes routing ambiguity worse by widening the single tool's applicability, and preserving successful empty results during outages means an access failure is still indistinguishable from no matches, so the incorrect refund still happens.

questions.scenario: Two search tools overlap. A compliance search misses an unreachable archive yet returns success with empty results, triggering an incorrect refund.
questions.explanation:
Overlapping tool descriptions cause misrouting, so split the general search into scoped tools with distinct applicability boundaries. An unreachable archive is an access failure, not a valid empty result, so the tool must return a structured error that distinguishes it from no matches; returning success with empty results led to the incorrect refund.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 2.1 Designing Tool Interfaces with Clear Descriptions and 2.2 Implementing Structured Error Responses for MCP Tools.

questions.prompt: Which design best reduces misrouting?

options.text: Rewrite misrouted fetch calls in a post-use hook after execution.
options.explanation: Rewriting after execution means the wrong tool has already run with the wrong reference, so side effects or bad data may already have landed. Misrouting must be fixed at selection time through clear tool boundaries, not patched retroactively.

options.text: Remove ambiguous verbs only from the system prompt text.
options.explanation: Tool descriptions, not the system prompt, are the primary selection signal, so editing prompt wording leaves the broad fetch tool overlapping the dedicated tools. The ambiguity that causes misrouting remains intact.

options.text: Scope external retrieval to its tool; reserve customer/local data.
options.explanation: The broad fetcher overlaps dedicated tools. Scoping external retrieval to its tool and reserving customer/local data for dedicated tools removes ambiguity at selection time.

options.text: Extend the customer tool to retrieve every URL and file.
options.explanation: Widening the customer tool increases the overlap instead of removing it, making selection between it and the local-file tool even more ambiguous. This moves in the opposite direction from a clear per-tool contract.

questions.scenario: A broad fetch tool overlaps customer-record and local-file tools. The model sends internal and local references to the wrong tool.
questions.explanation:
Ambiguous, overlapping descriptions cause misrouting. Removing the broad fetch tool and scoping external retrieval to its own tool, while reserving customer and local data for their dedicated tools, gives each tool a clear contract; post-hoc rewrites or wider tool scopes do not fix the selection problem.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 2.1 Designing Tool Interfaces with Clear Descriptions.

questions.prompt: How should execution and safety be enforced?

options.text: Force the SQL tool on every turn and forbid DROP in prose.
options.explanation: Forcing on every turn over-corrects: the SQL tool should only be forced on query turns, and a prose prohibition on destructive statements is not an enforcement mechanism and can be ignored by the model.

options.text: Use any tool choice and block destructive output afterward.
options.explanation: Leaving choice as any does not solve the skipped-execution problem, and filtering the output afterward means the destructive statement may already have been generated; blocking must happen server-side before execution.

options.text: Keep auto choice and rely on a read-only tool description.
options.explanation: Auto choice is exactly why the tool is sometimes skipped, and a description claiming read-only is only advisory — the model can still issue destructive statements that nothing deterministically rejects.

options.text: Force SQL only for query turns and reject DDL/DML server-side.
options.explanation: Skipped execution needs forced routing on query turns; destructive input needs server-side rejection. Prompt prose or output filtering alone is bypassable.

questions.scenario: A SQL tool under auto choice is sometimes skipped and sometimes receives destructive statements.
questions.explanation:
`tool_choice` solves execution, not safety: forced selection guarantees the SQL tool runs on query turns, while destructive statements must be blocked by a deterministic server-side check, since a tool description alone cannot be relied on to enforce authorization.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 2.3 Allocating Tools Across Agents and Configuring tool_choice.

questions.prompt: Select the changes that together fix isolation and partial-outage masking (Select TWO.)

options.text: Replace the general tool with tenant-scoped domain tools.
options.explanation: Tenant-scoped tools enforce boundaries; structured partial-failure errors stop masked outages. Together they fix isolation and observability; either alone is incomplete.

options.text: Return structured partial-failure errors instead of silent success.
options.explanation: Tenant-scoped tools enforce boundaries; structured partial-failure errors stop masked outages. Together they fix isolation and observability; either alone is incomplete.

options.text: Add tenant_id but keep the broad tool and silent partial success.
options.explanation: A tenant_id parameter does not give the tool a scoped description that improves selection in a large toolset, and keeping silent partial success still masks outages so downstream decisions keep consuming incomplete data.

options.text: Inject missing tenant fields after the tool returns.
options.explanation: Post-return field injection is a cosmetic fix: it neither establishes tenant isolation at the data-access boundary nor surfaces partial outages, so silently incomplete results still propagate into downstream decisions.

questions.scenario: A general multi-tenant data tool lacks tenant boundaries and masks partial outages. Silent partial success propagates into downstream decisions. A large co-located toolset worsens selection.
questions.explanation:
A large co-located toolset reduces selection reliability, so the general tool should be replaced with tenant-scoped domain tools. A partial outage must surface as a structured partial-failure error rather than silent success, because silent partial success propagates into downstream decisions.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 2.1 Designing Tool Interfaces with Clear Descriptions, 2.2 Implementing Structured Error Responses for MCP Tools, and 2.3 Allocating Tools Across Agents and Configuring tool_choice.

questions.prompt: Phase 1 — verification is indeterminate. Which gate prevents the refund cascade?

options.text: Block refunds only when account_id is null.
options.explanation: The account_id is present in this scenario, so the gate never fires; the problem is a pending verification status being read as verified. Null-checking an unrelated field does nothing to stop the refund.

options.text: Return transient indeterminate error; require verified status to refund.
options.explanation: Success with pending status must not read as verified. A transient indeterminate error plus a verified-status gate blocks the refund cascade and permits retry.

options.text: Use auto tool choice so verification can be skipped in outages.
options.explanation: Skipping verification during an outage makes the refund decision even less informed, and tool choice has no bearing on how a pending verification status is interpreted. This would widen the failure, not gate it.

options.text: Add 'verify first' instruction to the refund tool description.
options.explanation: A description instruction is advisory prose, not an authorization check: the coordinator can still read a pending status as verified and issue the refund. Enforcement must be a deterministic gate on verified status.

questions.scenario: Account verification returns success with pending status during an outage. The coordinator treats success as verified and issues a refund.
questions.explanation:
Success with a pending status during an outage is an indeterminate result, not a verified one. The tool must return a transient indeterminate error so the coordinator faces a retry decision, and the refund must require an explicit verified status; prose instructions in a tool description cannot enforce this authorization.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 2.2 Implementing Structured Error Responses for MCP Tools.

questions.prompt: Select the correct handling for each failure class (Select THREE.)

options.text: Retry the timeout with backoff and keep successful partials.
options.explanation: Timeout is retryable, invalid range is locally repairable, quota exhaustion must propagate with partial coverage. Blanket retries waste calls and discard useful partials.

options.text: Repair the invalid date range locally without another call.
options.explanation: Timeout is retryable, invalid range is locally repairable, quota exhaustion must propagate with partial coverage. Blanket retries waste calls and discard useful partials.

options.text: Propagate quota status with explicit partial-result coverage.
options.explanation: Timeout is retryable, invalid range is locally repairable, quota exhaustion must propagate with partial coverage. Blanket retries waste calls and discard useful partials.

options.text: Retry every failure uniformly, then return one generic error.
options.explanation: A uniform retry treats a non-retryable validation error and a permanent quota exhaustion as if they were transient, wasting calls without progress, and collapsing everything into one generic error discards which partial results succeeded — exactly the coverage the caller needs.

questions.scenario: Paper search returns a timeout, an invalid date range, and quota exhaustion. Blanket retries waste calls and discard successful partial results.
questions.explanation:
Failure classes require different handling: timeouts are transient and retryable with backoff, invalid input is a validation error to repair locally without another call, and quota exhaustion must be propagated with explicit coverage of which partial results succeeded. A uniform blanket retry discards successful partial results and prevents correct recovery decisions.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 2.2 Implementing Structured Error Responses for MCP Tools.

questions.prompt: How should the cases be distinguished?

options.text: Return retryable transient error and mark affected stock unknown.
options.explanation: Null conflates genuinely out-of-stock with unreachable warehouse. A retryable transient error plus unknown marking blocks backorder creation and enables retry.

options.text: Treat null as unknown through prompt instructions alone.
options.explanation: Prompt instructions are advisory: the tool still returns null, so the conflation between a confirmed empty result and an access failure persists in the data itself. Downstream consumers reading the raw value can still trigger backorders.

options.text: Force another stock call whenever any null value appears.
options.explanation: Forcing a retry on every null wastes calls on legitimately out-of-stock items, and if the warehouse remains unreachable the second call returns null again, so backorder creation is still possible.

options.text: Convert null to false in a post-use hook after return.
options.explanation: Converting null to false asserts a confirmed out-of-stock state that was never verified, which is precisely what triggers the backorders. The access failure remains masked, just with a different misleading value.

questions.scenario: Stock lookup returns null with a warehouse-unreachable note. The coordinator reads null as out of stock and creates backorders.
questions.explanation:
A null caused by an unreachable warehouse is an access failure that requires a retry decision, not a valid empty result. The tool must return a structured transient error and mark the affected stock as unknown, because prompt instructions or post-return conversion cannot distinguish missing data from a confirmed value.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 2.2 Implementing Structured Error Responses for MCP Tools.

questions.prompt: Which mitigation best limits the second-order failure?

options.text: Raise retry limits so real transient failures get more time.
options.explanation: Raising limits gives the mislabeled validation errors even more room to multiply across orchestration levels, increasing call volume without any progress. The root cause — a non-retryable error classified as retryable — is untouched.

options.text: Fingerprint errors and stop identical retries on unchanged input.
options.explanation: Mislabeled validation errors retry identically at every layer. Fingerprinting input+error and refusing identical retries breaks the multiplicative cascade.

options.text: Trust errorCategory and ignore the isRetryable field.
options.explanation: In this scenario the category itself is wrong (validation labeled transient), so trusting one field over the other does not fix the misclassification. Identical retries at every level would continue.

options.text: Retry only at the coordinator, never inside subagents.
options.explanation: Restricting retries to one level reduces but does not eliminate the loop: the coordinator will still retry the same mislabeled validation error indefinitely on unchanged input. The classification error itself remains.

questions.scenario: A tool mislabels validation failures as transient. Identical retries fire at multiple orchestration levels. Call volume multiplies without progress.
questions.explanation:
A validation error mislabeled as transient becomes retryable at every orchestration level, multiplying calls without progress. Fingerprinting the error and stopping identical retries on unchanged input breaks that loop; raising limits or trusting only one error field leaves the mislabeling in place.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 2.2 Implementing Structured Error Responses for MCP Tools.

questions.prompt: Which redesign preserves capability while improving selection?

options.text: Keep all tools and require some tool call on every turn.
options.explanation: Requiring a call every turn does not shrink the overlapping toolset, so the model still picks poorly among too many similar tools — and now it must also fabricate unnecessary calls on turns where none is needed.

options.text: Add a classifier tool while keeping all tools on one agent.
options.explanation: Adding a classifier grows the already-overloaded toolset and merely relocates the routing problem to another selection the model must make. The overlapping tools on one agent remain untouched.

options.text: Merge all domains into one broad handle_request tool.
options.explanation: A single broad tool sacrifices the distinct capabilities each domain tool provided and reintroduces the same ambiguity inside one interface. Capability is reduced, not preserved, and selection guidance does not improve.

options.text: Route to role-specific subagents with small relevant toolsets.
options.explanation: One agent with a large overlapping toolset cannot select reliably. Role-specific subagents with small relevant toolsets preserve capability while shrinking each selection space.

questions.scenario: One generalist agent holds a large overlapping toolset with poor selection. The team proposes forcing a tool call on every turn.
questions.explanation:
Too many tools per agent reduces selection reliability, and tools outside an agent's specialization tend to be misused. Routing to role-specific subagents with small, relevant toolsets preserves capability while improving selection; forcing a call on every turn does not fix the overlap that causes poor choice.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 2.3 Allocating Tools Across Agents and Configuring tool_choice.

questions.prompt: Phase 1 — credit retrieval fails for missing consent. How is order and attribution preserved?

options.text: Remove ordering and let the model choose each next step.
options.explanation: Removing ordering abandons the workflow guarantee that underwriting runs only after a successful credit check, which is exactly the dependency the scenario violates. It trades a sequencing bug for arbitrary, unguaranteed step order.

options.text: Keep forcing and add a warning to underwriting's description.
options.explanation: A description warning is advisory: forced selection will still execute underwriting after the credit failure, so the misleading missing-input error and the misattributed failure point persist unchanged.

options.text: Gate underwriting on credit success; propagate consent errors directly.
options.explanation: Forced sequencing without gating executes underwriting on missing consent, producing a misleading second error. Gating plus direct consent-error propagation preserves order and attribution.

options.text: Map the later missing-input error back to consent after execution.
options.explanation: Post-hoc remapping is a heuristic patch over a symptom: the underwriting call still runs on missing prerequisites and can fail for other reasons, making the reverse mapping unreliable. Attribution should come from gating, not guessing after the fact.

questions.scenario: A forced loan workflow calls underwriting even after credit retrieval fails for missing consent. The second call emits a misleading error. Attribution now points at the wrong step.
questions.explanation:
Forcing a tool ensures execution order but cannot make a failed prerequisite succeed. The workflow should gate underwriting on credit success and propagate the consent error directly, so attribution stays on the step that actually failed instead of surfacing later as a misleading missing-input error.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 2.2 Implementing Structured Error Responses for MCP Tools and 2.3 Allocating Tools Across Agents and Configuring tool_choice.

questions.prompt: Which redesign respects specialization?

options.text: Keep the shared tool and omit only obviously irrelevant URLs.
options.explanation: Manual filtering of only 'obviously' irrelevant URLs is unreliable and still hands each role a general-purpose loader, so cross-role retrieval of invoice or ticket URLs can continue whenever a URL looks plausibly relevant.

options.text: Move all URL access up to the coordinator agent.
options.explanation: Centralizing URL access at the coordinator does not give either subagent a role-scoped tool, and the coordinator now fetches content for both domains without a specialization boundary. The mixed-retrieval problem is relocated, not resolved.

options.text: Rename the shared tool identically in both subagents.
options.explanation: Renaming changes nothing about the tool's behavior or scope: both roles still share one general URL loader and both still receive invoice and ticket URLs, so cross-role retrieval continues exactly as before.

options.text: Give each role its loader and pass only role-relevant URLs.
options.explanation: A shared general loader plus unfiltered URLs guarantees cross-role retrieval. Role-specific loaders with only role-relevant URLs enforce specialization at the data plane.

questions.scenario: Billing and support subagents share a general URL tool and both receive invoice and ticket URLs, causing cross-role retrieval.
questions.explanation:
Agents with tools outside their specialization misuse them. Each role should hold its own loader and receive only role-relevant URLs, which respects the specialization boundary instead of relying on shared tool access and manual filtering.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 2.3 Allocating Tools Across Agents and Configuring tool_choice.

questions.prompt: How should context bloat be reduced without losing linting?

options.text: Force search during exploration and lint on every later turn.
options.explanation: Forcing tool calls on turns is a blunt workaround that doesn't fix the misleading 'analyzes code' description, and it over-constrains turns where neither pattern applies. The selection boundary is still undefined.

options.text: Remove custom file tools and rely only on lint output.
options.explanation: Relying only on lint output eliminates the search and read capability the exploration needs, so context bloat is replaced by an inability to investigate. Capability is destroyed rather than correctly routed.

options.text: Drop linting and invoke an equivalent command through Bash.
options.explanation: Dropping the lint tool loses its description-based selection guidance entirely, and routing the same linting through Bash reintroduces the same context-heavy outputs without fixing why exploration misuse happened.

options.text: Scope lint to verification-only; direct exploration to search/read.
options.explanation: A verification tool described as general analysis gets misused for exploration. Scoping lint to verification-only and routing exploration to search/read keeps capability while cutting context bloat.

questions.scenario: A lint tool described as 'analyzes code' is used for exploration, producing huge outputs instead of lightweight search and reads.
questions.explanation:
Tool descriptions are the primary selection mechanism, so a lint tool described as 'analyzes code' invites use for exploration. Scoping lint to verification-only and directing exploration to search and read tools fixes the selection problem while keeping linting available; removing linting or forcing tool calls addresses the symptom, not the description boundary.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 2.1 Designing Tool Interfaces with Clear Descriptions.

questions.prompt: Select the correct shared-configuration practices (Select THREE.)

options.text: Commit server definitions to shared project configuration.
options.explanation: Server definitions belong in shared project config, secrets belong in environment variables, and an available community ticket server should be reused instead of duplicated.

options.text: Inject tokens via environment variables, never hardcoded secrets.
options.explanation: Server definitions belong in shared project config, secrets belong in environment variables, and an available community ticket server should be reused instead of duplicated.

options.text: Adopt the available community ticket server over a duplicate.
options.explanation: Server definitions belong in shared project config, secrets belong in environment variables, and an available community ticket server should be reused instead of duplicated.

options.text: Keep user scope and distribute tokens through team chat.
options.explanation: User scope keeps team integrations invisible to other collaborators, and sharing tokens through team chat exposes the secret in plaintext history with no revocation path. Both practices contradict shared-config and environment-variable injection.

questions.scenario: Team MCP integrations are user-scoped; one hardcodes a personal token and another duplicates an available community ticket server.
questions.explanation:
Team MCP servers belong in shared project configuration (`.mcp.json`) rather than user scope, and tokens should be injected through environment variable substitution instead of being hardcoded. For standard integrations, prefer an existing community server over building a duplicate.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 2.4 Integrating MCP Servers into Claude Code and Agent Workflows.

questions.prompt: Select all the changes that reduce exploration and improve selection. (Select TWO.)

options.text: Expose the schema catalog as a first-class MCP resource.
options.explanation: Repeated describe calls signal undiscoverable schema. Exposing the catalog resource plus enriching tools with columns, relations, and examples lets the model plan without exploration calls.

options.text: Enrich table tools with columns, relations, and examples.
options.explanation: Repeated describe calls signal undiscoverable schema. Exposing the catalog resource plus enriching tools with columns, relations, and examples lets the model plan without exploration calls.

options.text: Merge all tables into one unrestricted query-any-table tool.
options.explanation: Merging tables into one unrestricted tool removes the per-table descriptions that carry applicability information, making selection guidance worse. It also invites unscoped queries rather than reducing exploration.

options.text: Require some table tool immediately via forced tool choice.
options.explanation: Forcing a table tool guarantees a call but not a correct one: with minimally described tools the model still lacks the schema knowledge to pick and query well, so exploratory describe calls continue.

questions.scenario: A database server exposes many minimally described table tools. The model repeatedly calls describe operations. An available schema catalog resource goes unused.
questions.explanation:
MCP resources act as content catalogs (such as database schemas) that reduce exploratory tool calls, so the schema catalog should be a first-class resource. Enriching the table tools' descriptions with columns, relations, and examples gives the model the applicability boundaries it currently lacks; merging tables or forcing a call removes the description guidance that drives selection.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 2.4 Integrating MCP Servers into Claude Code and Agent Workflows and 2.1 Designing Tool Interfaces with Clear Descriptions.

questions.prompt: Which change addresses collision and overload?

options.text: Namespace tool names; connect each role subagent to one server.
options.explanation: Colliding names plus a large flat toolset breaks selection. Namespacing removes collision and one-server-per-subagent shrinks each selection space.

options.text: Disable one server and rebuild its functions with shell commands.
options.explanation: Rebuilding server functions as shell commands recreates the same overlapping capability in a less structured form, and it forfeits the server's own tool descriptions and error handling. Collisions simply reappear as overlapping shell tools.

options.text: Force the colliding tool and rely on server ordering for choice.
options.explanation: Forcing a specific colliding tool hard-codes one choice regardless of task, and server ordering is an incidental detail the model cannot meaningfully reason about. Neither addresses the name collisions or the oversized toolset.

options.text: Keep all tools and explain duplicate names in the prompt.
options.explanation: Prompt prose cannot disambiguate tool invocations, and keeping all servers connected preserves the large flat toolset that degrades selection. The structural causes remain in place.

questions.scenario: Several MCP servers expose overlapping toolsets with colliding names. Selection reliability is poor.
questions.explanation:
Colliding tool names and large overlapping toolsets both degrade selection. Namespacing tool names removes ambiguity across servers, and connecting each role's subagent to a single server keeps each toolset small and role-relevant, the documented fix for poor selection reliability.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 2.3 Allocating Tools Across Agents and Configuring tool_choice and 2.4 Integrating MCP Servers into Claude Code and Agent Workflows.

questions.prompt: Select the fixes for scope and silent authentication failure (Select THREE.)

options.text: Move the server to shared project configuration for CI.
options.explanation: User scope plus hardcoded expiring token plus silent 401-as-null produces defective summaries in CI. Project config, environment token, and retryable 401 errors fix scope, secret, and observability.

options.text: Inject the token from the environment instead of hardcoding.
options.explanation: User scope plus hardcoded expiring token plus silent 401-as-null produces defective summaries in CI. Project config, environment token, and retryable 401 errors fix scope, secret, and observability.

options.text: Surface 401 as a structured retryable error, never silent null.
options.explanation: User scope plus hardcoded expiring token plus silent 401-as-null produces defective summaries in CI. Project config, environment token, and retryable 401 errors fix scope, secret, and observability.

options.text: Keep user scope and retry whenever a summary field is null.
options.explanation: Retrying on null summary fields treats an authentication failure as a data problem: the 401 will recur on every call while the scope and hardcoded-token defects persist. Null-triggered retries mask the root cause instead of surfacing it.

questions.scenario: CI uses a user-scoped ticket server with a hardcoded expiring token. A 401 returns as successful null data. Defective summaries propagate downstream.
questions.explanation:
CI is a team workflow, so the ticket server belongs in shared project configuration with the token injected from the environment rather than hardcoded and expiring. A 401 is an access failure and must surface as a structured, retryable error; returning successful null data lets defective summaries propagate downstream.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 2.4 Integrating MCP Servers into Claude Code and Agent Workflows and 2.2 Implementing Structured Error Responses for MCP Tools.

questions.prompt: Which strategy should have been used?

options.text: Read and rewrite every matching file in full.
options.explanation: Whole-file rewrites discard the surgical precision Edit is designed for and produce large diffs that collide with parallel changes to the same files. Broad discovery plus full rewrites is exactly the pattern that clobbered them.

options.text: Run a global in-place replacement across the repository.
options.explanation: A global replacement acts on raw text with no per-match validation, so unintended occurrences of the name (comments, strings, unrelated identifiers) get renamed silently. It also gives no opportunity to review each change site.

options.text: Grep occurrences, then Edit each with enough context.
options.explanation: Glob plus whole-file rewrite loses parallelism and clobbers edits. Grep for occurrences then Edit each with enough context for uniqueness keeps changes surgical.

options.text: Force Edit without changing its ambiguous match input.
options.explanation: Forcing Edit on ambiguous anchors defeats its safety rejection without resolving the ambiguity, so the underlying multiple-match problem remains and each call still fails or needs guessing.

questions.scenario: A rename uses broad file discovery then whole-file rewrites when Edit finds multiple matches. Parallel changes are clobbered.
questions.explanation:
Incremental understanding starts with Grep to locate occurrences, then targeted Edits with enough context to make each match unique. Whole-file rewrites after ambiguous matches discard the precision that Edit is designed for and invite parallel changes to clobber one another.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 2.5 Selecting and Applying Built-in Tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Grep, Glob).

questions.prompt: Which strategy balances safety and success?

options.text: Apply one multi-file patch for speed.
options.explanation: A single multi-file patch can partially apply, leaving some files changed and others untouched — an inconsistent state across coordinated changes. Speed here trades away the atomicity the scenario needs.

options.text: Expand Edit context per change; use full rewrite only if needed.
options.explanation: A multi-file patch risks partial application across files. Expanding Edit context per change with whole-file fallback only when necessary keeps each change atomic and validated.

options.text: Invoke the same patch through Bash instead of MCP.
options.explanation: Running the same patch through Bash changes the invocation channel, not the partial-application risk: an interrupted run still leaves files half-changed. The failure mode is unchanged.

options.text: Force the patch tool so validation cannot interrupt it.
options.explanation: Disabling validation makes partial application more likely and harder to detect, since interrupted or invalid diffs proceed unchecked. Removing safety checks worsens the exact risk the patch tool carries.

questions.scenario: Edit safely rejects ambiguous anchors; a patch tool can partially apply multi-file diffs. Several files need coordinated changes.
questions.explanation:
Edit's rejection of ambiguous anchors is a safety property, not an obstacle. The balanced strategy expands the context per change until the anchor is unique and falls back to a full rewrite only when needed; a partially applied multi-file patch trades correctness for speed and can leave files inconsistent.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 2.5 Selecting and Applying Built-in Tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Grep, Glob).

questions.prompt: Which incremental strategy is best?

options.text: Read all files completely to avoid missing hidden dependencies.
options.explanation: Exhaustive full reads are exactly what exhausted the context, and wrapper modules that merely re-export the target contribute no signal. Reading everything trades the investigation's token budget for redundancy.

options.text: Search names and aliases first, then read only matching sections.
options.explanation: Exhaustive full reads explode context when wrappers alias the target. Searching names and aliases first then reading only matching sections and wrappers minimizes tokens while preserving recall.

options.text: List files and read them from smallest to largest.
options.explanation: File size has no relationship to relevance: a small wrapper re-exporting the target matters more than a large unrelated module. This ordering heuristic still reads everything eventually and exhausts context.

options.text: Spawn one reader per file and retain every summary.
options.explanation: Retaining a summary of every file reintroduces the same unfiltered volume in compressed form, and parallel readers cannot see the alias relationships between wrappers that the investigation needs to trace.

questions.scenario: Bug investigation reads every imported file fully. Wrapper modules re-export the target under aliases, and context is exhausted.
questions.explanation:
Building understanding incrementally means searching for the names and aliases first (wrapper modules re-export the target under different names) and reading only the matching sections. Reading every imported file fully exhausts context without adding signal; Grep locates, Read traces the specific flow.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 2.5 Selecting and Applying Built-in Tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Grep, Glob).

questions.prompt: Which design guides selection without over-constraining it?

options.text: Force Grep for every search request.
options.explanation: Forcing literal search on every request discards semantic search entirely, so conceptual lookups where the exact wording is unknown lose their best tool. It over-constrains instead of guiding selection.

options.text: Delete semantic search and use literal search exclusively.
options.explanation: Deleting semantic search removes a genuine capability for conceptual queries where no exact string is known. The failure came from a boundary problem, not from the tool existing.

options.text: Rerank semantic results with Grep after every call.
options.explanation: Post-hoc reranking does not stop the model from choosing semantic search for literal lookups in the first place, and it adds an extra call to every search. The selection boundary remains undefined.

options.text: Scope semantic search to concepts; force Grep for literal lookups.
options.explanation: Broad semantic search hallucinates approximate matches for exact strings. Narrowing it to conceptual use while forcing Grep only for tagged literal lookups guides selection without removing capability.

questions.scenario: A broad semantic_search tool is chosen for exact error-string lookup and returns approximate hallucinated matches instead of using Grep.
questions.explanation:
Grep is the tool for literal content search such as exact error strings; semantic search suits conceptual lookups. Scoping each tool's description to its applicability boundary guides selection without over-constraining it, whereas forcing one tool for every search request discards the other capability.

Source: Exam Domain Notes, 2.1 Designing Tool Interfaces with Clear Descriptions and 2.5 Selecting and Applying Built-in Tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Grep, Glob).

snapshot.title: Exam Scenarios: Integration v1

questions.prompt: Which change closes the actual authorization gap?

options.text: Log every tool call together with its producing token
options.explanation: compliance-theater — logging records misuse after the fact; any foreign token is still accepted.

options.text: Issue a single shared service token for all sessions
options.explanation: convenience-over-safety — one shared token collapses per-user authorization and widens the blast radius.

options.text: Validate audience binding and mint a separate downstream token
options.explanation: Audience binding stops replayed foreign tokens at the door, and a separately minted downstream token replaces pass-through; both facts in the review are addressed.

options.text: State the token requirements in each tool description
options.explanation: prompt-as-guarantee — tool descriptions guide the model, they enforce nothing at the protocol layer.

questions.scenario: A security review of the travel-booking MCP server (Streamable HTTP) found that tokens minted for other resource servers are accepted, and that every downstream call to the booking API reuses whatever bearer token the client arrived with.
questions.explanation: Confused deputy: without audience binding any resource server's token replays, and passing the client's token upstream means the MCP server never establishes its own credential. Decisive: the review found two facts — acceptance and pass-through — so the fix must change both: validation and a separately-minted downstream token.

questions.prompt: Which retrieval change addresses both symptoms?

options.text: Retrieve more chunks per query to raise recall
options.explanation: knobs-not-design — more of the same near-identical chunks raises noise, not discriminability.

options.text: Swap the embedding model for a larger variant
options.explanation: scale-not-strategy — serials that are near-identical stay near-identical in a larger embedding space.

options.text: Re-embed the manuals at each weekly publication
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — freshness improves, but the lexical miss on TR-90442-B remains.

options.text: Fuse keyword and vector search, weighted by query type
options.explanation: Keyword/exact matching wins where embeddings lose — the serial — and query-type weighting keeps concept questions on the vector side; both symptoms, one change.

questions.scenario: A fleet-manuals assistant answers concept questions reliably, but lookups by exact trailer serial such as TR-90442-B fail half the time — the serials share near-identical embeddings — and the manuals are re-published weekly.
questions.explanation: Decisive: the two failures have different mechanics — near-identical embeddings lose lexical discriminability, while re-publication is a freshness cycle. Only a hybrid, query-weighted index serves both; every other option fixes one failure or neither.

questions.prompt: Which TWO actions fit the evidence? Select both.

options.text: Expand every tool description for clearer discrimination
options.explanation: louder-not-explicit — longer descriptions add tokens to every call; near-duplicates stay near-duplicates.

options.text: Prune unused and overlapping tools before adding more
options.explanation: Pruning the unused third shrinks exactly the surface the failures scale with, before the queued six enlarge it.

options.text: Move to a stronger model to handle the bigger catalogue
options.explanation: scale-not-strategy — failures grew with catalogue size, not with model capability.

options.text: Serve the catalogue through progressive discovery per intent
options.explanation: Progressive discovery keeps the model's working set at intent-size, so the queued growth stops compounding the error.

questions.scenario: An internal agent fronts 48 integration tools from six departments; selection accuracy has slipped as tools were added, latency grew with every addition, and a third of the catalogue saw no production call this quarter, while six more departmental tools are already queued.
questions.explanation: The measured evidence is catalogue bloat: unused third, slipping selection, growing latency, more additions queued. Decisive: shrink the working set now (prune) and keep it small as growth continues (progressive discovery) — both act on the measured cause.

questions.prompt: What should the architect do for this month's launch?

options.text: Ship direct now; revisit MCP at the second consumer
options.explanation: Direct meets the p99 today; the revisit trigger (second consumer) arrives next quarter, so the costly migration is not owed yet.

options.text: Wrap payments in MCP so the coming services inherit it
options.explanation: valid but early — inheritance benefits accrue next quarter while the p99 breach and new-host risk land this month.

options.text: Put MCP behind a cache to recover the added latency
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — a checkout check is not repeated within any TTL; the hop, and its latency, remain.

options.text: Proxy the launch through the existing chat agent's MCP
options.explanation: extra-hop — coupling the launch deadline to the chat agent's deploy adds the same latency problem it was meant to dodge.

questions.scenario: The payments check runs inline at checkout, where the direct REST call meets the 800 ms p99 at 99.9% success; the new MCP wrapper adds 180 ms and needs a new host, and while one service consumes it today, two more go live next quarter.
questions.explanation: Decisive: this month's launch has one consumer and a hard p99; MCP's reuse value arrives next quarter. The phase-gate for adopting the wrapper is the second consumer — it hasn't happened yet.

snapshot.description: Pilot of the exam_scenarios level: 4 Integration items with valid-but-inferior distractors, criterion hidden mid-stem.

snapshot.title: Exam Scenarios: Full A (60Q, 7 domains)

questions.prompt: What should the architect change?

options.text: Split the work across subagents coordinated by one orchestrator
options.explanation: over-orchestration — a coordinator plus subagents adds delegation overhead where a single call covers the whole task.

options.text: Upgrade the loop to the largest reasoning model tier
options.explanation: scale-not-strategy — a bigger model does not fix a pattern that is wrong for a bounded, deterministic task and raises cost further.

options.text: Add a longer system prompt that forbids looping retries
options.explanation: prompt-as-guarantee — instructions are guidance, not enforcement, and leave the unnecessary agent loop in place.

options.text: Replace it with a single augmented call plus a schema
options.explanation: A bounded, single-shot extraction is the case for one augmented call: the simplest solution meeting the requirement comes first and structure is added only when a measured failure demands it, cutting the loop and its cost.

questions.scenario: A telecom-ops team built an agent to pull four named fields out of outage notifications: one document in, one JSON record out, no branching and no open-ended reasoning. In production the agent loops on retries and costs three times the estimate, and leadership wants the extraction reliable and cheap, not smarter.
questions.explanation: A bounded, single-shot extraction is the case for one augmented call: the simplest solution meeting the requirement comes first and structure is added only when a measured failure demands it, cutting the loop and its cost.

questions.prompt: Which design principle does this follow?

options.text: Index frequent snapshots of past order history for faster recall
options.explanation: valid-but-early — a prebuilt index serves stable reference material, but the contract here is with a value that changes minute to minute.

options.text: Make an external system the call-time source of truth
options.explanation: Retrieval indexes static documents and stale snapshots, so it is the wrong tool for values that change during the conversation; answering from live state queried at call time is exactly the mechanism the notes prescribe.

options.text: Fine-tune the model on past order records each quarter
options.explanation: stale-fact — weights learned last quarter carry yesterday's statuses, which is precisely the staleness the constraint rules out.

options.text: Cache frequently asked order answers at the network edge
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — caching answers shortens the path but still serves the 10:00 snapshot to the 10:05 question.

questions.scenario: A retail order-lookup assistant answers where my order questions from production traffic. A proposal suggests calling the live order-status API and returning the retrieved record rather than trusting model knowledge, because the correct answer at 10:00 can be wrong at 10:05.
questions.explanation: Retrieval indexes static documents and stale snapshots, so it is the wrong tool for values that change during the conversation; answering from live state queried at call time is exactly the mechanism the notes prescribe.

questions.prompt: What architecture fits these tickets?

options.text: Route each classified ticket to its specialized single handler
options.explanation: Routing classifies an input and directs it to a specialized follow-up task, which is well suited when distinct categories are better handled separately; stable, well-understood categories are exactly the routing case, fixing both the overpay and the shallow handling.

options.text: Add one autonomous agent for every ticket category
options.explanation: over-orchestration — per-category agent loops are heavier than the dispatch to specialized single handlers they replace.

options.text: Cache the shared prompt prefix to cut token cost
options.explanation: premature-optimization — caching trims the cost of the wrong design while every ticket still takes one undifferentiated path.

options.text: Grow the catch-all prompt with instructions per category
options.explanation: louder-not-explicit — piling more instructions into one prompt stays less maintainable and never separates the categories.

questions.scenario: An IT service desk sends every inbound ticket, password resets, laptop procurement, security incidents, and billing questions, through one identical high-reasoning configuration with a giant catch-all prompt. Simple tickets are slow and overpaying, security tickets get the same shallow handling as password resets, and the categories are stable and well understood.
questions.explanation: Routing classifies an input and directs it to a specialized follow-up task, which is well suited when distinct categories are better handled separately; stable, well-understood categories are exactly the routing case, fixing both the overpay and the shallow handling.

questions.prompt: Which pattern fits each requirement?

options.text: Agent for both, since both take several steps
options.explanation: over-orchestration — granting planning autonomy to a fixed extract-validate-quote chain pays for flexibility the sequence never uses.

options.text: Workflow for both, hardened until forensics becomes predictable
options.explanation: prompt-as-guarantee — predefining steps for an inquiry whose next step is discovered mid-task replaces adaptation with guesswork.

options.text: Single augmented call for both, keeping the design simplest
options.explanation: valid-but-early — sufficient for the extraction step alone, but neither a fixed sequence nor adaptive investigation fits in one call.

options.text: Fixed workflow for quotes, autonomous agent for forensics
options.explanation: A workflow wires fixed steps in your code, exactly what a requirement that never varies needs; the investigation whose path emerges from intermediate results is the case for an agent planning its sequence. Each requirement gets the pattern it needs.

questions.scenario: A logistics fulfillment suite runs a quotes pipeline in which every request extracts shipment details, validates them against a rate card, and generates a quote. Requirements are stable and the steps never vary, while a parallel incident-forensics workstream only reveals its next diagnostic step from what the previous query returned.
questions.explanation: A workflow wires fixed steps in your code, exactly what a requirement that never varies needs; the investigation whose path emerges from intermediate results is the case for an agent planning its sequence. Each requirement gets the pattern it needs.

questions.prompt: Select TWO. Which conditions justify the multi-agent choice?

options.text: The synthesis is strictly linear, each step consuming the previous
options.explanation: over-orchestration — a dependent sequence is prompt chaining, not parallel breadth-first work; splitting it into agents adds coordination the task cannot use.

options.text: The problem is breadth-first with many independently explorable directions
options.explanation: Multi-agent systems earn their keep on breadth-first queries: many independent directions can be pursued at once, which is precisely the shape of a landscape scan.

options.text: Reducing total token consumption per run is the primary goal
options.explanation: scale-not-strategy — multi-agent designs spend more tokens than a single chat, so picking them to cut cost inverts the documented trade-off.

options.text: Every thread's source material exceeds a single context window
options.explanation: When source material exceeds one window, parallel subagents each carrying their own isolated window is exactly the mechanism that helps; isolated context per subagent is what raises coverage without overflowing.

questions.scenario: A pharma competitive-landscape assistant scans dozens of independent research threads: trials, patents, and publications. Each thread's source material exceeds a single context window on its own, per-run cost stays acceptable, and leadership wants coverage of the whole landscape improved, not per-thread polish. The proposal on the table is a coordinator dispatching isolated subagents.
questions.explanation: Multi-agent systems earn their keep on breadth-first queries: many independent directions can be pursued at once, which is precisely the shape of a landscape scan.

questions.prompt: How should the verification requirement be enforced?

options.text: Restate the verification rule once more at the prompt's start
options.explanation: louder-not-explicit — repeating wording adds emphasis, not an enforcement point; the payout can still precede verification.

options.text: Raise the model tier so that instruction adherence improves
options.explanation: scale-not-strategy — adherence improves statistically while the requirement stays probabilistic, which the controller does not accept.

options.text: Add a programmatic precondition that blocks payouts before verification
options.explanation: Programmatic enforcement, hooks and preconditions, gives a deterministic guarantee where prompt guidance stays probabilistic; blocking the downstream call until a verified customer ID exists is exactly the mechanism for requirements that must never be skipped.

options.text: Summarize the twelve confirmation flows into the policy prompt
options.explanation: prompt-as-guarantee — an enlarged prompt documents what should happen while the ordering still depends on the model remembering it.

questions.scenario: An insurance-claims platform executes refunds through a refund agent that holds a six-thousand-token policy prompt and a history of twelve accepted confirmation flows. The controller requires that no payout runs before customer identity is verified, and so far compliance rests entirely on wording in the prompt.
questions.explanation: Programmatic enforcement, hooks and preconditions, gives a deterministic guarantee where prompt guidance stays probabilistic; blocking the downstream call until a verified customer ID exists is exactly the mechanism for requirements that must never be skipped.

questions.prompt: Which overlooked property explains this?

options.text: Knowledge boundary, since new resume formats appeared
options.explanation: stale-fact — nothing in the incident is about training data; the same inputs produced differing outputs.

options.text: Context rot, because long sessions degraded recall
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — accuracy here degraded across identical short jobs, not inside an accumulating session window.

options.text: Non-determinism, so demos cannot certify repeated behavior
options.explanation: The same input can produce different outputs across runs, which is why evaluation frameworks exist: you cannot certify behavior you only observed once; a clean demo is not evidence of determinism.

options.text: Working-memory limits, because documents exceeded the window
options.explanation: scale-not-strategy — the requests were small; a window ceiling would return errors, not divergent categorizations.

questions.scenario: A recruiter-ops team shipped its resume-parsing agent after a demo ran cleanly five times, then built the reconciliation accounting around outputs that repeated exactly. In week two of production the same statement, reprocessed, produced a different categorization, and the discrepancy surfaced only when an analyst re-ran a batch.
questions.explanation: The same input can produce different outputs across runs, which is why evaluation frameworks exist: you cannot certify behavior you only observed once; a clean demo is not evidence of determinism.

questions.prompt: What should the architect record first?

options.text: The four discovery buckets: do, not-do, cost, prove
options.explanation: A preference like seamless signals that discovery is needed, not a requirement; forcing the statement into what the system must do, must not do, must cost, and must prove turns it into testable, bounded constraints the design can build against.

options.text: A reference architecture that realizes the stated preference
options.explanation: valid-but-early — the pattern matters, but selecting it against an untested experience word inherits assumptions into the design.

options.text: A translation of the vendor's preferences into constraints
options.explanation: valid-but-early — translating is the right move, but without the four question buckets the yield stays whatever happens to come up.

options.text: The escalation path for cases the assistant cannot resolve
options.explanation: valid-but-early — a handoff rule is one likely constraint, yet it emerges from the must-not-do category rather than anchoring the whole call.

questions.scenario: A SaaS vendor briefs the architect that the deployment must feel seamless to the pharmacy operations staff who will live in it daily. The team is tempted to sketch the retrieval design immediately, because the brief sounds precise enough to start building against this week.
questions.explanation: A preference like seamless signals that discovery is needed, not a requirement; forcing the statement into what the system must do, must not do, must cost, and must prove turns it into testable, bounded constraints the design can build against.

questions.prompt: How should these choices be structured?

options.text: The direct route, for flexibility in renegotiating the agreement
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — the route is chosen for the cloud commitment, while the entry point serves the user, so one layer cannot dictate the others.

options.text: AWS Bedrock, because the existing BAA agreement covers it
options.explanation: compliance-theater — the same model underneath does not merge the questions; each layer answers to a different stakeholder.

options.text: Google Vertex, since another health network runs there
options.explanation: Entry point is chosen for the user and the work, build-time interface for the engineering team, delivery route for cloud commitments and compliance posture; three conversations with three different stakeholders, and one layer rarely dictates the others.

options.text: Microsoft Foundry, to diversify the model provider dependency further
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — convenience for the coding team answers the build-time question only and leaves the audience and procurement decisions unfixed.

questions.scenario: A registrar workflows builder is choosing how its public exam-booking assistant talks to Claude. Engineers want SDK convenience, the operations director wants branch staff to use one shared workflow, and procurement wants the request traffic inside the university's existing Google Cloud agreement.
questions.explanation: Entry point is chosen for the user and the work, build-time interface for the engineering team, delivery route for cloud commitments and compliance posture; three conversations with three different stakeholders, and one layer rarely dictates the others.

questions.prompt: Which delivery route fits?

options.text: The direct route, for flexibility in renegotiating the agreement
options.explanation: valid-but-early — flexibility is real but costs a second agreement negotiation, while one route is already covered.

options.text: AWS Bedrock, because the existing agreement covers it
options.explanation: Governance and regulated-industry constraints rule out a route before any cost or latency trade-off applies; the agreement that already covers the governed configuration closes the compliance question, exactly how the healthcare-network case is decided in the notes.

options.text: Google Vertex, since another capital-markets desk runs there
options.explanation: stale-fact — another deployment's precedent does not extend this network's agreement; coverage is what decides.

options.text: Microsoft Foundry, to diversify the model provider dependency
options.explanation: gold-plating — adding a third route adds procurement and operations surface with no requirement in the brief behind it.

questions.scenario: A medical-records assistant drafts clinical documentation from dictated notes. The network holds its business-associate agreement with AWS, runs standardized there, and the competing proposal would sign a separately negotiated agreement on the direct route. The record retains its clinical-authorization rule whatever the route, and only one configuration is already covered by the existing agreement.
questions.explanation: Governance and regulated-industry constraints rule out a route before any cost or latency trade-off applies; the agreement that already covers the governed configuration closes the compliance question, exactly how the healthcare-network case is decided in the notes.

questions.prompt: What explains the late-shift lapses?

options.text: The accumulated history finally reached the window limit
options.explanation: stale-fact — the scenario says the window is far from its limit; an exceeded edge errors the request instead of bending recall.
