options.text: Attention degraded well before the window's hard limit
options.explanation: Context that accumulates turn over turn pays cost and latency scaling linearly with input, and attention quality can degrade on long contexts well before the hard limit; that is the mid-morning codes coming unstitched while the morning answers stayed accurate.

options.text: The model tier is too small for billing work
options.explanation: scale-not-strategy — the morning answers were correct on the same tier; capability is not what changed by late afternoon.

options.text: A prompt edit shifted the insurance code definitions
options.explanation: prompt-as-guarantee — nothing reports a prompt change, and the same instructions produced the correct morning codes.

questions.scenario: A hospital group's charge-capture assistant joins physician rounds, and its context accumulates patient, volume, and billing notes turn over turn through a twelve-hour shift. By late afternoon the clerk's mid-morning insurance codes come back unstitched while the bill still passes, and the afternoon cost per prompt runs visibly higher. The window is far from its limit, and nothing failed.
questions.explanation: Context that accumulates turn over turn pays cost and latency scaling linearly with input, and attention quality can degrade on long contexts well before the hard limit; that is the mid-morning codes coming unstitched while the morning answers stayed accurate.

questions.prompt: What explains the near-zero cached reads?

options.text: Enable a second breakpoint immediately after the promotions banner
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — a second breakpoint still freezes a prefix that changes on every call, so reads stay near zero.

options.text: Move the static policy text into each user message
options.explanation: knobs-not-design — relocating blocks does not alone create a stable prefix; the dynamic fields still lead every request.

options.text: Place the dynamic fields after the policy and breakpoint there
options.explanation: Caches match identical prefixes, and a breakpoint marks where the prefix ends. With dynamic fields first, the shared static tail sits after them, so nothing before the breakpoint repeats; ordering static content first, with the breakpoint on its last block, turns the policy into cheap reads.

options.text: Double the model tier so the long prompt processes faster
options.explanation: scale-not-strategy — the prompt already fits the window; a bigger model changes neither the prefix order nor its reuse.

questions.scenario: A retail support bot answers policy questions at 4,000 conversations a day, and its engineers prepend the current date, the store id, and a rotating promotions banner to the top of the system prompt, followed by eight thousand tokens of static policy text. Caching was switched on, yet usage shows reads at almost zero and the latency budget keeps slipping.
questions.explanation: Caches match identical prefixes, and a breakpoint marks where the prefix ends. With dynamic fields first, the shared static tail sits after them, so nothing before the breakpoint repeats; ordering static content first, with the breakpoint on its last block, turns the policy into cheap reads.

questions.prompt: What restores the lost conversation context?

options.text: Resend the complete conversation history with every new API request
options.explanation: The API is stateless: it stores nothing between requests, so memory lives entirely in what the client resends. Appending each assistant reply and sending the full history restores the reference every follow-up question needs.

options.text: Store the transcript in the portal and show it above replies
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — a readable transcript improves the interface while the model still never receives prior turns in the request.

options.text: Tell the model inside the prompt to remember earlier answers
options.explanation: prompt-as-guarantee — instructions cannot reference turns the request never carried; guidance does not substitute for the missing history.

options.text: Lower the sampling temperature so replies track the newest question
options.explanation: knobs-not-design — sampling controls affect wording variety, not which turns of the conversation reach the model.

questions.scenario: An insurance claims portal lets adjusters keep chatting with a claims-explainer assistant, but since the last deployment follow-up questions like 'summarize that in one line' return answers about the wrong claim, because the integration ships only the newest user question to the API while the conversation keeps growing on screen.
questions.explanation: The API is stateless: it stores nothing between requests, so memory lives entirely in what the client resends. Appending each assistant reply and sending the full history restores the reference every follow-up question needs.

questions.prompt: Why does caching produce no savings?

options.text: The one-hour cache lifetime expires between these sparse calls
options.explanation: stale-fact — the hour matters only after something qualifies; nothing here ever entered the cache to expire.

options.text: Raise every diagnostic prompt above one thousand padded tokens
options.explanation: valid-but-early — padding prompts past the threshold can qualify them, yet short, varying diagnostics rarely amortize the write.

options.text: Cache the generated answers so repeated questions skip generation
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — the cache stores input preprocessing work, not the generated answers, so copying questions buys nothing.

options.text: Content below the 1024-token minimum never qualifies for caching
options.explanation: Caching has a minimum threshold: everything being cached must sum to at least 1024 tokens. These brief, ever-changing diagnostics sit far under it, so each request is processed and billed as ordinary input and usage shows no read.

questions.scenario: A telecom diagnostics agent examines one network device at a time; its entire prompt, instructions included, measures roughly three hundred tokens, and each device's question differs from the previous one. Operations enabled prompt caching expecting cost relief, yet the usage report still shows ordinary input tokens, and month-end cost review finds no relief at all.
questions.explanation: Caching has a minimum threshold: everything being cached must sum to at least 1024 tokens. These brief, ever-changing diagnostics sit far under it, so each request is processed and billed as ordinary input and usage shows no read.

questions.prompt: Select TWO. Which statements match documentation?

options.text: Prompt caching stores the generated answers rather than the input
options.explanation: stale-fact — the cache stores input preprocessing work, so the model still generates every answer fresh at reply time.

options.text: Cached prefixes still occupy the window; caching changes their price
options.explanation: A cached prefix remains fully present in the context; the usage fields distinguish cheap cache reads from fresh processing. Caching is a billing optimization, so the fix for sagging late-conversation quality is curation, not a billing change.

options.text: Cache reads prove the history no longer consumes window space
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — reads measure the billing side, not occupancy; the cached prefix still sits fully in the window, so a read proves price, never presence.

options.text: Changing one character inside the cached prefix forces a fresh write
options.explanation: Cache content must be identical up to the breakpoint; even adding one word invalidates it and pushes the changed portion through a fresh, costlier cache write.

questions.scenario: A hospital discharge-summary service carries every prior conversation turn in the window and just enabled prompt caching, yet engineering still debates what the feature actually buys. One engineer claims cached history stops crowding the context; another claims a one-character edit to the summary guidelines defeats the whole cache. Select the TWO statements the documentation supports.
questions.explanation: A cached prefix remains fully present in the context; the usage fields distinguish cheap cache reads from fresh processing. Caching is a billing optimization, so the fix for sagging late-conversation quality is curation, not a billing change.

questions.prompt: What should gate enabling extended thinking?

options.text: Enable thinking by default since deeper reasoning reliably lifts accuracy
options.explanation: knobs-not-design — deeper reasoning helps some tasks, but the documented order still puts prompt optimization first at far less latency.

options.text: Enable thinking only when also upgrading to the strongest model
options.explanation: scale-not-strategy — pairing thinking with a bigger model stacks two latency costs before evaluations show either one is needed.

options.text: Exhaust prompt optimization first; think only if accuracy stays short
options.explanation: The documented rule: evaluate without thinking first, and enable extended thinking only when accuracy still misses requirements after prompt optimization. Thinking tokens are billed as output and add latency, which the two-second inline target pays for on every interaction.

options.text: Raise the sampling temperature so the generation explores more possibilities
options.explanation: knobs-not-design — temperature reshuffles word choice rather than adding the reasoning steps the failing scores want.

questions.scenario: A legal-ops team's clause-extraction prompt scores below target on its evaluation, and the senior partner wants answers faster, not slower. A colleague proposes enabling extended thinking immediately to raise quality. The existing bill already treats thinking tokens as output, and the workflow must stay under a two-second latency target for inline reviewer assistance.
questions.explanation: The documented rule: evaluate without thinking first, and enable extended thinking only when accuracy still misses requirements after prompt optimization. Thinking tokens are billed as output and add latency, which the two-second inline target pays for on every interaction.

questions.prompt: How should the model decision be made?

options.text: Move every workload to the flagship because premium quality pays
options.explanation: scale-not-strategy — the most capable tier spends more on workloads whose quality the labeled outputs already measure.

options.text: Keep Sonnet the default; move tiers only when evaluations justify it
options.explanation: Sonnet balances intelligence, speed, and cost, so it stays the production default. Moving up needs an eval proving the quality bar is missed; moving down needs proof the quality tradeoff holds. The weekly labeled outputs supply exactly that evidence.

options.text: Move every workload to the cheapest tier because cost dominates
options.explanation: eval-blindness — cost alone cannot confirm the cheaper tier holds quality; no measurement defends the downgrade.

options.text: Split the workloads randomly across both tiers to hedge the bet
options.explanation: knobs-not-design — random hedging ignores the labeled evidence the team already collects; model decisions are meant to be measured, not reflexive.

questions.scenario: A settlements team runs one reconciliation summarizer on Sonnet. The CFO wants premium quality everywhere and an engineer wants the cheapest model everywhere, and both proposals would change every workload at once. The team does collect labeled reconciliation outputs every week from the banking reviewers, yet nobody has agreed what better would even mean before switching.
questions.explanation: Sonnet balances intelligence, speed, and cost, so it stays the production default. Moving up needs an eval proving the quality bar is missed; moving down needs proof the quality tradeoff holds. The weekly labeled outputs supply exactly that evidence.

questions.prompt: Which refinement targets the stubborn misclassifications?

options.text: Rewrite the category instructions once more, now more explicitly
options.explanation: louder-not-explicit — rewriting the same rule a third time restates the boundary the reports already miss; demonstration stays absent.

options.text: Upgrade to the most capable reasoning model now available
options.explanation: scale-not-strategy — the current tier handles routine reports fine; capability is not what the failing corner cases lack.

options.text: Lower the sampling temperature so classifications become consistent
options.explanation: knobs-not-design — variance in wording is not the reported symptom; the category boundary itself is what fails.

options.text: Add examples of the failing reports, labeled, within tags
options.explanation: Examples show rather than tell: the failing, sarcastic, unusually worded reports become sample input and ideal output pairs, the documented remedy for corner cases that instructions cannot capture. Delimiting tags keep each pair clearly separated from the surrounding instructions.

questions.scenario: A freight-claims assistant classifies damage reports as approved, rejected, or escalated. Straightforward photographic reports classify cleanly, but sarcastic surveyor remarks and unusually worded adjustment notes keep coming back wrong. Two prompt rewrites have not closed the gap, and the team archives every classified report together with its final grading.
questions.explanation: Examples show rather than tell: the failing, sarcastic, unusually worded reports become sample input and ideal output pairs, the documented remedy for corner cases that instructions cannot capture. Delimiting tags keep each pair clearly separated from the surrounding instructions.

questions.prompt: Which context strategy addresses all symptoms?

options.text: Retrieve only the document sections that each question needs
options.explanation: Cost and latency scale linearly with input length, and attention quality can degrade on very long contexts well before the hard limit. Progressive loading sends only what the current question needs, cutting both while lifting mid-document reliability.

options.text: Upgrade to the largest-window model and keep the full dossier
options.explanation: scale-not-strategy — a larger window raises the ceiling while linear cost and attention degradation both continue inside it.

options.text: Cache the dossier so repeated questions skip its preprocessing
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — caching skips preprocessing of the prefix while the full dossier still ships, costs, and dilutes attention on every call.

options.text: Review the dossier with several parallel subagents on every question
options.explanation: over-orchestration — several full-dossier reviews multiply the very input length the symptoms blame, multiplying cost and latency too.

questions.scenario: A cadastre team scanned ninety years of property records into one knowledge base. Today the assistant pastes the entire matched dossier, sometimes five hundred pages, into the window on every question, so each inquiry is slow and expensive, and answers citing deeds buried mid-document come back less reliably than answers citing the opening pages.
questions.explanation: Cost and latency scale linearly with input length, and attention quality can degrade on very long contexts well before the hard limit. Progressive loading sends only what the current question needs, cutting both while lifting mid-document reliability.

questions.prompt: Which integration approach fits this requirement?

options.text: Freeze EHR changes until the three integrations converge on one schema
options.explanation: valid-but-early — convergence never arrives while each team keeps its own definitions and deploys on its own cadence, so the divergence this question describes persists.

options.text: Move the EHR calls into one shared library every team forks
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — a forked shared library drifts apart exactly like today's schemas, so the three-way maintenance burden survives the refactor untouched.

options.text: Expose the EHR functions through MCP servers any application can reach
options.explanation: An MCP server centralizes the tool definitions and the vendor integration in one place, so a single tested update reaches every connected application at once instead of through three divergent forks.

options.text: Grant each application direct database credentials to read EHR tables
options.explanation: convenience-over-safety — raw database credentials couple every application directly to the storage schema and bypass the vendor's contractual interface entirely.

questions.scenario: A hospital network runs three separate Claude applications, discharge summaries, coding support, and referral triage, and each integration team maintains its own hand-written tool definitions for the same EHR functions. Whenever the EHR vendor ships an update, all three teams patch their schemas independently, and the fixes reach production at different speeds.
questions.explanation: An MCP server centralizes the tool definitions and the vendor integration in one place, so a single tested update reaches every connected application at once instead of through three divergent forks.

questions.prompt: Which transport should this connection use?

options.text: Keep stdio but tunnel the streams through a permanent SSH tunnel
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — a tunnel masks the hop, but stdio still requires the client to launch the server as a subprocess on the same machine.

options.text: Switch the integration to streamable HTTP across the two networks
options.explanation: stdio only works when client and server run on the same machine, while streamable HTTP carries the JSON messages between networked hosts, which is exactly what a second data center demands.

options.text: Embed the conversion service directly inside the pricing engine process
options.explanation: scale-not-strategy — collapsing the service into one application couples the pricing engine to conversion logic and answers nothing about the remote deployment requirement.

options.text: Duplicate the server beside each client and use stdio locally
options.explanation: gold-plating — duplicating the service beside every client multiplies deployment, versioning, and consistency work just to avoid a networked transport.

questions.scenario: A retailer's pricing engine needs a currency-conversion MCP server. During the pilot, the platform team launched the server as a subprocess on the same VM, exchanging messages over standard input and output. Now the conversion service must run in another data center, and the transport assumption quietly breaks.
questions.explanation: stdio only works when client and server run on the same machine, while streamable HTTP carries the JSON messages between networked hosts, which is exactly what a second data center demands.

questions.prompt: Which pattern should absorb these failures?

options.text: Fail over to a smaller model whenever 429 responses appear
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — a different model tier does not govern admission control; 429 responses concern request pacing, not model capability, so the incidents repeat.

options.text: Move to the enterprise tier so the rate limits disappear
options.explanation: scale-not-strategy — higher limits move the threshold, but the burst behavior, the 429 semantics, and the incident noise stay exactly the same.

options.text: Enqueue every single request through a second fairness-queueing service
options.explanation: over-orchestration — a queueing layer adds infrastructure between the caller and the API without implementing the documented cure for transient 429 and 529 responses.

options.text: Retry transient responses with exponential backoff, waits doubling each attempt
options.explanation: 429 and 529 are transient conditions that normally clear with backoff, so exponentially longer waits, typically doubling each attempt, absorb the afternoon bursts without ever failing the whole rebalancing run.

questions.scenario: A portfolio-rebalancing service calls the Claude API during North American market hours, when request volume triples. Every afternoon the integration logs bursts of HTTP 429 and 529 responses, the on-call rotation treats each one as a sev-2 incident, and the service fails the whole rebalancing run when a single burst arrives.
questions.explanation: 429 and 529 are transient conditions that normally clear with backoff, so exponentially longer waits, typically doubling each attempt, absorb the afternoon bursts without ever failing the whole rebalancing run.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the MCP handshake is correct?

options.text: The client's InitializeRequest triggers a capabilities reply from the server
options.explanation: valid-but-early — the InitializeRequest does open the exchange, but it names only the first message; the early failures come from tool calls fired before the exchange completed.

options.text: The Initialized Notification requires a matching result from the server
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — the Initialized Notification is the one handshake message sent without expecting any reply, so awaiting a result stalls every connection at startup.

options.text: Tool calls are only valid after the three-message exchange completes
options.explanation: The specification sequences InitializeRequest, InitializeResult with capabilities, and the Initialized Notification before anything else, so tool calls issued ahead of the exchange are precisely the version-dependent failures the reviewers saw.

options.text: stdio connections may skip initialization when the server was used before
options.explanation: convenience-over-safety — assuming remembered state skips the required handshake, yet every MCP connection, stdio included, starts from the same three-message initialization.

questions.scenario: A telecom integration team adds its first MCP server to a network-operations assistant, and reviewers question when protocol state actually begins. The connection currently issues ListToolsRequests immediately after the transport opens, before any capability exchange, and some early calls fail depending on the server version.
questions.explanation: The specification sequences InitializeRequest, InitializeResult with capabilities, and the Initialized Notification before anything else, so tool calls issued ahead of the exchange are precisely the version-dependent failures the reviewers saw.

questions.prompt: What restores reliable tool selection?

options.text: Rewrite all eighteen tool descriptions with much longer, detailed wording
options.explanation: louder-not-explicit — longer descriptions do not remove the overlap that produced the misselections; eighteen partly relevant tools still ride along on every single call.

options.text: Scope each conversation's toolset to the four or five role-relevant tools
options.explanation: Selection reliability drops as the registered tool count grows, so each conversation performs best when it sees only the handful of tools its role actually needs, with cross-role utilities narrowly granted.

options.text: Upgrade to a stronger model before touching any tool configuration
options.explanation: scale-not-strategy — a stronger model does not shrink the catalogue that diluted selection; the traced billing-utility misselections would recur on the same eighteen choices.

options.text: Force the model to justify its choice before every invocation
options.explanation: knobs-not-design — a spoken justification adds latency and tokens while the competing, oversized catalogue that caused the wrong pick remains unchanged.

questions.scenario: A litigation-support assistant exposes eighteen registered tools covering docket pulls, citation checks, billing timers, calendar booking, and matter updates. Tool-selection accuracy keeps slipping, and traces show the model selecting billing utilities during research questions, because every conversation carries every tool.
questions.explanation: Selection reliability drops as the registered tool count grows, so each conversation performs best when it sees only the handful of tools its role actually needs, with cross-role utilities narrowly granted.

questions.prompt: How should live status reach the model?

options.text: Retrieve the newest dispatch snapshot from the nightly indexed corpus
options.explanation: stale-fact — a snapshot that was correct at ten can be wrong at 10:05, because retrieved data may already be stale by the time the model reads it.

options.text: Re-embed the dispatch corpus every fifteen minutes around the clock
options.explanation: knobs-not-design — quarter-hourly re-embedding narrows the staleness window but never closes it, and dispatch state keeps moving between indexing runs.

options.text: Increase retrieval depth so more tracking articles reach the context
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — deeper retrieval raises recall over the same stored articles; the returned-to-depot case stays wrong until the next nightly indexing run completes.

options.text: Call the dispatch system through a tool whenever status is needed
options.explanation: Retrieval suits static or slow-moving knowledge, but an answer that changes by the minute needs the system of record, so a tool call to dispatch delivers the true current state at question time.

questions.scenario: A freight carrier's support assistant answers delivery-status questions from a knowledge base indexed nightly, and customers receiving out-for-delivery answers for parcels already returned to the depot are filing complaints. The tracking status lives in the dispatch system and changes several times per hour, while the indexed articles describe claims procedures that barely change.
questions.explanation: Retrieval suits static or slow-moving knowledge, but an answer that changes by the minute needs the system of record, so a tool call to dispatch delivers the true current state at question time.

questions.prompt: Which capability satisfies this requirement?

options.text: Enable citations on the document blocks passed with each question
options.explanation: Citations enabled on the source documents make the model return the exact quoted text supporting each statement, so adjusters can verify every coverage answer against the precise policy passage without a manual keyword hunt.

options.text: Ask the model to quote its sources politely in output
options.explanation: prompt-as-guarantee — a courteous instruction yields references that may be invented, not the verified quoted span, and nothing ties the citation to the source document.

options.text: Raise the maximum output tokens so answers grow longer
options.explanation: scale-not-strategy — longer answers still arrive unattributed, so the manual clause hunt that motivated the change continues, just with more text to scan.

options.text: Add a second verification pass that re-reads the retrieved chunks
options.explanation: over-orchestration — a second verification pass raises cost and latency while still producing the same unattributed prose that adjusters cannot check.

questions.scenario: An insurer's claims assistant gives adjusters answers about coverage limits, and underwriting now demands that every answer be checkable against the subscribed policy documents. The assistant returns free-text answers from retrieved policy chunks, and adjusters spend much of the day locating the original clause by keyword search.
questions.explanation: Citations enabled on the source documents make the model return the exact quoted text supporting each statement, so adjusters can verify every coverage answer against the precise policy passage without a manual keyword hunt.

questions.prompt: Which TWO statements about MCP sampling are true? Select TWO.

options.text: The server asks the connected client to run the model call
options.explanation: Under sampling the server asks the connected client to run the generation, because the client already holds a working Claude connection, so the public server never touches the provider itself.

options.text: The server then no longer needs its own provider credentials
options.explanation: The generation burden moves to the client, which already authenticates, so the server retains no model provider credentials of its own to leak, rotate, or fund.

options.text: Generation costs stay on the server's own provider budget line
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — keeping the provider credential on the server preserves exactly the concentration of cost and secret-keeping that the controllers asked to remove.

options.text: Summarization executes inside the server process under its own credential
options.explanation: stale-fact — sampling shifts generation responsibility to the client; the server gathers its data, issues the sampling request, and waits rather than executing anything.

questions.scenario: A records office publishes a public MCP server that searches archived ordinances. Each citizen query currently triggers a summarization the office pays for directly, because the server authenticates to the model provider with its own credential, and usage grows every quarter while controllers want costs to follow the questioner.
questions.explanation: Under sampling the server asks the connected client to run the generation, because the client already holds a working Claude connection, so the public server never touches the provider itself.

questions.prompt: Which retrieval design serves both question styles?

options.text: Split the assistant into two separate concept-lookup and parts-lookup interfaces
options.explanation: over-orchestration — two parallel assistants double the integration surface while each retrieval path still misses the other question style entirely.

options.text: Re-embed the entire catalogue with a larger, stronger embedding model
options.explanation: scale-not-strategy — a bigger embedding space keeps near-identical part codes near-identical, so the neighboring-SKU confusion survives the more expensive re-embedding.

options.text: Weight keyword and vector retrieval differently depending on the query
options.explanation: Exact part codes match lexically where embeddings tie, while concept phrasing stays on the semantic side; weighting the two signals by query type lets one retrieval pipeline serve both question styles.

options.text: Increase retrieval depth so more candidates survive the final filter
options.explanation: knobs-not-design — deeper retrieval floods the context with more neighboring SKUs of the same confusable material rather than separating the two failure styles.

questions.scenario: A pump manufacturer's spares assistant handles two question styles: concept questions such as what causes cavitation, and exact lookups of part codes like 6204-2RS engraved on nameplates. Concept questions retrieve correctly, but similar-looking part codes return neighboring SKUs, and technicians distrust the assistant exactly when they need it most.
questions.explanation: Exact part codes match lexically where embeddings tie, while concept phrasing stays on the semantic side; weighting the two signals by query type lets one retrieval pipeline serve both question styles.

questions.prompt: How should the access boundary be enforced?

options.text: Check each requested path against the client's roots inside every tool
options.explanation: The SDK exposes the client's declared roots but does not enforce them, so each tool must verify that the requested path falls inside an approved root before it touches the file.

options.text: Trust the granted directories, since customers picked those paths themselves
options.explanation: convenience-over-safety — trusting the grant without a check lets any tool read beyond the approved directories, which is how the beta pulled in unrelated folders.

options.text: Move conversion state into the model's context so paths stay visible
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — visibility inside the model's context informs nobody about the file system; the conversion tool still opens whatever paths its arguments name.

options.text: Expose the whole customer disk and filter the results after conversion
options.explanation: extra-hop — converting everything and filtering afterwards wastes work per conversion and keeps the boundary check duplicated outside the tool, where support already copied it.

questions.scenario: A SaaS document-automation vendor ships an MCP conversion server, and each customer's Claude session may only read files inside directories that customer explicitly granted. During the beta, conversions sometimes pulled in spreadsheets from unrelated folders, and support duplicated the same path checks inside every deployment.
questions.explanation: The SDK exposes the client's declared roots but does not enforce them, so each tool must verify that the requested path falls inside an approved root before it touches the file.

questions.prompt: What does the executed BAA actually cover?

options.text: Any Claude product, because one BAA travels with the subscription
options.explanation: compliance-theater — the subscription assumption papers over which configuration the agreement enumerates; the same surface can be covered on one delivery route and not another.

options.text: A specific deployment configuration, since coverage differs between delivery routes
options.explanation: BAA coverage attaches to the configuration, not the product, so the architect must confirm that the chosen delivery route is precisely the configuration the executed agreement covers before any record flows.

options.text: The product brand, however the traffic's delivery route is configured
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — naming the brand answers the product question while the agreement's actual scope, the configured delivery route, goes unchecked.

options.text: Only the cloud provider routes, which carry separately negotiated agreements
options.explanation: stale-fact — neither route class is universally covered; each configuration, direct or through a cloud provider, must be checked against the executed agreement itself.

questions.scenario: A national civil-registry agency routes scanned birth records, which carry protected personal data, through a Claude integration, and procurement assumes its signed BAA covers the data whichever delivery route the agency chooses. During architecture review, the intended route turns out not to be the configuration the agreement covers.
questions.explanation: BAA coverage attaches to the configuration, not the product, so the architect must confirm that the chosen delivery route is precisely the configuration the executed agreement covers before any record flows.

questions.prompt: Which golden-dataset change predicts production reliability?

options.text: Add adversarial documents: scans, missing fields, unusual layouts, ambiguous entries
options.explanation: An eval only predicts production if its inputs mirror the production distribution, so the set gains the messy cases it never contained: imperfect scans, missing fields, and entries experts parse differently. The trade-off is heavier golden-set curation.

options.text: Raise the passing threshold from 98 percent to 99 percent
options.explanation: knobs-not-design — a higher bar on the same clean distribution adds coverage of nothing and still misses every production failure mode.

options.text: Replicate every clean document ten times to tighten statistical confidence
options.explanation: scale-not-strategy — more samples from the same clean distribution raise statistical confidence in exactly the wrong measurement.

options.text: Switch the grading from code assertions to a model judge
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — the 98 percent on clean data is real, so the defect is coverage, not how the outputs are graded.

questions.scenario: An insurer's claims-extraction assistant scores 98 percent on its golden set, yet production misses structured fields whenever claims arrive as faxed scans with handwritten sections or missing policy numbers. The golden set holds only clean, digital-born claims. The release ships next week and the team wants scores that predict production behavior.
questions.explanation: An eval only predicts production if its inputs mirror the production distribution, so the set gains the messy cases it never contained: imperfect scans, missing fields, and entries experts parse differently. The trade-off is heavier golden-set curation.

questions.prompt: Which grading type fits the mechanical checks?

options.text: A judge model scoring every field against the schema
options.explanation: scale-not-strategy — paying a judge per mechanical check adds cost without adding any signal a function does not already determine.

options.text: Code-based checks: schema validation, field presence, exact lookups
options.explanation: Schema compliance, field presence, and exact lookups are unambiguous: a function either passes them or fails, in milliseconds, at no per-item cost. The judge budget then goes to the tone judgments that genuinely need interpretation.

options.text: Human review of every record before its nightly acceptance
options.explanation: gold-plating — human review is the slowest, most expensive rung, wasted on checks a function settles deterministically.

options.text: Regex assertions checking that the response sounds consistently professional
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — a regex proves the word professional appears; it does not judge whether the tone actually fits.

questions.scenario: A telecom provider's nightly pipeline extracts contract fields for renewals. Each response must be valid JSON with the required field names present, and reviewers also want each summary's tone judged. Costs rose after the team decided that an LLM judge should grade every output, including the purely mechanical checks.
questions.explanation: Schema compliance, field presence, and exact lookups are unambiguous: a function either passes them or fails, in milliseconds, at no per-item cost. The judge budget then goes to the tone judgments that genuinely need interpretation.

questions.prompt: What isolates which decision caused the gain?

options.text: Ask a judge model which of the three changes helped most
options.explanation: knobs-not-design — attribution is a property of experiment design; no judge prompt recovers it after the fact.

options.text: Ship the same combined release again and watch the aggregate score
options.explanation: eval-blindness — rerunning a blended release repeats the experiment without ever separating its variables.

options.text: Test one variable at a time against the versioned golden set
options.explanation: Iterative improvement is gated by comparison against a stable reference: the eval that defines the capability, then A/B the change against it. Isolating one variable per run makes the gain attributable, at the price of more sequential runs.

options.text: Freeze the current prompt, then rerun the whole combined release twice
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — repeating a blended release measures the mixture again; the variables stay permanently entangled.

questions.scenario: A retailer's support assistant just shipped a release that changed the system prompt, swapped the retrieval embedding model, and raised retrieved-chunk depth in the same week. Agreement scores moved four points, but leadership wants to know which decision drove the gain. The next roadmap decision depends on it.
questions.explanation: Iterative improvement is gated by comparison against a stable reference: the eval that defines the capability, then A/B the change against it. Isolating one variable per run makes the gain attributable, at the price of more sequential runs.

questions.prompt: What step is missing before trusting the scores?

options.text: Grade every output twice and average the two resulting scores
options.explanation: knobs-not-design — averaging two uncalibrated readings yields another uncalibrated number, not agreement with human judgment.

options.text: Force the judge to emit reasoning before every nightly score
options.explanation: valid-but-early — forced reasoning makes inconsistency easier to detect, but it neither proves nor improves agreement with humans.

options.text: Run the judge against human-labeled outputs to measure agreement
options.explanation: A judge is itself a system that can be wrong, so calibrate it against human-labeled outputs and confirm agreement with human judgment. An uncalibrated judge seems trustworthy, which is exactly why its confident scores go unchallenged.

options.text: Raise the judge model's temperature until its scores stop varying
options.explanation: knobs-not-design — a sampling knob addresses run-to-run noise, not whether the verdicts track human judgment at all.

questions.scenario: A bank deployed an LLM judge to grade its dispute-resolution answers, and the judge returns confident scores on every nightly run. Nobody ever compared its verdicts against human reviewers' labeled outputs, yet the team treats each score as release-ready. Leadership asks what principled step the rollout skipped.
questions.explanation: A judge is itself a system that can be wrong, so calibrate it against human-labeled outputs and confirm agreement with human judgment. An uncalibrated judge seems trustworthy, which is exactly why its confident scores go unchallenged.

questions.prompt: Select TWO. Which checklist items need the judge?

options.text: Whether every response is valid JSON against the schema
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — schema validity is deterministic; a function parses it in milliseconds and a judge only adds cost.

options.text: Whether the summary's tone reassures without alarming the families
options.explanation: Tone is interpretation: the range of appropriate voice is too wide and context-dependent for a function, so a judge scores it against a rubric. The trade-off is paying roughly one extra model call per graded item.

options.text: Whether the care reasoning is sound and complete throughout
options.explanation: Reasoning quality requires judgment; whether an analysis is logically complete cannot be encoded as a function, which is exactly the judge's job. The cost matches the generation call, so the budget goes only to interpretive checks.

options.text: Whether all required discharge sections are present in output
options.explanation: scale-not-strategy — section presence is a mechanical checklist; routing it through a judge wastes the interpretation budget.

questions.scenario: A hospital network's intake assistant drafts discharge-confirmation summaries. The quality lead splits the review checklist into two buckets: behaviors a function checks deterministically, and behaviors that need interpretation. Two checklist items remain unassigned, because judge calls cost as much as the generation itself.
questions.explanation: Tone is interpretation: the range of appropriate voice is too wide and context-dependent for a function, so a judge scores it against a rubric. The trade-off is paying roughly one extra model call per graded item.

questions.prompt: What maintenance keeps the suite trustworthy?

options.text: Run the unchanged suite after every deploy, only much more often
options.explanation: eval-blindness — frequency re-measures the wrong behavior more often; nothing tests what the prompt now produces.

options.text: Regenerate expected outputs so the golden dataset tracks current behavior
options.explanation: An out-of-date suite measures behavior the system no longer produces and grants false confidence precisely when regression risk peaks, so expectations are regenerated whenever the prompt moves. The trade-off is golden-set upkeep on every prompt revision.

options.text: Add regression cases that cover only the truncation failure mode
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — one rescued failure mode leaves every remaining stale expectation measuring a retired prompt.

options.text: Freeze the shipped prompt until the passing suite stops passing
options.explanation: knobs-not-design — freezing the prompt slows change but never restores the dataset's fidelity to shipped behavior.

questions.scenario: A legal-ops team revised its contract-summarization prompt twice, and the eval suite kept passing every run. Two weeks after the prompt shipped, summaries truncate long multi-clause obligation sentences. The golden dataset predates the prompt changes and its expected outputs still mirror the retired prompt's behavior.
questions.explanation: An out-of-date suite measures behavior the system no longer produces and grants false confidence precisely when regression risk peaks, so expectations are regenerated whenever the prompt moves. The trade-off is golden-set upkeep on every prompt revision.

questions.prompt: Which mechanism turns corrections into regression checks?

options.text: Ship the model upgrade and compare the aggregate scores afterward
options.explanation: eval-blindness — the upgrade lands into the same blind spot; aggregate comparison replaces the missing regression signal with none.

options.text: Add technicians' anecdotal complaint patterns to the assistant's system prompt
options.explanation: prompt-as-guarantee — folding anecdotes into instructions is guidance, not an enforced check the suite can run.

options.text: Publish a live dashboard counting corrected answers by product line
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — counting edits reports where misses happened after the fact; it never gates the next release.

options.text: Pipe the corrected outputs into a labeled eval regression set
options.explanation: Production corrections are free labeled examples of the failure modes the field actually exposes; adding them to the golden set keeps it current and gates every later change against them. The trade-off is a standing pipeline that captures corrections.

questions.scenario: A manufacturer's troubleshooting assistant has run for a quarter; technicians silently correct its wrong answers in the ticketing tool, and nothing routes those corrections back into any evaluation. Meanwhile a model upgrade ships next month. The architect must turn field corrections into an input the eval suite consumes.
questions.explanation: Production corrections are free labeled examples of the failure modes the field actually exposes; adding them to the golden set keeps it current and gates every later change against them. The trade-off is a standing pipeline that captures corrections.

questions.prompt: Where should the passing threshold come from?

options.text: Derive thresholds from the business requirement, not the prototype
options.explanation: valid-but-early — directionally right, but as written it names no source; the committee still gets no derivable number.

options.text: Anchor the threshold at 91 percent to keep early momentum
options.explanation: stale-fact — 91 percent memorializes early spot checks; it measures what the prototype achieved, not what the business demanded.

options.text: Set the threshold at 100 percent because summaries are critical
options.explanation: gold-plating — one hundred percent on a probabilistic summarizer buys a certainty the requirement never priced.

options.text: Keep whichever threshold the final prototype happens to attain
options.explanation: Thresholds come from what the business requires, and the system builds until it clears them. Anchoring to whatever the prototype already achieves inverts that order and merely certifies the status quo.

questions.scenario: A SaaS onboarding assistant summarizes support tickets. The product manager wrote "summarize accurately" as the only success criterion. The final prototype reached 91 percent on the team's early spot checks, and the steering committee meets Thursday wanting to approve a concrete pass threshold.
questions.explanation: Thresholds come from what the business requires, and the system builds until it clears them. Anchoring to whatever the prototype already achieves inverts that order and merely certifies the status quo.

questions.prompt: Which measurement practice exposes the buried error?

options.text: A stricter confidence interval around the 97 percent mean
options.explanation: knobs-not-design — narrowing the interval measures the mixture more precisely while every segment stays invisible inside it.

options.text: Upgrade the extraction model and prioritize the legacy registers
options.explanation: scale-not-strategy — a bigger model changes extraction, not the measurement that hides the register-specific defect.

options.text: Stratified accuracy reporting by document type and field
options.explanation: Aggregate metrics mask segments, so accuracy is measured by document type and field before any automation decision; stratified sampling surfaces the error pattern the 97 percent mean conceals. The cost is segmenting the golden set and its reporting.

options.text: Add legacy registers until the aggregate score reaches 99
options.explanation: eval-blindness — more of the same aggregate raises a number that never resolves the buried segment.

questions.scenario: A registrar's extraction assistant reports 97 percent aggregate accuracy, and leadership therefore approves automation of the digital archive. Document types and fields, however, score very differently: a legacy register error hides beneath the mean. Nobody has measured accuracy separately by document type and field.
questions.explanation: Aggregate metrics mask segments, so accuracy is measured by document type and field before any automation decision; stratified sampling surfaces the error pattern the 97 percent mean conceals. The cost is segmenting the golden set and its reporting.

questions.prompt: What should gate the change before shipping?

options.text: A/B against a versioned golden set, keeping only non-regressing winners
options.explanation: Changes ship only when the versioned golden set shows the new prompt winning on tracked metrics without regressing any category. The comparison is reproducible; the trade-off is versioning discipline and golden-set upkeep.

options.text: Send both prompt versions to a larger model and compare outputs
options.explanation: scale-not-strategy — a bigger model is an unmeasured, unrelated variable that attributes nothing cleanly to the prompt.

options.text: Raise the manual spot-check sample from eight up to thirty
options.explanation: eval-blindness — more ad hoc glances are still unversioned, and the regressed hub was never in the sample.

options.text: Watch inbound customer complaints for one week at full traffic
options.explanation: convenience-over-safety — full-traffic exposure makes every traveler absorb the regression while the team waits for signals.

questions.scenario: An airline's baggage-claim assistant prompt was rewritten one evening; the engineer eyeballed eight answers, called the tone sharper, and merged. Days later, connection-time answers for one hub airport regressed quietly. The architect must define what gates every prompt change before it reaches production from now on.
questions.explanation: Changes ship only when the versioned golden set shows the new prompt winning on tracked metrics without regressing any category. The comparison is reproducible; the trade-off is versioning discipline and golden-set upkeep.

questions.prompt: How should the handbook rule be enforced?

options.text: Retrain the deployed model on the handbook during the next alignment pass
options.explanation: scale-not-strategy — training-time alignment is general by design and happens before any deployment, so it never sees the firm's handbook.

options.text: Trust the refusals observed in testing as proof of handbook coverage
options.explanation: compliance-theater — observed refusals cover broad harm classes and prove nothing about a specific rule that lives in no layer.

options.text: Encode the handbook rules as application-layer instructions paired with runtime controls
options.explanation: The alignment boundary leaves deployment-specific policy to the application layer: trained behavior reduces broad harm but never saw the firm's handbook, so instructions must be paired with screening, authorization, or review, or the rule lives in no layer.

options.text: Add a system-prompt paragraph summarizing the handbook and close the gap
options.explanation: prompt-as-guarantee — instructions steer one request but are not enforcement; without a paired control, the steering leaves the rule unenforced.

questions.scenario: A litigation-support assistant for a 200-attorney firm drafts answers from transcripts and pleading templates. In testing, Claude refused every harmful request the team tried, so the safety boundary was signed off as covered. In production, partners report the assistant advising outside the firm's approved intake script, a handbook rule that maps to no harmful-output class; nobody encoded the handbook anywhere.
questions.explanation: The alignment boundary leaves deployment-specific policy to the application layer: trained behavior reduces broad harm but never saw the firm's handbook, so instructions must be paired with screening, authorization, or review, or the rule lives in no layer.

questions.prompt: Which screening points does the design still lack?

options.text: Input screening before the model call and authorization before side effects
options.explanation: A guarded path has three control points at different places answering different questions; with only output screening, nothing decides whether requests reach the model and nothing authorizes side-effecting actions, which is exactly the payout that executed unchecked.

options.text: A second judge on the response so toxicity scoring gains redundancy
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — both checks would sit at the same final point; the duplicates still decide nothing about inputs or tool actions.

options.text: Longer system instructions telling the model when to call the payment tool
options.explanation: prompt-as-guarantee — instructions steer behavior but do not authorize the payout; the side effect still runs without a permission check.

options.text: A fail-closed switch that blocks responses whenever the toxicity judge errors
options.explanation: valid-but-early — worthwhile once the path has more than one control, but it only hardens the single filter already there.

questions.scenario: An insurance-claims copilot got one guardrail: a toxicity judge that scores the final response before delivery, praised in the last security review as the system's safety layer. During a quarterly drill, the payments tool executed a duplicate payout that no caller had approved, and the judge never flagged anything. Compliance asks which decision points the current design actually covers.
questions.explanation: A guarded path has three control points at different places answering different questions; with only output screening, nothing decides whether requests reach the model and nothing authorizes side-effecting actions, which is exactly the payout that executed unchecked.

questions.prompt: Which control closes this injection vector?

options.text: Add stronger phrase-matching patterns to the existing user-input screening rules
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — the instructions ride in after input screening has already passed the request, so the entry-point check cannot see them.

options.text: Pin the supplier list so no new senders reach the model
options.explanation: convenience-over-safety — a sender allowlist does nothing for instructions embedded inside an approved supplier's own documents.

options.text: Wrap retrieved documents in quotes so the model treats them as data
options.explanation: prompt-as-guarantee — marking text as data steers the model's reading but does not enforce which embedded instructions it follows.

options.text: Screen retrieved content and tool outputs before they enter context
options.explanation: The dominant injection vector in deployments with retrieval or tool use rides in through retrieved content and tool outputs, so those sources need their own screening pass, with the classifier used on user input, before they are appended to context.

questions.scenario: A logistics-visibility agent reads thousands of supplier emails and pays invoices through connected tools. A buyer noticed that a vendor's emailed banner, styled as a small instruction, changed the delivery terms the agent then repeated; the same instruction arrived inside retrieved content the model treats as trusted, after the chat-input screening had already passed the request.
questions.explanation: The dominant injection vector in deployments with retrieval or tool use rides in through retrieved content and tool outputs, so those sources need their own screening pass, with the classifier used on user input, before they are appended to context.

questions.prompt: What behavior must the architect decide explicitly?

options.text: Cache the last known-good verdicts and reuse them during screening outages
options.explanation: stale-fact — reused verdicts describe the previous conversation state, not the unscreened response currently waiting on delivery.

options.text: Whether the guardrail fails open, passing traffic, or fails closed
options.explanation: A screening service that errors while traffic keeps flowing gives the appearance of protection without the function; the failure direction is a deliberate architectural choice, because the surrounding code's default almost always lets requests through the unprotected path.

options.text: Move the screening call after delivery to remove its latency
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — screening after delivery observes nothing; the check exists to decide whether the response is safe to reach the user.

options.text: Set a stricter confidence threshold so the judge blocks more responses
options.explanation: knobs-not-design — a threshold trades false positives for coverage; it says nothing about what happens when the screening dependency itself errors.

questions.scenario: A telecom's moderation service screens every customer-chat response before delivery. During a dependency upgrade the screening endpoint returns timeouts, and the integration's existing retry-and-continue logic keeps the chat traffic flowing, so customers converse while the control does none of the work it was placed there to do. The availability dashboard stayed green throughout.
questions.explanation: A screening service that errors while traffic keeps flowing gives the appearance of protection without the function; the failure direction is a deliberate architectural choice, because the surrounding code's default almost always lets requests through the unprotected path.

questions.prompt: Which TWO pairings are correct? Select TWO.

options.text: Token-budget exhaustion — replay archived audit logs to reconstruct past requests
options.explanation: scale-not-strategy — replaying logs documents what happened; it neither caps padded archived scans nor watches the budget they consume.

options.text: Indirect prompt injection — treat the retrieved archive text as untrusted before screening
options.explanation: Retrieved content carries instructions the model treats as trusted; mitigation is to treat that text as untrusted and screen tool and content inputs, not just the citizen's typed question.

options.text: Direct prompt injection — the audit log records every request the user makes
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — logging observes the request after the fact; only input screening stands between the user's override and the model.

options.text: Data exposure — redact sensitive fields server-side before anything reaches the logs
options.explanation: Sensitive fields enter the context window or the logs where they should not, so the mitigation is server-side redaction of those fields before anything is written to the audit store.

questions.scenario: A national records agency runs an assistant that summarizes archived files and answers citizen questions over retrieved archives, writing every request to a long-lived audit log. Drafting the written risk assessment, the architect must pair each recurring LLM risk category the design exposes with a workable mitigation.
questions.explanation: Retrieved content carries instructions the model treats as trusted; mitigation is to treat that text as untrusted and screen tool and content inputs, not just the citizen's typed question.

questions.prompt: What positions the workload inside the authorized boundary?

options.text: Attach the model card and reuse the earlier proof-of-concept assessment
options.explanation: stale-fact — the model card describes the software, not the deployment; a proof-of-concept sign-off is not the workload's authorization record.

options.text: Enable request logging so assessors can trace every eligibility call
options.explanation: compliance-theater — logging produces an audit trail but does not place the workload inside an authorized boundary.

options.text: Route the workload through a FedRAMP-authorized government cloud environment
options.explanation: FedRAMP authorization attaches to the cloud service and environment, not the model; the delivery route must be authorized at the workload's required impact level and the workload must run exclusively through it.

options.text: Add a compliance notice to the eligibility assistant's system prompt
options.explanation: prompt-as-guarantee — a compliance notice in the prompt asserts the deployment's posture without placing any component inside an authorized boundary.

questions.scenario: A federal benefits agency approved a proof of concept after reading that the model itself is FedRAMP authorized, then chose the vendor's standard commercial endpoint for the eligibility workload. At the authority-to-operate review, the assessor asks where the workload actually runs and which authorization record covers that path. The engineer points at the model card.
questions.explanation: FedRAMP authorization attaches to the cloud service and environment, not the model; the delivery route must be authorized at the workload's required impact level and the workload must run exclusively through it.

questions.prompt: What must exist before PHI reaches the vendor?

options.text: A signed BAA, HIPAA compliance enabled, and only eligible features
options.explanation: PHI through a third party requires a signed Business Associate Agreement; the evidence a reviewer accepts is the signed BAA, the admin setting showing HIPAA compliance enabled, and the eligible-feature list.

options.text: The SOC 2 Type II report, which attests HIPAA processing
options.explanation: compliance-theater — a SOC 2 report attests security controls under another framework; it is not a BAA and does not by itself authorize PHI processing.

options.text: A confidentiality clause added to the assistant's deployed system prompt
options.explanation: prompt-as-guarantee — a confidentiality instruction is unenforced model guidance; it satisfies none of the contractual or configuration requirements HIPAA imposes.

options.text: Consumer sign-in upgraded to the vendor's most expensive enterprise tier
options.explanation: scale-not-strategy — the top tier buys capacity, not the signed agreement and the enabled configuration the obligation actually names.

questions.scenario: A hospital group will let its triage assistant process patient histories through the model vendor. Legal confirms the vendor publishes a SOC 2 Type II report; deployment today uses the consumer sign-in flow and default settings. Before any patient data flows, the architect lists what compliance actually requires of the configuration.
questions.explanation: PHI through a third party requires a signed Business Associate Agreement; the evidence a reviewer accepts is the signed BAA, the admin setting showing HIPAA compliance enabled, and the eligible-feature list.

questions.prompt: Which evidence would have caught this drift?

options.text: The signed residency clause agreed with the infrastructure procurement contract
options.explanation: stale-fact — the clause was true at signing; it cannot show where this month's copies, including monitoring writes, actually land.

options.text: A quarterly attestation that the configured region setting remains EU
options.explanation: compliance-theater — the setting never changed; residency covers copies in logs and caches, which a setting attestation never inspects.

options.text: A convergence check comparing the primary database's regional replica copies
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — replica convergence concerns the primary store, while the drift was a monitoring path writing outside the approved boundary.

options.text: A data-flow record tracing every copy the deployment retains
options.explanation: Data residency covers processing and storage within the approved region, including copies in logs, caches, and retention paths; a living data-flow record, kept by an accountable owner, would have flagged the second-region write when it happened.

questions.scenario: A payments group pinned its assistant's processing and storage to the EU region to satisfy its residency regulator. Months later, a new tracing feature quietly began writing request metadata to a store in a second region. The residency configuration itself had never changed, so the discrepancy surfaced only when the regulator's questionnaire asked where every copy of the data lives.
questions.explanation: Data residency covers processing and storage within the approved region, including copies in logs, caches, and retention paths; a living data-flow record, kept by an accountable owner, would have flagged the second-region write when it happened.

questions.prompt: What should discovery produce from this preference?

options.text: A feature list mirroring the sponsor's experience words
options.explanation: louder-not-explicit — repeating the experience word more prominently still records a preference; the bounded constraint beneath it is what the design actually needs.

options.text: A stakeholder-approved summary of the current claims workflow
options.explanation: stale-fact — a workflow summary describes what happens today; it leaves the unconfirmed experience word standing in for a testable constraint.

options.text: A prototype demonstrated at the next steering committee
options.explanation: valid-but-early — the sketch feels like progress, but it ends the questioning that would surface the latency budget, the handoff rule, and the failure path.

options.text: Testable constraints: a latency target, handoff rule, failure path
options.explanation: Follow-up questions convert the experience word into testable constraints: a bounded latency target, a handoff rule, and a failure state that hides internals. That costs minutes of questioning and buys a design the team can actually build and measure against.

questions.scenario: An insurance carrier's claims lead tells the discovery call that the new correspondence assistant should 'feel seamless' for adjusters. The architect writes 'seamless' into the requirements, treats it as the experience to deliver, and starts designing the case-assignment flow. The design review that follows has nothing bounded to build against, because the word still hides what the system must never exceed.
questions.explanation: Follow-up questions convert the experience word into testable constraints: a bounded latency target, a handoff rule, and a failure state that hides internals. That costs minutes of questioning and buys a design the team can actually build and measure against.

questions.prompt: What must the architect now investigate?

options.text: A feature list mirroring the sponsor's words
options.explanation: louder-not-explicit — the outcomes were already captured; asking for them again spends discovery time on a bucket the call has answered.

options.text: The must-not-do boundaries: prohibited actions and human-escalation cases
options.explanation: The call holds must-do outcomes, a cost constraint, and a proof obligation; missing is the must-not-do bucket. Stakeholders rarely volunteer boundaries, so the architect asks which actions are prohibited and which cases route to a human.

options.text: A prototype demonstrated at the next steering meeting
options.explanation: knobs-not-design — the ceiling is already stated; stress-testing it is a design exercise, not the missing requirement category.

options.text: Testable constraints: latency target, handoff rule, failure path
options.explanation: compliance-theater — the proof obligation is on the table; the gap is the unasked must-not-do question, not stronger evidence.

questions.scenario: A telecom architect scopes an incident-ticket drafting assistant. The operations lead lists the outcomes they want, a cost ceiling per interaction, and the compliance report the rollout must produce, but nobody on the call has said what the assistant is forbidden to do or which cases must still reach a human. Which discovery question closes the remaining category?
questions.explanation: The call holds must-do outcomes, a cost constraint, and a proof obligation; missing is the must-not-do bucket. Stakeholders rarely volunteer boundaries, so the architect asks which actions are prohibited and which cases route to a human.

questions.prompt: What does the translation-table discipline require?

options.text: One row: implied constraint, forced decision, documented assumption
options.explanation: Each discovery item becomes one translation-table row: the statement, the implied constraint, the decision it forces, and the assumption documented while unconfirmed. An unlabeled assumption inherits silently into the design, which is how ownership gaps resurface. One extra column, traceability.

options.text: A priority ranking of the sponsor's stated expectations
options.explanation: scale-not-strategy — ranking preferences preserves their wording, not the constraint, and never separates what is confirmed from what is assumed.

options.text: A sketch the sponsor approves during the call
options.explanation: valid-but-early — a sketch accelerates the meeting, but it stops the questioning that turns the remark into a constraint with an owner.

options.text: An escalation route reserved for later compliance blockers
options.explanation: convenience-over-safety — reserving a future path defers the confirmation; the assumption ships unmarked and the blocker arrives at review, when changing course costs the most.

questions.scenario: During discovery for a customs-summaries assistant, the logistics sponsor says their reviewers will catch anything the model misses. The architect records the remark as a confirmed requirement and starts designing accordingly. Weeks later the reviewer team explains that nobody actually owns the review step, and nothing in the design record marks it as unconfirmed.
questions.explanation: Each discovery item becomes one translation-table row: the statement, the implied constraint, the decision it forces, and the assumption documented while unconfirmed. An unlabeled assumption inherits silently into the design, which is how ownership gaps resurface. One extra column, traceability.

questions.prompt: Select TWO. Which practices keep discovery questions alive?

options.text: Record the proposed sketch as the agreed design
options.explanation: valid-but-early — the sketch is useful, but adopting it as agreed ends the four-category questioning before licensure and retention rules surface.

options.text: Finish the four-category question set before proposing anything
options.explanation: The protective move is deliberately boring: run must-do, must-not-do, must-cost, and must-prove to completion before any sketch. A confident proposal is what makes a sponsor stop volunteering constraints, precisely the ones a compliance review later misses.

options.text: Treat each 'quick check' remark as a constraint
options.explanation: Every 'it's just a review' hides an architectural gate: who authorizes, when, and with what evidence. Chasing the remark costs one question; skipping it plants a constraint that resurfaces when changing the design costs most.

options.text: Demonstrate a prototype within the same week
options.explanation: gold-plating — a same-week prototype adds motion, not requirements; it does not recover the must-not-do and must-prove answers the call skipped.

questions.scenario: In a discovery call for a clinic's note-drafting assistant, the architect hears two stakeholder statements and proposes an architecture on the spot; the sponsor nods because it sounds competent. Two weeks later a compliance review surfaces a licensed-authorization gate and an unrecorded record-retention rule. Both constraints were one direct question away.
questions.explanation: The protective move is deliberately boring: run must-do, must-not-do, must-cost, and must-prove to completion before any sketch. A confident proposal is what makes a sponsor stop volunteering constraints, precisely the ones a compliance review later misses.

questions.prompt: Which tradeoff element did the presentation miss?

options.text: What the choice gains for the initial design effort
options.explanation: louder-not-explicit — the gain was named and heard; repeating the simplicity argument cannot recover the element the approval actually lacked.

options.text: What the choice gives up at production retrieval quality
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — the sacrifice was partly covered when the per-call price came up; what was never spoken was the cost of the unwind.

options.text: What unwinding the decision costs at production volume
options.explanation: Every tradeoff carries three elements: what the choice gains, what it gives up, and what reversal costs once the system is built around it. The third is what most presentations skip; it turns a correct verdict into a defensible choice.

options.text: Whether the choice also alters the later compliance posture
options.explanation: compliance-theater — the posture question matters in regulated rooms, but this approval failed on a business number, not on an obligation.

questions.scenario: An architect proposes keeping a full regulatory-notice document in context for a payments scale-up, answers the CTO's question about the per-call price, and the room approves. Six weeks later the production invoice shows a five-figure monthly line, because call volume multiplied the quoted per-interaction figure and nobody had priced undoing the design.
questions.explanation: Every tradeoff carries three elements: what the choice gains, what it gives up, and what reversal costs once the system is built around it. The third is what most presentations skip; it turns a correct verdict into a defensible choice.

questions.prompt: How should the decision be framed for approval?

options.text: A package: options, criteria, recommendation, and remaining risks
options.explanation: The stakeholder is not adopting the architecture; they are accepting a decision they must justify to their own leadership. Options considered, criteria weighed, the recommendation, and the risks that remain give the room that justification, which makes the presentation approvable.

options.text: A verdict naming the technically superior option only
options.explanation: convenience-over-safety — a verdict shortens the meeting but leaves the sponsor without the criteria they need to defend the choice upward.

options.text: A ranked comparison of the options by effort
options.explanation: knobs-not-design — an effort ranking answers feasibility, not the criteria the committee weighed or the risks they still carry.

options.text: An executive summary of the winning design's benefits
options.explanation: compliance-theater — a benefits-only summary hides the risks the directors will ask about when the downside appears later.

questions.scenario: A city permitting office's steering committee must approve the intake-assistant design. The architect will present one recommendation, and committee members must each defend the choice to their own directorate afterward. What the committee adopts is less an architecture than a decision they can carry, provided the presentation supplies its grounds.
questions.explanation: The stakeholder is not adopting the architecture; they are accepting a decision they must justify to their own leadership. Options considered, criteria weighed, the recommendation, and the risks that remain give the room that justification, which makes the presentation approvable.

questions.prompt: Which change converts buyer interest into confidence?

options.text: More agentic features that show the platform's sophistication
options.explanation: gold-plating — more features answer what the system can do, the question the buyer has already moved past.

options.text: A second feature pass rehearsed by the sales team
options.explanation: extra-hop — another sales-led feature pass inserts distance between the buyer and proof that the design fits their workflow.

options.text: A glossier recording of the same generic demonstration
options.explanation: louder-not-explicit — a glossier presentation of the same generic content repeats the miss with better production values.

options.text: A scenario-specific demo built on the buyer's workflow
options.explanation: A capabilities demo answers what the system can do; a scenario-specific demo answers what it does with the buyer's problem, workflow, and constraints. Only the second creates confidence: recognition of their vocabulary, approvals, and failures proves the fit.

questions.scenario: A law-firm buyer watches a due-diligence demo that is polished, feature-rich, and entirely generic, calls it interesting, then asks what the system does with their own matter workflow. Discovery had aligned both sides on the problem; the demonstration, not the diagnosis, is what now feels unproven to the firm.
questions.explanation: A capabilities demo answers what the system can do; a scenario-specific demo answers what it does with the buyer's problem, workflow, and constraints. Only the second creates confidence: recognition of their vocabulary, approvals, and failures proves the fit.

questions.prompt: Select TWO. Which choices most build the demo's credibility?

options.text: A warranty workflow the buyer recognizes, failures included
options.explanation: Buyers trust what feels familiar; their own vocabulary, approval steps, and failure points on screen turn a feature tour into proof. Recognition persuades more than polish, because it answers what the system does with their problem, their data, their constraints.

options.text: The broadest feature tour available on the platform
options.explanation: gold-plating — breadth answers what the system can do, which creates interest, not the confidence that the solution fits the buyer's context.

options.text: Limitations deferred to the question period to stay positive
options.explanation: convenience-over-safety — deferring limits keeps the narrative positive until the buyer discovers a weakness mid-flow, and discovered weakness reads as accident, not scope.

options.text: One or two limitations named upfront as intentional scope
