options.explanation: Naming one or two constraints in advance, framed as what the solution deliberately does not do, signals discipline. In regulated rooms a stated boundary reads as rigor, while a mid-flow discovery drops confidence. Less impressive, but trust that survives scrutiny.

questions.scenario: An industrial-equipment vendor prepares a warranty-triage demo for a procurement panel working under regulated disclosure duties. Four decisions precede any screens: the scenario, which limitations to name, sales collaboration, and data preparation. Getting them wrong costs the trust that discovery earned, because buyers judge the demo by whether it resembles their operations.
questions.explanation: Buyers trust what feels familiar; their own vocabulary, approval steps, and failure points on screen turn a feature tour into proof. Recognition persuades more than polish, because it answers what the system does with their problem, their data, their constraints.

questions.prompt: Where should the shared conventions and configuration live?

options.text: Ask each engineer to mirror the conventions into their personal user settings
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — user-level settings are personal scope that no pasting keeps synchronized, so the drift continues across laptops exactly as before.

options.text: Version the conventions in an internal wiki and link it from onboarding
options.explanation: louder-not-explicit — a wiki page documents the baseline but nothing loads it into the assistant, so conventions reach nobody's session automatically.

options.text: Check the project instructions file and shared settings into the repository
options.explanation: Project-scoped instructions and settings are meant to be versioned in the repository, so every collaborator inherits identical conventions, permissions, and MCP configuration automatically from source control.

options.text: Upgrade everyone to the most capable model tier for consistent output behavior
options.explanation: scale-not-strategy — a larger model does not distribute shared permissions or project context; each laptop still starts from whatever was configured locally.

questions.scenario: Engineers at a university ITS department copied their coding conventions into personal user-level CLAUDE.md files, so agents behave differently on every laptop: new hires miss the pull-request checklist, reviewers re-explain conventions, and nobody shares the MCP server configuration for the registrar's records system, while onboarding stretches across lost days.
questions.explanation: Project-scoped instructions and settings are meant to be versioned in the repository, so every collaborator inherits identical conventions, permissions, and MCP configuration automatically from source control.

questions.prompt: Which distribution mechanism fits these failure symptoms?

options.text: Bundle the procedure into an owner-managed plugin with version-controlled updates and rollback
options.explanation: Plugins carry the governance this failure exposed: version-controlled updates from a connected repository, group targeting, and a documented path back, so one bad edit stops shipping to everyone at once.

options.text: Re-upload a corrected copy of the skill through Organization settings for everyone
options.explanation: knobs-not-design — repeating the flat upload adds another manual fix, not the versioning and rollback mechanism the requirement names; that channel has no native rollback.

options.text: Move the skill into each affected project repository as a filesystem artifact
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — project skills version with their repository but reach only the projects that carry it, not sixty engineers across every team.

options.text: Expose the procedure as an API Skill called by the partner's products
options.explanation: gold-plating — API Skills serve programmatic, machine-to-machine reuse; this procedure is human-facing, so the mechanism does not match who consumes it.

questions.scenario: A telecom platform team distributes its incident-writeup procedure to sixty engineers as a flat skill upload. Two weeks later an unnoticed prompt edit makes every writeup fail the compliance template, the same wrong output ships for six days, and there is no way back to the last good version.
questions.explanation: Plugins carry the governance this failure exposed: version-controlled updates from a connected repository, group targeting, and a documented path back, so one bad edit stops shipping to everyone at once.

questions.prompt: Which spend posture decision comes first?

options.text: Leave the vendor defaults in place until monthly spend justifies tighter guards
options.explanation: convenience-over-safety — inheriting the defaults means every untended tier choice multiplies silently across forty clinicians before anyone connects it to the doubled invoice.

options.text: Cap the team's total monthly spend but leave model choice to individuals
options.explanation: knobs-not-design — a single ceiling catches overspend after the fact instead of steering defaults, allowlists, and effort at the point where the choice is made.

options.text: Remove model switching altogether so that nobody can ever pick another tier
options.explanation: scale-not-strategy — hard-locking the tier discards cheaper models that simpler reporting steps should use; an allowlist keeps control without sacrificing that flexibility.

options.text: Set model defaults, an allowlist, effort guidance, and per-user spend caps
options.explanation: Spend posture means deciding the starting model, the allowed alternatives, effort guidance, and the spend, rate, and per-user caps that keep consumption bounded as usage scales across dozens of people.

questions.scenario: A diagnostic-imaging vendor onboards forty clinicians onto an assistant that drafts scan summaries. The first invoice arrives at twice the forecast: every session starts on the largest model by default, engineers switch tiers freely mid-task, and nobody set effort guidance or usage caps because the rollout prioritized features over guardrails.
questions.explanation: Spend posture means deciding the starting model, the allowed alternatives, effort guidance, and the spend, rate, and per-user caps that keep consumption bounded as usage scales across dozens of people.

questions.prompt: Select TWO. Which actions convert license-day access into real adoption?

options.text: Announce the rollout company-wide and let each developer's enthusiasm set the pace
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — another announcement grows awareness, but the failure is enablement; access without workflow integration stalls the team at basic chat.

options.text: Name a champion per department who proves a real workflow first
options.explanation: A champion absorbs the early friction, builds the local example, and seeds adoption batch by batch, so usage spreads deliberately instead of concentrating in a few early enthusiasts.

options.text: Restrict the assistant to senior engineers until the rest finish formal training
options.explanation: valid-but-early — training-first sequencing delays the champions who absorb friction and produce the worked examples the later batches depend on.

options.text: Wire assistance into the editor, review, and test loop they already use
options.explanation: Enablement means configuring assistance inside the workflow developers already use, so conventions become skills and project configuration applied consistently rather than knowledge that depends on who happens to be present.

questions.scenario: A grocery retailer bought seats for its four hundred developers on license day. Usage logs show three enthusiasts shipping twice as fast while everyone else treats the assistant as a question box, and reviewers now face a doubled volume of confident diffs. Adoption has gone lumpy.
questions.explanation: A champion absorbs the early friction, builds the local example, and seeds adoption batch by batch, so usage spreads deliberately instead of concentrating in a few early enthusiasts.

snapshot.description: Full-length scenarios exam: 60 items across the 7 blueprint domains, valid-but-inferior distractors, criterion hidden mid-stem.

snapshot.title: Exam Scenarios: Full B (60Q, 7 domains)

questions.prompt: Which pattern does each workstream need?

options.text: Agent for both, because both follow several gates
options.explanation: over-orchestration — granting a planning loop to work whose order is known adds unpredictability the filing process never benefits from.

options.text: A multi-agent orchestrator for both, sharing the clause context
options.explanation: over-orchestration — coordination overhead across subagents buys breadth, not reliability, for a legally fixed filing sequence.

options.text: Workflow for the filing gates, agent for clause research
options.explanation: When the steps are known in advance and identical for every request, the fixed workflow makes each step auditable; the research task whose next move becomes clear mid-task is the case for the autonomous agent that plans, acts, and observes.

options.text: Single augmented call for each, run in parallel
options.explanation: valid-but-early — each workstream takes more than one call, so a single call covers neither the gates nor the research trail.

questions.scenario: A legal-ops intake system reviews vendor contracts against the firm's playbook. Every filing moves through the same gates, extract, classify, flag, draft a summary, in a fixed order, while a separate clause-research task follows trails that depend entirely on what each retrieved precedent reveals.
questions.explanation: When the steps are known in advance and identical for every request, the fixed workflow makes each step auditable; the research task whose next move becomes clear mid-task is the case for the autonomous agent that plans, acts, and observes.

questions.prompt: Which adjustment fixes the rider errors?

options.text: Front-load the tariff riders at the top of context
options.explanation: Front-loading critical information is the documented mitigation for working memory: what the decision needs goes first, because attention degrades on long contexts well before the hard limit, and the figures at the top are precisely the ones that survive. The riders trade narrative order for reliability.

options.text: Summarize the whole record once more, more carefully
options.explanation: louder-not-explicit — the fluency is not the defect; a fuller narration still leaves the rider buried where the errors happen.

options.text: Move the model up to a stronger reasoning tier
options.explanation: scale-not-strategy — the interval reads near the top are already right; capability is not what separates the buried riders.

options.text: Chunk the record and retrieve only the cited passages
options.explanation: valid-but-early — chunking serves records beyond the window; this record fits with room to spare, so the dispatch adds hops without recovering what position hid.

questions.scenario: A regional utility's reading-validation assistant receives one dense meter record: interval reads, calculation notes, tariff riders, and exception flags in narrative order. Summaries come back fluent but cite the wrong tariff rider on disputed statements, while the interval figures, which sit near the top, are always right. The record fits the window with room to spare.
questions.explanation: Front-loading critical information is the documented mitigation for working memory: what the decision needs goes first, because attention degrades on long contexts well before the hard limit, and the figures at the top are precisely the ones that survive. The riders trade narrative order for reliability.

questions.prompt: Which proposal serves both questions?

options.text: Index nightly snapshots of both balances and rules
options.explanation: valid-but-early — a snapshot index serves the quarterly policy text, but pointing it at balances too leaves the 10:05 balance answered from the 10:00 record.

options.text: Answer balances from model knowledge, retrieve policies
options.explanation: stale-fact — parametric knowledge carries the training-time snapshot; it cannot return a current balance at 10:05.

options.text: Query the ledger live, retrieve the policy documents
options.explanation: Retrieval is built for static documents and stale snapshots, and should not be substituted for live state; the balance needs a direct read of the source of truth, and the quarterly policy text is the stable reference material retrieval serves.

options.text: Cache ledger answers briefly to absorb transaction spikes
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — a short cache still serves one 10:00 value into the 10:05 question, which the brief excludes.

questions.scenario: A bank's service-ops assistant must answer what is my current balance and can I overdraft. Balances change with every transaction, while overdraft rules and eligibility policy sit in reference documents that update quarterly. One proposal indexes everything nightly; another queries the core-banking ledger live and retrieves the policy documents.
questions.explanation: Retrieval is built for static documents and stale snapshots, and should not be substituted for live state; the balance needs a direct read of the source of truth, and the quarterly policy text is the stable reference material retrieval serves.

questions.prompt: What architecture fits these categories?

options.text: One multi-agent team, one agent per ticket category
options.explanation: gold-plating — coordinated agents exceed what stable categories need, when dispatch to single specialized handlers suffices.

options.text: A routing step dispatching to specialized per-category handlers
options.explanation: Routing classifies an input and directs it to a specialized follow-up task, well suited when distinct categories are better handled separately; that is exactly what lets simple questions take the cheap path and escalations the deep one.

options.text: Cache the shared prompt prefix to cut token spend
options.explanation: premature-optimization — caching trims the cost of the wrong design while every ticket still rides one undifferentiated path.

options.text: Extend the catch-all prompt with per-category ticket instructions
options.explanation: louder-not-explicit — more instructions in one prompt stays harder to maintain and never separates the categories.

questions.scenario: A retail support desk sends password resets, warranty registrations, incident escalations, and billing questions through one identical high-reasoning configuration behind a giant catch-all prompt. Simple questions arrive slowly and overpay, escalations get the same shallow handling as password resets, and the categories are stable and well understood.
questions.explanation: Routing classifies an input and directs it to a specialized follow-up task, well suited when distinct categories are better handled separately; that is exactly what lets simple questions take the cheap path and escalations the deep one.

questions.prompt: Select TWO. Which conditions justify the multi-agent choice?

options.text: The synthesis is a strictly linear, dependent sequence
options.explanation: over-orchestration — a linear dependent sequence is prompt chaining; agents add coordination the sequence cannot use.

options.text: Reducing total tokens per run is the primary goal
options.explanation: scale-not-strategy — multi-agent systems cost more tokens than a single chat, the opposite of the engagement's stated priority.

options.text: The problem is breadth-first with many independent directions
options.explanation: Multi-agent systems earn their keep on breadth-first queries with many independent directions, which is what a diligence sweep across precedents, disclosures, and patents actually looks like.

options.text: Each direction's source material exceeds a single context window
options.explanation: When sources exceed one window, parallel subagents each carrying their own isolated window is exactly the mechanism that helps, since isolated context per subagent raises coverage without overflow.

questions.scenario: A due-diligence review at a law firm produces a synthesis from dozens of independent research threads: precedents, financial disclosures, and patents. Each thread's materials exceed a single context window, and answer quality matters more than token cost for this engagement. A coordinator proposal would dispatch isolated parallel subagents.
questions.explanation: Multi-agent systems earn their keep on breadth-first queries with many independent directions, which is what a diligence sweep across precedents, disclosures, and patents actually looks like.

questions.prompt: How should the ordering requirement be enforced?

options.text: Add a programmatic precondition blocking disbursements before verification
options.explanation: Where business rules require guaranteed compliance, programmatic enforcement, hooks and preconditions, replaces prompt guidance's probabilistic compliance; blocking the disbursement call until a verified identity exists is the deterministic guarantee the lender asked for.

options.text: A compliance judge scoring each transcript after funding
options.explanation: compliance-theater — judging completed payouts records misses after the fact without ever holding one back before it ran.

options.text: A compliance-acknowledgment paragraph at the top of the prompt
options.explanation: prompt-as-guarantee — the wording already produces probabilistic compliance, and a stronger paragraph does not change that class of guarantee.

options.text: Upgrade to the model tier with best instruction adherence
options.explanation: scale-not-strategy — adherence improves statistically while the disbursement ordering still carries no deterministic guarantee at all.

questions.scenario: A mortgage lender's processing agent funds disbursements only after identity verification, and the operations chief wants that rule enforced deterministically. Today the guarantee rests on wording in the agent's prompt, and on an orderly history of thirteen completed disbursements cited as evidence that the wording works.
questions.explanation: Where business rules require guaranteed compliance, programmatic enforcement, hooks and preconditions, replaces prompt guidance's probabilistic compliance; blocking the disbursement call until a verified identity exists is the deterministic guarantee the lender asked for.

questions.prompt: Which overlooked property explains this?

options.text: Steerability, because the precise numerical computation had drifted
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — the computation was never routed to deterministic code; but the divergence here needs no numerical explanation.

options.text: Working memory, because reports exceeded the context window
options.explanation: scale-not-strategy — the documents fit; an exceeded window would error the request, not quietly alter its categorization.

options.text: Knowledge boundary, because the report terminology had changed
options.explanation: stale-fact — terminology freshness is not the mechanism here; identical inputs produced different outputs across runs.

options.text: Non-determinism, so demos cannot certify repeated behavior
options.explanation: The same input can produce different outputs across runs, so evaluation frameworks, not one clean demonstration, are how you certify behavior; the sign-off treated a repeated observation as a guarantee.

questions.scenario: A manufacturing-forecasting assistant summarizes production reports; the architect watched five runs and concluded the outputs were deterministic, then signed off the monthly financial rollup as a repeatable, check-free step. Weeks later the same statement, reprocessed, produced a different categorization, found only when an auditor re-ran a batch.
questions.explanation: The same input can produce different outputs across runs, so evaluation frameworks, not one clean demonstration, are how you certify behavior; the sign-off treated a repeated observation as a guarantee.

questions.prompt: What should the architect establish first?

options.text: The four discovery buckets: do, not-do, cost, prove
options.explanation: Experience words like simple signal more discovery, not a requirement; forcing the statement through must-do, must-not-do, must-cost, and must-prove yields testable, bounded constraints, and finishing that question set before proposing anything is the documented discipline.

options.text: A translation table of the statements into constraints
options.explanation: valid-but-early — the table is where discoveries land, but it records whatever the questions surfaced rather than driving them.

options.text: A prototype residents can react to in usability tests
options.explanation: valid-but-early — testing a sketch feels productive, yet it duplicates what the four question buckets would have established earlier.

options.text: The documentation standards the municipality's record office uses
options.explanation: valid-but-early — documentation conventions matter at handoff, not before the requirements exist that they would document.

questions.scenario: A municipal-records vendor hears the registrar say the booking assistant must feel simple for residents. The delivery team wants to start the interface design the same afternoon, because the registrar confirmed the summary sounded right and momentum matters politically this quarter.
questions.explanation: Experience words like simple signal more discovery, not a requirement; forcing the statement through must-do, must-not-do, must-cost, and must-prove yields testable, bounded constraints, and finishing that question set before proposing anything is the documented discipline.

questions.prompt: How should the decision record be split?

options.text: Three decisions, by audience: user, engineer, procurement
options.explanation: Entry point is chosen for the user and the work, build-time interface for the engineering team, delivery route for cloud commitments and compliance posture; three conversations with three different stakeholders, which is what the one-page record collapses.

options.text: One record, since one model serves every audience
options.explanation: compliance-theater — naming the shared model does not reconcile three decisions; the conflicting readings prove the page answers different questions at once.

options.text: Split by latency, compliance, and integration-cost rankings
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — those criteria are real, but they grade options within a layer instead of separating which stakeholder decides which layer.

options.text: Ratify whichever reading the engineering audience defends
options.explanation: convenience-over-safety — one audience's interpretation governs its layer only, leaving the end-user and procurement decisions unrecorded.

questions.scenario: A publishing group's editorial suite reaches the model through a web application the engineers built, while its rights-licensing team uses a ready-made product and its transit of articles runs inside the partner's contracted hyperscaler. A departing architect left one page titled Claude platform decision, without subdivisions, that all three audiences now read differently.
questions.explanation: Entry point is chosen for the user and the work, build-time interface for the engineering team, delivery route for cloud commitments and compliance posture; three conversations with three different stakeholders, which is what the one-page record collapses.

questions.prompt: Which delivery route fits?

options.text: AWS Bedrock, because the desk'sAmazon cloud commitment fits it
options.explanation: stale-fact — the desk runs on Google Cloud, so an AWS route adds a second relationship instead of reusing the platform they hold.

options.text: Google Vertex, keeping the request path inside their cloud
options.explanation: Latency decides when compliance clears on several routes: keeping the 400-millisecond path inside the firm's existing Google Cloud environment minimizes network round-trips, which is exactly how the trade-commentary case is decided in the notes.

options.text: The direct route, because governance already clears it
options.explanation: valid-but-early — clearing the compliance pre-filter answers the governed-workload question, not the lowest-latency placement of the hop.

options.text: Microsoft Foundry, to diversify the model provider dependency
options.explanation: gold-plating — a third procurement relationship buys redundancy with no requirement in the brief behind it.

questions.scenario: A capital-markets desk is designing trade commentary delivered the moment each trade prints. Every governance constraint in the brief already clears on the direct route, yet the desk runs entirely on Google Cloud and needs each summary delivered within 400 milliseconds of execution.
questions.explanation: Latency decides when compliance clears on several routes: keeping the 400-millisecond path inside the firm's existing Google Cloud environment minimizes network round-trips, which is exactly how the trade-commentary case is decided in the notes.

questions.prompt: Which adjustment restores the lost detail?

options.text: Enable the prompt caching on this growing conversation
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — caching changes what the accumulated transcript costs, not how reliably dawn notes survive inside the window.

options.text: Upgrade the assistant to the very widest-window model
options.explanation: scale-not-strategy — the window already coasts; more room does not restore attention over the notes the summaries drop.

options.text: Raise the sampling temperature so answers keep more detail
options.explanation: knobs-not-design — sampling shapes wording variety, not which captured turns of the transcript survive into each summary.

options.text: Summarize across turns when the context grows long
options.explanation: When context gets long, the documented practice is to summarize across turns: periodic compaction curates what stays in scope while the conversation continues, which both restores the dawn notes' influence and trims the cost that climbs with every untrimmed pass.

questions.scenario: An insurer's adjustment-notes assistant runs voice-of-customer summaries through a conversation that gains a documents-sent preamble, an adjuster's annotations, and a running tally of excuses on every turn. Late-morning turns coast on the working window, yet summaries start dropping pretext notes captured at dawn, and cost climbs with each untrimmed pass. Nothing in the transcript failed validation.
questions.explanation: When context gets long, the documented practice is to summarize across turns: periodic compaction curates what stays in scope while the conversation continues, which both restores the dawn notes' influence and trims the cost that climbs with every untrimmed pass.

questions.prompt: Which steering change makes totals dependable?

options.text: Reduce the temperature so the totals stop varying between runs
options.explanation: knobs-not-design — lower variance makes wrong totals quieter rather than correct; the prompt still computes them itself.

options.text: Restate the computation instruction in bold at the prompt's top
options.explanation: louder-not-explicit — emphasis restates an instruction the model already follows in the letter while the intent keeps drifting.

options.text: Paste every rate sheet twice so the model can double-check itself
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — duplicating the pasted input adds tokens and a second chance to disagree, not a calculation.

options.text: Compute totals in deterministic code; let the model explain them
options.explanation: Steerability is weakest on precise numerical computation, so deterministic code should own the answer while the model explains it. That separates the guaranteed arithmetic from the fluent narration, and the printed rationale stops citing a different number than the billed one.

questions.scenario: A city permits office has its assistant compute excavation-fee totals itself from rate sheets pasted into the prompt. Totals disagree between runs, rounding rules get applied inconsistently, and the printed rationale sometimes cites a number different from the one billed. Fee payments depend on these totals, and another prompt rewrite is not affordable this quarter.
questions.explanation: Steerability is weakest on precise numerical computation, so deterministic code should own the answer while the model explains it. That separates the guaranteed arithmetic from the fluent narration, and the printed rationale stops citing a different number than the billed one.

questions.prompt: Which refinement restores traceable separation?

options.text: Repeat the sectioning instructions once more at the very end
options.explanation: louder-not-explicit — the instructions are already clear enough; what is missing is any boundary between the pasted documents.

options.text: Wrap each content type in descriptive, distinct delimiting tags
options.explanation: Mixing content types is exactly when these boundaries earn their keep: descriptive tags like incident notes, alarms, and complaints give each block a named edge the model can attribute conclusions to, and the more descriptive the name, the clearer the purpose.

options.text: Trim the pasted evidence until the prompt fits one screen
options.explanation: scale-not-strategy — trimming the evidence to fit sacrifices exactly the provenance the conclusions need to cite later.

options.text: Upgrade to a model that untangles interleaved content better
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — a stronger reader still sees the same undifferentiated stream; the defect is missing boundaries, not reading power.

questions.scenario: A telecom incident-intake prompt interleaves technician notes, raw alarm logs, and customer complaint threads with its instructions, so the model copies alarm codes into conclusions and quotes complaints as if they were diagnostics. No rule is violated, yet content boundaries are invisible, and the operations lead keeps rejecting answers that cannot show which material produced each conclusion.
questions.explanation: Mixing content types is exactly when these boundaries earn their keep: descriptive tags like incident notes, alarms, and complaints give each block a named edge the model can attribute conclusions to, and the more descriptive the name, the clearer the purpose.

questions.prompt: Which refinement anchors the feedback tone fastest?

options.text: Turn the archived perfect answers into labeled worked examples
options.explanation: The strongest examples already exist: perfect past outputs become sample input and ideal output pairs, which shows rather than describes the target. Explaining why each archived answer counts as ideal adds the reasoning, so the model generalizes the standard instead of guessing it.

options.text: Add a paragraph stressing the importance of consistent tone
options.explanation: louder-not-explicit — praising consistency tells the model what to value without showing one sentence of what it sounds like.

options.text: Rewrite the grading rubric so its criteria read more precisely
options.explanation: gold-plating — the rubric is not in doubt, so rewriting criteria nobody questioned spends effort beside the actual failure.

options.text: Run evaluations more often so tone drift gets caught sooner
options.explanation: eval-blindness — measuring the drift more often does not narrow it; the prompt still lacks a target to imitate.

questions.scenario: An online-education company's grading-feedback assistant matches its rubric only loosely, and graders report that feedback tone drifts between sessions and question types. The prompt-evaluation pipeline scores every output from one to ten and has archived several perfect answers from earlier prompt versions. The instruction wording has survived three reviews, and nobody doubts the rubric itself.
questions.explanation: The strongest examples already exist: perfect past outputs become sample input and ideal output pairs, which shows rather than describes the target. Explaining why each archived answer counts as ideal adds the reasoning, so the model generalizes the standard instead of guessing it.

questions.prompt: Select TWO. Which diagnoses fit the evidence?

options.text: The transcript now needs the largest-window model to fit
options.explanation: scale-not-strategy — the transcript already fits; the failure is degradation inside the window, not capacity at its edge.

options.text: Caching the growing transcript will arrest the quality decay
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — caching changes what the transcript costs, not how reliably the model recalls what sits inside it.

options.text: Attention quality degrades long before the context limit is reached
options.explanation: Attention quality can degrade on very long contexts well before the hard limit, which is exactly the documented failure and explains the mid-session lapses without any limit being hit.

options.text: Periodic compaction should summarize and compress the accumulated history
options.explanation: Compaction, periodically summarizing or compressing accumulated context, is the documented response: it curates what stays in context rather than assuming more room fixes recall, and it also trims the cost that grows with every added turn.

questions.scenario: A retail-banking adviser copilot stays sharp through the first dozen exchanges of a servicing chat, then quoting fee schedules and earlier answers turns unreliable even though the context window is far from full, while every added turn keeps raising cost and response latency. Select the TWO diagnoses that match this documented behavior.
questions.explanation: Attention quality can degrade on very long contexts well before the hard limit, which is exactly the documented failure and explains the mid-session lapses without any limit being hit.

questions.prompt: How should the shared setting be decided?

options.text: Pick a middle value both jobs can tolerate equally
options.explanation: knobs-not-design — a middle value leaves extraction noisier than needed and the copy tamer than welcome, pleasing neither owner.

options.text: Set it to maximum so the assistant stays maximally flexible
options.explanation: knobs-not-design — maximum randomness helps the marketing copy but makes copied codes and tolerances more variable, the opposite of what records need.

options.text: Match the setting to the job: low extraction, high copy
options.explanation: The documented guidance ties the setting to the task: extraction and data work run at low temperatures, while brainstorming and marketing copy run high. The shared failure is one value answering two opposite jobs, so the fix applies the right setting per job.

options.text: Set it to zero so every job returns identical wording
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — zero determinism serves the records yet flattens exactly the variety the catalog copy exists to provide.

questions.scenario: A lighting manufacturer gives one assistant two jobs: copying defect codes, batch numbers, and tolerances from inspection sheets into records, and drafting playful copy for the consumer catalog. One sampling setting serves both, and neither the record error rate nor the marketing team is happy with the shared result they both receive today.
questions.explanation: The documented guidance ties the setting to the task: extraction and data work run at low temperatures, while brainstorming and marketing copy run high. The shared failure is one value answering two opposite jobs, so the fix applies the right setting per job.

questions.prompt: Which technique guarantees a pasteable JSON body?

options.text: Add stronger formatting instructions demanding bare JSON without decoration
options.explanation: prompt-as-guarantee — formatting instructions remain guidance the model honors approximately, so fences and stray remarks still survive into the widget.

options.text: Prefill the assistant turn and stop at the closing fence
options.explanation: Opening the assistant turn with the code fence makes the model continue inside it, and a stop sequence ends generation exactly at the closing fence. The reply arrives as the delimited payload alone, with nothing more for the widget to strip.

options.text: Parse the reply in the page and strip decoration there
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — parsing downstream keeps the problem alive: every formatting slip still reaches the page before code repairs it.

options.text: Generate each quotation twice and keep whichever output parses
options.explanation: over-orchestration — a second generation doubles latency and cost to settle what the stop sequence settles deterministically in one pass.

questions.scenario: An insurer's quotation widget embeds the model's reply directly, so the pricing JSON must arrive alone: no markdown fences, no commentary, nothing the page cannot paste straight into its rating calculator. Today corrections wait for editors to trim fences and stray sentences by hand, and every trimming mistake ships a broken quotation to the brokerage portal.
questions.explanation: Opening the assistant turn with the code fence makes the model continue inside it, and a stop sequence ends generation exactly at the closing fence. The reply arrives as the delimited payload alone, with nothing more for the widget to strip.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes the two documented failures?

options.text: The first concerns the request's byte limit; the second, permissions
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — permissions and byte size explain a rejected request, but neither explains a reply that stops early mid-table.

options.text: Both failures mean the accumulated conversation must be resent smaller
options.explanation: prompt-as-guarantee — shrinking one resend addresses neither boundary specifically because the two failures sit at different limits entirely.

options.text: Both failures are transient faults that will retry successfully next run
options.explanation: stale-fact — both failures reproduce deterministically on identical inputs, so retrying cannot succeed where the limit itself was exceeded.

options.text: One rejects the prompt; the other truncates generation at the ceiling
options.explanation: An oversized prompt is rejected before generation begins, while a prompt that fits returns a distinct stop reason when its reply reaches the window ceiling. Both failures are documented distinctly, and checking the usage field plus the token-counting API warns before either occurs.

questions.scenario: A grid-operations vendor pastes each entire week of sensor exports into the context window to draft its regulatory exposure report. Twice this month the failures differed: one night the request died before generation because the prompt alone exceeded the token limit, and another sailed through until the reply stopped early mid-table. They want warnings that fire before either failure, not after.
questions.explanation: An oversized prompt is rejected before generation begins, while a prompt that fits returns a distinct stop reason when its reply reaches the window ceiling. Both failures are documented distinctly, and checking the usage field plus the token-counting API warns before either occurs.

questions.prompt: What does this evidence say comes next?

options.text: Enable extended thinking on every note before measuring anything
options.explanation: premature-optimization — turning on thinking before cheaper instruction work is exhausted pays its latency and tokens without measured need.

options.text: Keep sharpening the explicit guidelines and targeted process steps
options.explanation: The gain came from clarity, then specificity: output guidelines plus process steps lifted scores from roughly 4 toward 8. The documented iteration loop keeps hunting the next measurable instruction change, which beats reaching for heavier machinery first.

options.text: Swap to the flagship tier since reasoning quality drove gains
options.explanation: scale-not-strategy — the doubled scores credited wording and structure, not capability, so the evidence favors the prompt over the upgrade.

options.text: Freeze the prompt now that evaluation scores have doubled
options.explanation: valid-but-early — freezing preserves a good score while the iteration loop exists precisely to find the next gain.

questions.scenario: A documentation SaaS feeds structured changelog entries to a generator that writes customer-facing release notes. Early versions asked vaguely what to emphasize and the outputs wandered; after the team added explicit guidelines for length, sections, and which entries to skip, evaluation scores more than doubled. Leadership now wants the next gain and asks what unlocks it.
questions.explanation: The gain came from clarity, then specificity: output guidelines plus process steps lifted scores from roughly 4 toward 8. The documented iteration loop keeps hunting the next measurable instruction change, which beats reaching for heavier machinery first.

questions.prompt: Which pattern-to-failure pairing is correct?

options.text: Retries with exponential backoff absorb transient 5xx and 429 responses
options.explanation: 429 and 529 indicate transient, server-side conditions, so retrying with exponential backoff, each successive wait longer than the last, is precisely the documented remedy these bursts need.

options.text: A circuit breaker blocks calls during a dependency's error-threshold cooldown
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — the breaker trips during the wave and stops calling, but it cannot absorb; requests still fail until the dependency recovers, only at a controlled rate.

options.text: Fallback chains repeat the identical failing call until it succeeds
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — repeating the identical call is the retries pattern; fallback chains swap to an alternate path in the orchestration layer instead of repeating anything.

options.text: Timeouts always indicate permanent faults that no retry can resolve
options.explanation: convenience-over-safety — a timeout may signal temporary stress, a slow dependency, or a permanent fault, so treating every one as unrecoverable discards the transient majority.

questions.scenario: A telecom runs an incident-notes service, and during one weekend the model provider returned 5xx errors in long waves. The service retried immediately, hammering the recovering dependency, and stayed unavailable far longer than the dependency itself, so reviewers now ask which control owns which failure.
questions.explanation: 429 and 529 indicate transient, server-side conditions, so retrying with exponential backoff, each successive wait longer than the last, is precisely the documented remedy these bursts need.

questions.prompt: Which pipeline change fixes these mixed answers?

options.text: Retrieve longer slices so each one carries its own admission header
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — longer slices dilute retrieval precision and still arrive stripped of the identifying header that made them ambiguous in the first place.

options.text: Compress the corpus so more of it fits the context window
options.explanation: scale-not-strategy — compression cannot make a retrieved slice self-identifying, and the corpus already exceeds the window, which is the very constraint it runs into again.

options.text: Raise retrieval depth so conflicting evidence is more likely present
options.explanation: knobs-not-design — deeper retrieval floods the context with more of the same anonymous slices instead of fixing what made each one ambiguous.

options.text: Prepend admission context to each chunk and add BM25 lexical search
options.explanation: Chunks lacking identifying context force the model to guess provenance; prepending patient, ward, and admission context before indexing, backed by a BM25 lexical index, gives every slice its identifying context and adds the exactness lexical search provides.

questions.scenario: A hospital indexes 400-token slices of its discharge summaries for a clinical question-answering assistant. Retrieved slices say continue current medication without naming the patient, the ward, or the admission, so the model composes confident answers mixing one patient's medication with another's admission, and the corpus far exceeds any context window.
questions.explanation: Chunks lacking identifying context force the model to guess provenance; prepending patient, ward, and admission context before indexing, backed by a BM25 lexical index, gives every slice its identifying context and adds the exactness lexical search provides.

questions.prompt: What actually enforces the geography requirement?

options.text: Choosing a model tier whose training occurred inside the required geography
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — where a model once trained says nothing about where inference executes; the requirement binds the traffic's termination, not the training data's origin.

options.text: Setting the request language always to the jurisdiction's official language
options.explanation: knobs-not-design — request language changes the answer's wording, not the infrastructure; execution still lands wherever the cheapest endpoint happens to run.

options.text: Data-residency pinning at the delivery route, depending on the cloud provider
options.explanation: Residency pinning is configured at the delivery-route level so that execution terminates in the required geography, and it may depend on the chosen cloud provider, which is exactly the property the policy constrains.

options.text: Adding a clause to the processing agreement promising domestic execution
options.explanation: compliance-theater — a promised clause asserts the obligation on paper while the request path still terminates wherever that day's lowest latency points.

questions.scenario: A regional tax administration moves its ruling-assistant workload to Claude, and its data-protection policy requires that model execution happen inside its jurisdiction. An engineer proposes routing traffic to whichever endpoint currently quotes the lowest latency, treating geography as a billing detail rather than an execution property.
questions.explanation: Residency pinning is configured at the delivery-route level so that execution terminates in the required geography, and it may depend on the chosen cloud provider, which is exactly the property the policy constrains.

questions.prompt: Which integration point fits today's reality?

options.text: A dedicated MCP server maintained for future, currently unplanned consumers
options.explanation: gold-plating — a dedicated MCP server serves future, unplanned consumers; today it adds protocol surface and integration cost that a single-application estate never justifies.

options.text: A direct API integration with approval logic in deterministic server code
options.explanation: A single application with no second client planned gains nothing from a protocol layer; the direct API integrates exactly one consumer, and approval logic lives as deterministic code where the compliance rules already sit.

options.text: A shared MCP layer run by the compliance department for its audits
options.explanation: compliance-theater — handing the integration to a governance-owned layer adds review surface without changing that the approval rules already enforce deterministically in code.

options.text: A second Claude application shipped early to justify the protocol layer
options.explanation: over-orchestration — building a second application just to legitimize the integration pattern spends effort the single-use-case requirement never requested.

questions.scenario: A retailer's platform team proposes delivering its markdown-approval assistant as an MCP integration, citing long-term reuse. Exactly one Claude application exists today, no second client is planned, and the approval logic needs only deterministic code where the compliance rules already live.
questions.explanation: A single application with no second client planned gains nothing from a protocol layer; the direct API integrates exactly one consumer, and approval logic lives as deterministic code where the compliance rules already sit.

questions.prompt: Which change closes the authorization gap?

options.text: Log every tool call together with the token used for it
options.explanation: compliance-theater — logs record the borrowed identity after each request succeeds; they neither validate the audience nor stop the pass-through.

options.text: Raise the token's scope so one credential serves every downstream API
options.explanation: convenience-over-safety — widening one credential's scope enlarges the blast radius across every system, the opposite of closing the gap the review found.

options.text: Restate the calling conventions in the system prompt the agents share
options.explanation: prompt-as-guarantee — restated conventions in a system prompt are model guidance, not an authorization boundary enforced at the server.

options.text: Validate each inbound token's audience and mint a separate upstream token
options.explanation: An MCP server acting as a resource server must validate that each token was issued specifically for it and obtain its own credential for the upstream API; together those two habits close the confused-deputy class of failure.

questions.scenario: An industrial-automation vendor fronts its line-monitoring SaaS with an MCP server. The server accepts whichever bearer token arrives, without checking who the token was issued for, and forwards that same client token unchanged to the factory's maintenance API, so one service answers with another's identity.
questions.explanation: An MCP server acting as a resource server must validate that each token was issued specifically for it and obtain its own credential for the upstream API; together those two habits close the confused-deputy class of failure.

questions.prompt: What is the load-bearing constraint here?

options.text: A larger context window that holds both document versions at once
options.explanation: scale-not-strategy — extra capacity holds both versions without distinguishing them, so answers quoting the superseded schedule recur exactly as before.

options.text: Weekly human spot-checks of sampled answers against current fee schedules
options.explanation: eval-blindness — a weekly sample inspects a handful of answers after the fact, while the midweek exposure between publication and indexing remains structurally untouched.

options.text: Retrieval index coverage and freshness, validated whenever the corpus changes
options.explanation: The knowledge mitigation works only while the retrieval index contains the current documents, so validating completeness and consistency whenever the corpus changes is the condition the whole system rests on, and it is exactly what the weekly cycle skips.

options.text: A stronger model that reads the retrieved terms more carefully
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — a stronger reader interprets whatever the index holds, so a stale index yields the same superseded terms, merely read more carefully.

questions.scenario: A bank's product-terms assistant answers from an index refreshed every Sunday, while pricing PDFs published midweek reach the document store the same day. Supervisors keep finding answers quoted from superseded fee schedules, yet the cost and latency dashboards show the system perfectly healthy.
questions.explanation: The knowledge mitigation works only while the retrieval index contains the current documents, so validating completeness and consistency whenever the corpus changes is the condition the whole system rests on, and it is exactly what the weekly cycle skips.

questions.prompt: How is the grounding lookup guaranteed?

options.text: Describe the ticketing tool's importance more persuasively in the prompt
options.explanation: louder-not-explicit — persuasion raises the probability of calling the lookup but leaves the skip path open, which is precisely where the auditors' two stale answers came from.

options.text: Add a scoring penalty so plain text answers score lower
options.explanation: knobs-not-design — no sampling penalty converts a maybe-call into a guaranteed call; the decision between answering and looking up stays probabilistic.

options.text: Cache repeated ticket lookups so repeated identical calls become cheaper
options.explanation: premature-optimization — caching lowers the cost of the calls that happen, yet the audited failures occurred on turns where the model never called at all.

options.text: Set tool_choice so every request must return a tool call
options.explanation: With tool_choice set to any, or forced to the ticket-lookup tool itself, the response must be a tool invocation, turning the grounding lookup into a structural guarantee rather than a judgment call.

questions.scenario: A support-desk SaaS requires that every answer be grounded in the customer's current ticket state. The assistant often answers from conversational memory when the lookup feels unnecessary to the model, and auditors flagged two stale-state answers in their last review, even though the lookup itself never failed.
questions.explanation: With tool_choice set to any, or forced to the ticket-lookup tool itself, the response must be a tool invocation, turning the grounding lookup into a structural guarantee rather than a judgment call.

questions.prompt: Which reliability pattern provides the degradation?

options.text: Retries against the identical primary tier with exponentially longer waits
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — retries retrace the same slow dependency; during a latency doubling, each retry waits longer and still returns after the four-second budget has passed.

options.text: A circuit breaker that suspends the assistant until provider latency recovers
options.explanation: convenience-over-safety — a breaker's binary pass-or-suspend behavior turns every spike into a full outage, when dispatch asked for degradation rather than another failure mode.

options.text: A fallback chain that serves from a faster tier during spikes
options.explanation: A fallback chain operates in the orchestration layer: while the primary tier's latency spikes, the same request is served from a faster model, trading some answer quality for answered questions instead of stalled sessions.

options.text: A second regional deployment of the identical primary model configuration
options.explanation: scale-not-strategy — replicating the identical configuration in another region inherits the very same latency spike, so nothing diverse stands by when the primary stalls.

questions.scenario: A telecom's technician assistant must answer within four seconds at the 95th percentile. During regional network events, provider latency occasionally doubles, sessions time out, and the design offers no second path, so dispatch wants graceful degradation, not a stalled assistant.
questions.explanation: A fallback chain operates in the orchestration layer: while the primary tier's latency spikes, the same request is served from a faster model, trading some answer quality for answered questions instead of stalled sessions.

questions.prompt: Which TWO statements about MCP resources hold? Select TWO.

options.text: Resources expose data directly to prompts without requiring tool calls
options.explanation: Resources follow a read-only request-response pattern: the client's ReadResourceRequest returns the content, and your code may inject it straight into the prompt, with no model-initiated tool call anywhere in the path.

options.text: Templated resource URIs include parameters that the SDK passes onward
options.explanation: Templated resources give a URI pattern with parameters; the client fills them and the SDK passes them onward, so the same memorandum can be read by identifier without hand-built URIs. Read-only, they suit the consultation flow the partners described.

options.text: Resource reads trigger side-effecting writes on the originating MCP server
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — mutation belongs to tools; resources follow a read-only request-response pattern, which is exactly why they suit the consultation flow the partners described.

options.text: Resources always require a model-initiated tool call before any retrieval
options.explanation: extra-hop — the resource pattern returns content for direct prompt injection, so routing every read through a model-initiated tool call reinstates the round-trip the partners criticized.

questions.scenario: A law firm's precedent MCP server exposes thousands of archived memoranda. Reading a memorandum never modifies anything, yet every read costs a full tool round-trip, and partners ask why consultation cannot simply inject the passage when a colleague is mentioned, while drafting must stay interactive and state-changing.
questions.explanation: Resources follow a read-only request-response pattern: the client's ReadResourceRequest returns the content, and your code may inject it straight into the prompt, with no model-initiated tool call anywhere in the path.

questions.prompt: Which instrumentation catches this failure class?

options.text: An anomaly alarm on the daily token consumption of the workload
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — skipped embeddings consume almost no additional tokens, so consumption stays level while the answers quietly lose their newly ingested decades.

options.text: A scheduled comparison of the monthly inference spend against its forecast
options.explanation: compliance-theater — spend variance describes the finance ledger, not retrieval; the skipped embeddings move the bill too little to flag and the latency not at all.

options.text: A quarterly satisfaction survey of the researchers who use the assistant
options.explanation: eval-blindness — a survey surfaces complaints quarters later and cannot point to the ingestion batch whose skipped embeddings caused the misses.

options.text: Retrieval precision measured on every request, with alerts on significant drops
options.explanation: Retrieval quality is the failure surface, so measuring precision on every request and alerting when it falls below threshold is the instrumentation that catches indexing gaps neither cost nor latency will ever show.

questions.scenario: A records office's declassification assistant has run for two quarters, and its cost per record and p95 latency are flat and green. Researchers report that newly ingested 1970s case files rarely surface in answers, because the ingest batch skipped embedding for scanned pages, and nothing in today's dashboards would have caught that.
questions.explanation: Retrieval quality is the failure surface, so measuring precision on every request and alerting when it falls below threshold is the instrumentation that catches indexing gaps neither cost nor latency will ever show.

questions.prompt: What should the failing tool return?

options.text: Structured errors that distinguish error category, retryability, and human-readable cause
options.explanation: Structured errors carry a category — transient, validation, business, or permission — plus an isRetryable flag, so the agent retries transient failures locally, stops on business answers, and treats access failures as its own re-authentication problem.

options.text: Longer tool descriptions teaching the model when failures usually occur
options.explanation: louder-not-explicit — prose about failure modes carries no machine-readable decision, so the agent still cannot tell a timeout from a policy rejection.

options.text: A single success flag that collapses every failure into one boolean
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — one boolean is the present defect; a generic status hides the difference between an access failure, which needs a retry decision, and a valid empty result.

options.text: An automatic retry wrapper placed around every MCP tool invocation
options.explanation: over-orchestration — uniform retries ignore the error's nature, so business rejections and expired credentials re-fail identically while consuming the same scarce quota.

questions.scenario: An insurer's claims-triage agent calls a fraud-scoring MCP tool whose failures all return the same text, operation failed. When scoring returned business rejections the agent retried valid requests, when credentials expired it retried those too, and the retries hammered the login endpoint during peaks.
questions.explanation: Structured errors carry a category — transient, validation, business, or permission — plus an isRetryable flag, so the agent retries transient failures locally, stops on business answers, and treats access failures as its own re-authentication problem.

questions.prompt: What does the guidance recommend instead?

options.text: Many automatically gradable cases beat a handful of manual ones
options.explanation: Broad, cheap, automatically graded coverage catches more regressions than a small, painstaking, manually graded set, and it can rerun on every change. The trade-off is less scrutiny per case, which volume and rerunnability more than repay.

options.text: Automate the same five cases with a stronger judge model
options.explanation: scale-not-strategy — the case count is the constraint, not the judge's power; five items still miss everything else.

options.text: Assign two more reviewers to grade the same five cases
options.explanation: gold-plating — duplicating painstaking effort raises gating cost while coverage remains five items.

options.text: Route production failures into a weekly human grading queue
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — grading failures after production turns misses into reports, not gates for the next release.

questions.scenario: A pharmacy-benefits manager grades extraction quality with five painstakingly hand-verified cases, rerun after every prompt tweak. Coverage stays narrow, so rare failure modes keep slipping into production. Operations wants wider protection this quarter without slowing the release cadence, and the next release review meets in two weeks.
questions.explanation: Broad, cheap, automatically graded coverage catches more regressions than a small, painstaking, manually graded set, and it can rerun on every change. The trade-off is less scrutiny per case, which volume and rerunnability more than repay.

questions.prompt: Which evaluation category fits this gap?

options.text: A stricter code-based threshold on per-answer accuracy
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — tightening a per-answer check cannot see a failure that only emerges across turns.

options.text: Longer single-turn inputs until the context window fills
options.explanation: scale-not-strategy — a fuller window measures capacity, not whether context survives ten exchanges later.

options.text: Parallel sub-evals, one per sentence of prior context
options.explanation: over-orchestration — splitting one conversation into per-sentence evaluations discards exactly the cross-turn behavior being graded.

options.text: Multi-turn evals scored across whole conversation transcripts
options.explanation: A multi-turn eval scores the conversation: whether prior context holds, whether follow-ups invent details, whether quality survives as the session lengthens. It needs its own golden dataset of transcripts with known-good turns; the cost is building conversations, not pairs.

questions.scenario: A telecom assistant aces every single-turn evaluation, yet production transcripts show it forgetting account details stated earlier in the conversation. The golden set holds only isolated question-and-answer pairs. Callers report the assistant's quality visibly decaying as conversations run longer, so the architect must add the missing kind of evaluation.
questions.explanation: A multi-turn eval scores the conversation: whether prior context holds, whether follow-ups invent details, whether quality survives as the session lengthens. It needs its own golden dataset of transcripts with known-good turns; the cost is building conversations, not pairs.

questions.prompt: Which grading belongs at launch?

options.text: The cheapest available judge, graded nightly across all volumes
options.explanation: knobs-not-design — cheaper grading wins later, once the judge is trusted; the launch bears unnoticed judgment risk.

options.text: Regex assertions on notice length, structure, and required sign-offs
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — regexes prove formatting, not the novel, judgment-heavy correctness the reviewing counsel will litigate.

options.text: Human review scored by rubric, reused to calibrate the judge
options.explanation: Human grading is the most expensive rung, reserved for high-stakes or novel behaviors that neither code nor a calibrated judge yet covers, and its labels later calibrate the judge. The cost is throughput: expect sampled, not complete, notice review.

options.text: Ship without grading, because the notices are legally routine documents
options.explanation: compliance-theater — declaring the notices routine skips the assessment the launch needs; routine is the claim, not the finding.

questions.scenario: A regulatory agency's assistant drafts enforcement notices, and a wrong notice triggers a formal appeal, so mistakes carry real cost. The behaviors are novel with no established rubric, and neither code checks nor the judge inspire trust yet. The reviewing counsel demands the strongest grading for the launch window.
questions.explanation: Human grading is the most expensive rung, reserved for high-stakes or novel behaviors that neither code nor a calibrated judge yet covers, and its labels later calibrate the judge. The cost is throughput: expect sampled, not complete, notice review.

questions.prompt: What determines how much evidence the rollout needs?

options.text: The consequence of a wrong call, not how early numbers look
options.explanation: The confidence requirement is set by the consequence of being wrong, not by an encouraging first sample; in a high-consequence routing a small positive-looking sample proves little. The cost is patience: enough sessions per group before claiming the win.

options.text: A few hundred sessions suffice when the early effect looks clearly positive
options.explanation: premature-optimization — an encouraging early sample is anecdote, not statistical power; the rollout proceeds on luck.

options.text: Sample size matters only for cost metrics, never for quality
options.explanation: stale-fact — quality effects also need sizing; the module requires sample estimates for accuracy just as for cost.

options.text: Ship to thirty percent of traffic and extrapolate whatever results arrive
options.explanation: eval-blindness — extrapolating whatever arrives forgives neither the traffic mix nor the effect's uncertainty.

questions.scenario: A retail bank will reroute thirty percent of its advisory traffic through a new retrieval configuration, and a wrong call costs the quarterly revenue plan. The experiment team proposes deciding after two days because the early numbers already look positive. Leadership asks what should actually decide the sample size.
questions.explanation: The confidence requirement is set by the consequence of being wrong, not by an encouraging first sample; in a high-consequence routing a small positive-looking sample proves little. The cost is patience: enough sessions per group before claiming the win.

questions.prompt: Select TWO. Which practices make the grading rigorous?

options.text: Detailed rubrics with a small, fixed verdict set
options.explanation: Detailed rubrics with constrained verdicts force consistent, comparable judgments instead of drifting scores. The trade-off: the judge prompt becomes engineered, tested infrastructure in its own right.

options.text: Calibration against a held-out set of human-labeled outputs
options.explanation: Calibration against human-labeled examples proves the judge agrees with human judgment before its verdicts gate anything. The cost is assembling and periodically refreshing that labeled calibration set.

options.text: Grading with the same model that produced each output
options.explanation: stale-fact — self-preference is the documented weakness: a model judging its own outputs retains its reasoning context and rarely challenges itself.

options.text: Free-form scores returned with no reasoning alongside them
options.explanation: eval-blindness — free-form scores without forced reasoning make borderline inconsistency invisible precisely where the judge wobbles.

questions.scenario: A marketplace's moderation assistant now passes through an LLM judge whose nightly verdicts wobble on borderline cases. The judge currently grades the very outputs it produced, returns free-form scores, and has never met a human-labeled example. The platform lead wants the TWO practices that make the grading rigorous.
questions.explanation: Detailed rubrics with constrained verdicts force consistent, comparable judgments instead of drifting scores. The trade-off: the judge prompt becomes engineered, tested infrastructure in its own right.

questions.prompt: Which control catches the next regression early?

options.text: Run the eval suite as the gate for every change
options.explanation: Every production change — model swap, prompt revision, context strategy, retrieval configuration — runs the eval suite during development before shipping. It is the only reliable way to know whether the change helped. The trade-off is keeping that suite trustworthy.

options.text: Freeze all configuration until the production complaint rate settles
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — freezing configuration stops future change but explains none of the three regressions already shipped.

options.text: Escalate every third complaint to a standing human review board
options.explanation: compliance-theater — an escalation board records misses; it never tests the next change the pipeline wants to ship.

options.text: Compare quarterly complaint rates across the last four shipped releases
options.explanation: eval-blindness — quarter-over-quarter rates narrate history; they cannot attribute damage to the change that caused it.

questions.scenario: An insurer swapped its model, then rewrote the retrieval prompt, then changed its context strategy; each change landed directly in production because the demo looked fine. Complaints climbed after the third, and nobody can attribute the damage to a named change. The steering committee demands one standing control.
questions.explanation: Every production change — model swap, prompt revision, context strategy, retrieval configuration — runs the eval suite during development before shipping. It is the only reliable way to know whether the change helped. The trade-off is keeping that suite trustworthy.

questions.prompt: Which reading of the results catches it?

options.text: A stricter overall threshold, one point above the new mean
options.explanation: knobs-not-design — the threshold arbitrates the mixture, while the rare segment still swings freely beneath it.

options.text: A larger golden set to stabilize the overall noisy mean
options.explanation: scale-not-strategy — more mixed samples tighten the mean while the buried segment stays statistically invisible.

options.text: Re-run the full suite nightly until complaint patterns fully settle
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — nightly reruns measure the same mixture; frequency cannot reveal a segment the set never isolates.

options.text: A per-category breakdown, not the aggregate mean by itself
options.explanation: Interpretation means reading where the score moved, not just how far: a change that raises the mean while quietly degrading a rare, expensive segment is not an improvement. The cost is segmenting the golden set and reading it by category.

questions.scenario: A forklift maker's document assistant shipped a retrieval prompt that raised the overall golden-set mean. Engineering celebrated until warranty analysts reported that answers on rare legacy diagrams quietly got worse in the same week. The next release gate must catch this pattern without slowing the team down.
questions.explanation: Interpretation means reading where the score moved, not just how far: a change that raises the mean while quietly degrading a rare, expensive segment is not an improvement. The cost is segmenting the golden set and reading it by category.

questions.prompt: Which evaluation property decides the recommendation?

options.text: Agents always produce higher answer quality than fixed chains do
options.explanation: eval-blindness — 'always higher quality' assumes what only measurement shows; the documented trade-off is lower completion rates.

options.text: Workflows are far easier to evaluate, since each step is known
options.explanation: With the steps known in advance, each one can be tested, scored, and regression-checked on its own, which is why workflows suit production reliability targets; agents buy flexibility at the price of unpredictability.

options.text: Workflows consume fewer tokens because their prompts stay much shorter
options.explanation: knobs-not-design — token cost is an optimization property, not the evaluation property the committee asked about.

options.text: Autonomy guarantees correct recovery whenever any single tool call fails
options.explanation: prompt-as-guarantee — guaranteed recovery is asserted, not measured; unpredictability is the documented cost of agency.

questions.scenario: A SaaS team debates its support redesign: the fixed chain is easy to regression-test because every step is known, while the proposed autonomous agent answers more creatively but takes a different tool path every run. The steering committee asks why the recommendation favors the chain despite the agent's appeal.
questions.explanation: With the steps known in advance, each one can be tested, scored, and regression-checked on its own, which is why workflows suit production reliability targets; agents buy flexibility at the price of unpredictability.

questions.prompt: How should the criterion be rewritten?

options.text: Keep the vague wording but let three senior reviewers vote
options.explanation: eval-blindness — reviewer voting polls opinions; it still never defines what passing means for any single case.

options.text: Name the fields to extract, the thresholds, and failure modes
options.explanation: Success criteria must be specific and measurable: the behavior stated concretely, the threshold set by the business, and each named failure mode becoming a category in the golden set. The trade-off is that inspiring, vague wording cannot survive.

options.text: Track satisfaction ratings from business users after each release
options.explanation: compliance-theater — satisfaction surveys measure sentiment after shipping; they do not define the behavior the eval must check.

options.text: Trust the model's self-rated confidence as the passing mark
options.explanation: stale-fact — self-rated confidence is an unreliable proxy; the notes treat confidence self-ratings as poorly calibrated signals.

questions.scenario: A contracts vendor's written requirement reads "assess indemnification accurately." The architect must turn that sentence into something the eval suite can actually measure, because today nobody agrees what passing means and two reviewers scored the same output differently last quarter. Legal signs off only on criteria they can defend.
questions.explanation: Success criteria must be specific and measurable: the behavior stated concretely, the threshold set by the business, and each named failure mode becoming a category in the golden set. The trade-off is that inspiring, vague wording cannot survive.

questions.prompt: Why does the order of work matter?

options.text: Ordinary tests would work, since tests and evals check identical behavior
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — ordinary tests pin implementation; an eval pins the behavior a probabilistic system must reliably reproduce.

options.text: Developers ship slower because the eval suite adds parallel maintenance
options.explanation: gold-plating — the parallel suite does cost effort, but it is the verifying mechanism itself, not avoidable overhead.

options.text: Writing evals first makes success measurable and every change verifiable
options.explanation: Defining the eval before production code forces success into measurable terms, exposes design assumptions while they are still cheap to change, and gives every later change a gate. Without it, no change to the behavior can ever be verified.

options.text: Model swaps get cheaper because comparisons then need no written baseline
options.explanation: premature-optimization — comparing without a defined baseline compares against nothing; the gate, not the price, is what changes.

questions.scenario: A records office inherits working extraction code that shipped with no evaluations. The developer proposes building the eval suite afterward, as a QA step once the system runs, and the board wants to know why the order matters. Budget pressure backs the delay — which outcome does the deferral actually cost?
questions.explanation: Defining the eval before production code forces success into measurable terms, exposes design assumptions while they are still cheap to change, and gives every later change a gate. Without it, no change to the behavior can ever be verified.

questions.prompt: Which redesign restores meaningful human review?

options.text: Split the queue across more reviewers and a second shift
options.explanation: scale-not-strategy — doubling reviewers absorbs yesterday's volume; each item still arrives stripped of what a reviewer needs to judge it.

options.text: Route by confidence, reversibility, and cost, showing reviewers inputs and flag reasons
options.explanation: Oversight that covers everything reviews nothing; the routing rule sends only decisions whose stakes warrant attention, and the reviewer view must show the inputs the decision relied on and the flag reason, so there is something to weigh.

options.text: Add an Agree checkbox so reviewer approvals can be recorded faster
options.explanation: compliance-theater — recording approvals faster documents the skim without changing what reviewers can actually see about each case.

options.text: Escalate only the items customers formally dispute after the fact
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — post-dispute escalation discovers the failure through the customer; it never sends the quietly skimmed cases to anyone.

questions.scenario: A claims-automation lead routed every adjudication output to a human queue where reviewers see the final recommendation and an Approve button, nothing else. Queue depth sits near four hundred items daily; by mid-morning reviewers approve continuously to keep pace, and a contested denial later turns out to have been skimmed. Compliance wants the oversight made meaningful again.
questions.explanation: Oversight that covers everything reviews nothing; the routing rule sends only decisions whose stakes warrant attention, and the reviewer view must show the inputs the decision relied on and the flag reason, so there is something to weigh.

questions.prompt: How should the checkpoints be placed?
