options.text: Gate every single action so that nothing executes without a prior approval
options.explanation: over-orchestration — gating the routine setpoint suggestions floods reviewers, and oversight collapses into approvals, the consent-fatigue failure.

options.text: Keep the nightly review but add a much richer action summary
options.explanation: compliance-theater — by then the purchase orders have shipped; a richer summary of a shipped calibration cannot stop the next one.

options.text: Remove the controller write from the agent and apply it by hand
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — deleting the write solves the gate by removing the capability the deployment exists to deliver.

options.text: Gate each irreversible, high-stakes action before execution; sample routine ones
options.explanation: The checkpoint is a gate positioned by risk and reversibility: it pauses execution before any irreversible or high-stakes action the agent would otherwise take autonomously, while lower-stakes actions are sampled rather than gated one by one.

questions.scenario: A factory-automation agent adjusts dozens of production-setpoint suggestions per shift, edits purchase orders when suppliers report shortages, and occasionally writes a new calibration to the line controller. The lead proposes one nightly review of everything the agent did, since gates add latency; orders ship before anyone reads, and the controller once shipped an unsafe calibration.
questions.explanation: The checkpoint is a gate positioned by risk and reversibility: it pauses execution before any irreversible or high-stakes action the agent would otherwise take autonomously, while lower-stakes actions are sampled rather than gated one by one.

questions.prompt: Which TWO placements match the guidance? Select TWO.

options.text: Input screening: use a lightweight model to catch jailbreak patterns
options.explanation: Input intent is ambiguous and jailbreak patterns cannot be exhaustively captured by rules, so a lightweight model classifies the input before the request reaches the model; deterministic checks chain behind it for what they can guarantee.

options.text: Tool-call authorization: judge each caller's scope with a model
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — authorization must be deterministic, an allowlist plus identity and scope, so the decision is provable and replayable; a judged score is neither.

options.text: Output screening: validate returned tickets against the expected schema
options.explanation: A known structure is exactly what a validator catches with certainty; the model-based judge is reserved for qualities like toxicity or policy compliance that language understanding, not a schema, decides.

options.text: Input screening: a fixed regex as the only jailbreak defense
options.explanation: knobs-not-design — the guidance pairs a model-based classifier with deterministic checks because each misses what the other catches; the brittle rule alone blocks only what it anticipated.

questions.scenario: A B2B SaaS firm is wiring guardrails into its support assistant. In one workshop the team debates each decision point: whether jailbreak-style screening needs a classifier, whether the schema check on returned tickets can be a validator, and whether tool authorization can stay an allowlist that auditors can replay. Two placements match the published guidance.
questions.explanation: Input intent is ambiguous and jailbreak patterns cannot be exhaustively captured by rules, so a lightweight model classifies the input before the request reaches the model; deterministic checks chain behind it for what they can guarantee.

questions.prompt: What turns the register into auditable proof?

options.text: Expand the design document with more detailed descriptions per control
options.explanation: compliance-theater — a thicker design document still names controls nobody can demonstrate; a control no one can prove is indistinguishable from one that is not running.

options.text: Attach a named owner and a living evidence artifact to each obligation
options.explanation: Each obligation becomes a technical control, an accountable owner, and an evidence artifact a reviewer can inspect, because a control specified without an owner and proof can silently stop operating and then surface only as an audit finding.

options.text: Snapshot the current configuration and archive it as final evidence
options.explanation: stale-fact — a frozen snapshot ages immediately; configurations drift, so the artifact must stay alive and be revalidated on a cadence.

options.text: Route every obligation question to the security lead as single accountable owner
options.explanation: over-orchestration — collapsing accountability onto one role loses the per-obligation owner that security, legal, and platform each must agree to hold.

questions.scenario: A retail group's assistant deployment maps each compliance obligation to a control — access limits, residency, transparency — in a design-time document. Nobody owns the entries, and nothing shows they operate; meanwhile a configuration change this quarter retired the redaction step unnoticed. The access-records audit is next month, and the register is a narrative.
questions.explanation: Each obligation becomes a technical control, an accountable owner, and an evidence artifact a reviewer can inspect, because a control specified without an owner and proof can silently stop operating and then surface only as an audit finding.

questions.prompt: Which distinction does the operations lead miss?

options.text: Treat the training exclusion as also ending retention and monitoring
options.explanation: stale-fact — the exclusion is real but speaks only to training; it says nothing about the retention claim.

options.text: Retention obligations apply only while training use stays enabled
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — retention exists independently for logging, abuse prevention, legal compliance, and configured audit purposes, whether or not training continues.

options.text: Disable retention entirely so the training exclusion becomes trustable
options.explanation: knobs-not-design — retention feeds logging, abuse prevention, legal compliance, and configured audit, so deleting it trades real obligations for a simpler story.

options.text: Training exclusion and retention are two distinct claims made separately
options.explanation: Data may be excluded from model training by default while still being retained or monitored for logging, abuse prevention, legal compliance, or configured audit purposes, so diligence asks both questions and the vendor answers each separately.

questions.scenario: A media-archiving vendor assures publishers that their footage transcripts are excluded from model training by default. A publisher's counsel, during diligence, asks whether the vendor still retains and monitors the transcripts after processing, and for which purposes. The operations lead answers that training exclusion covers everything, and counsel quietly notes the answer missed the question.
questions.explanation: Data may be excluded from model training by default while still being retained or monitored for logging, abuse prevention, legal compliance, or configured audit purposes, so diligence asks both questions and the vendor answers each separately.

questions.prompt: Which mechanism should the architect mandate?

options.text: Least-privilege, action-scoped tool credentials enforced at the integration's server side
options.explanation: Each tool operates with the minimum privileges its action needs, and identity is enforced at the server side rather than trusted from the model, so a wrong-field write stays inside the blast radius of one scoped permission.

options.text: Longer tool descriptions so the model picks the right fields
options.explanation: prompt-as-guarantee — better descriptions guide tool selection but leave every credential as powerful as before; guidance is not authorization.

options.text: A nightly reconciliation sweep that detects any cascading wrong-field writes
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — reconciliation repairs downstream after the cascade; it never constrains what the original write could touch.

options.text: A larger servicing-transaction audit report prepared for the risk committee
options.explanation: compliance-theater — richer reporting observes the cascade afterward while the credential pool that made it wide stays untouched.

questions.scenario: A bank connected its servicing assistant through one pool of powerful credentials: whatever the model decides to touch, the credentials may read or write, because granular wiring seemed like spare work. The model calls its tools competently, but one wrong-field write once cascaded through three downstream servicing systems. Security asks the architect for the mechanism, not intentions.
questions.explanation: Each tool operates with the minimum privileges its action needs, and identity is enforced at the server side rather than trusted from the model, so a wrong-field write stays inside the blast radius of one scoped permission.

questions.prompt: Which addition serves all three audiences?

options.text: Longer, more customer-friendly verdict wording drafted with the legal team
options.explanation: premature-optimization — nicer wording answers only the shipper; the examiner and the tuning team still cannot see what the decision relied on.

options.text: A louder disputes queue so contested verdicts get human attention
options.explanation: louder-not-explicit — routing disputes faster never explains the uncontested ones; reconstruction still starts from a bare verdict.

options.text: Decision logging of inputs, context, output, and routing, replay-keyed
options.explanation: The same instrumentation answers why a decision happened: the log captures inputs, retrieved context, output, and routing, keyed so one decision replays for the shipper, the regulator, and the tuning team; without reconstruction, no explanation is reliable.

options.text: A statistics dashboard of aggregate accuracy by coverage decision type
options.explanation: compliance-theater — aggregates describe the population while each contested decision still cannot be reconstructed from its stored verdict.

questions.scenario: A freight-dispute assistant returns coverage decisions that shippers contest weekly. Users want the reason in their terms, the regulator's examiners want the inputs the decision relied on, and the tuning team wants the retrieved context that shaped each answer. Today the assistant stores only its final verdicts, so every investigation starts from nothing.
questions.explanation: The same instrumentation answers why a decision happened: the log captures inputs, retrieved context, output, and routing, keyed so one decision replays for the shipper, the regulator, and the tuning team; without reconstruction, no explanation is reliable.

questions.prompt: Which handling matches the platform's refusal contract?

options.text: Retry on the same history until the refusal finally clears
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — the same refused context returns further refusals; the trigger condition never changes, so the retry loop rides the same context.

options.text: Hardcode all of today's refusal categories into the switch statement
options.explanation: stale-fact — the enumerated category set changes, so the switch reads the category but the list itself is re-checked at publish time, not frozen.

options.text: Treat every arriving refusal as one single undifferentiated failure event
options.explanation: compliance-theater — a single undifferentiated refusal path looks controlled but forfeits the category and explanation the platform already returns.

options.text: Read stop_reason and stop_details, reset context, and route by category
options.explanation: Refusals report stop_reason refusal with a stop_details policy category so different refusal classes route differently; after a refusal, reset or clear the conversation context, because the same refused context returns further refusals, and tolerate an absent stop_details.

questions.scenario: An edTech homework helper occasionally streams a mid-lesson refusal; its handler treats every refusal as identical, logs it, and replays the same conversation history for the next question, where another refusal often lands. A junior proposes hardcoding today's category strings into a switch statement so responses can branch. The architect reviews the handling code.
questions.explanation: Refusals report stop_reason refusal with a stop_details policy category so different refusal classes route differently; after a refusal, reset or clear the conversation context, because the same refused context returns further refusals, and tolerate an absent stop_details.

questions.prompt: Which addition makes gradual drift visible early?

options.text: A larger model tier that stabilizes the answer quality
options.explanation: scale-not-strategy — a bigger model lowers the error rate, but nobody is watching the trend, so the erosion continues unreviewed.

options.text: Longer trace retention covering the complete ninety-day window
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — deeper traces support diagnosis after the fact; they do not decide when a decline deserves a review.

options.text: A governance rule: quality trigger, named owner, required action
options.explanation: A dashboard collects signals; a feedback loop maps each to a trigger, an owner, and a required action, the decision layer the stack lacks. Without it, a drift crossing no hard threshold stays invisible, because nothing decides the signals mattered.

options.text: An error-rate alert retuned to far stricter failure thresholds
options.explanation: eval-blindness — the score was already falling; another threshold on the error rate misses a drift that never crosses one.

questions.scenario: A retailer's support assistant launched solid: quick answers, steady tone, common questions handled. Ninety days later customers report it feels less useful, yet every dashboard stayed nominal, because the eval score slid gradually while the error rate never crossed any alert threshold and nobody owned the trend. Which addition would have caught the slide weeks earlier?
questions.explanation: A dashboard collects signals; a feedback loop maps each to a trigger, an owner, and a required action, the decision layer the stack lacks. Without it, a drift crossing no hard threshold stays invisible, because nothing decides the signals mattered.

questions.prompt: Select TWO. Which rows belong in the governance table?

options.text: A quarterly compliance-owned output audit, whatever the scores
options.explanation: Regulated reviews fire on a schedule, not at a threshold: the obligation requires periodic output audits even when every metric looks good. Without a calendar trigger and named owner, the checkpoint surfaces only when a reviewer asks for the record.

options.text: A pager alert wired to every collected signal
options.explanation: louder-not-explicit — paging on every signal buries the judgment; a signal routed nowhere still decides nothing.

options.text: A drift trigger that forces an iterate-versus-re-architect diagnosis
options.explanation: The quality row turns a signal into a judgment: diagnose prompt, data, or model drift, then decide to iterate or to re-architect. That decision layer separates a feedback loop from monitoring, and it is what a pager cannot supply.

options.text: A monthly metric report sent to every stakeholder
options.explanation: compliance-theater — a periodic report records what happened but assigns no trigger, no owner, and no action, so no signal is ever decided to matter.

questions.scenario: A regulated clinical-documentation deployment is writing its governance table before launch. Observability collects eval scores, latency, cost, and residency configuration, and the compliance reviewer expects a defined trigger behind every obligation the deployment carries, not a report assembled after the fact. Which TWO rows belong in that table?
questions.explanation: Regulated reviews fire on a schedule, not at a threshold: the obligation requires periodic output audits even when every metric looks good. Without a calendar trigger and named owner, the checkpoint surfaces only when a reviewer asks for the record.

questions.prompt: How should the commitment be rewritten?

options.text: Promise the largest available model tier to reduce errors
options.explanation: scale-not-strategy — even the most capable tiers still err, so the guarantee stays undischarged; the wording, not the model, is the defect.

options.text: Name the metric, the breach condition, the remedy
options.explanation: An SLA makes three things clear: what is measured, what counts as breach, and what happens when one occurs. Reduction techniques help but never eliminate errors, so a probabilistic system promises measured rates with consequences, not determinism. Guarantees become percentages.

options.text: Instruct the model, through the prompt, to answer accurately
options.explanation: prompt-as-guarantee — prompt instructions are guidance, not enforcement, and they cannot convert a probabilistic system into a certainty.

options.text: Log every answered request so disputes can be audited
options.explanation: compliance-theater — audit logging documents breaches after they happen; it never defines the measured metric, the breach condition, or the remedy.

questions.scenario: A SaaS vendor's assistant SLA promises fast, accurate answers, guaranteed. When a client disputes a breach, nobody can say what was measured, what counts as a breach, or what the affected client receives, and the numbers were never tied to anything the business actually expects. Which revision makes the commitment defensible?
questions.explanation: An SLA makes three things clear: what is measured, what counts as breach, and what happens when one occurs. Reduction techniques help but never eliminate errors, so a probabilistic system promises measured rates with consequences, not determinism. Guarantees become percentages.

questions.prompt: Which threshold traces to a tangible source?

options.text: A p95 latency budget traced to the user-experience expectation
options.explanation: Latency thresholds reflect the user-experience expectation named in discovery; because the number traces to how long the workflow may take, it stays defensible. A rounded figure invites the dispute the commitment exists to settle.

options.text: An availability figure chosen because it sounded rigorous
options.explanation: knobs-not-design — an untethered number cannot be traced to any source, so it reads as a preference dressed up as a commitment.

options.text: A quality target borrowed from another deployment's criteria
options.explanation: convenience-over-safety — borrowed acceptance criteria describe a different workflow; quality must trace to the eval results this deployment established.

options.text: A cost ceiling copied from the pilot's measured numbers
options.explanation: stale-fact — production volume routinely runs one to two orders of magnitude above the pilot, so pilot figures answer the wrong question.

questions.scenario: An insurer drafts thresholds for its policy-questions assistant's SLA. The drafter wants numbers that survive a client dispute, and the notes are blunt: a threshold nobody can trace to a source is just a target that sounded reasonable. Which of the four traces to something tangible?
questions.explanation: Latency thresholds reflect the user-experience expectation named in discovery; because the number traces to how long the workflow may take, it stays defensible. A rounded figure invites the dispute the commitment exists to settle.

questions.prompt: What would have kept the change safe?

options.text: A more detailed diagram of the resulting architecture
options.explanation: compliance-theater — a diagram records what the system is; it cannot tell the successor which choices are load-bearing, so the reversal still looks safe.

options.text: The decision, the rejected alternatives, the tradeoff each resolved
options.explanation: The completeness test: can a competent architect who was not in the room make a safe change after reading it? That takes the decision, the rejected alternatives, the tradeoff resolved; a diagram shows what, never why, so choices wrongly reverse.

options.text: Meeting recordings and the chat threads behind each decision
options.explanation: convenience-over-safety — recordings exist, but nobody replays them under pressure; rationale must be written while it is held, not archived for later.

options.text: A versioned permission list inherited from the previous team
options.explanation: stale-fact — a permissions snapshot describes who may change the system, not why the context strategy was residency-load-bearing.

questions.scenario: A wealth manager's assistant has its context strategy redesigned by an inherited engineer to fix a performance complaint; the switch quietly reintroduces a data-handling pattern the original design had retired, breaking the residency constraint. The architecture diagram was thorough, but it recorded only the final design. What should the decision log have carried?
questions.explanation: The completeness test: can a competent architect who was not in the room make a safe change after reading it? That takes the decision, the rejected alternatives, the tradeoff resolved; a diagram shows what, never why, so choices wrongly reverse.

questions.prompt: Which fields let the sponsor justify expansion?

options.text: Deeper latency percentiles and a real-time error dashboard
options.explanation: louder-not-explicit — sharper technical metrics describe the same thing the document already proves: that the system runs.

options.text: A larger monitored sample spread across more storefront regions
options.explanation: scale-not-strategy — more samples of the same technical metrics raise confidence in exactly what the CFO never asked about.

options.text: A reuse note licensing the pattern to sister brands
options.explanation: valid-but-early — the reuse note matters, but it cannot answer the missing question: what the deployment changed in business terms.

options.text: The before-and-after business metric and its auditable control
options.explanation: Volume, latency, and error rate prove the system runs; the before-and-after on the business metric, auditable by a control, tells the CFO what changed. Without the before number there is no story; without the control, the after figure asserts.

questions.scenario: A retail sponsor takes the deployment's outcome document to the CFO: forty thousand requests a month, sub-two-second latency, error rate under half a percent. The CFO answers that the numbers prove the system runs, then asks what changed for the business, and the document has no field that answers it.
questions.explanation: Volume, latency, and error rate prove the system runs; the before-and-after on the business metric, auditable by a control, tells the CFO what changed. Without the before number there is no story; without the control, the after figure asserts.

questions.prompt: Which habit prevents the residency failure?

options.text: Set the region parameter explicitly, not the default
options.explanation: Regional availability on mediated routes requires explicit configuration, and defaulting to a global endpoint is the pattern that breaks residency; the habit is setting the region parameter explicitly rather than inheriting the provider default.

options.text: Document the entry-point responsibility map before writing integration code
options.explanation: extra-hop — the responsibility map keeps task boundaries honest across entry points, but it does not change which region executes the regulated inference.

options.text: Verify feature availability parity across the two chosen routes
options.explanation: stale-fact — feature lag is real across mediated routes, but residency breaks through default configuration, not through parity gaps.

options.text: Move all traffic onto one endpoint for simplicity
options.explanation: convenience-over-safety — collapsing routes deletes the documented secondary path and invites the silent scope creep the responsibility map exists to prevent.

questions.scenario: A public-records authority deploys its filing-summarization assistant across the direct API for search tuning and a cloud-provider route for the regulated path, under a strict in-region residency rule. The integration team keeps the provider's default endpoint configuration to save setup time. Which habit prevents the residency failure?
questions.explanation: Regional availability on mediated routes requires explicit configuration, and defaulting to a global endpoint is the pattern that breaks residency; the habit is setting the region parameter explicitly rather than inheriting the provider default.

questions.prompt: Select TWO. Which judgments satisfy the phase gate?

options.text: Proceed to expansion now because the before metric exists
options.explanation: valid-but-early — the before number proves intent, not outcome; deciding expansion before the after-metric exists substitutes appetite for the evidence the gate demands.

options.text: Schedule the outcome document at a defined post-launch milestone
options.explanation: The gate needs the before-and-after comparison complete, and the after side requires enough production runtime to measure. Naming when the document completes converts an unfilled gate into a scheduled obligation; expansion decided before the after-metric exists is appetite, not evidence.

options.text: Freeze configuration until the after-metric can be measured
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — freezing configuration slows drift, but it neither produces the after-metric nor makes the comparison auditable, so the gate stays unsatisfied either way.

options.text: Name the measurement owner and confirm the control logs
options.explanation: The week-four action makes the coming document complete in principle: an owner accountable for ongoing measurement, and a control whose evidence accrues automatically. With those, the after-metric needs only time, which further meetings cannot supply.

questions.scenario: A healthcare network is four weeks into a clinical-note deployment, and the CFO wants the expansion case now. The outcome document gates the transition and requires a before-and-after business metric, an auditable control, and a named measurement owner. The baseline before-metric exists from discovery, while post-deployment runtime is still short.
questions.explanation: The gate needs the before-and-after comparison complete, and the after side requires enough production runtime to measure. Naming when the document completes converts an unfilled gate into a scheduled obligation; expansion decided before the after-metric exists is appetite, not evidence.

questions.prompt: Which checklist dimension did the team skip?

options.text: Human understanding — the author can explain what shipped and why
options.explanation: Diligence requires the human-understanding check: whoever merges the change explains what the code does and why, including inputs it was never tested against, because passing shallow checks is where judgment erosion starts.

options.text: Correctness — automated tests exist, pass, and match the stated behavior requirement
options.explanation: eval-blindness — the tests were green and behavior matched, so this dimension passed; the miss was that nobody could explain the code.

options.text: Security — no secrets committed, inputs validated, and least-privilege external tool access
options.explanation: valid-but-early — input validation was indeed missing, yet the decisive evidence is that nobody, starting with the author, could explain the deployed behavior.

options.text: Maintainability — the module reads clearly, follows conventions, and hides no surprises
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — readability governs the merged code after the fact but would not have forced anyone to explain the unvalidated input's behavior.

questions.scenario: A retail bank's cards platform credited AI assistance for a quarter of forty percent faster delivery. Then a generated change passed review with green tests yet leaked cardholder data through an input nobody had validated, and in the post-mortem even the author who merged it could not explain its behavior.
questions.explanation: Diligence requires the human-understanding check: whoever merges the change explains what the code does and why, including inputs it was never tested against, because passing shallow checks is where judgment erosion starts.

questions.prompt: Which symptom-to-cause path belongs in the runbook?

options.text: Trace the slowest request span and check whether prompt caching still hits
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — that path answers latency spikes, not gradual quality decline with no code change, so it confirms what nobody disputes.

options.text: Compare answers against an eval set; check model, prompt, and retrieval drift
options.explanation: Gradual quality decline without a code change points at a model or prompt change, or retrieval drift as the corpus grew; the eval comparison turns the symptom into a measured cause.

options.text: Inspect tool authorization, rate limits, and unhandled error paths across integrations
options.explanation: knobs-not-design — that path diagnoses intermittent tool failures through authorization and rate limits; nothing here failed intermittently or at the integration layer.

options.text: Check the per-request model tier and the cache hit rate against budget
options.explanation: eval-blindness — that path explains cost rising without a usage change; this incident says nothing about spend, and its signal is quality, not money.

questions.scenario: Over eight weeks a logistics provider's freight-visibility assistant degraded gradually: answer quality slipped while dashboards stayed green, no deploy touched the service, and the incident sat unexplained until a quarterly review, because the team's runbook never mapped this symptom to its cause.
questions.explanation: Gradual quality decline without a code change points at a model or prompt change, or retrieval drift as the corpus grew; the eval comparison turns the symptom into a measured cause.

questions.prompt: Which control pair delivers that guarantee?

options.text: A weekly governance committee reviews every production release after it has deployed
options.explanation: extra-hop — a retrospective committee adds a hop and a week; the guarantee must hold while the agent acts, not afterward.

options.text: Release-discipline instructions written into the signed prompt the production agent reads
options.explanation: prompt-as-guarantee — prompt instructions are guidance rather than enforcement and weaken exactly when attention drifts or the prompt gets edited.

options.text: A production deploy hook requiring a named release manager, with branch protection
options.explanation: Hooks enforce the production gate: the deploy hook blocks the release until a named release manager authorizes it, and branch protection turns anything the agent writes into a reviewed pull request with no direct route to main.

options.text: Tiered permission profiles that let the agent deploy anywhere without further approvals
options.explanation: convenience-over-safety — per-environment tiers set how much the agent may do en route, but without the deploy hook production still ships on the agent's authority alone.

questions.scenario: A customs agency lets its delivery agent prepare production releases, triage failed builds, and open fix pull requests while running unwatched inside the deployment pipeline. Leadership wants the documented guarantee that the agent acts freely up to the production gate yet cannot pass it alone.
questions.explanation: Hooks enforce the production gate: the deploy hook blocks the release until a named release manager authorizes it, and branch protection turns anything the agent writes into a reviewed pull request with no direct route to main.

questions.prompt: Select TWO. Which statements describe the closing-the-loop design?

options.text: The detection script stays deterministic; Claude is invoked only after a breach
options.explanation: Detection stays deterministic on a rolling baseline, and the model enters only once a control band is breached, so invocation cost tracks anomalies rather than the clock.

options.text: At the 3σ tier the agent acts only through gated, pre-approved routes
options.explanation: At 3σ the agent may open a pull request into the review gate or trigger a runbook approved in advance, so autonomy stays inside gates the organization already controls.

options.text: Claude watches the breach metric continuously and decides when tiers trip
options.explanation: over-orchestration — the design deliberately keeps a model out of the detection loop; a model there adds cost and nondeterminism to a statistical check.

options.text: Findings the agent produces ship through its own automated deployment route
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — findings re-enter as intent.md and ship through the normal review gate; a private deployment route would strand the change outside the audit trail.

questions.scenario: An insurer feeds its post-deploy 5xx rate through a closing-the-loop arrangement: a versioned detection script watches the metric and invokes the assistant when a control band breaches, findings arrive with the firing tier recorded, and triage happens each morning before the on-call engineer starts.
questions.explanation: Detection stays deterministic on a rolling baseline, and the model enters only once a control band is breached, so invocation cost tracks anomalies rather than the clock.

snapshot.description: Full-length scenarios exam: 60 items across the 7 blueprint domains, valid-but-inferior distractors, criterion hidden mid-stem.

snapshot.title: CCAR-P Exam Scenarios — Full C (60Q, dificultad superior)

questions.prompt: Which pattern should the architect pick?

options.text: A single autonomous agent that plans its own lookup sequence freely
options.explanation: over-orchestration — planning autonomy adds unpredictability and cost where every step is already documented and identical on each request.

options.text: A supervisor agent that delegates every lookup step to specialist subagents
options.explanation: over-orchestration — specialist delegation adds coordination overhead on every answer while the documented sequence already orders the steps reliably.

options.text: A single monolithic prompt holding every maintenance manual and lookup rule
options.explanation: prompt-as-guarantee — concentrating everything in one call leaves the ordering, the tools, and the enforcement emergent rather than owned by surrounding code.

options.text: A fixed workflow that executes each documented step in sequence
options.explanation: Predictability, latency, and error cost are the binding factors here: the steps are known, identical, and synchronous, so the workflow orders them in code and keeps every step observable and auditable, exactly the guarantees a planning loop cannot promise.

questions.scenario: An airframer's maintenance-operations assistant answers technicians' fault-code questions. Volume peaks during certification audits, mechanics wait synchronously for every answer, wrong answers have grounded test fleets, and each lookup follows the same documented extract, check, and report sequence despite taking several recorded steps. The steps never vary between shifts, and leadership wants the ordering guaranteed rather than improvised.
questions.explanation: Predictability, latency, and error cost are the binding factors here: the steps are known, identical, and synchronous, so the workflow orders them in code and keeps every step observable and auditable, exactly the guarantees a planning loop cannot promise.

questions.prompt: Which orchestration satisfies the compliance contract?

options.text: Peer-to-peer handoffs where each specialist decides the next step itself
options.explanation: valid-but-early — direct handoffs shorten the path but fragment ownership of the ordering, so nobody guarantees an exception actually stops the downstream chain.

options.text: A supervisor invoking specialists in sequence, recording outcomes, halting on exceptions
options.explanation: The coordinator owns all inter-agent communication, routing, and error handling, so the ordering, the exception halts, and the ordered record are all enforced at one chokepoint; the trail the officer signs is complete by construction instead of reconstructed afterward.

options.text: All four specialists running fully in parallel, their outputs merged afterwards
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — parallelism destroys the ordering the audit requires, and the tariff exception arrives after dependent passes have already run and been recorded.

options.text: A shared event log that every specialist opportunistically monitors and answers
options.explanation: valid-but-early — opportunistic consumption leaves invocation order emergent, so gaps and missed exception handling surface only when an auditor reconstructs the trail.

questions.scenario: A port authority's berth-booking suite runs four specialists: berthing rules, tariff calculation, customs documentation, and pilotage. Each booking must leave a complete, ordered record of every decision, later specialists must not run when the tariff step flags an exception, and the compliance officer personally signs the resulting audit trail. Today the specialists coordinate through one shared message log with no owner.
questions.explanation: The coordinator owns all inter-agent communication, routing, and error handling, so the ordering, the exception halts, and the ordered record are all enforced at one chokepoint; the trail the officer signs is complete by construction instead of reconstructed afterward.

questions.prompt: Select TWO. Which characteristics favor the autonomous agent?

options.text: The verification steps are known in advance and identical for every submitted registration
options.explanation: over-orchestration — a known, identical step sequence is the fixed workflow's case, so granting a planning loop pays for flexibility those submissions never exercise.

options.text: Input formats arrive unpredictably and demand dynamic handling on every drive
options.explanation: Unpredictable input formats demand exactly the adaptation a planning loop provides: it observes each result and chooses the next action where a wired sequence would have guessed the handling in advance.

options.text: Which checks run only becomes clear from each intermediate result returned
options.explanation: When a step's necessity only becomes clear mid-task, the documented fit is the loop that plans, acts, observes, and decides its next step; fixed steps would guess at paths they cannot foresee.

options.text: Every verification step must remain individually auditable and reproducible for the record
options.explanation: valid-but-early — auditability argues for the workflow, whose fixed, individually reproducible steps are precisely what a planning loop makes harder to certify.

questions.scenario: An electoral consultancy prototypes the address-verification assistant for registration drives. Some counties deliver spreadsheets, others scanned ledgers, and whether a bounds check or a duplicate-records check comes next only becomes clear once the previous records check returns. Qualifying counts publish on statutory dates, so leadership asks which failures a fixed workflow would leave uncovered.
questions.explanation: Unpredictable input formats demand exactly the adaptation a planning loop provides: it observes each result and chooses the next action where a wired sequence would have guessed the handling in advance.

questions.prompt: Which adjustment restores the buried findings?

options.text: Front-load the key admissibility findings with explicit, clearly labeled section headings
options.explanation: Attention holds the start and end of long inputs reliably and loses material from the middle; placing the findings the decision needs at the beginning of the aggregated packet, explicitly sectioned, trades the narrative order for recall, which is the documented positional mechanism.

options.text: Move the conclusions block to the very top, above the metadata
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — the conclusions already process reliably because they sit at the start; their promotion does nothing for findings positioned in the middle of the packet.

options.text: Chunk the packet and retrieve only the passages each question cites
options.explanation: valid-but-early — retrieval earns its extra hop when material exceeds the window; this packet fits comfortably, so dispatching passages cannot recover what position hid.

options.text: Re-run every summary through a second, fully independent reviewing instance
options.explanation: extra-hop — a second reading duplicates the same positional exposure, so whatever the middle hid from the first pass it hides from the reviewer too.

questions.scenario: A national forensics institute's evidence-summaries assistant reads each chain-of-custody packet: personnel changes, transfer timestamps, and storage conditions in narrative order, conclusions at the top, admissibility findings buried mid-packet. The conclusions always surface; the mid-packet findings surface intermittently, and reviewers catch the misses by hand. The packet was shortened twice and the misses returned both times, while the packet fits the context window with room to spare.
questions.explanation: Attention holds the start and end of long inputs reliably and loses material from the middle; placing the findings the decision needs at the beginning of the aggregated packet, explicitly sectioned, trades the narrative order for recall, which is the documented positional mechanism.

questions.prompt: Which addition measures production correctness?

options.text: Token-consumption alerts that fire whenever daily usage drifts from its norms
options.explanation: compliance-theater — spend alerts watch the bill, not the answers; a forecast can stay perfectly cheap and still miss every day of the season unnoticed.

options.text: A larger reasoning model, since forecast accuracy generally improves with capability
options.explanation: scale-not-strategy — capability shifts accuracy statistically, yet without captured corrections the team still never learns how often the published forecasts miss.

options.text: A feedback loop turning downstream corrections into labelled evaluation cases
options.explanation: A feedback loop captures the corrections managers already make and routes a sample of production outputs into a labelled evaluation set; that converts scattered overrides into a measured accuracy signal, the only way production correctness becomes observable at all.

options.text: A scheduled quarterly review that re-reads the whole forecast prompt's wording
options.explanation: eval-blindness — reviewing wording inspects the instructions and never the outputs, so the managers' overrides, which are the ground truth, stay unmeasured and unused.

questions.scenario: A theme-park group's ride-forecast assistant has survived one full season. Operations dashboards show healthy latency and cost, direction managers routinely override the published forecasts downstream, and nobody can quantify how often the forecasts actually miss. Twice the team revised the prompt wording and the override rate never moved, because the corrections land in chat threads nobody aggregates.
questions.explanation: A feedback loop captures the corrections managers already make and routes a sample of production outputs into a labelled evaluation set; that converts scattered overrides into a measured accuracy signal, the only way production correctness becomes observable at all.

questions.prompt: Select TWO. Which conditions warrant the multi-agent design?

options.text: Each strand needs specialists, tools, and context that overload one agent
options.explanation: Distinct sub-tasks needing different specialisations, tools, and context would swamp a single agent's window; focused agents with their own isolated context are exactly the mechanism that lifts that ceiling.

options.text: Several strands are independent and can run fully in parallel
options.explanation: Independent sub-tasks that run in parallel cut the end-to-end synthesis time, matching a cost-tolerant, coverage-driven brief; the coordinator dispatches the strands simultaneously and aggregates their results.

options.text: The consortium's primary goal is minimizing total token consumption per run
options.explanation: scale-not-strategy — every subagent runs its own isolated context, so multi-agent designs multiply token spend; choosing them to economize inverts the documented trade-off.

options.text: The programme sponsor explicitly asked for the most sophisticated architecture available
options.explanation: gold-plating — sponsor preference is not a property of the work; the design is justified by the strands' independence, specialization, and context weight, which the brief already fixes.

questions.scenario: A polar-observatory consortium briefs a synthesis across independent evidence streams: borehole thermal series, satellite imagery, and instrument-interference investigations. Each strand demands its own specialists, instruments, and dense reference context that would crowd a single assistant's window, the strands share no dependencies, and the review board accepted a higher per-run cost in exchange for deeper coverage. Volume is low and weekly.
questions.explanation: Distinct sub-tasks needing different specialisations, tools, and context would swamp a single agent's window; focused agents with their own isolated context are exactly the mechanism that lifts that ceiling.

questions.prompt: Where should the penalty arithmetic live?

options.text: A few extra few-shot examples of correctly computed contractual penalty calculations
options.explanation: prompt-as-guarantee — examples raise the odds, but the amounts stay emergent model output, so finance keeps reconciling them against the calculator every cycle.

options.text: A second, independent reviewing instance that checks each penalty figure afterwards
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — a reviewer flags mismatches after the fact, but the nondeterministic arithmetic itself still produces the figure that was signed.

options.text: A longer system prompt that restates the contractual penalty formula precisely
options.explanation: louder-not-explicit — restating the formula more precisely improves adherence statistically, while the same inputs still need not yield the same amounts across runs.

options.text: Penalty amounts computed in existing code, narrative drafted by Claude
options.explanation: The decomposition lens assigns deterministic, same-input-same-output work to existing systems and keeps judgment and narrative with the model; computed in code, the penalty repeats exactly, which is the repeatability finance's reference calculator already proved the business needs.

questions.scenario: A biotech cold-chain monitor summarizes carrier temperature excursions and computes the contractual penalty amount for every shipment. One prompt currently asks the model for both the narrative and the amounts. Finance reports penalty figures that occasionally disagree with its reference calculator while the prose reads perfectly, and two reruns of the same shipment have produced different penalty amounts.
questions.explanation: The decomposition lens assigns deterministic, same-input-same-output work to existing systems and keeps judgment and narrative with the model; computed in code, the penalty repeats exactly, which is the repeatability finance's reference calculator already proved the business needs.

questions.prompt: What decides the cost question here?

options.text: Parallel research subagents, since dividing the work divides the token bill
options.explanation: stale-fact — splitting work duplicates overhead rather than sharing it, because each subagent's isolated context window adds its own spend to the total.

options.text: The single augmented assistant, because breadth-light questions avoid the multiplier
options.explanation: Multi-agent systems multiply token spend, roughly fifteen times a single chat, because every subagent carries its own isolated context; breadth-light questions under a hard cost ceiling gain nothing from that, so the retrieval-backed single assistant is the only shape the ceiling permits.

options.text: Prompt caching, which trims the repeated policy corpus's retrieval token overhead
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — caching changes what a repeated prefix costs, not the duplication; the subagent contexts multiply what gets read, however cheaply.

options.text: A larger reasoning model, because sharper answers would end conversations sooner
options.explanation: scale-not-strategy — capability changes neither the question's breadth nor the duplication; the multiplier is structural, not a function of answer quality.

questions.scenario: A cruise line's shoreside team answers itinerary-policy questions for call-center agents, each answered from one policy corpus retrieved at call time. Daily volume is modest, the questions never need breadth or parallel exploration, and the CFO holds the deployment to an explicit per-question cost ceiling. A remaining proposal would add a coordinator dispatching parallel research subagents for every question.
questions.explanation: Multi-agent systems multiply token spend, roughly fifteen times a single chat, because every subagent carries its own isolated context; breadth-light questions under a hard cost ceiling gain nothing from that, so the retrieval-backed single assistant is the only shape the ceiling permits.

questions.prompt: Which factor picks the pattern here?

options.text: Latency, because fleet certification deadlines punish even a slow summarization pipeline
options.explanation: valid-but-early — the brief says answers are not latency-bound, so buying speed purchases a constraint that nothing in this operation is actually feeling.

options.text: Cost, because certification volumes stay modest through the current fiscal year
options.explanation: premature-optimization — the memo states budget is not binding, so optimizing around cost distracts from the constraint the review boards genuinely feel.

options.text: Error cost, since missed conditions delay certifications for multiple weeks
options.explanation: When the five factors pull differently, the tightest constraint decides: here a missed condition costs weeks of fleet availability, so the office buys the most predictable, observable pattern and pays whatever cost or latency that guarantee asks.

options.text: Observability, because the boards ask to trace each conclusion they sign
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — traceability is a demand the binding constraint must satisfy, not the selecting factor; whichever pattern error cost picks, the traceability follows from it.

questions.scenario: A certification-operations office at a national nuclear operator summaries clearance records for review boards. A missed certification condition delays fleets for weeks; a wrong sentence invites a regulator's question; the boards demand conclusions they can trace step by step. Volume is modest, answers are not latency-bound, and the procurement memo notes budget is not the binding constraint this fiscal year.
questions.explanation: When the five factors pull differently, the tightest constraint decides: here a missed condition costs weeks of fleet availability, so the office buys the most predictable, observable pattern and pays whatever cost or latency that guarantee asks.

questions.prompt: Which coordinator change fixes this?

options.text: Longer, more detailed instruction sheets attached to every dispatched lore subagent
options.explanation: louder-not-explicit — sharper instructions change what subagents produce, not whether anything evaluates the aggregated synthesis before it ships.

options.text: An iterative refinement loop where the coordinator evaluates and re-routes
options.explanation: The coordinator's refinement loop evaluates the aggregated synthesis against its quality criteria and re-routes tasks where coverage falls short; that added evaluation step, not more instruction or more workers, catches missing canon before publication, which is what the forums were doing.

options.text: A standing fifth subagent dedicated exclusively to detecting contradictions against canon
options.explanation: gold-plating — yesterday's gap gets a permanent worker while the canon keeps moving; judging whether the synthesis covers it remains the coordinator's responsibility.

options.text: Narrower task decomposition, splitting every dispatch into smaller and safer units
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — finer decomposition shrinks what each subagent sees but never adds the evaluation that decides whether the aggregated synthesis is actually complete.

questions.scenario: A games studio's lore-continuity coordinator dispatches subagents across quest texts, codex entries, and dialogue records, then aggregates their synthesis into continuity notes. Recent expansions shipped notes that contradicted the region's established canon, the forums noticed before reviewers did, and the canon now grows faster than editors can read. The coordinator currently forwards every synthesis it receives, unchanged, to publication.
questions.explanation: The coordinator's refinement loop evaluates the aggregated synthesis against its quality criteria and re-routes tasks where coverage falls short; that added evaluation step, not more instruction or more workers, catches missing canon before publication, which is what the forums were doing.

questions.prompt: Select TWO. Which designs strengthen the coordinator's oversight?

options.text: Coordinator prompts written as goals with quality criteria, never step-by-step instructions
options.explanation: Goals-and-criteria prompts keep delegation comprehensive, which is what prevents the overly narrow decomposition that fragmented the analyses here; step-by-step instructions are the documented cause of that narrowing.

options.text: All inter-agent communication routed through the coordinator, which owns every decision
options.explanation: Routing all communication through the coordinator makes every delegation, result, and error pass one chokepoint, so the authorship of each intermediate call becomes reconstructable; that is precisely the oversight the board asked to audit.

options.text: Peer specialists negotiating their own handoffs directly for much faster turnaround
options.explanation: valid-but-early — direct negotiation trims latency but dissolves the coordinator's ownership of communication, so the decision record the board wants never assembles.

options.text: Decomposition pushed to the narrowest steps each specialist can individually accept
options.explanation: over-orchestration — extremely fine steps manufacture the very fragmentation the observatory felt; granularity of scope, not of steps, is what the coordinator controls.

questions.scenario: A radio observatory's duty-archivist coordinator delegates across calibration, timing, and interference specialists for night-shift astronomers. Twice this quarter, fragmented analyses duplicated one another's coverage, and nobody could afterwards reconstruct which coordinator decision had commissioned each intermediate call. The director wants delegation the oversight board can audit without narrowing the science the specialists perform.
questions.explanation: Goals-and-criteria prompts keep delegation comprehensive, which is what prevents the overly narrow decomposition that fragmented the analyses here; step-by-step instructions are the documented cause of that narrowing.

questions.prompt: Which refinement removes the interpretation drift?

options.text: Restate each instruction once more, this time rendered everywhere in bold emphasis
options.explanation: louder-not-explicit — repeating each instruction a second time restates wording the reviewers already read differently; nothing in it becomes checkable or measurable for either the model or the disputes.

options.text: Replace the indefinites with measurable, checkable targets: lengths, sections, tone markers
options.explanation: Swapping indefinites for precise, measurable targets — a maximum length, named sections, checkable tone markers — makes every rule verifiable, so both reviewers and the model grade the same way, and reply quality stops depending on who interprets 'short'.

options.text: Sample several temperatures so outputs spread across the full plausible style range
options.explanation: knobs-not-design — sampling variance reshuffles wording, while the instructions themselves stay exactly as open to each reviewer's interpretation as they were before the knobs moved.

options.text: Adopt one reviewer's interpretation as the standard while the dispute stays open
options.explanation: valid-but-early — one interpretation imposed today guides this quarter's replies while 'short' and 'formal' remain exactly as unverifiable for the next guideline dispute.

questions.scenario: A hotel group's guest-communication assistant drafts pre-arrival and post-stay emails. Its instructions tell the model to keep messages short, avoid a formal tone, and mention relevant amenities. Two reviewers disagree about what those rules mean, reply lengths swing between three lines and three paragraphs, and the tone wobbles. Another round of gentler wording is proposed.
questions.explanation: Swapping indefinites for precise, measurable targets — a maximum length, named sections, checkable tone markers — makes every rule verifiable, so both reviewers and the model grade the same way, and reply quality stops depending on who interprets 'short'.

questions.prompt: Select TWO. Which statements match the documented mechanism?

options.text: Reordered or rewritten tool definitions break the shared prefix, keeping reads near zero
options.explanation: The cache is extremely sensitive: changing even one character of the tools or system prompt invalidates the cache for that component. Definitions regenerated and reordered each deploy never present an identical prefix, so every call pays a fresh write and reads stay near zero.

options.text: A successful cache read proves those tokens no longer occupy the window
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — reads measure the billing side, not occupancy; the cached prefix still sits fully inside the window, so a read proves price, never presence.

options.text: Cache writes cost more than standard input until repeated reads amortize them
options.explanation: Caching is granular and economic: writes carry a higher per-token cost than standard input, so savings arrive only when many repeat requests read the same prefix. Near-zero reads mean the portal pays the write premium repeatedly with nothing amortizing it.

options.text: Caching stores the generated answers so identical questions skip generation entirely
options.explanation: stale-fact — the cache preserves input preprocessing work, not answers; the model still generates every reply fresh at response time regardless of what the prefix shares.

questions.scenario: An airline's flight-status portal calls Claude with fare, airport, and rebooking tool definitions — regenerated and occasionally reordered at each deploy — followed by the per-request status payload. Usage shows cache_read_input_tokens near zero on repeat calls while cache_creation_input_tokens spikes. One engineer argues a successful read would prove cached tokens leave the window; another wants caching pushed much harder.
questions.explanation: The cache is extremely sensitive: changing even one character of the tools or system prompt invalidates the cache for that component. Definitions regenerated and reordered each deploy never present an identical prefix, so every call pays a fresh write and reads stay near zero.

questions.prompt: Which change best lifts the mid-document accuracy?

options.text: Front-load the critical payment clauses and add descriptive navigation headings throughout
options.explanation: Models reliably process the start and end of long inputs but may miss findings from the middle. Front-loading puts the payment clauses where attention is dependable, and headings give the model anchors for navigating the specialty content that remains mid-input.

options.text: Repeat the payment-clause instructions verbatim in bold at the very prompt end
options.explanation: louder-not-explicit — restating a rule the model already reads adds emphasis at the end without giving the mid-document content any positional or navigational anchors.

options.text: Truncate the specification down to just its general conditions before every question
options.explanation: scale-not-strategy — trimming trades away the specialty divisions the missed questions are actually about, shrinking the input at the cost of the answers' grounding.

options.text: Raise the sampling temperature so clauses are retrieved more creatively each time
options.explanation: knobs-not-design — a sampling control changes how wording varies, not which portion of a long input reliably receives the model's attention.

questions.scenario: A construction firm's assistant answers subcontractor questions over a 90,000-token project specification pasted whole into every request. Payment-clause questions answered from the opening general-conditions section come back reliably, while the same clauses mirrored mid-document in the specialty divisions are regularly missed or misquoted. Procurement allows one structural prompt change this quarter, not a model migration.
questions.explanation: Models reliably process the start and end of long inputs but may miss findings from the middle. Front-loading puts the payment clauses where attention is dependable, and headings give the model anchors for navigating the specialty content that remains mid-input.

questions.prompt: What does the pattern indicate, and what follows?

options.text: The window is nearly full, so the larger-window model surely fixes recall
options.explanation: scale-not-strategy — degradation here tracks how much accumulates in context, so a larger window raises the ceiling without slowing the late-session slip the stem reports.

options.text: Caching frees the accumulated history from the window once its reads succeed
options.explanation: stale-fact — cached prefixes still occupy the window; caching changes what those tokens cost, never whether they count against it.

options.text: Raising the sampling temperature stabilizes recall across the increasingly long review sessions
options.explanation: knobs-not-design — a sampling knob reshuffles wording while accuracy degradation driven by how much sits in the window continues exactly as before.

options.text: Curate what stays: summarize across turns and extract persistent case facts
options.explanation: As token count grows, accuracy and recall degrade — context rot — regardless of how much window remains, so the lever is curation: summarize across turns, keep a persistent facts block for identifiers, and treat caching purely as the billing optimization it is.

questions.scenario: A pharmacovigilance team's assistant reviews cumulative adverse-event narratives for signal detection, and engineers enabled prompt caching across the growing case history expecting it to relieve the window. Weeks later, early-session summaries stay sharp while end-of-session accuracy keeps slipping, per-request input cost still rises with every retained narrative, and finance disputes the growing bill while leadership debates the one-million-token model.
questions.explanation: As token count grows, accuracy and recall degrade — context rot — regardless of how much window remains, so the lever is curation: summarize across turns, keep a persistent facts block for identifiers, and treat caching purely as the billing optimization it is.

questions.prompt: Which refinement targets the stubborn misgradings?

options.text: Escalate all of the borderline narratives to the flagship reasoning model instead
options.explanation: scale-not-strategy — routine lots already grade correctly, so capability is not what the uncommon defect wording lacks; the extra tier buys latency, not the distinction.

options.text: Rewrite the defect definitions a third time, this time with stronger emphasis
options.explanation: louder-not-explicit — stronger emphasis restates the same definition boundary the uncommon wording already crosses; nothing demonstrates what separates the two defect families.

options.text: Turn the archived narratives into labeled examples of the failing distinctions
options.explanation: Examples show rather than tell: the failing narratives become sample input and ideal output pairs, the documented remedy for corner cases instructions cannot capture, while XML tags keep each example clearly separated and the one-second latency target survives intact.

options.text: Lower the sampling temperature so the grades stop oscillating between the bins
options.explanation: knobs-not-design — variance is not the reported symptom; the defect boundary itself is what fails whenever uncommon wording arrives, so randomness control cannot close it.

questions.scenario: A produce-import desk grades every lot from inspection narratives. Routine wording grades cleanly, but uncommon defect descriptions — bacterial spotting versus chill injury — keep landing in the wrong bins, and two prompt rewrites have not moved the error rate. Supervisors have archived dozens of correctly resolved narratives with their final grades, and grading latency must stay under one second.
questions.explanation: Examples show rather than tell: the failing narratives become sample input and ideal output pairs, the documented remedy for corner cases instructions cannot capture, while XML tags keep each example clearly separated and the one-second latency target survives intact.

questions.prompt: What mechanism explains the errors, and what fixes them?

options.text: Give the compaction prompts even firmer instructions to preserve every single detail
options.explanation: prompt-as-guarantee — firmer instructions cannot make a compression step retain the figures it was built to collapse; the fidelity loss is structural, not motivational.

options.text: Cache the original filings so that the summaries regenerate faster every turn
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — caching accelerates the preprocessing of filings while the summary itself remains the step where the identifiers and amounts quietly disappear.

options.text: Summaries inherently drop load-bearing detail; extract a persistent case-facts block outside them
options.explanation: Summarization inherently loses precise detail — exact identifiers, numeric values, prior decisions — so compaction itself drives the errors. Extracting the transactional facts into a persistent block included in every prompt outside the summarized history keeps them reliably available no matter how many turns were summarized.

options.text: Ship the new one-million-token model and thereby stop the summarization step entirely
options.explanation: scale-not-strategy — dropping compaction restores full fidelity but also restores the per-request cost growth the summaries existed to cut, undoing the finance win.

questions.scenario: A newsroom's litigation-coverage assistant condenses months of accumulated reporting about an ongoing merger case into running summaries, so later answers stay cheap. Since compaction began, the cited indemnity amounts disagree with the published filings, previously agreed citation formats quietly revert, and deadlines agreed in week one resurface a week late. The reference filings remain available in the archive.
questions.explanation: Summarization inherently loses precise detail — exact identifiers, numeric values, prior decisions — so compaction itself drives the errors. Extracting the transactional facts into a persistent block included in every prompt outside the summarized history keeps them reliably available no matter how many turns were summarized.

questions.prompt: What most likely explains the repeated write charges?

options.text: The breakpoint sits too late, after the analysis prompt's final content block
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — a correctly placed breakpoint cannot hold a prefix whose five-minute lifetime expires long before the next weekly report arrives.

options.text: The 2,000-token analysis prompt sits below the 1,024-token minimum threshold for caching
options.explanation: stale-fact — a 2,000-token prompt clears the 1,024-token minimum comfortably, so eligibility was never the failing condition in this week's usage report.

options.text: The model version changed between the reports and reset the shared cache
options.explanation: valid-but-early — a release does reset caches, yet the stem reports nothing changing in prompt, tools, or ordering between these runs.

options.text: The five-minute default cache TTL expires between the weekly report runs
options.explanation: The default cache lifetime is five minutes, so workloads whose request frequency falls below the TTL pay a fresh creation write every time without realizing any reads. Nothing changed in the prompt; the weekly cadence itself is why each report bills as a new cache creation.

questions.scenario: An archaeological field unit's finds-reporting assistant runs a 2,000-token stable analysis prompt once a week, when each excavation summary concludes. Usage reports show cache_creation_input_tokens billed on every run and cache_read_input_tokens at zero, although nothing in the prompt, tools, or ordering has changed between reports. The morning debate blames the breakpoint placement and the recent model version.
questions.explanation: The default cache lifetime is five minutes, so workloads whose request frequency falls below the TTL pay a fresh creation write every time without realizing any reads. Nothing changed in the prompt; the weekly cadence itself is why each report bills as a new cache creation.

questions.prompt: Select TWO. Which statements match the documented tradeoff?

options.text: Chain-of-thought reasoning improves accuracy equally on the simple extraction workloads too
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix — explicit reasoning pays off when the answer depends on conditional steps, not on the bounded extraction workloads where instructions already suffice.

options.text: Thinking tokens are billed as output and add latency every call
options.explanation: With extended thinking engaged you pay the thinking tokens and the additional latency on every call, so the two-second interactive target pays continuously. The case for enabling it comes from a measured accuracy gap, never from the assumption that it cannot hurt.

options.text: Heavier techniques make the prompts faster because they catch the errors earlier
options.explanation: stale-fact — each added technique spends tokens and latency on the very call that runs it; catching errors later never speeds that request up.

options.text: Enable it only after prompt work, once evals show the gap
options.explanation: Run evaluations without thinking first: if accuracy still misses requirements after the prompt itself has been worked, then consider enabling it. The documented progression starts zero-shot and adds examples and reasoning only as the task's structure demands, because every added technique costs tokens and latency.

questions.scenario: An aerospace MRO team must lift its discrepancy-disposition accuracy and proposes extended thinking across every workload. Billing treats thinking tokens as output, the disposition workflow must stay inside a two-second interactive target, and the platform runs evals each release. One engineer argues thinking cannot hurt because accuracy never decreases; another plans to enable it before the next eval cycle, skipping a release.
questions.explanation: With extended thinking engaged you pay the thinking tokens and the additional latency on every call, so the two-second interactive target pays continuously. The case for enabling it comes from a measured accuracy gap, never from the assumption that it cannot hurt.

questions.prompt: Which transport fits this production deployment?

options.text: Streamable HTTP, because it connects clients to remotely hosted servers over standard HTTP
options.explanation: valid-but-early: the transport is right, but the reasoning cites protocol familiarity rather than the decisive constraint that clients and the server no longer share a machine.

options.text: Stdio, mounting the production host's drives so every client keeps sharing one machine
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix: the constraint is that clients run on different hosts, and no drive mount changes that stdio only works when both sides share one machine.

options.text: Streamable HTTP, because it enables remote hosted connections that stdio cannot provide
options.explanation: Stdio requires client and server on one machine, so shared hosting breaks it; streamable HTTP trades some functionality for exactly the remote, multi-client access this deployment needs.

options.text: A postcard-style WebSocket-only channel, because MCP excludes remote network transports entirely
options.explanation: stale-fact: MCP is transport agnostic and explicitly supports HTTP, WebSockets, and other network protocols beyond same-machine stdio.

questions.scenario: A freight-visibility startup prototypes its fleet-status MCP server locally: the client launches the server as a subprocess and exchanges JSON over standard input and output. This worked because both processes ran on the same laptop. Now the team must host the server on a shared production machine while two applications, running on entirely different hosts, call it concurrently.
questions.explanation: Stdio requires client and server on one machine, so shared hosting breaks it; streamable HTTP trades some functionality for exactly the remote, multi-client access this deployment needs.

questions.prompt: Which mechanism explains the breakage?

options.text: Those features ride the SSE channel carrying server-initiated requests, which restrictive settings drop
options.explanation: Progress notifications and Create Message requests depend on the streamable-HTTP workaround that pushes messages from server to client; stateless or plain-JSON modes operate within plain request-reply semantics, so these exactly break while ordinary tool calls survive.

options.text: Stdio, mounting the production host's drives so every client still keeps sharing one machine
options.explanation: knobs-not-design: reliability patterns recover from transient errors, but here the channel carrying the requests was disabled, so no retry succeeds.

options.text: The gateway adds one extra network hop before the requests reach the MCP server
options.explanation: extra-hop: an additional hop adds latency, yet hops do not selectively disable notifications while tool calls succeed.

options.text: A client instruction telling the assistant to retry whenever summaries are missing
options.explanation: prompt-as-guarantee: prompting cannot recreate a transport channel; the missing SSE connection, not model behavior, drops the messages.

questions.scenario: An energy-grid alarm assistant keeps its summarization tool implemented as a server-initiated sampling flow: during each outage the MCP server sends a Create Message request back through the connection and the client returns generated text. The team then deploys the server behind their gateway with stateless_http and json_response enabled. Outage summaries silently stop appearing and progress notifications vanish, although simple tool calls still succeed.
questions.explanation: Progress notifications and Create Message requests depend on the streamable-HTTP workaround that pushes messages from server to client; stateless or plain-JSON modes operate within plain request-reply semantics, so these exactly break while ordinary tool calls survive.

questions.prompt: Which TWO resource designs satisfy both requirements? Select TWO.

options.text: One templated resource whose URI takes a paragraph number as its only parameter
options.explanation: wrong-layer-fix: the templated URI must key on the term identifier; a paragraph index still gives autocomplete no list of defined terms to read.

options.text: A direct resource with a static URI that lists every defined glossary term
options.explanation: Direct resources have fixed, parameterless URIs, which is exactly what the autocomplete listing needs; read-only content flows into the prompt without model tool calls.

options.text: A prompt template that instructs the model to search the glossary itself
options.explanation: extra-hop: turning every mention into a model round-trip duplicates what a resource read already delivers directly into the prompt.

options.text: A templated resource, glossary/{term_id}, whose URI parameter selects one glossary entry
options.explanation: Templated resources carry parameters in their URI and the SDK passes them to the function, so one pattern covers every entry, injected without model tool calls.

questions.scenario: A standards publisher's MCP server exposes its technical glossary. Editors type mention syntax such as @term, and the client must, first, offer an autocomplete list of every defined term without supplying any parameters and, second, fetch the complete entry for whichever identifier the editor mentioned, so the content enters the prompt without the model calling any tool.
questions.explanation: Direct resources have fixed, parameterless URIs, which is exactly what the autocomplete listing needs; read-only content flows into the prompt without model tool calls.

questions.prompt: Why does MCP sampling reduce the server's operating cost?

options.text: Waiting for the Initialize Result to arrive before sending any further request
options.explanation: knobs-not-design: smaller output caps trim each call, yet the server still holds the credential and pays the entire inference bill.

options.text: Generation moves through the connected client, so the client's credentials pay
options.explanation: The server ends its work by sending a Create Message request; the client, already holding a connection and credentials, calls the model and returns the text, so the server needs no key and pays no inference bill.

options.text: Issuing a fresh ListTools call before sending the very first CallTool request
options.explanation: premature-optimization: caching trims tokens on repeated prefixes, but the paying party stays the server for every citizen's request.

options.text: A rate limit caps how much each citizen's session can generate per day
options.explanation: convenience-over-safety: throttling constrains the bill without changing who pays; the cost still accrues to the server's credential.

questions.scenario: A national-records office publishes one MCP records-search server that hundreds of citizens' assistants connect to.
